sotto_argomento: Apply and manage tags on resources
domanda: Contoso tags every resource group with a CostCenter tag. The finance team reports that Microsoft Cost Management shows no CostCenter value for several hundred virtual machines and managed disks that already exist inside those resource groups. You must ensure that every existing resource, and every resource created in the future, carries the CostCenter value of its parent resource group. Any CostCenter value already set on a resource must be overwritten with the resource group's value. You must minimize administrative effort. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Built-in policy definition to assign: [Require a tag on resources | Inherit a tag from the resource group | Append a tag and its value from the resource group]
opzione_b: Policy effect that this definition uses: [Append | Deny | Modify]
opzione_c: Prerequisite for the policy assignment: [A managed identity that is granted a role including tag write permissions | A Log Analytics workspace in each resource group | An Azure Automation account with a Run As account]
opzione_d: Action required to tag the resources that already exist: [Wait for the next policy evaluation cycle | Create a remediation task | Redeploy each resource from its ARM template]
risposta_corretta: Inherit a tag from the resource group,Modify,A managed identity that is granted a role including tag write permissions,Create a remediation task
spiegazione: Correct dropdown 1: 'Inherit a tag from the resource group'. Microsoft describes this built-in definition as: 'Adds or replaces the specified tag and value from the parent resource group when any resource is created or updated. Existing resources can be remediated by triggering a remediation task.' The addOrReplace behaviour matches the requirement to overwrite an existing value. 'Require a tag on resources' only enforces the existence of a tag with the deny effect and never applies a value. 'Append a tag and its value from the resource group' uses the append effect and 'Does not modify the tags of resources created before this policy was applied until those resources are changed', so it cannot fix the existing resources. Correct dropdown 2: 'Modify'. The 'Inherit a tag from the resource group' definition uses the modify effect, which adds, updates, or removes tags on a subscription or resource during creation or update, and supports remediating existing non-compliant resources. Correct dropdown 3: 'A managed identity that is granted a role including tag write permissions'. Policy assignments with effect set as Modify require a managed identity to do remediation; the identity can be system-assigned or user-assigned, and the role defined in roleDefinitionIds must include all operations granted to the Contributor or Tag Contributor role. A Log Analytics workspace and an Automation account are unrelated to Modify remediation. Correct dropdown 4: 'Create a remediation task'. When a policy definition using the modify effect is run as part of an evaluation cycle, it doesn't make changes to resources that already exist - it only marks them non-compliant so they can be remediated through a remediation task. Waiting therefore never tags them, and redeploying every resource is possible but is the opposite of minimizing administrative effort.
tags: tags,azure policy,modify effect,remediation task,managed identity,tag inheritance

sotto_argomento: Apply and manage tags on resources
domanda:
You use the Azure portal to assign the built-in policy definition named 'Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing' at the scope of a subscription. You configure the tag name Department and select a system-assigned managed identity for the assignment. The subscription already contains hundreds of resources, many of which have no Department tag. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true.

1. The resources that already exist and are missing the Department tag are tagged automatically at the end of the next policy evaluation cycle.
2. If a new resource is created with a Department tag whose value differs from the value on its parent resource group, the policy replaces the resource's value with the resource group's value.
3. Because you created the assignment in the Azure portal, Azure Policy grants the system-assigned managed identity the roles that are listed in the definition's roleDefinitionIds property.
opzione_a: The resources that already exist and are missing the Department tag are tagged automatically at the end of the next policy evaluation cycle.
opzione_b: If a new resource is created with a Department tag whose value differs from the value on its parent resource group, the policy replaces the resource's value with the resource group's value.
opzione_c: Because you created the assignment in the Azure portal, Azure Policy grants the system-assigned managed identity the roles that are listed in the definition's roleDefinitionIds property.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No. This is the most commonly missed behaviour of the modify effect. When a policy definition using the modify effect is run as part of an evaluation cycle, it doesn't make changes to resources that already exist; instead, it marks any resource that meets the if condition as non-compliant so it can be remediated through a remediation task. Modify evaluates before the request is processed by a resource provider, so it only acts on creation or update requests. You must create a remediation task to tag the existing resources. Statement 2 - No. The chosen definition is the 'if missing' variant, which Microsoft describes as: 'Adds the specified tag with its value from the parent resource group when any resource missing this tag is created or updated... If the tag exists with a different value it will not be changed.' It uses the Add operation, not addOrReplace. To overwrite a differing value you would assign 'Inherit a tag from the resource group' instead. Statement 3 - Yes. Policy assignments with the modify effect require a managed identity to do remediation. When you use the portal, Azure Policy automatically grants the managed identity the listed roles once assignment starts; the roles must be granted manually only when you create the assignment with an SDK, PowerShell, or the CLI. Note that if roleDefinitionIds are later edited in the definition, the new permissions must be granted manually even in the portal.
tags: tags,azure policy,modify effect,inherit a tag,remediation task,managed identity

sotto_argomento: Apply and manage tags on resources
domanda: You assign the Tag Contributor built-in role to a cost analyst named Ava at the scope of a subscription. Ava signs in to the Azure portal, opens the Tags page of a resource group, adds a tag, and selects Save - but the operation fails. Ava must be able to apply tags to resource groups and to individual resources in the subscription. Ava must not be able to create, modify, or delete the resources themselves, and you must follow the principle of least privilege. What should you do?
opzione_a: Assign Ava the Reader role at the subscription scope in addition to Tag Contributor.
opzione_b: Assign Ava the Contributor role at the subscription scope instead of Tag Contributor.
opzione_c: Remove the subscription-scoped assignment and assign Tag Contributor separately at each resource group scope.
opzione_d: Instruct Ava to apply the tags by using Azure PowerShell, the Azure CLI, or the REST API instead of the Azure portal.
spiegazione: Correct: d. This is a documented limitation of the role, not a misconfiguration. Tag Contributor grants write access to the Microsoft.Resources/tags resource type, which lets the holder tag any resource even without access to the resource itself. However, Microsoft states that this role can't apply tags to resources or resource groups through the Azure portal, although it can apply tags to subscriptions through the portal, and it supports all tag operations through Azure PowerShell and the REST API. Using a non-portal client is therefore the fix that keeps least privilege intact. Wrong: a. The failure is not caused by missing read access. Adding Reader grants only */read on the resources and does not change the portal's behaviour for tagging resources and resource groups. Wrong: b. Contributor does grant the required access to apply tags to any entity through the portal, because it grants write access to the resource itself - but it also grants full access to manage all resources, which breaks both stated requirements. Wrong: c. The portal limitation is a property of the Tag Contributor role, not of the scope at which it is assigned; re-assigning it lower in the hierarchy changes nothing.

sotto_argomento: Apply and manage tags on resources
domanda: Your organization is drafting a tagging standard for all Azure workloads and needs to document the platform constraints correctly. Which statements about Azure resource tags are true? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Each resource, resource group, and subscription can have a maximum of 50 tag name-value pairs.
opzione_b: A tag name is limited to 512 characters, except for storage accounts, where the tag name is limited to 128 characters.
opzione_c: Tag names are case-insensitive for operations, but tag values are case-sensitive.
opzione_d: Tags can be applied to management groups in the same way that they are applied to subscriptions.
opzione_e: A tag value is limited to 1,024 characters.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft documents that each resource, resource group, and subscription can have a maximum of 50 tag name-value pairs. If you need more, use a JSON string as a single tag value to pack multiple values under one tag name. Correct: b. The tag name has a limit of 512 characters and the tag value has a limit of 256 characters; for storage accounts, the tag name limit is 128 characters (the value limit stays 256). Correct: c. Tag names are case-insensitive for operations - an operation updates or retrieves a tag regardless of casing, although the resource provider might preserve the casing you supplied and you see that casing in cost reports. Tag values are case-sensitive. Wrong: d. You can apply tags to Azure resources, resource groups, and subscriptions but not to management groups. Wrong: e. 1,024 is not the tag value limit. The tag value has a limit of 256 characters. Also worth knowing for the standard: tag names can't contain the characters < > % & \ ? / and some services (Azure Automation, Azure CDN, Azure Public and Private DNS zones and A records, Log Analytics saved searches) support only 15 tags.

sotto_argomento: Apply and manage tags on resources
domanda: A resource group named RG-Finance is tagged with CostCenter = CC-4410 and Environment = Production. A colleague deploys a new storage account into RG-Finance by using a Bicep file that does not define any tags. No Azure Policy assignments exist in the subscription. You open the storage account in the Azure portal and view its Tags page. What do you see?
opzione_a: The storage account has CostCenter = CC-4410 and Environment = Production, inherited from RG-Finance.
opzione_b: The storage account has both tags, but they are displayed as read-only and cannot be changed on the storage account.
opzione_c: The storage account has no tags.
opzione_d: The storage account has no tags now, but inherits both tags automatically at the end of the next Azure Policy evaluation cycle.
spiegazione: Correct: c. Microsoft documents this explicitly: resources don't inherit the tags you apply to a resource group or a subscription. Tag inheritance is not a built-in behaviour of Azure Resource Manager, so a resource deployed with no tags has no tags, regardless of what its parent resource group carries. Wrong: a. This is the classic misconception. Tags on a resource group describe only the resource group object itself; they are never automatically copied down to the resources inside it. Wrong: b. There is no notion of an inherited, read-only tag on a child resource. Tags applied to a resource are always writable by anyone with tag write access on that resource. Wrong: d. Automatic tag inheritance only happens if you assign a tag policy such as 'Inherit a tag from the resource group', and even then the modify effect does not change resources that already exist during an evaluation cycle - it marks them non-compliant so they can be fixed with a remediation task. With no policy assigned, no evaluation cycle will ever add the tags.

sotto_argomento: Configure cost management
domanda: Case study: Litware, Inc. holds an Enterprise Agreement with Azure Prepayment. Azure spend is spread across 12 subscriptions organized under a management group named MG-Litware. The finance controller reports that the engineering subscription named Sub-Eng repeatedly overruns its allocated monthly spend, and the overrun is only discovered after the invoice arrives. Litware's requirements are: the finance mailbox must be notified before the monthly spend for Sub-Eng is projected to exceed 50,000 USD; no running workload may be stopped or throttled as a result of the notification; and the solution must require the least administrative effort. You need to recommend a solution. What should you configure?
opzione_a: A budget scoped to Sub-Eng with a monthly reset period and a forecasted cost alert that notifies the finance mailbox.
opzione_b: A credit alert on the Enterprise Agreement billing account, configured to fire when spending is projected to exceed 50,000 USD.
opzione_c: An Azure Advisor cost recommendation with an alert configured on the Cost category for Sub-Eng.
opzione_d: An Azure spending limit of 50,000 USD on Sub-Eng.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Budgets are supported at the subscription scope, and Microsoft Learn states that forecasted alerts provide advanced notification that your spending trends are likely to exceed your budget, generating alerts when the forecasted cost projection exceeds the set threshold. A monthly reset period matches the monthly requirement, and email recipients are configured directly on the budget's alert conditions. Critically, this meets the 'no workload may be stopped' requirement: the documentation states that when budget thresholds are exceeded, resources aren't affected and your consumption isn't stopped. Wrong: b - credit alerts notify you when your Azure Prepayment is consumed and are generated automatically at 90% and 100% of the prepayment credit balance. They are not configurable to an arbitrary currency amount, they are not forecast-based, they are scoped to the prepayment balance rather than to a single subscription, and they are sent to account owners rather than an arbitrary recipient list. Wrong: c - Azure Advisor's Cost category recommends optimizations such as right-sizing or shutting down underutilized virtual machines. It analyzes resource configuration and usage telemetry to suggest savings; it does not track spend against a monetary threshold and cannot notify anyone that a projected monthly spend will exceed 50,000 USD. Wrong: d - the Azure spending limit is not available on Enterprise Agreement subscriptions, cannot be set to a custom amount, and would violate the requirement that no workload be stopped, because reaching a spending limit disables deployed resources for the remainder of the billing period.
tags: cost management, budgets, forecasted alert, azure advisor, credit alert, spending limit, enterprise agreement

sotto_argomento: Configure cost management
domanda: Your organization uses an Enterprise Agreement and has purchased Azure Prepayment. You are documenting how Cost Management alerts behave so that the finance team knows what is automatic and what must be configured. Select the correct value for each statement.
opzione_a: Automatic thresholds at which credit alerts are generated: [50% and 75% | 80% and 100% | 90% and 100%]
opzione_b: Alert type that is supported for Enterprise Agreement but NOT for Microsoft Customer Agreement or pay-as-you-go: [Budget alert | Credit alert | Cost anomaly alert]
opzione_c: Maximum number of email recipients that can be configured in a single budget: [3 | 5 | 10]
opzione_d: Alert conditions you can configure on a budget: [Actual cost only | Forecasted cost only | Actual cost and forecasted cost]
risposta_corretta: 90% and 100%,Credit alert,5,Actual cost and forecasted cost
spiegazione: Correct values: 90% and 100% / Credit alert / 5 / Actual cost and forecasted cost. Microsoft Learn states that credit alerts notify you when your Azure Prepayment is consumed and are generated automatically at 90% and at 100% of your Azure Prepayment credit balance, and that Azure Prepayment is for organizations with Enterprise Agreements. The supported alert features table shows Credit and Department spending quota alerts are supported for Enterprise Agreement only, whereas Budget alerts are supported for Enterprise Agreement, Microsoft Customer Agreement, and Web direct/Pay-As-You-Go. The budgets tutorial states you can optionally include up to five thresholds and five email addresses in a single budget, and that you configure both actual cost and forecasted budget alerts, switching between them with the Type field. Wrong values: 50%/75% and 80%/100% are not the documented credit alert thresholds (50% or 75% are cited only as examples of department spending quota thresholds, which are configured, not automatic). Budget alerts are available across all three offer types, so they are not EA-exclusive; cost anomaly alerts are a separate, opt-in feature. 3 and 10 contradict the documented maximum of five email recipients. 'Actual cost only' and 'Forecasted cost only' each omit a supported alert type.
tags: cost management, cost alerts, credit alerts, azure prepayment, enterprise agreement, budgets

sotto_argomento: Configure cost management
domanda: You are briefing a new cloud administrator on how Microsoft Cost Management budgets behave. Which statements about budgets are correct? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A budget can be created at the management group, subscription, or resource group scope.
opzione_b: A single budget supports up to five cost thresholds and up to five email recipients.
opzione_c: A budget scoped to a subscription or a resource group can be configured to trigger an action group when a threshold is met.
opzione_d: When the budget amount is exceeded, Azure automatically stops the resources within the budget scope to prevent further charges.
opzione_e: Budgets support only actual cost alerts; to alert on projected spending you must create a separate Azure Monitor metric alert rule.
spiegazione: Correct: a, b, c. (a) Microsoft Learn lists the supported Azure RBAC budget scopes as management group, subscription, and resource group (plus EA and Microsoft Customer Agreement billing scopes). (b) Budgets require at least one cost threshold and a corresponding email address, and you can optionally include up to five thresholds and five email addresses in a single budget. (c) When you create or edit a budget for a subscription or resource group scope, you can configure it to call an action group, which can then run automation such as an Azure Function or a webhook. Wrong: d - this is the single most common misconception about budgets. The documentation states that notifications are triggered when the budget thresholds are exceeded, but resources aren't affected and your consumption isn't stopped. Budgets are an alerting and accountability tool, not an enforcement tool. Wrong: e - budgets natively support both actual cost alerts and forecasted cost alerts; you toggle between them with the Type field when configuring the alert, and forecasted alerts fire when the forecasted cost projection exceeds the set threshold. No separate Azure Monitor rule is needed.
tags: cost management, budgets, thresholds, forecasted alerts, action groups, scopes

sotto_argomento: Configure cost management
domanda: The FinOps team at Litware creates a budget scoped to a management group named MG-Production and wants the budget to invoke an Azure Function through an action group when 80 percent of the budget amount is reached. While configuring the budget, the option to select an action group is not available. You need to enable the automation with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opzione_a: Re-create the budget at a subscription scope, because action groups are supported only for subscription and resource group budget scopes.
opzione_b: Assign the Cost Management Contributor role to the FinOps team at the MG-Production management group scope.
opzione_c: Enable the common alert schema on the action group so that budgets can integrate with it.
opzione_d: Change the budget alert type from actual cost to forecasted cost, because only forecasted alerts can trigger action groups.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Budgets can be created at the management group, subscription, and resource group scopes, but Microsoft Learn states that when you create or edit a budget for a subscription or resource group scope you can configure it to call an action group, and that action groups are currently only supported for subscription and resource group scopes. Moving the budget down to a subscription scope is therefore the required change. Wrong: b - this is a permissions role, and lack of permission is not why the control is hidden. Cost Management Contributor lets a user create and modify budgets, but no role makes action groups available at management group scope. Wrong: c - the documentation states you can integrate budgets with action groups regardless of whether the common alert schema is enabled or disabled in those groups, so the schema setting is irrelevant here. Wrong: d - both actual cost and forecasted cost budget alerts exist, and the alert type has no bearing on action group support; the limitation is the budget's scope.
tags: cost management, budgets, action groups, management group, scope, automation

sotto_argomento: Configure management groups
domanda:
Anna is assigned the Global Administrator role in your Microsoft Entra tenant, but she has no Azure role assignments on any subscription or management group. She needs to assign the Owner role to a security group at the root management group scope. In the Azure portal she browses to Microsoft Entra ID > Manage > Properties and sets the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to Yes, then signs out and signs back in. Evaluate each of the following statements:
1. Setting the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to Yes assigns Anna the User Access Administrator role in Azure RBAC at root scope (/).
2. The elevated access is a global tenant property, so every user assigned the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID gains the same access.
3. After elevating access, Anna can assign the Owner role to a security group at the root management group scope.
opzione_a: Setting the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to Yes assigns Anna the User Access Administrator role in Azure RBAC at root scope (/).
opzione_b: The elevated access is a global tenant property, so every user assigned the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID gains the same access.
opzione_c: After elevating access, Anna can assign the Owner role to a security group at the root management group scope.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. Microsoft Learn states that when you set the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to Yes, you are assigned the User Access Administrator role in Azure RBAC at root scope (/), which grants permission to assign roles in all Azure subscriptions and management groups associated with the tenant. The toggle is only available to users assigned the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID. Statement 2 - No. The documentation is explicit that this setting is not a global property and applies only to the currently signed-in user; you can't elevate access for all members of the Global Administrator role. Each Global Administrator who needs elevated access must set the toggle individually. Statement 3 - Yes. The User Access Administrator role includes Microsoft.Authorization/*, so once elevated at root scope Anna can assign any Azure role, including Owner, at the root management group. Microsoft also documents that after the tenant administrator elevates access, the administrator can assign any Azure role to other directory users or groups to manage the hierarchy. Note that Microsoft recommends removing the elevated access (setting the toggle back to No) once the required changes at root scope are complete.
tags: elevate access, root management group, user access administrator, global administrator, entra id, rbac

sotto_argomento: Configure management groups
domanda: Fabrikam is designing a management group hierarchy for its Microsoft Entra tenant and needs to record the supported platform limits and default behaviors in a design document. Select the correct value for each statement.
opzione_a: Maximum number of management groups in a single directory: [1000 | 10000 | 50000]
opzione_b: Maximum levels of management group depth, excluding the root level and the subscription level: [4 | 6 | 8]
opzione_c: Maximum number of parent management groups that a subscription can have: [1 | 2 | Unlimited]
opzione_d: Default parent of a newly created subscription: [Root management group | No parent until assigned | The most recently created management group]
spiegazione: Correct values: 10000 / 6 / 1 / Root management group. Microsoft Learn's 'Important facts about management groups' states that a single directory can support 10,000 management groups; that a management group tree can support up to six levels of depth, not including the root level or the subscription level; and that each management group and subscription can support only one parent (while each management group can have many children). The 'Important facts about the root management group' section states that new subscriptions automatically default to the root management group when they're created, which is also why you don't need permissions on the root management group to move an item into or out of it. Wrong values: 1000 and 50000 are not the documented directory limit. 4 is a common Cloud Adoption Framework design guideline rather than the platform maximum, and 8 exceeds the limit. 2 and Unlimited contradict the single-parent rule that keeps all subscriptions and management groups within one hierarchy per directory. 'No parent until assigned' and 'The most recently created management group' contradict the documented default landing spot for new subscriptions.
tags: management groups, limits, hierarchy, root management group, subscriptions

sotto_argomento: Configure management groups
domanda: An auditor asks you to explain how the top of your organization's Azure governance hierarchy works. Which statement about the root management group is TRUE?
opzione_a: The root management group's ID is the same value as the Microsoft Entra tenant ID, and unlike other management groups it cannot be moved or deleted.
opzione_b: The root management group can be deleted after all child management groups and subscriptions have been moved out of it.
opzione_c: Users who are assigned the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID are granted the Owner role on the root management group by default.
opzione_d: You can create additional root management groups in a directory to keep production and development hierarchies completely separate.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft Learn's 'Important facts about the root management group' states that the ID is the same value as the Microsoft Entra tenant ID, that the default display name is 'Tenant root group', and that the root management group can't be moved or deleted, unlike other management groups. Wrong: b - the root management group can never be deleted, regardless of whether it still has children. (The rule that a management group must have no child management groups or subscriptions before deletion applies to non-root management groups.) Wrong: c - this is the classic misconception. No one has default access to the root management group. Microsoft Entra Global Administrators are the only users who can elevate themselves to gain access, which assigns them the User Access Administrator role at root scope; only after elevating can they assign roles such as Owner. Wrong: d - each directory has a single top-level root management group, and all subscriptions and management groups are within a single hierarchy in each directory. This single hierarchy exists specifically so that global access and policy assignments cannot be bypassed.
tags: management groups, root management group, tenant root group, entra id, governance

sotto_argomento: Configure management groups
domanda: While planning a management group hierarchy for a large enterprise, you need to document the maximum nesting supported. Up to how many levels of depth can a management group tree support, excluding the root management group level and the subscription level?
spiegazione: Correct: b. Microsoft Learn's 'Important facts about management groups' states that a management group tree can support up to six levels of depth, and that this limit does not include the root level or the subscription level. Wrong: a - 4 is a commonly cited Cloud Adoption Framework design recommendation for practical hierarchy depth, but it is not the platform limit. Wrong: c and d - 8 and 10 exceed the documented limit; the other published management group limits are 10,000 management groups per single directory and one parent per management group or subscription.
tags: management groups, hierarchy, depth, limits, governance

sotto_argomento: Configure resource locks
domanda: A resource group named RG-Web contains a web app named app-web01 and the App Service plan that hosts it, named ASP-Web. A CanNotDelete lock named lock-web is applied to app-web01 only. No other management locks exist anywhere in the subscription. All administrators hold the Owner role on the subscription. Select the outcome of each operation.
opzione_a: An administrator deletes the RG-Web resource group: [Succeeds | Fails - the entire delete operation is blocked | Succeeds - every resource except app-web01 is deleted]
opzione_b: An administrator deletes a diagnostic setting that is applied to app-web01: [Succeeds | Fails - the extension resource inherits the lock from app-web01 | Succeeds - but only after the lock notes are cleared]
opzione_c: A developer deploys updated application code to app-web01: [Succeeds | Fails - the lock blocks all write operations | Fails - the lock blocks data plane requests]
opzione_d: An engineer scales up ASP-Web to a higher pricing tier: [Succeeds | Fails - ASP-Web inherits the lock from app-web01 | Fails - the lock blocks POST requests to the subscription]
risposta_corretta: Fails - the entire delete operation is blocked,Fails - the extension resource inherits the lock from app-web01,Succeeds,Succeeds
spiegazione: Correct dropdown 1: 'Fails - the entire delete operation is blocked'. Microsoft states that if you have a Delete lock on a resource and attempt to delete its resource group, the whole delete operation is blocked - even if the resource group and the other resources in it are unlocked - because a partial deletion isn't possible. Correct dropdown 2: 'Fails - the extension resource inherits the lock from app-web01'. Extension resources inherit locks from the resource to which they're applied, and Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings is an extension resource type. Because the diagnostic setting's full resource ID is nested under app-web01's resource ID, the lock on app-web01 blocks the delete. Correct dropdown 3: 'Succeeds'. CanNotDelete means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it. Only ReadOnly blocks write operations, so a code deployment is unaffected. Correct dropdown 4: 'Succeeds'. Locks are inherited downward from a parent scope to the resources within it; ASP-Web is a sibling resource in the same resource group, not a child of app-web01, so it inherits nothing from lock-web. (Had the lock been a ReadOnly lock on RG-Web instead, this scale-up would have failed, because a read-only lock on a resource group that contains an App Service plan prevents scaling the plan up or out.)
tags: resource locks,cannotdelete,lock inheritance,extension resources,diagnostic settings,app service

sotto_argomento: Configure resource locks
domanda: Contoso runs a business-critical virtual machine named VM-ERP in a resource group named RG-Prod. Operations engineers must still be able to resize VM-ERP, attach data disks, and restart it, but no one in the organization - including subscription owners - may delete it. What should you configure?
opzione_a: A CanNotDelete (Delete) lock on VM-ERP
opzione_b: A ReadOnly (Read-only) lock on VM-ERP
opzione_c: A ReadOnly (Read-only) lock on RG-Prod
opzione_d: An Azure Policy assignment that uses the deny effect, scoped to RG-Prod
spiegazione: Correct: a. A CanNotDelete lock (shown as 'Delete' in the portal) means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it. Because a management lock applies across all users and roles and overrides user permissions, even a subscription Owner cannot delete VM-ERP while the lock exists, yet resize, disk attach, and restart operations still succeed. Wrong: b. A ReadOnly lock means authorized users can read a resource but can't delete or update it - it is similar to restricting all users to the permissions of the Reader role, so it would block the required resize and disk-attach operations. Wrong: c. A ReadOnly lock on the resource group is inherited by every resource in it and is even more restrictive: a read-only lock on a resource group that contains a virtual machine prevents all users from starting or restarting that virtual machine, because those operations require a POST request. Wrong: d. The deny effect of Azure Policy evaluates create and update requests against resource properties; it is not the mechanism for blocking deletion. The effect designed to block delete calls is denyAction, whose only supported action name today is 'delete'. A management lock is the feature Microsoft documents for protecting resources from accidental deletion.

sotto_argomento: Configure resource locks
domanda: During a change freeze, your team applies a Read-only lock at the scope of a resource group named RG-Shared. RG-Shared contains a storage account, an App Service plan that hosts a web app, a network security group, and an Azure Automation account. You must warn the operations team about what will stop working. Which operations does the lock block? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Listing the storage account's access keys from the Azure portal
opzione_b: Uploading a blob to an existing container by using a shared access signature that was issued before the freeze
opzione_c: Scaling up the App Service plan to a higher pricing tier
opzione_d: Viewing the security rules of the network security group in the Azure portal
opzione_e: Starting a runbook in the Automation account
spiegazione: Correct: a. A read-only lock on a storage account prevents users from listing the account keys, because the List Keys operation is handled by a POST request to Azure Resource Manager and locks prevent the POST method from sending data to the ARM API. Correct: c. A read-only lock on a resource group that contains an App Service plan prevents you from scaling up or out of the plan. Correct: e. A read-only lock on a resource group that contains an automation account prevents all runbooks from starting, because those operations require a POST method request. Wrong: b. Locks only apply to control plane Azure operations and not to data plane operations. A blob upload goes to the service endpoint rather than to management.azure.com, so the lock does not block it - a read-only or cannot-delete lock on a storage account doesn't protect the data in a blob, queue, table, or file. Wrong: d. ReadOnly means authorized users can read the resource; it is similar to restricting all authorized users to the permissions that the Reader role provides. Reading the NSG's rules is exactly what the lock still permits. (Note that a read-only lock on an NSG would block creation of the corresponding NSG flow log, which is a write.)
tags: resource locks,readonly lock,automation account,app service plan,post method,data plane

sotto_argomento: Configure resource locks
domanda: A platform engineer named Diego is assigned the Contributor role at the scope of a subscription. When Diego tries to create a Delete lock on a resource group, the request fails with an authorization error. Diego must be able to create and remove management locks, but must not be granted the ability to create, modify, or delete the resources themselves. Which built-in role should you assign to Diego?
opzione_a: Owner
opzione_b: User Access Administrator
opzione_c: Resource Policy Contributor
opzione_d: Management Group Contributor
spiegazione: Correct: b. To create or delete management locks, you need access to Microsoft.Authorization/* or Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* actions, and Microsoft names Owner and User Access Administrator as the built-in roles that have the required access. User Access Administrator's Actions are */read, Microsoft.Authorization/*, and Microsoft.Support/* - it therefore grants the lock actions while granting no write access to resources, which satisfies the constraint. This also explains the failure: Contributor grants Actions '*' but carries the NotActions Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete, so it cannot create or delete locks. Wrong: a. Owner does have the required access (Actions '*' with no NotActions), but it grants full access to manage all resources, which violates the requirement that Diego must not be able to create, modify, or delete resources. Wrong: c. Resource Policy Contributor covers Azure Policy definitions and assignments, not Microsoft.Authorization/locks. Wrong: d. Management Group Contributor lets you manage management groups; it does not grant the lock actions at subscription or resource group scope, and locks cannot be applied to management groups at all.

sotto_argomento: Configure resource locks
domanda: A support engineer applies a Read-only lock to a storage account named stcontoso01. Shortly afterward, a line-of-business application that retrieves its connection string from the storage account's Access keys page starts to fail, and the engineer can no longer display the account keys in the Azure portal even though the engineer is an Owner of the subscription. What explains this behaviour?
opzione_a: A ReadOnly lock blocks all data plane requests to the storage account, so the keys can no longer be used.
opzione_b: The List Keys operation is handled by a POST request to the Azure Resource Manager API, and a ReadOnly lock blocks it.
opzione_c: Applying a ReadOnly lock automatically disables shared key authorization on the storage account.
opzione_d: Applying a ReadOnly lock automatically rotates both storage account keys, invalidating the cached connection string.
spiegazione: Correct: b. Microsoft documents that a read-only lock on a storage account prevents users from listing the account keys, because a POST request handles the Azure Storage List Keys operation, and locks prevent the POST method from sending data to the Azure Resource Manager API. The lock overrides any user permissions, so being an Owner does not help. Users who don't have the account keys need to use Microsoft Entra credentials to access blob or queue data. Wrong: a. Locks only apply to control plane Azure operations (requests to management.azure.com) and not to data plane operations. Clients that already hold a key or SAS can still read and write blob data; the lock does not protect the data itself. Wrong: c. A lock never changes a resource's configuration. Disabling shared key authorization is a separate storage account property (allowSharedKeyAccess) that an administrator must set explicitly - and a ReadOnly lock would in fact block that change. Wrong: d. Locks do not perform any action on the resource; key rotation is a deliberate administrative operation (and it is itself a control plane POST that the lock would block).
tags: resource locks,readonly lock,storage account,list keys,control plane

sotto_argomento: Configure resource locks
domanda:
Your organization protects production workloads with management locks. A subscription named Sub-Prod sits under a management group named MG-Production and contains a resource group named RG-Core. RG-Core contains a storage account named stcore01. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true.

1. A CanNotDelete lock applied to RG-Core also prevents the deletion of resources that are added to RG-Core after the lock was created.
2. You can apply a ReadOnly lock to MG-Production to protect every subscription beneath it.
3. A CanNotDelete lock on stcore01 prevents a user from deleting a blob in stcore01 by using AzCopy with a valid account key.
opzione_a: A CanNotDelete lock applied to RG-Core also prevents the deletion of resources that are added to RG-Core after the lock was created.
opzione_b: You can apply a ReadOnly lock to MG-Production to protect every subscription beneath it.
opzione_c: A CanNotDelete lock on stcore01 prevents a user from deleting a blob in stcore01 by using AzCopy with a valid account key.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. When you apply a lock at a parent scope, all resources within that scope inherit the same lock, and Microsoft explicitly notes that even resources you add later inherit the same parent lock. Inheritance is evaluated at request time, not captured when the lock is created. Statement 2 - No. Microsoft states that you can't add a lock to management groups. Locks can be scoped to a subscription, a resource group, or an individual resource only. To protect every subscription under MG-Production you would have to place a lock on each subscription. Statement 3 - No. Locks only apply to control plane Azure operations and not to data plane operations. Deleting a blob with AzCopy and an account key is a data plane request to the storage service endpoint, so the lock does not block it - Microsoft states that a read-only lock or cannot-delete lock on a storage account doesn't protect the data in a blob, queue, table, or file. Note the contrast: the same lock would block a control plane delete such as the File Shares - Delete ARM operation.
tags: resource locks,lock inheritance,management groups,data plane,storage account

sotto_argomento: Configure resource locks
domanda: The governance team applies a Read-only lock at the scope of a resource group named RG-App1. RG-App1 contains a virtual machine named VM-App1, an App Service plan named ASP-App1, and a storage account named stapp101. All administrators hold the Owner role on the subscription. Which operation still succeeds while the lock is in place?
opzione_a: Starting VM-App1 after it has been stopped (deallocated)
opzione_b: Scaling up ASP-App1 to a higher pricing tier
opzione_c: Reading blob data from stapp101 by using a client application and an account key that was retrieved before the lock was applied
opzione_d: Moving VM-App1 from RG-App1 to a different resource group
spiegazione: Correct: c. Locks only apply to control plane Azure operations and not to data plane operations. A read-only or cannot-delete lock on a storage account doesn't protect its data from being read, modified, or deleted, so an application holding a valid account key continues to read blob data through the data plane endpoint (for example https://stapp101.blob.core.windows.net). Wrong: a. A read-only lock on a resource group that contains a virtual machine prevents all users from starting or restarting that virtual machine, because those operations require a POST method request. Wrong: b. A read-only lock on a resource group that contains an App Service plan prevents you from scaling up or out of the plan. Wrong: d. A read-only lock on a resource group prevents you from moving existing resources in or out of that resource group. (Note the asymmetry Microsoft calls out: you can move a resource that itself carries a read-only lock to another resource group - it is the lock on the resource group that blocks the move here.)
tags: resource locks,readonly lock,control plane,data plane,app service plan

sotto_argomento: Configure resource locks
domanda: In a subscription named Sub-Prod, a CanNotDelete lock named lock-sub is applied at the subscription scope. A resource group in that subscription named RG-Data has a ReadOnly lock named lock-rg. RG-Data contains an Azure SQL logical server named srv-data01. An engineer who holds the Owner role on Sub-Prod attempts to add a server-level firewall rule to srv-data01 through the Azure portal. What is the result?
opzione_a: The operation succeeds, because the CanNotDelete lock at the subscription scope is applied first and takes precedence over locks at lower scopes.
opzione_b: The operation succeeds, because management locks restrict only users who are not assigned the Owner role.
opzione_c: The operation fails, because srv-data01 inherits the ReadOnly lock from RG-Data and the most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence.
opzione_d: The operation fails, because a CanNotDelete lock at the subscription scope blocks every write operation in the subscription.
spiegazione: Correct: c. When you apply a lock at a parent scope, all resources within that scope inherit the same lock, and the most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence. srv-data01 therefore inherits both CanNotDelete (from the subscription) and ReadOnly (from RG-Data); ReadOnly is the more restrictive, so authorized users can read the server but can't delete or update it. Creating a firewall rule is a control plane write, so it fails. Wrong: a. Precedence is not determined by scope order or by which lock is 'closest' - it is always the most restrictive lock that wins. Wrong: b. Unlike Azure RBAC, management locks apply a restriction across all users and roles; the lock overrides any user permissions, including Owner. Wrong: d. CanNotDelete means authorized users can read and modify the resource but can't delete it. It does not block write operations - the ReadOnly lock is what blocks this request.

sotto_argomento: Configure self-service password reset (SSPR)
domanda: Case study: Litware, Inc. has a Microsoft Entra tenant named litware.onmicrosoft.com with the verified custom domain litware.com. A Microsoft Entra Connect server synchronizes the on-premises Active Directory Domain Services forest to the tenant by using password hash synchronization. All 2,000 users are assigned Microsoft Entra ID P1 licenses. On the Password reset blade, Self service password reset enabled is set to All and Number of methods required to reset is set to 2. All users have registered a mobile phone and an authentication email. On the Microsoft Entra Connect server, the Password writeback check box is selected on the Optional features page, and the synchronization account has been granted Reset password, Change password, Write lockoutTime, Write pwdLastSet, and the Unexpire Password extended right. Cloud-only users can reset their passwords at https://aka.ms/sspr without any problem. Every synchronized user who attempts a reset is instead told to contact an administrator to reset the password. You need to resolve the issue for the synchronized users. What should you do?
opzione_a: In the Microsoft Entra admin center, browse to Entra ID > Password reset > On-premises integration and select "Write back passwords to your on-premises directory".
opzione_b: In the Microsoft Entra admin center, browse to Entra ID > Password reset > Properties and set Number of methods required to reset to 1.
opzione_c: Reconfigure Microsoft Entra Connect to use pass-through authentication instead of password hash synchronization.
opzione_d: In the Microsoft Entra admin center, browse to Entra ID > Password reset > On-premises integration and set "Allow users to unlock accounts without resetting their password" to Yes.
spiegazione: Correct: Enabling password writeback is a two-part configuration. Selecting Password writeback on the Optional features page of Microsoft Entra Connect is only the first half; you must also enable writeback for SSPR in the Microsoft Entra admin center under Entra ID > Password reset > On-premises integration by checking "Write back passwords to your on-premises directory" (as at least a Hybrid Identity Administrator). Microsoft Learn states that when this option is set to No, writeback is disabled and federated, pass-through authentication, or password hash synchronized users aren't able to reset their passwords. This matches the symptom exactly: during the SSPR checks, Microsoft Entra ID determines that the user's password is managed on-premises, and if SSPR writeback isn't deployed the user is asked to contact their administrator - while cloud-only users are unaffected. B is wrong: all users have registered two methods, so the method count check is already satisfied; lowering it to 1 would weaken security and would not change the on-premises password management check (and the setting lives on the Authentication methods page, not Properties). C is wrong: pass-through authentication also leaves the password managed on-premises, so the same writeback check applies - switching sign-in methods does not enable writeback. D is wrong: "Allow users to unlock accounts without resetting their password" only separates the account-unlock operation from the password-reset operation for users whose writeback is already working; it does not enable writeback.
tags: sspr,password writeback,on-premises integration,microsoft entra connect,password hash synchronization,troubleshooting

sotto_argomento: Configure self-service password reset (SSPR)
domanda: The Microsoft Entra tenant for Contoso, Ltd. has the custom domain contoso.com verified, and Microsoft Entra Connect synchronizes identities from an on-premises directory. On the Password reset blade, Self service password reset enabled is set to All, Number of methods required to reset is set to 1, and the methods available to users are Mobile phone and Security questions. A cloud-only account that is assigned the Helpdesk Administrator role has registered security questions only, and cannot complete a reset at https://aka.ms/sspr. All non-administrator users can reset their passwords successfully. What is the most likely cause?
opzione_a: Cloud-only accounts cannot use SSPR when Microsoft Entra Connect is synchronizing identities into the tenant.
opzione_b: Accounts with an administrator role are subject to the strong two-gate password reset policy, which requires two authentication methods and prohibits security questions.
opzione_c: Number of days before users are asked to reconfirm their authentication information is set to 0, which blocks administrator resets.
opzione_d: Password writeback is not enabled in Microsoft Entra Connect.
spiegazione: Correct: Administrator accounts are enabled for SSPR by default and are governed by a strong default two-gate password reset policy that cannot be changed. The two-gate policy requires two pieces of authentication data - such as an email address, authenticator app, or phone number - and it prohibits security questions. Helpdesk Administrator appears in the list of roles affected by the two-gate policy, and because a custom domain is configured and Microsoft Entra Connect is synchronizing identities, the two-gate policy applies rather than the one-gate exception. A is wrong: cloud-only accounts are fully supported for SSPR in a hybrid tenant; the presence of Microsoft Entra Connect only affects whether the two-gate policy applies and whether writeback is needed for synchronized users. C is wrong: setting the reconfirmation interval to 0 means users are never asked to confirm their authentication information - it does not block resets, and it is only available when Require users to register when signing in is enabled. D is wrong: the account is cloud-only, so its password is managed in Microsoft Entra ID and writeback is not involved; writeback only matters for federated, pass-through authentication, or password hash synchronized users. Correction: option A was rewritten - it previously claimed the account was not a member of the group selected under Self service password reset enabled, which is incoherent because the scenario sets the scope to All, so no group is selected at all.

sotto_argomento: Configure self-service password reset (SSPR)
domanda:
The Microsoft Entra tenant for Contoso, Ltd. has the custom domain contoso.com verified, and Microsoft Entra Connect synchronizes identities from an on-premises Active Directory Domain Services forest. On the Password reset blade, Self service password reset enabled is set to Selected and scoped to a group named Sales. Number of methods required to reset is set to 2. The members of Sales previously registered only a mobile phone, because the policy formerly required a single method. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true.
1. A member of Sales who has registered only a mobile phone can still reset a forgotten password by using SSPR.
2. A cloud-only user who is assigned the User Administrator role can register security questions and use them as one of the two methods required to reset the password.
3. To prevent administrator accounts from using SSPR, you must set the AllowedToUseSspr property on the tenant authorization policy to false.
opzione_a: A member of Sales who has registered only a mobile phone can still reset a forgotten password by using SSPR.
opzione_b: A cloud-only user who is assigned the User Administrator role can register security questions and use them as one of the two methods required to reset the password.
opzione_c: To prevent administrator accounts from using SSPR, you must set the AllowedToUseSspr property on the tenant authorization policy to false.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: The "Change authentication methods" table on Microsoft Learn documents the outcome of changing the number of required methods: 1 method registered with 2 methods required gives the result "Unable to reset or unlock". Users who do not register the minimum number of required methods see an error page and must request that an administrator reset their password. Statement 2 - No: User Administrator is one of the administrator roles listed as being affected by the strong default two-gate password reset policy, and because the tenant has a custom domain configured and Microsoft Entra Connect synchronizing identities, the two-gate policy applies rather than the one-gate exception. The two-gate policy requires two pieces of authentication data such as an email address, authenticator app, or phone number, and it explicitly prohibits security questions. Statement 3 - Yes: You can disable the use of SSPR for administrator accounts by setting the value of the AllowedToUseSspr property on the tenant authorization policy to false, for example with Update-MgPolicyAuthorizationPolicy -AllowedToUseSspr:$false, or by PATCHing allowedToUseSSPR on the authorizationPolicy in Microsoft Graph. Administrators are enabled for SSPR by default and the administrator two-gate policy itself cannot be edited, so this tenant-level property is the supported way to turn it off. Policy changes can take up to 60 minutes to take effect.
tags: sspr,two-gate policy,allowedtousesspr,authorization policy,number of methods required,administrator reset policy

sotto_argomento: Configure self-service password reset (SSPR)
domanda:
You are deploying self-service password reset (SSPR) for Northwind Traders. The deployment must meet the following requirements:
- SSPR must be enabled only for the members of a single Microsoft Entra group named NW-Pilot.
- Users must provide two authentication methods to reset or unlock their password.
- Users must be prompted to register their authentication methods the next time they sign in to a Microsoft Entra integrated application.
- After they register, users must never be prompted to reconfirm their authentication information.
Select the appropriate option for each setting under Entra ID > Password reset.
opzione_a: Self service password reset enabled (Properties page): [None | Selected | All]
opzione_b: Number of methods required to reset (Authentication methods page): [1 | 2 | 3]
opzione_c: Require users to register when signing in (Registration page): [Yes | No]
opzione_d: Number of days before users are asked to reconfirm their authentication information (Registration page): [0 | 180 | 730]
spiegazione: Correct: (1) Self service password reset enabled must be Selected, because SSPR can be scoped to None, Selected, or All, and only Selected scopes SSPR to a single chosen Microsoft Entra group - None would disable SSPR and All would enable every user in the tenant. (2) Number of methods required to reset must be 2; Microsoft Learn states this value can be set to either one or two, so 3 is not a valid choice and 1 would not meet the requirement. (3) Require users to register when signing in must be Yes, which prompts users to complete SSPR registration when they use modern authentication or a web browser to sign in to applications that use Microsoft Entra ID; No means users are never prompted during sign-in and must register manually at https://aka.ms/ssprsetup. (4) The reconfirmation interval accepts values from 0 to 730 days, and setting the value to 0 means users are never asked to confirm their authentication information - 180 and 730 would both prompt users to reconfirm. Note that the reconfirmation setting is only available when Require users to register when signing in is enabled. Correction: the stem and options were clarified to name the page that hosts each setting - the four settings are not all on the Properties page; scope is on Properties, the method count is on Authentication methods, and both registration settings are on Registration.
tags: sspr,registration,number of methods required,reconfirm authentication information,microsoft entra id

sotto_argomento: Configure self-service password reset (SSPR)
domanda: You are preparing to enable self-service password reset (SSPR) password writeback for a hybrid Microsoft Entra tenant. You must configure the on-premises Active Directory Domain Services permissions for the account that Microsoft Entra Connect uses to synchronize the directory. Which permissions and rights must you grant to that account? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Reset password
opzione_b: Write permissions on pwdLastSet
opzione_c: Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All
opzione_d: Write permissions on lockoutTime
opzione_e: Membership in the Enterprise Admins group of the forest root domain
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft Learn lists the permissions and options that must be set on the account specified in Microsoft Entra Connect for SSPR writeback: Reset password, Change password, Write permissions on lockoutTime, Write permissions on pwdLastSet, and the Extended rights for Unexpire Password on the root object of each domain in that forest. Of the options offered, Reset password, Write pwdLastSet and Write lockoutTime are the three that appear in that list; they are applied to Descendant User objects in Active Directory Users and Computers. (Change password and the Unexpire Password extended right are also required in a real deployment but are not offered as options here.) C is wrong: Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All are the directory replication permissions used by Microsoft Entra Connect for password hash synchronization; they are not part of the documented writeback permission set. E is wrong: Enterprise Admins membership is never listed as a requirement - granting it would violate least privilege, and the documented approach is to delegate the specific permissions on the domain root instead. If you do not assign the documented permissions, writeback might appear to be configured correctly but users encounter errors when they manage their on-premises passwords from the cloud.

sotto_argomento: Configure self-service password reset (SSPR)
domanda: Password writeback is enabled in Microsoft Entra Connect and the option "Write back passwords to your on-premises directory" is selected on the On-premises integration page. Synchronized users can reset their forgotten passwords successfully. However, a user who resets her password and then realizes she mistyped it receives an error when she tries to change it again the same day. Password writeback works normally the next day. What should you configure to resolve the issue?
opzione_a: Grant the Microsoft Entra Connect account the Unexpire Password extended right on the root object of the domain.
opzione_b: Set the Minimum password age group policy setting to 0 in the on-premises domain.
opzione_c: Set Allow users to unlock accounts without resetting their password to Yes on the On-premises integration page.
opzione_d: Set Number of days before users are asked to reconfirm their authentication information to 0.
spiegazione: Correct: On-premises password policies can prevent password resets from being processed. Microsoft Learn states that for password writeback to work most efficiently the Minimum password age group policy must be set to 0, and explicitly notes that if you need to allow users to change or reset passwords more than once per day, you must set Minimum password age to 0. The setting is under Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies in gpmc.msc. A is wrong: the Unexpire Password extended right is a required writeback permission, but a missing one would break writeback consistently, not only for a second reset within the same day - and writeback already works for the first reset. C is wrong: that setting only separates the account-unlock operation from the password-reset operation; it has no effect on how frequently a password can be changed. D is wrong: the reconfirmation interval governs how often users are prompted to confirm their registered authentication information; it does not influence on-premises password age policy.
tags: sspr,password writeback,minimum password age,group policy,troubleshooting,microsoft entra connect

sotto_argomento: Configure self-service password reset (SSPR)
domanda: Contoso plans to pilot self-service password reset (SSPR) before a tenant-wide rollout. Only the members of a Microsoft Entra security group named Pilot-Users must be able to reset their own passwords. All other users must continue to call the help desk. You sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center as an Authentication Policy Administrator and browse to Entra ID > Password reset > Properties. What should you configure?
opzione_a: Set Self service password reset enabled to All, then create a Conditional Access policy that blocks the password reset flow for everyone except Pilot-Users.
opzione_b: Set Self service password reset enabled to Selected, then choose the Pilot-Users group.
opzione_c: Set Self service password reset enabled to None, then assign Microsoft Entra ID P1 licenses only to the members of Pilot-Users.
opzione_d: Set Self service password reset enabled to All, then set Number of methods required to reset to 2.
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft Entra ID lets you enable SSPR for None, Selected, or All users. Selected scopes SSPR to the members of a chosen Microsoft Entra group, which is exactly the pilot requirement. A is wrong: the SSPR scope is controlled on the Password reset > Properties page, not by Conditional Access; Conditional Access does not gate the SSPR portal in this way, and setting the scope to All would already enable SSPR for everyone. C is wrong: None disables SSPR for all users, and licensing does not define the SSPR scope - the documentation explicitly states that although some unlicensed users may technically be able to access SSPR, licensing is not the scoping mechanism. D is wrong: Number of methods required to reset controls how many authentication methods a user must provide (the value can be set only to 1 or 2); it does not restrict which users are enabled for SSPR, and All would enable every user. Note also that Number of methods required to reset is configured on the Authentication methods page, not on the Properties page named in the scenario.
tags: sspr,self-service password reset,microsoft entra id,password reset scope,selected group

sotto_argomento: Configure self-service password reset (SSPR)
domanda: Fabrikam, Inc. synchronizes an on-premises Active Directory Domain Services forest to Microsoft Entra ID by using Microsoft Entra Connect. Every user is licensed for Microsoft 365 Business Standard only. You must allow the synchronized users to reset a forgotten password from https://aka.ms/sspr and have the new password written back to the on-premises directory. You need to identify the minimum licensing change required. What should you do?
opzione_a: Assign Microsoft 365 Business Basic licenses to the synchronized users.
opzione_b: Assign Microsoft Entra ID P1 licenses to the synchronized users.
opzione_c: Make no licensing change; Microsoft 365 Business Standard already includes self-service password reset with on-premises writeback.
opzione_d: Make no licensing change; enable password hash synchronization in Microsoft Entra Connect instead.
spiegazione: Correct: The SSPR licensing table on Microsoft Learn marks "Hybrid user password change or reset with on-prem writeback" as available only in Microsoft 365 Business Premium and Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2. Of the choices offered, Microsoft Entra ID P1 is the minimum that enables writeback. A is wrong: the documentation explicitly warns that standalone Microsoft 365 Basic and Standard licensing plans do not support SSPR with on-premises writeback, so moving to Business Basic makes the situation worse (Basic does not even cover cloud-only password reset in the same way Standard does). C is wrong: Microsoft 365 Business Standard covers cloud-only user password change and cloud-only user password reset, but not on-premises writeback. D is wrong: password hash synchronization determines how sign-in is authenticated and synchronizes hashes from on-premises to the cloud - it does not write cloud password changes back to Active Directory, and it does not grant any license entitlement.
tags: sspr,password writeback,licensing,microsoft entra id p1,hybrid identity

sotto_argomento: Configure self-service password reset (SSPR)
domanda: Six months ago you enabled self-service password reset (SSPR) by setting Self service password reset enabled to Selected and choosing a group named SSPR-Sales. The pilot succeeded, and the business now wants the members of a second group named SSPR-Finance to be enabled for SSPR as well. No other users may be enabled for SSPR. You must minimize administrative effort. What should you do from the Microsoft Entra admin center?
opzione_a: On the Password reset > Properties page, select both SSPR-Sales and SSPR-Finance under Selected.
opzione_b: Create a new group, add SSPR-Sales and SSPR-Finance as members of it, and select the new group under Selected.
opzione_c: On the Password reset > Properties page, set Self service password reset enabled to All.
opzione_d: Create a second password reset policy that is scoped to SSPR-Finance.
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft Learn states that you can currently enable only one Microsoft Entra group for SSPR using the Microsoft Entra admin center, and that Microsoft Entra ID supports nested groups as part of a wider SSPR deployment. Creating a parent group that contains both existing groups as members and selecting that single parent group satisfies the requirement with the least effort. A is wrong: the admin center allows only one group to be selected for SSPR, so you cannot pick two groups. C is wrong: All would enable SSPR for every user in the tenant, which violates the requirement that no other users be enabled. D is wrong: Microsoft Entra ID has a single tenant-level SSPR policy for users - you cannot create multiple SSPR policies scoped to different groups (the separate, unchangeable administrator two-gate policy is the only other policy, and it is not something you create).
tags: sspr,nested groups,password reset scope,microsoft entra id,selected group

sotto_argomento: Create custom role definitions
domanda: Contoso defines an Azure custom role named Storage Ops with the following permissions block: Actions contains 'Microsoft.Storage/*'; NotActions contains 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/delete'; DataActions contains 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/*'; NotDataActions contains 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/delete'. A user named User7 is assigned the Storage Ops custom role at the scope of a storage account named sa2. User7 is also assigned the Storage Blob Data Contributor built-in role at the scope of sa2. User7 has no other role assignments, and no deny assignments or management locks exist. Select the answer choice that completes each statement based on the information presented.
opzione_a: User7 can delete the storage account sa2: [Yes | No]
opzione_b: User7 can delete a blob in a container in sa2: [Yes | No]
opzione_c: User7 can read a blob in a container in sa2: [Yes | No]
opzione_d: The effective control plane permissions of the Storage Ops role alone are computed as: [Actions minus NotActions | Actions plus NotActions | NotActions minus Actions]
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/delete' is subtracted from the Storage Ops wildcard by NotActions, and no other assigned role grants it. Storage Blob Data Contributor's Actions cover blob containers and the generateUserDelegationKey action, not deletion of the storage account resource itself. Because nothing grants the action, access is not allowed - not because NotActions denies it, but because no role grants it. Statement 2 - Yes: this is the key distinction. NotDataActions removed the blob delete action from the Storage Ops role, but the docs state that 'if a user is assigned a role that excludes a data action in NotDataActions, and is assigned a second role that grants access to the same data action, the user is allowed to perform that data action. NotDataActions is not a deny rule.' Storage Blob Data Contributor includes 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/delete' in its DataActions, and RBAC is additive, so the deletion is allowed. Statement 3 - Yes: both roles grant the blob read data action; Storage Ops grants it through its blobs wildcard (blob read is not excluded by NotDataActions) and Storage Blob Data Contributor grants it explicitly. Statement 4 - Actions minus NotActions: Microsoft Learn defines the formula as 'Actions - NotActions = Effective control plane permissions', with the matching 'DataActions - NotDataActions = Effective data permissions' for the data plane. NotActions is never added to Actions, and the subtraction is never performed in the reverse direction; the subtraction is also computed per role definition, then the results of all of a user's role assignments are summed.
tags: azure rbac,custom role,notactions,notdataactions,dataactions,storage blob data contributor,effective permissions

sotto_argomento: Create custom role definitions
domanda: Contoso creates an Azure custom role named VM Operator. In the role definition, Actions is set to 'Microsoft.Compute/*' and NotActions is set to 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete'. A user named User2 is assigned the VM Operator custom role at the scope of a resource group named RG-App. Separately, User2 is also assigned the Virtual Machine Contributor built-in role at the scope of RG-App. User2 attempts to delete a virtual machine in RG-App. What is the result, and why?
opzione_a: The deletion fails, because listing an action in NotActions creates an explicit deny for that action.
opzione_b: The deletion fails, because Azure subtracts the NotActions of every assigned role from the union of all Actions granted to the user.
opzione_c: The deletion succeeds, because Virtual Machine Contributor grants the delete action and NotActions is not a deny rule.
opzione_d: The deletion succeeds, but only after an administrator removes the VM Operator role assignment from User2.
spiegazione: Correct answer (c): NotActions is scoped to the role definition that contains it, not to the user. Microsoft Learn states this directly: 'If a user is assigned a role that excludes an action in NotActions, and is assigned a second role that grants access to the same action, the user is allowed to perform that action. NotActions is not a deny rule - it is simply a convenient way to create a set of allowed actions when specific actions need to be excluded.' The subtraction 'Actions - NotActions = Effective control plane permissions' is computed per role definition; the results are then combined additively across the user's role assignments. The Virtual Machine Contributor built-in role includes 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete' in its Actions and has an empty NotActions, so the delete is granted and succeeds. (a) is wrong because it states the single most common misconception about NotActions; only a deny assignment produces an explicit deny in Azure RBAC. (b) is wrong because it describes an evaluation model Azure does not use: NotActions is never applied across role boundaries, so the VM Operator role's exclusion cannot reach into the Virtual Machine Contributor assignment. (d) is wrong because no removal is needed; the deletion already succeeds while both assignments are in place. To genuinely prevent the deletion, Contoso would need to remove the Virtual Machine Contributor assignment, since a wildcard-based custom role cannot subtract permissions that another role independently grants.
tags: azure rbac,notactions,custom role,virtual machine contributor,effective permissions,not a deny rule

sotto_argomento: Create custom role-based access control (RBAC) roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
domanda: The operations team at Northwind Traders needs a single Azure custom role that meets the following requirements: team members can perform every action in the Microsoft.Compute resource provider except deleting virtual machines; the role must be available for assignment in two subscriptions, sub-prod01 and sub-prod02, that trust the same Microsoft Entra tenant. You author the role definition in JSON. Select the correct option for each drop-down.
opzione_a: Property that must contain "Microsoft.Compute/*": [Actions | DataActions | NotActions | AssignableScopes]
opzione_b: Property that must contain "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete": [Actions | DataActions | NotActions | NotDataActions]
opzione_c: Property that must contain the two subscription IDs: [Scope | AssignableScopes | Condition | NotActions]
opzione_d: Maximum number of custom roles allowed per Microsoft Entra tenant: [500 | 2000 | 4000 | 5000]
spiegazione: Drop-down 1 - Actions: The Actions property 'specifies the control plane actions that the role allows to be performed.' Microsoft.Compute/* 'Grants access to all actions for all resource types in the Microsoft.Compute resource provider,' which matches the requirement. DataActions holds only data plane actions (where isDataAction is true), and compute management operations are control plane actions. NotActions and AssignableScopes do not grant anything. Drop-down 2 - NotActions: NotActions 'specifies the control plane actions that are subtracted or excluded from the allowed Actions that have a wildcard (*),' and effective permissions are computed as Actions - NotActions. Because Actions uses the Microsoft.Compute/* wildcard, subtracting the delete action with NotActions is exactly the documented pattern. Actions would grant the delete instead of excluding it; NotDataActions only subtracts from DataActions, and virtual machine delete is not a data action. Drop-down 3 - AssignableScopes: AssignableScopes is 'an array of strings that specifies the scopes that the custom role is available for assignment,' and "/subscriptions/{subscriptionId1}", "/subscriptions/{subscriptionId2}" is the documented example for making a role available in two subscriptions. Custom roles can be shared between subscriptions that trust the same Microsoft Entra tenant. Scope is a property of a role assignment, not of a role definition; Condition holds an ABAC condition statement; NotActions holds excluded actions. Drop-down 4 - 5000: Microsoft Learn states 'There is a limit of 5,000 custom roles per tenant' and 'Each tenant can have up to 5000 custom roles.' 2000 is the limit only for Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet; 4000 is the role assignments limit per subscription; 500 is the role assignments limit per management group.

sotto_argomento: Create custom role-based access control (RBAC) roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
domanda: You are authoring an Azure custom role definition for the Contoso tenant and you are reviewing the rules that govern the AssignableScopes property. Which three statements are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: AssignableScopes can't be set to the root scope ("/").
opzione_b: Wildcards (*) can't be used in AssignableScopes.
opzione_c: You can define only one management group in the AssignableScopes of a custom role.
opzione_d: AssignableScopes must contain at least one subscription, because management groups aren't supported as assignable scopes for custom roles.
opzione_e: Listing a scope in AssignableScopes grants the role's permissions at that scope, even when no role assignment exists.
spiegazione: Correct: a. The documented custom role limits state 'You cannot set AssignableScopes to the root scope ("/").' The root scope is reserved for built-in roles, whose AssignableScopes is "/". Correct: b. The limits also state 'You cannot use wildcards (*) in AssignableScopes. This wildcard restriction helps ensure a user can't potentially obtain access to a scope by updating the role definition.' Note that wildcards ARE allowed inside Actions, NotActions, DataActions, and NotDataActions strings (one wildcard per action string). Correct: c. 'You can define only one management group in AssignableScopes of a custom role.' This limits situations where role definitions and role assignments become disconnected when a subscription or management group moves to a different parent. Wrong: d. Management groups are explicitly supported: a valid example is "/providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/{groupId1}", and you can define a management group as an assignable scope so the role is available on that management group and everything under it. The requirement is only that you use at least one management group, subscription, or resource group. Wrong: e. AssignableScopes only specifies where the role is available for assignment (and controls who can create, update, delete, or view the custom role). It grants nothing by itself.
