Microsoft Learn states 'the level of access is determined by the custom role assignment (scope + role permissions + security principal) and not the AssignableScopes listed in the custom role.'
tags: azure rbac,custom role,assignablescopes,root scope,wildcards,management group,role definition

sotto_argomento: Create custom role-based access control (RBAC) roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
domanda: A custom role named Sandbox Operator has its AssignableScopes set to /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/mg-sandbox. The role is assigned to a Microsoft Entra group at the scope of a subscription named sub-dev01, which is currently a child of mg-sandbox. A governance change requires sub-dev01 to be moved so that it becomes a child of a different management group named mg-corp. The move fails with an error stating that it would break the relationship between the role assignment and the role definition. Which action resolves the issue while keeping the existing role assignment on sub-dev01 in place?
opzione_a: Add /subscriptions/{sub-dev01-id} to the AssignableScopes of the Sandbox Operator role, then move the subscription.
opzione_b: Add /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/mg-corp as a second management group in the AssignableScopes of the Sandbox Operator role, then move the subscription.
opzione_c: Remove the Sandbox Operator role assignment from sub-dev01, then move the subscription.
opzione_d: Set the AssignableScopes of the Sandbox Operator role to the root scope ("/"), then move the subscription.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Moving sub-dev01 out from under mg-sandbox breaks the hierarchy path from the role assignment on the subscription up to the role definition on the management group, which is why Azure blocks the move. Microsoft Learn lists 'Add the subscription to the role definition's assignable scope' as a documented fix. AssignableScopes accepts subscriptions alongside a management group, so after adding the sub-dev01 scope the definition remains reachable from the assignment regardless of the new parent, and the assignment survives. Wrong: b. 'You can define only one management group in the assignable scopes of a new role.' The definition already contains mg-sandbox, so mg-corp cannot be added as a second management group. Wrong: c. Removing the role assignment before the move is a documented option and would allow the move to succeed, but it does not satisfy the requirement to keep the existing role assignment on sub-dev01 in place - the access would have to be recreated afterwards. Wrong: d. Custom roles cannot use the root scope: 'You cannot set AssignableScopes to the root scope ("/").' The root scope is reserved for built-in roles. (Retargeting AssignableScopes to the root management group would be valid, but that is a management group, not the root scope "/".)
tags: azure rbac,custom role,assignablescopes,management group,move subscription,troubleshooting,role definition

sotto_argomento: Create custom role-based access control (RBAC) roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
domanda: An engineer authors an Azure custom role that includes the DataActions entry Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/read and sets AssignableScopes to a single management group named mg-data. Azure creates the role definition successfully. However, when the engineer tries to assign the role at the mg-data management group scope, the assignment fails. What is the reason?
opzione_a: Custom roles that contain DataActions can't be assigned at management group scope, but the role can be assigned at the subscriptions, resource groups, or resources under mg-data.
opzione_b: AssignableScopes must include the root scope (/) before a custom role can be assigned at any management group scope.
opzione_c: A custom role can list only one management group in AssignableScopes, so mg-data must be replaced with the Tenant Root Group.
opzione_d: Data plane permissions can't be granted through Azure RBAC role definitions and must be assigned in the Microsoft Entra admin center instead.
spiegazione: Correct: a. The documented custom role limits state 'Custom roles with DataActions can't be assigned at the management group scope' and clarify: 'You can create a custom role with DataActions and one management group in AssignableScopes. You can't assign the custom role at the management group scope itself; however, you can assign the custom role at the scope of the subscriptions within the management group.' This is why the definition was created but the assignment failed. Wrong: b. Custom roles cannot set AssignableScopes to the root scope (/) at all - that is an explicit documented limit. The root scope is reserved for built-in roles. Wrong: c. The one-management-group rule is real, but the role already lists exactly one management group (mg-data), so it isn't violated. Swapping in the Tenant Root Group would not help, because the DataActions restriction applies to any management group scope. Wrong: d. Azure RBAC does support data plane permissions: the same authorization model used for control plane actions has been extended to data plane actions via the DataActions and NotDataActions properties. Built-in roles such as Storage Blob Data Reader use DataActions.

sotto_argomento: Create users and groups
domanda: Litware Inc. uses the following membership rule on a Dynamic User security group. No parentheses are present in the rule: user.country -eq "US" -and user.department -eq "Marketing" -or user.department -eq "Sales". Based on the documented operator precedence for dynamic membership rules, determine whether each user is added to the group. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: A user whose country is US and whose department is Marketing: [Added | Not added]
opzione_b: A user whose country is Canada and whose department is Sales: [Added | Not added]
opzione_c: A user whose country is Canada and whose department is Marketing: [Added | Not added]
opzione_d: A user whose country is US and whose department is Finance: [Added | Not added]
spiegazione: Microsoft Learn documents operator precedence from highest to lowest as: the comparison operators (-eq, -ne, -startsWith, -notStartsWith, -contains, -notContains, -match, -notMatch, -in, -notIn), then -not, then -and, then -or, then -any and -all. Because -and binds more tightly than -or, the rule is evaluated as (user.country -eq "US" -and user.department -eq "Marketing") -or (user.department -eq "Sales"). Dropdown 1 = Added: The user satisfies both halves of the -and branch. Dropdown 2 = Added: The -or branch is satisfied by department Sales on its own; country is irrelevant to that branch, which is the common misreading of this rule. Dropdown 3 = Not added: The -and branch fails because country is not US, and the -or branch fails because the department is not Sales. Dropdown 4 = Not added: The -and branch fails on department, and the -or branch fails on department. Learn notes you need parentheses only when the default precedence doesn't meet your requirements. Writing user.country -eq "US" -and (user.department -eq "Marketing" -or user.department -eq "Sales") would instead require US for every member and would exclude the Canadian Sales user, and setting operator precedence explicitly is one of the cases that requires the rule syntax text box rather than the rule builder. Correction: the final sentence previously asserted only that parentheses "would change the result" without saying how; it now states the specific alternate grouping and which user it excludes.
tags: microsoft entra id,dynamic membership,operator precedence,membership rule,and,or

sotto_argomento: Create users and groups
domanda: Adatum Corporation collaborates with several partner firms whose users have been invited into the Adatum tenant through B2B collaboration. You must create a group that always contains every guest user in the tenant so that a Conditional Access policy can target them. The group must not provision a mailbox or a SharePoint site, and membership must never be maintained by hand. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Group type: [Security | Microsoft 365 | Mail-enabled security]
opzione_b: Membership type: [Assigned | Dynamic User | Dynamic Device]
opzione_c: Membership rule: [user.userType -eq "Guest" | user.objectId -ne null | device.deviceOwnership -eq "Personal"]
opzione_d: Minimum license required for each unique member: [Microsoft Entra ID Free | Microsoft Entra ID P1 | Microsoft Entra ID P2]
spiegazione: Group type = Security: Security groups are used to manage access to shared resources and do not provision a mailbox or SharePoint site, unlike Microsoft 365 groups. Mail-enabled security groups cannot be managed in the Microsoft Entra admin center at all; Learn states they can only be managed in the Exchange admin center or the Microsoft 365 admin center. Membership type = Dynamic User: Guests are user objects, and only Dynamic User membership evaluates user attributes automatically. Assigned would require manual maintenance, and Dynamic Device evaluates device attributes only. Membership rule = user.userType -eq "Guest": userType is a supported string property whose allowed values are member, guest, and null, and Guest indicates a user who is not internal to the company. user.objectId -ne null is the documented "all users" rule that adds both guests and members, and device.deviceOwnership is a device attribute that cannot be used in a user rule. Minimum license = Microsoft Entra ID P1: Learn states dynamic membership groups require a Microsoft Entra ID P1 license (or an Intune for Education license) for each unique user who is a member of one or more dynamic membership groups, and that you must hold enough licenses to cover all such users even though you do not have to assign them. Microsoft Entra ID Free does not include the feature, and P2 exceeds the documented minimum.
tags: microsoft entra id,dynamic membership,usertype,guest,licensing,entra id p1,security group

sotto_argomento: Create users and groups
domanda: You are documenting what can be a member of each Microsoft Entra group type for your organization's identity standards. Which of the following membership scenarios are supported? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A device object can be a member of a security group.
opzione_b: A device object can be a member of a Microsoft 365 group.
opzione_c: A service principal can be a member of a security group.
opzione_d: A security group can be added as a member of a Microsoft 365 group.
opzione_e: A security group can be added as a member of another security group.
spiegazione: Correct (a): Microsoft Learn states that members of a security group can include users, devices, and service principals. Correct (c): Service principals are explicitly listed as supported members of a security group; users and service principals can also own a security group. Correct (e): For the security group type you can add an existing group to another group (nested groups). Nesting is supported for membership and Conditional Access scopes, but members of the nested child group do not gain access to shared resources and applications assigned to the parent group, and licenses cannot be applied to nested security groups. Wrong (b): Members of a Microsoft 365 group can only include users, so devices cannot be added. Wrong (d): Adding security groups to Microsoft 365 groups is explicitly listed as unsupported, as is adding Microsoft 365 groups to security groups or to other Microsoft 365 groups. Correction: sotto_argomento was "Manage external users", which did not match a question about group types, and has been set to "Create users and groups". The explanation of option (e) previously said members of the parent group gain access; it has been rewritten to state the documented behavior, that nested groups do not gain access to resources assigned to the parent.
tags: microsoft entra id,group types,security group,microsoft 365 group,nested groups,service principal

sotto_argomento: Create users and groups
domanda: A sales manager whose user object ID is aaaaaaaa-0000-1111-2222-bbbbbbbbbbbb needs a group that always contains the people who report directly to her. The Manager property is correctly populated for all users in the tenant. Which membership rule should you enter for the Dynamic User group?
opzione_a: Direct Reports for "aaaaaaaa-0000-1111-2222-bbbbbbbbbbbb"
opzione_b: user.manager -eq "aaaaaaaa-0000-1111-2222-bbbbbbbbbbbb"
opzione_c: Direct Reports for "manager@contoso.com"
opzione_d: (Direct Reports for "aaaaaaaa-0000-1111-2222-bbbbbbbbbbbb") -and (user.department -eq "Sales")
spiegazione: Correct (a): Microsoft Learn documents the direct reports rule syntax as Direct Reports for "{objectID_of_manager}", where the value is the object ID of the manager. This rule must be authored in the rule syntax text box because the rule builder does not support it, and note that the manager is also added to the group. Wrong (b): manager is not listed among the supported user properties for building a single-expression dynamic membership rule; the documented mechanism for direct reports is the dedicated Direct Reports for syntax. Wrong (c): The direct reports rule requires the manager's object ID, which you find in the manager's profile, not a user principal name or email address. Wrong (d): Learn explicitly states that you can't combine the direct reports rule with any other membership rules. It also supports only the manager's direct reports, not the reports of those reports. Correction: option (d) previously used the unsupported user.manager property, which made it a duplicate of the flaw in option (b) rather than testing the documented "cannot be combined with other rules" restriction. It has been rewritten to use the correct Direct Reports for syntax combined with a second expression, so it is now wrong for exactly one clear reason.
tags: microsoft entra id,dynamic membership,direct reports,membership rule,manager

sotto_argomento: Create users and groups
domanda: Contoso Ltd. manages 400 corporate-owned Windows laptops that are registered in Microsoft Entra ID. The security team wants a group whose membership is populated automatically from the device attribute deviceOwnership so that a Conditional Access policy can target only company-owned hardware. No mailbox or SharePoint site should be created for the group. Which group type and membership type should you select when you create the group?
opzione_a: Group type: Microsoft 365; Membership type: Dynamic Device
opzione_b: Group type: Security; Membership type: Dynamic Device
opzione_c: Group type: Security; Membership type: Dynamic User
opzione_d: Group type: Microsoft 365; Membership type: Assigned
spiegazione: Correct (b): A security group can contain either devices or users, and the Dynamic Device membership type evaluates device attributes such as device.deviceOwnership -eq "Company" to add and remove devices automatically. Security groups have no mailbox or SharePoint site, which satisfies the requirement. Wrong (a): Microsoft 365 groups can include only users as members, so Dynamic Device is not a valid membership type for them. Wrong (c): Dynamic User evaluates user attributes and populates the group with user objects, not devices; a dynamic group can target users or devices, never both. Wrong (d): Assigned membership requires an administrator to add each member manually, which is not automatic, and a Microsoft 365 group cannot contain devices and does provision a mailbox and SharePoint site. Correction: url_riferimento was a bare page link and has been replaced with the #group-types deep link that actually carries the membership statements. Note that device-based dynamic membership groups can only be created with the rule syntax text box, because the rule builder supports user-based groups only.
tags: microsoft entra id,groups,security group,microsoft 365 group,dynamic device,membership type

sotto_argomento: Create users and groups
domanda: A helpdesk technician reports that a Dynamic User group intended to contain "every user who has any value in the Department field" is returning zero members, even though hundreds of users clearly have a department populated. The current membership rule is user.department -ne "null". You must correct the rule. Which membership rule should you configure?
opzione_a: user.department -ne null
opzione_b: user.department -notContains null
opzione_c: -not (user.department -eq null)
opzione_d: user.department -notMatch "null"
spiegazione: Correct (a): Microsoft Learn states that to specify a null value in a rule you use -eq or -ne when comparing the null value, and gives user.mail -ne null as the correct way to reference the null value, without quotation marks. The original rule failed because quotation marks around null make it a literal string comparison, so it only matched users whose department was literally the text "null". Wrong (b): -notContains performs a partial string match and is not the documented way to perform a null check; Learn also cautions to minimize the use of Match and Contains operators because they slow dynamic group processing. Wrong (c): Learn explicitly states you must not use the -not operator as a comparative operator for the null value, and that doing so returns an error whether you use null or $null. Wrong (d): -match and -notMatch are regular expression operators and, with null in quotation marks, this again compares against the literal string "null" rather than performing a null check.
tags: microsoft entra id,dynamic membership,null values,troubleshooting,membership rule,operators

sotto_argomento: Create users and groups
domanda: Northwind Traders wants a Dynamic User security group that contains every internal employee in the tenant but excludes all B2B collaboration guests. The group must stay accurate as employees join and leave. Which membership rule should you configure?
opzione_a: user.objectId -ne null
opzione_b: (user.objectId -ne null) -and (user.userType -eq "Member")
opzione_c: user.userType -ne "Guest"
opzione_d: (user.objectId -ne "null") -and (user.userType -eq "Member")
spiegazione: Correct (b): Microsoft Learn documents this exact pattern. The rule user.objectId -ne null selects all users, and combining it with user.userType -eq "Member" restricts membership to member users and excludes guests. Wrong (a): This is the documented "all users" rule, but Learn explicitly states it adds both business-to-business guest users and member users, so guests would not be excluded. Wrong (c): The userType property allows the values member, guest, and null. A rule that only tests -ne "Guest" would also match user objects whose userType is null, so it does not reliably select just internal members. Wrong (d): Putting null in quotation marks makes it a literal string comparison. Learn states you should use quotation marks around the word null only if you want it interpreted as a literal string value; the correct null check is user.objectId -ne null without quotes.

sotto_argomento: Create users and groups
domanda: An administrator at Fabrikam is authoring membership rules for Dynamic Device security groups in the Microsoft Entra admin center. Devices are enrolled in Microsoft Intune, and a mix of Microsoft Entra joined, Microsoft Entra hybrid joined, and Microsoft Entra registered devices exists in the tenant. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. 1) The rule device.deviceOwnership -eq "Corporate" adds the company-owned devices to the group. 2) The rule device.deviceTrustType -eq "ServerAD" adds the Microsoft Entra hybrid joined devices to the group. 3) A Dynamic Device rule can reference the department attribute of the device's registered owner.
opzione_a: The rule device.deviceOwnership -eq "Corporate" adds the company-owned devices to the group.
opzione_b: The rule device.deviceTrustType -eq "ServerAD" adds the Microsoft Entra hybrid joined devices to the group.
opzione_c: A Dynamic Device rule can reference the department attribute of the device's registered owner.
spiegazione: Statement 1 = No: This is the classic Intune trap. Microsoft Learn states that when you use deviceOwnership to create dynamic membership groups for devices, you need to set the value equal to "Company". The allowed values are Personal, Company, and Unknown. Intune represents the same ownership as Corporate in its own reporting, but the dynamic rule must use Company. Statement 2 = Yes: For deviceTrustType, Learn documents AzureAD to represent Microsoft Entra joined devices, ServerAD to represent Microsoft Entra hybrid joined devices, and Workplace to represent Microsoft Entra registered devices. Statement 3 = No: Learn explicitly states you can't create a device membership group based on the user attributes of the device owner; device membership rules can reference only device attributes. A single dynamic group can target users or devices, never both.

sotto_argomento: Create users and groups
domanda: Your organization is standardizing how administrators author dynamic membership rules. You need to identify which rules cannot be created with the rule builder in the Microsoft Entra admin center and must be authored in the rule syntax text box. Which rules require the text box? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A rule that combines six expressions with the -and and -or operators.
opzione_b: A rule that uses the Direct Reports for "{objectID_of_manager}" syntax.
opzione_c: A rule that uses the -notContains operator.
opzione_d: A single-expression rule such as user.department -eq "Sales".
opzione_e: A two-expression rule that uses the -startsWith operator on user.displayName.
spiegazione: Correct (a): Microsoft Learn lists a rule with more than five expressions as requiring the text box, because the rule builder supports only up to five expressions. Correct (b): A rule for direct reports is explicitly listed as requiring the text box. Correct (c): A rule with a -contains or -notContains operator is explicitly listed as requiring the text box. Wrong (d): A single simple expression is exactly the kind of rule the rule builder is designed for. Wrong (e): Two expressions is well within the five-expression limit and -startsWith is a standard operator the rule builder handles. Other documented text-box-only cases include setting operator precedence, complex expressions such as (user.proxyAddresses -any (_ -startsWith "contoso")), and all device-based dynamic membership groups, since the rule builder is available only for user-based groups.
tags: microsoft entra id,dynamic membership,rule builder,rule syntax,operators,direct reports

sotto_argomento: Create users and groups
domanda: You download the bulk upload CSV template from Microsoft Entra ID > Users > Bulk create. You plan to create 60 new internal user accounts. Which set of columns must contain a value in every data row for the file to pass validation?
opzione_a: Name [displayName], User name [userPrincipalName], Initial password [passwordProfile], Block sign in (Yes/No) [accountEnabled]
opzione_b: Name [displayName], User name [userPrincipalName], First name [givenName], Last name [surname]
opzione_c: User name [userPrincipalName], Initial password [passwordProfile], Usage location [usageLocation], Department [department]
opzione_d: Name [displayName], User name [userPrincipalName], Initial password [passwordProfile], Usage location [usageLocation]
spiegazione: Correct (a): Microsoft Learn states that only the first four columns of the bulk create template are required: Name, User name (userPrincipalName), Initial password, and Block sign in (Yes/No). All other columns are optional and can be left empty. Wrong (b): First name and Last name are optional properties in the template, and Initial password and Block sign in are missing from this set. Wrong (c): Usage location and Department are optional, and this set omits the required Name and Block sign in columns. Wrong (d): Usage location is optional; the fourth required column is Block sign in (Yes/No), which maps to accountEnabled. Note that the version:v1.0 row and the column header row must be preserved exactly as downloaded or the upload cannot be processed, the examples row must be removed, and bulk create requires at least the User Administrator role.
tags: microsoft entra id,bulk create,csv template,users,required columns

sotto_argomento: Create users and groups
domanda: An administrator opens the dynamic membership rule builder in the Microsoft Entra admin center to configure a Dynamic User group. What is the maximum number of expressions the rule builder supports before the rule must be authored in the rule syntax text box instead?
spiegazione: Correct (b): Microsoft Learn states that the rule builder supports the construction of up to five expressions; a rule with more than five expressions is explicitly listed as requiring the rule syntax text box. Wrong (a): Three is not the documented limit; the builder accepts more than three expressions. Wrong (c): Ten is not a documented rule builder limit for dynamic membership rules. Wrong (d): 15 is not the expression limit. It is easily confused with the 15 extensionAttribute properties (extensionAttribute1-15) that are supported in dynamic rules, and with the 15,000 dynamic membership groups a single tenant can have.

sotto_argomento: Create, configure, and manage groups
domanda: Tailspin Toys is documenting its recovery procedures for accidentally deleted Microsoft Entra ID objects. Select the correct value to complete each statement.
opzione_a: Period during which a deleted user account remains in a suspended state and can be restored: [14 days | 30 days | 90 days]
opzione_b: Group types that can be restored after deletion: [Distribution groups only | Microsoft 365 groups and cloud security groups | All group types, including distribution groups]
opzione_c: The group restoration period can be customized: [Yes | No]
risposta_corretta: 30 days,Microsoft 365 groups and cloud security groups,No
spiegazione: Correct values are 30 days, Microsoft 365 groups and cloud security groups, and No. For users, the documentation states that after you delete a user the account remains in a suspended state for 30 days and can be restored during that window. For groups, the documentation states that restore functionality is available for Microsoft 365 groups and cloud security groups in Microsoft Entra ID, that it isn't available for distribution groups, that the deleted group is retained but not visible for 30 days from the deletion date, and that the 30-day group restoration period isn't customizable. Incorrect - 14 days or 90 days: the user soft-delete window is fixed at 30 days. Incorrect - Distribution groups only: this is the inverse of the truth, since distribution groups are precisely the type excluded from restore. Incorrect - All group types including distribution groups: distribution groups are explicitly not supported. Incorrect - Yes for customization: the retention period is fixed by the service and cannot be changed by an administrator.
tags: microsoft entra id,restore,deleted groups,deleted users,soft delete,retention

sotto_argomento: Create, configure, and manage users
domanda: A misconfigured offboarding script at Fourth Coffee deleted 120 Microsoft Entra ID user accounts yesterday. You sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center as a User Administrator and browse to Entra ID > Users > Deleted users. You must restore all 120 accounts in a single operation by using bulk restore. Arrange the following actions in the correct order.
opzione_a: Browse to the completed CSV file and select Submit to start validation of the file.
opzione_b: Review the outcome of the job on the Bulk operation results page.
opzione_c: On the Deleted users page, select Bulk restore.
opzione_d: Download the CSV template and add a row containing the Object ID of each user to restore.
opzione_e: After the file passes validation, select Submit to start the bulk restore operation.
spiegazione: The documented bulk restore sequence is: (1) On the Deleted users page, select Bulk restore to upload a valid CSV file of properties of the users to restore. (2) Open the CSV template and add a line for each user you want to restore; the only required value is ObjectID, and the version row and column header row must be kept exactly as downloaded or the upload can't be processed. (3) Under Upload your csv file, browse to the file and select Submit, which starts validation of the CSV file. (4) When the file contents are validated you see File uploaded successfully; if there are errors you must fix them before you can submit the job. When your file passes validation, select Submit to start the bulk operation that restores the users. (5) You can see the status of all of your pending bulk requests on the Bulk operation results page, and if you experience errors you can download the results file, which contains the reason for each error. The most common ordering mistake is attempting to upload before selecting Bulk restore, or treating the first Submit (validation) as the action that performs the restore; validation and execution are two distinct Submit steps.
tags: microsoft entra id,bulk restore,deleted users,csv,bulk operations

sotto_argomento: Create, configure, and manage users
domanda: Relecloud has a hybrid identity environment. User1 is a cloud-only account that was deleted 20 days ago. User2 was synchronized from Windows Server Active Directory by using Microsoft Entra Connect, was deleted in Microsoft Entra ID for security reasons, and still exists in the on-premises directory. User3 was deleted 45 days ago and has already been permanently removed. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true. 1) User1 can be restored from the Deleted users page in the Microsoft Entra admin center. 2) Microsoft Support can restore User3 on request. 3) The synchronization engine may restore User2 during the next synchronization cycle.
opzione_a: User1 can be restored from the Deleted users page in the Microsoft Entra admin center.
opzione_b: Microsoft Support can restore User3 on request.
opzione_c: The synchronization engine may restore User2 during the next synchronization cycle.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: User1 was deleted 20 days ago, which is inside the 30-day window. The documentation states you can see all the users that were deleted less than 30 days ago and that these users can be restored, along with all their properties. Statement 2 - No: User3 was deleted 45 days ago, so the automatic permanent deletion process has already run. The documentation is explicit that after the 30-day window passes the permanent deletion process automatically starts and can't be stopped, and that after a user is permanently deleted, neither you nor Microsoft Support can restore them. The only remedy is to create a new user and manually re-enter the information. Statement 3 - Yes: the documentation notes that although you can delete synced users in Microsoft Entra ID for security purposes, Microsoft Entra ID isn't the source of authority for synced users, and if the user still exists in your on-premises directory the sync engine may restore the user during the next synchronization cycle. To remove such a user durably, the account must be handled in the on-premises directory.
tags: microsoft entra id,restore deleted users,permanent deletion,hybrid identity,microsoft entra connect,source of authority

sotto_argomento: Create, configure, and manage users
domanda: An employee's account was deleted 10 days ago. At the time of deletion, the account had a Microsoft 365 E5 license assigned directly. Since then, the licenses have been consumed by new hires, and the tenant now shows zero available Microsoft 365 E5 licenses. An administrator restores the deleted account from the Deleted users page. What is the result?
opzione_a: The restore operation fails until an E5 license is freed or purchased.
opzione_b: The account is restored but with no licenses assigned, and the administrator must reassign a license manually.
opzione_c: The E5 license that was assigned at the time of deletion is restored with the account, and the organization can be temporarily out of compliance for license usage.
opzione_d: The account is restored and is automatically downgraded to a Microsoft Entra ID Free license until an E5 license becomes available.
spiegazione: Correct: The license is restored and the tenant can be temporarily out of compliance. The documentation explicitly notes that once a user is restored, licenses that were assigned to the user at the time of deletion are also restored even if there are none available, and that if you're consuming more licenses than you purchased, your organization could be temporarily out of compliance for license usage. Incorrect - The restore fails: license availability is not a gate on the restore operation; Microsoft Entra ID prioritizes returning the account to its previous state. Incorrect - Restored with no licenses: this contradicts the documented behavior. When a user account is deleted the account's organization information is preserved, and when you restore a user that information, including the license assignments, is restored. Incorrect - Automatically downgraded to Microsoft Entra ID Free: there is no automatic downgrade mechanism. The original assignment is reinstated as-is, which is precisely what creates the temporary compliance gap.

sotto_argomento: Create, configure, and manage users
domanda: An administrator needs to review which user accounts were recently deleted in Microsoft Entra ID and restore one of them from the Deleted users page in the Microsoft Entra admin center. Which is the least privileged built-in role that can perform this task?
opzione_a: Directory Readers
opzione_b: Reports Reader
opzione_c: User Administrator
opzione_d: Global Reader
spiegazione: Correct: User Administrator. The documented procedure for viewing restorable users and restoring a deleted user directs you to sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center as at least a User Administrator, then browse to Entra ID > Users > Deleted users. The same role is documented for permanently deleting a user and for bulk restore. Incorrect - Directory Readers: this role grants read access to basic directory information only; it cannot restore objects. Incorrect - Reports Reader: this role only reads sign-in and audit reporting data and usage reports; it has no user management permissions. Incorrect - Global Reader: Global Reader has broad read-only access across the tenant and can view deleted users, but read-only roles cannot perform the write operation of restoring an account. Restoring requires User Administrator.

sotto_argomento: Create, configure, and manage users
domanda: A User Administrator at Fabrikam deletes the Microsoft Entra ID account of an employee who left the company. Two weeks later, HR reports that the employee is returning and the original account should be recovered with all of its properties. For how long after deletion does a user account remain in a suspended state where it can still be restored?
opzione_a: 14 days
opzione_b: 30 days
opzione_c: 60 days
opzione_d: 90 days
spiegazione: Correct: 30 days. The documentation states that after you delete a user, the account remains in a suspended state for 30 days, and during that 30-day window the user account can be restored along with all its properties. After the 30-day window passes, the permanent deletion process automatically starts and can't be stopped. Incorrect - 14 days: no 14-day soft-delete window exists for Microsoft Entra user accounts. Incorrect - 60 days: 60 days is not the Microsoft Entra soft-delete retention period. Incorrect - 90 days: 90 days is a retention value used by other Microsoft services (for example, certain sign-in and audit reporting retention scenarios), but it is not the deleted user restore window, which is fixed at 30 days.
tags: microsoft entra id,deleted users,restore,soft delete,30 days

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: A colleague is authoring a custom policy definition that uses the modify effect and asks you to review the JSON. Which statements about the modify effect are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: The Remove operation is supported only for resource tags.
opzione_b: If conflictEffect is not specified, its default value is deny.
opzione_c: During a standard evaluation cycle, modify automatically applies its operations to resources that already exist.
opzione_d: The details property must include a roleDefinitionIds array.
opzione_e: Modify can add or replace the identity.type field on any Azure resource type.
spiegazione: A is correct: of the three supported operations (addOrReplace, add, remove), Microsoft documents that remove is only supported for resource tags - you cannot use it to strip an arbitrary alias-mapped property. B is correct: conflictEffect determines which definition wins when more than one modifies the same property or when the operation does not work on the specified alias, its available values are audit, deny, and disabled, and its default value is deny (Microsoft nonetheless recommends audit for definitions that include aliases, to avoid failing requests on API versions where the property is not Modifiable). D is correct: roleDefinitionIds is a required subproperty of details, and it must contain full role resource IDs, not short role names, because these are the roles the assignment's managed identity needs in order to remediate. C is incorrect - this is the classic misconception. Modify is a skipped modification for existing resources: when it runs as part of an evaluation cycle it makes no changes to resources that already exist, it only marks them non-compliant so they can be remediated through an explicitly created remediation task. E is incorrect: you can only modify identity.type on virtual machines and Virtual Machine Scale Sets. On any other resource type, policy evaluation is skipped altogether and the resource is considered not applicable to the policy.

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: Your governance team is planning a large-scale remediation of non-compliant resources across several subscriptions. Which statements about Azure Policy remediation tasks are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Remediation tasks can be created only for assignments whose policy definitions use the deployIfNotExists or modify effect.
opzione_b: When the assignment is created in the Azure portal, Azure Policy can automatically grant the managed identity the roles listed in roleDefinitionIds.
opzione_c: A single remediation task can remediate every deployIfNotExists policy contained in an initiative at the same time.
opzione_d: The location chosen for a system-assigned managed identity determines which regions the remediation task is able to target.
opzione_e: A single remediation task can remediate a maximum of 50,000 resources.
spiegazione: A is correct: Microsoft states that resources non-compliant to policies with deployIfNotExists or modify effects can be put into a compliant state through remediation, and the portal's Policies to remediate tab lists only those two effect types. B is correct: when you create the assignment and its identity through the portal, Azure Policy automatically grants the identity the roles defined in the definition's roleDefinitionIds; for SDK, CLI, or PowerShell the roles must be granted manually. Note the caveat that if roleDefinitionIds are edited later, the new permissions must be granted manually even in the portal. E is correct: the maximum number of resources for a remediation task is 50,000 (the -ResourceCount parameter defaults to 500). C is incorrect: when remediation is initiated from an initiative assignment you must select which policy to remediate from a drop-down, because only one deployIfNotExists or modify policy can be remediated through a single remediation task at a time. D is incorrect: although a location must be specified when a system-assigned identity is created, Microsoft states that the location of the managed identity doesn't affect its operation with Azure Policy. The resources a task targets are filtered by scope and by the optional Locations filter on the task, not by the identity's location.

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: An engineer uses Azure CLI to assign a built-in policy definition that has a deployIfNotExists effect, passing --location and --mi-system-assigned so that a system-assigned managed identity is created. The compliance dashboard correctly lists dozens of non-compliant resources, but every deployment started by the remediation task fails with an authorization error. What should you do first to resolve the issue?
opzione_a: Grant the assignment's managed identity the roles listed in the policy definition's roleDefinitionIds property.
opzione_b: Change the assignment's enforcementMode property from DoNotEnforce to Default.
opzione_c: Delete the assignment and re-create it with a user-assigned managed identity instead.
opzione_d: Run Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan against the subscription to refresh the compliance data.
spiegazione: Granting the roles manually is correct. Azure Policy uses the assignment's managed identity to perform the template deployment, and that identity must hold the minimum RBAC roles declared in the definition's roleDefinitionIds. Only the Azure portal grants those roles automatically when the assignment is created; for every other method - Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, or any SDK - Microsoft states the roles must be granted manually or the remediation deployment will fail. That is exactly the symptom described. Option B is wrong: enforcementMode affects whether the effect fires during resource creation or update, and Microsoft documents that remediation tasks can be started for deployIfNotExists policies even when enforcementMode is DoNotEnforce - it would not produce an authorization error. Option C is wrong because the identity type is irrelevant to the failure: a user-assigned identity created outside the portal needs the same roles granted manually, so re-creating the assignment reproduces the problem. Option D is wrong because compliance evaluation and remediation use different identities - evaluation uses the caller's identity and is clearly working here, since the non-compliant resources are already listed. Re-scanning cannot fix an authorization failure on the deployment.

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: A new administrator is being onboarded to Azure Policy. Select the correct answer for each drop-down to complete the onboarding cheat sheet.
opzione_a: Scopes at which a policy definition can be stored: [Management group or subscription | Subscription or resource group | Resource group or individual resource]
opzione_b: Assignment property used to exclude a child scope from evaluation: [notScopes | exemptionCategory | resourceSelectors]
opzione_c: Compliance state reported for a resource covered by a policy exemption: [Compliant | Exempted | Non-compliant]
opzione_d: Effect that blocks a non-compliant resource creation request: [Audit | Deny | Append]
spiegazione: A policy definition can be saved in either a management group or a subscription; those are the only two definition locations. Resource groups and individual resources are assignment scopes, not definition locations, so the other two choices are wrong. notScopes is the array property on the assignment object that determines what to exclude from evaluation; exemptionCategory is wrong because it belongs to a separate policyExemptions object and only classifies an exemption as Waiver or Mitigated, and resourceSelectors is wrong because it narrows evaluation by resource location or type for safe deployment practices rather than excluding a named scope. Exempted is the state shown for exempted resources - this is the defining benefit of an exemption over an exclusion, since the resource is still tracked in compliance reports rather than disappearing from them; Compliant would misrepresent the resource, and Non-compliant is the state the exemption is specifically meant to override. Deny is the effect that blocks the create or update request: Audit only logs the non-compliance and marks the resource, and Append alters the request by adding fields rather than blocking it (though it does fall back to deny behaviour if it would overwrite a conflicting value in the request).

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: Contoso has a management group named Corp that contains three subscriptions: Sub1, Sub2, and Sub3. A cloud engineer created a custom policy definition while Sub1 was the selected definition location. You must now assign that same custom definition to all three subscriptions, using the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opzione_a: Assign the existing definition from Sub1 directly to the Corp management group.
opzione_b: Re-create the policy definition using the Corp management group as its definition location, then assign it to Corp.
opzione_c: Export the definition and re-create a separate copy in Sub2 and Sub3, then create three assignments.
opzione_d: Add the existing Sub1 definition to a new initiative in Sub1 and assign the initiative to Corp.
spiegazione: Re-creating the definition at the Corp management group is correct: the definition location determines the scope to which a definition can be assigned, and resources must be within the resource hierarchy of that definition location. A definition stored in a management group can be assigned to that management group and to any child management group or child subscription, so a single definition and a single assignment at Corp covers Sub1, Sub2, and Sub3. Microsoft states explicitly that if you plan to apply a definition to several subscriptions, the definition location must be a management group that contains each subscription. Option A is wrong because a definition whose location is Sub1 can only be assigned within Sub1's hierarchy - the Corp management group is a parent, not a child, so it is outside that hierarchy and the assignment cannot be created. Option C is technically workable but is the opposite of least administrative effort: it produces three definitions and three assignments to keep in sync. Option D is wrong because an initiative inherits the same definition-location constraint; an initiative stored in Sub1 that references a Sub1-scoped definition still cannot be assigned up at the Corp management group.

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: You are documenting the difference between excluded scopes (notScopes) on a policy assignment and Azure Policy exemptions for your governance team. Which statements are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Resources within a scope listed in the assignment's notScopes array are not evaluated and are not included in the assignment's compliance count.
opzione_b: A policy exemption is created as a child object on the resource hierarchy or the individual resource that is granted the exemption.
opzione_c: A policy exemption can be made time-bound by setting its expiresOn property.
opzione_d: Adding a scope to notScopes requires creating a Microsoft.Authorization/policyExemptions object at that scope.
opzione_e: Resources covered by a policy exemption are reported in the compliance dashboard with a state of Compliant.
spiegazione: A is correct: exclusion is implemented through the properties.notScopes array on the assignment object, and Microsoft states that resources within these scopes aren't evaluated or included in the compliance count. B is correct: an exemption is a separate Resource Manager object created as a child of the resource hierarchy or individual resource being exempted - which is why deleting the parent resource also removes the exemption. C is correct: the optional expiresOn property (Universal ISO 8601 DateTime) sets when the resource is no longer exempt; note that the object itself is preserved for record-keeping after that date, it just stops being honoured. D is incorrect because it conflates the two features: notScopes is a property of the policy assignment object itself, so excluding a scope means modifying the assignment - no policyExemptions object is involved, and unlike an exemption it requires no exempt/Action permission on the assignment. E is incorrect: the whole point of an exemption over an exclusion is that the resource is still tracked, so it appears with a distinct compliance state of Exempted, not Compliant. Reporting it as Compliant would hide the accepted risk.

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: Your team is authoring a custom policy definition that uses the deployIfNotExists effect to deploy a diagnostic setting when one is missing, and you are preparing the corresponding assignment. Select the correct answer for each drop-down to complete the design notes. (The definition's details property omits evaluationDelay, existenceScope, and deploymentScope.)
opzione_a: Value used for evaluationDelay: [PT5M | PT10M | PT30M]
opzione_b: Value used for existenceScope: [ResourceGroup | Subscription | ManagementGroup]
opzione_c: Template style supported inside the deployment property: [Linked templates | Nested templates | Both linked and nested templates]
opzione_d: Managed identities that can be associated with the assignment: [One system-assigned or one user-assigned identity | One system-assigned identity and one user-assigned identity | Any number of user-assigned identities]
risposta_corretta: PT10M,ResourceGroup,Nested templates,One system-assigned or one user-assigned identity
spiegazione: evaluationDelay defaults to PT10M (10 minutes): it specifies when the existence of the related resources is evaluated after a create or update request, and accepts AfterProvisioning, AfterProvisioningSuccess, AfterProvisioningFailure, or an ISO 8601 duration between 0 and 360 minutes. PT5M and PT30M are valid values you could set, but neither is the default. existenceScope defaults to ResourceGroup, which limits the query for the related resource to the evaluated resource's resource group; Subscription is a valid alternative that queries the whole subscription (and requires the assignment scope to be at subscription level or higher), but it is not the default, and ManagementGroup is not an allowed value for existenceScope at all. Nested templates are supported with deployIfNotExists, while Microsoft states that linked templates are currently not supported - which rules out both other choices. Finally, a single policy assignment can be associated with only one managed identity, either system-assigned or user-assigned; that one identity can hold multiple role assignments, but you cannot attach both types or several user-assigned identities to the same assignment.

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: Fabrikam requires that every resource in a subscription carry a costCenter tag. Several hundred resources already exist without the tag. You must use Azure Policy to apply the tag to those existing resources and to ensure that resources created in the future receive it automatically. Which effect should the policy definition use?
opzione_a: Append
opzione_b: Modify
opzione_c: Audit
opzione_d: AuditIfNotExists
spiegazione: Modify is correct: it adds, updates, or removes tags on a resource during creation or update, and - critically for this requirement - existing non-compliant resources can be brought into a compliant state through a remediation task, which is supported only for the modify and deployIfNotExists effects. Microsoft explicitly recommends Modify over Append when managing tags, because Modify offers more operation types (addOrReplace, add, remove) and the ability to remediate existing resources. Append is wrong: although it can add a tag on a create or update request, when it runs during an evaluation cycle it makes no changes to resources that already exist - it only marks them non-compliant, and no remediation task can be created for it. Audit is wrong because it only reports the non-compliant resources in the compliance dashboard; it never alters a resource on creation or afterwards. AuditIfNotExists is wrong for the same reason and is additionally the wrong tool here: it assesses a related child or extension resource's properties rather than the tags on the resource itself, and like Audit it cannot remediate.

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: A custom policy definition uses the append effect with a single field/value pair that targets the non-[*] alias Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/networkAcls.ipRules in order to set an approved IP rule on storage accounts. A developer submits a request to create a storage account whose payload already specifies a different set of values in networkAcls.ipRules. What is the outcome of the request?
opzione_a: The append effect silently overwrites the developer's ipRules with the policy value, and the storage account is created.
opzione_b: The request is rejected, because append behaves as a deny effect when it would override a value in the original request with a different value.
opzione_c: The policy value is added alongside the developer's entries and the storage account is created with the combined array of IP rules.
opzione_d: The storage account is created with the developer's values and is then flagged as non-compliant in the next evaluation cycle.
spiegazione: Option B is correct. Append evaluates before the request is handed to the Resource Provider, and Microsoft documents that if the append effect would override a value in the original request with a different value, then it acts as a deny effect and rejects the request. With a non-[*] alias that maps to an array, append tries to write the value as the entire array, so a pre-existing array causes exactly this conflict and a deny event occurs. Option A is wrong because append never silently overwrites a conflicting value - overwriting behaviour on an existing value is what the modify effect's addOrReplace operation provides, not append. Option C is wrong because it describes the [*] version of the alias: using Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/networkAcls.ipRules[*] appends the value to a potentially pre-existing array (and creates the array if absent). That is the correct authoring fix here, but it is not what the non-[*] alias in this scenario does. Option D is wrong because the request never reaches the Resource Provider - it is rejected up front - so there is no created resource to mark non-compliant.

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: Several policy assignments in Resource Manager mode apply to a single subscription. A user submits a request to create a resource. Drag the policy effects into the order in which Azure Policy evaluates them for that request, from first evaluated to last evaluated.
opzione_a: Deny
opzione_b: Disabled
opzione_c: AuditIfNotExists
opzione_d: Append and Modify
opzione_e: Audit
spiegazione: The documented order of evaluation for a Resource Manager mode request is: Disabled is checked first, to determine whether the policy rule should be evaluated at all. Append and Modify are evaluated next, because either can alter the request, and a change they make might prevent an audit or deny effect from triggering afterwards - these two effects are available only in Resource Manager mode. Deny is then evaluated; evaluating deny before audit prevents double logging of an undesired resource. Audit is evaluated next (Manual would follow it, and DenyAction is evaluated last of all). AuditIfNotExists is evaluated after audit, because unlike audit it inspects a related child or extension resource; together with deployIfNotExists it runs only after the Resource Provider returns a success code, to determine whether more compliance logging or action is required. A common error is placing Deny first on the assumption that Azure Policy blocks bad requests before doing anything else - in fact Append and Modify run first and may make the request compliant, so Deny never fires.
tags: azure policy,effects,order of evaluation,resource manager mode

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda:
Contoso assigns a custom initiative that contains policy definitions using the deployIfNotExists, modify, and append effects to a management group. The assignment was created through the Azure portal with a system-assigned managed identity, and its enforcementMode property is set to DoNotEnforce. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is correct.
1. A remediation task can be started for the deployIfNotExists policies in this assignment even though enforcementMode is set to DoNotEnforce.
2. The append policy in the initiative can bring existing non-compliant resources into a compliant state through a remediation task.
3. The assignment can be associated with both its current system-assigned managed identity and an additional user-assigned managed identity.
opzione_a: A remediation task can be started for the deployIfNotExists policies in this assignment even though enforcementMode is set to DoNotEnforce.
opzione_b: The append policy in the initiative can bring existing non-compliant resources into a compliant state through a remediation task.
opzione_c: The assignment can be associated with both its current system-assigned managed identity and an additional user-assigned managed identity.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes: Microsoft documents explicitly that remediation tasks can be started for deployIfNotExists policies even when enforcementMode is set to DoNotEnforce. DoNotEnforce suppresses the effect during resource creation or update and suppresses Activity log entries, but evaluation still runs, compliance is still reported, and manual remediation remains available. Statement 2 is No: remediation is available only for the deployIfNotExists and modify effects. When an append policy runs during an evaluation cycle it makes no changes to resources that already exist - it only marks any resource meeting the if condition as non-compliant. This is precisely why Microsoft recommends modify over append when you need to remediate existing resources. Statement 3 is No: each Azure Policy assignment can be associated with only one managed identity, which is either system-assigned or user-assigned. That single identity can be granted multiple roles if the initiative's definitions require several, but a second identity of any type cannot be attached to the same assignment.

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: Before enforcing a new standard, you assign a policy definition that uses the Deny effect to a production subscription and set the assignment's enforcementMode property to DoNotEnforce. What is the result?
opzione_a: Resources are still evaluated and their compliance state is still reported, but non-compliant create or update requests are not blocked and no Azure Activity log entry is written.
opzione_b: The policy rule is not evaluated at all, so no compliance data is generated for the assignment.
opzione_c: Non-compliant create or update requests are still blocked, but no Azure Activity log entry is written.
opzione_d: Existing non-compliant resources are automatically brought into a compliant state without a remediation task.
spiegazione: Option A is correct. enforcementMode set to DoNotEnforce is the documented 'What If' capability: it lets you test the outcome of a policy on existing resources without initiating the policy effect and without triggering entries in the Azure Activity log. Evaluation still happens, so the compliance dashboard shows you which resources would be affected. Option B is wrong because it describes the Disabled effect, which Microsoft explicitly contrasts with enforcementMode - Disabled prevents resource evaluation from happening at all, whereas DoNotEnforce only suppresses enforcement of the effect. Option C is wrong because it inverts the behaviour: DoNotEnforce is precisely what stops the Deny effect from blocking the request. Option D is wrong on two counts: remediation applies only to deployIfNotExists and modify (never to Deny), and even for those effects existing resources require an explicitly created remediation task - although, notably, such a task can still be started while enforcementMode is DoNotEnforce.

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: While configuring a policy assignment in the Azure portal, the Remediation tab prompts you to create a managed identity and select a location for it. Which policy effect makes a managed identity mandatory on the assignment?
opzione_a: Audit
opzione_b: Append
opzione_c: DeployIfNotExists
opzione_d: DenyAction
spiegazione: DeployIfNotExists is correct: policy assignments with the deployIfNotExists effect must have an identity property because Azure Policy executes an ARM template deployment on your behalf, and it authenticates that deployment with a managed identity associated with the assignment. Modify is the only other effect with the same requirement. Audit is wrong because it only assesses the resource's own properties and writes a compliance record - it never changes or deploys anything, so it has no identity to authenticate as. Append is wrong because it alters the request payload before the Resource Provider processes it, inside the policy engine itself; it performs no deployment and therefore explicitly does not require a managed identity (Microsoft recommends Append precisely for cases where you cannot create a managed identity). DenyAction is wrong because it simply blocks a matching action request and, like Deny, takes no action that requires authorization as a separate principal.

sotto_argomento: Implement and manage Azure Policy
domanda: How frequently does Azure Policy automatically re-evaluate already-assigned policies and initiatives as part of the standard compliance evaluation cycle?
opzione_a: Every 15 minutes
opzione_b: Every hour
opzione_c: Every 24 hours
opzione_d: Every 7 days
spiegazione: Every 24 hours is correct: Microsoft documents the standard compliance evaluation cycle as occurring once every 24 hours, at which point all assignments are automatically re-evaluated and updated compliance results become available in the portal and SDKs. Every 15 minutes is wrong - it confuses the cycle with a different documented figure: when a single resource is created or updated in a scope that has an assignment, the effect event and that individual resource's compliance status appear roughly 15 minutes later, but this does not re-evaluate any other resource. Every hour is wrong; no Azure Policy evaluation trigger is documented on an hourly cadence. Every 7 days is wrong - the seven-day figure relates to the compliance-over-time chart shown on the Policy Overview page, not to the evaluation frequency. If you cannot wait for the cycle, trigger an on-demand scan with Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan or az policy state trigger-scan.

sotto_argomento: Interpret access assignments
domanda: An analyst is assigned the Owner role at the scope of a subscription that contains a storage account named sa1. When the analyst opens a blob container in the Azure portal and selects Microsoft Entra User Account as the authentication method, the blob list fails to load. Which built-in role should you assign to sa1 so that the analyst can read the blob contents with their Microsoft Entra identity?
opzione_a: Storage Account Contributor
opzione_b: Reader
opzione_c: Storage Blob Data Reader
opzione_d: Storage Account Key Operator Service Role
spiegazione: Correct answer C: Storage Blob Data Reader is described as 'Allows for read access to Azure Storage blob containers and data' and is the role that supplies the data plane permission Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/read in its DataActions. Owner grants only Actions = '*', which is a control plane wildcard; Microsoft Learn's worked example states that a user with Owner 'cannot perform data plane actions without taking additional steps. For example, by default, Alice cannot read the blobs inside a container.' Control plane access is deliberately not inherited into the data plane when the container authentication method is Microsoft Entra User Account, which stops wildcard roles from silently gaining data access. A is wrong because Storage Account Contributor is a control plane role for managing the account and does not add blob DataActions. B is wrong because Reader only grants */read on the control plane, which is a subset of what Owner already provides. D is wrong because Storage Account Key Operator Service Role manages access keys, which is not reading blob data with a Microsoft Entra identity.
tags: data plane,control plane,storage blob data reader,owner,dataactions

sotto_argomento: Interpret access assignments
domanda: An engineer holds the Contributor role on a resource group that hosts a production database. When the engineer tries to add a CanNotDelete lock to the resource group, the operation fails with an authorization error. Which additional built-in role should you assign to resolve the failure while granting the fewest additional permissions?
opzione_a: Owner
opzione_b: User Access Administrator
opzione_c: Management Group Contributor
opzione_d: Resource Policy Contributor
spiegazione: Correct answer B: Management locks are Microsoft.Authorization/locks resources. Microsoft Learn states 'To create or delete management locks, you need access to Microsoft.Authorization/* or Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* actions. Users assigned to the Owner and the User Access Administrator roles have the required access.' Contributor fails because its NotActions subtract Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete from its wildcard, which removes lock creation. User Access Administrator supplies Microsoft.Authorization/* and, because roles are additive, the engineer keeps Contributor's resource management rights. A is wrong not because it fails but because it is excessive: Owner would also work, yet it grants full resource control plus role assignment, violating the least-privilege requirement. C is wrong because Management Group Contributor manages management group objects, not locks on a resource group. D is wrong because Resource Policy Contributor covers Azure Policy, not Microsoft.Authorization/locks.

sotto_argomento: Interpret access assignments
domanda:
A user named User1 is assigned the Contributor role at the scope of a resource group named RG1. RG1 contains a virtual machine and a storage account. User1 has no other Azure role assignments and no Microsoft Entra role assignments. Evaluate each of the following statements about what User1 can do. Does each statement evaluate to Yes?
1. User1 can create an additional virtual machine in RG1.
2. User1 can assign the Reader role on RG1 to a user named User2.
3. User1 can delete RG1 and all of the resources it contains.
opzione_a: User1 can create an additional virtual machine in RG1.
opzione_b: User1 can assign the Reader role on RG1 to a user named User2.
opzione_c: User1 can delete RG1 and all of the resources it contains.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes: Contributor's Actions are the wildcard '*', which covers Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write, and no compute action is excluded by its NotActions, so User1 can create VMs anywhere in RG1. Statement 2 is No: creating a role assignment requires Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, but Contributor's NotActions include Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write, which subtracts that action from the wildcard. This is the defining limitation of Contributor: 'does not allow you to assign roles in Azure RBAC'. Granting access would require Owner, User Access Administrator, or Role Based Access Control Administrator. Statement 3 is Yes: deleting a resource group requires Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups/delete, which is included in the '*' wildcard and is not excluded by any NotAction. Contributor's NotActions only remove Microsoft.Authorization, Microsoft.Blueprint, image gallery sharing and Microsoft.Purview consent actions, so full resource lifecycle management, including deletion, remains permitted.

sotto_argomento: Interpret access assignments
domanda: A colleague is assigned the Contributor role at the scope of a resource group named RG1. Which task will the colleague be UNABLE to perform in RG1?
opzione_a: Create a virtual machine and attach a managed disk to it.
opzione_b: Grant a second user the Reader role on RG1.
opzione_c: Delete a storage account that already exists in RG1.
opzione_d: Deploy an ARM template that provisions a virtual network.
spiegazione: Correct answer B: The Contributor role is defined as Actions = '*' with NotActions that include Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete. Because creating a role assignment requires Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, that action is subtracted from the wildcard and Contributor cannot grant access to anyone. This is why the official role description reads 'Grants full access to manage all resources, but does not allow you to assign roles in Azure RBAC, manage assignments in Azure Blueprints, or share image galleries.' A is wrong because creating VMs and disks are ordinary Microsoft.Compute actions covered by the '*' wildcard. C is wrong because deleting resources is also covered by '*'; the NotActions only exclude the Microsoft.Authorization, Microsoft.Blueprint, Microsoft.Compute/galleries/share and Microsoft.Purview/consents actions, not resource deletion. D is wrong because Microsoft.Resources/deployments actions are included in the wildcard, so a Contributor can deploy templates.

sotto_argomento: Interpret access assignments
domanda: A developer named User1 has two Azure role assignments: Contributor at the scope of Subscription1, and Role Based Access Control Administrator at the scope of a resource group named RG1 inside Subscription1. RG1 contains a virtual machine named VM1. What can User1 do in RG1?
opzione_a: Manage VM1 and assign roles on RG1, because the permissions from the two role assignments are combined.
opzione_b: Manage VM1, but not assign roles on RG1, because Contributor's NotActions deny role assignment at every scope beneath Subscription1.
opzione_c: Assign roles on RG1, but not manage VM1, because the more specific resource group assignment overrides the subscription assignment.
opzione_d: Neither manage VM1 nor assign roles on RG1, because conflicting role assignments at different scopes cancel each other out.
spiegazione: Correct answer A: Azure RBAC is additive. A role assignment at a parent scope is inherited by child scopes, so Contributor at Subscription1 applies within RG1, and the Role Based Access Control Administrator assignment on RG1 adds Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write and /delete there. Microsoft Learn is explicit that NotActions is not a deny rule: 'If a user is assigned a role that excludes an action in NotActions, and is assigned a second role that grants access to the same action, the user is allowed to perform that action.' B is wrong precisely because it treats NotActions as a deny rule rather than as a subtraction from a single role's wildcard. C is wrong because a narrower assignment does not override or replace an inherited one; only deny assignments block access this way. D is wrong because role assignments never cancel one another out; effective permissions are the union of all assignments that apply at the scope.

sotto_argomento: Interpret access assignments
domanda: Which statements correctly describe the differences between Azure RBAC roles and Microsoft Entra roles? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Azure roles can be assigned at management group, subscription, resource group, or resource scope.
opzione_b: A Global Administrator can manage all Azure subscriptions in the tenant without any additional configuration.
opzione_c: Microsoft Entra roles can be scoped to the tenant, to an administrative unit, or to an individual object such as a specific application.
opzione_d: Both Azure RBAC and Microsoft Entra ID support custom roles.
opzione_e: Assigning the Owner role at root scope in Azure RBAC automatically grants the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID.
spiegazione: Correct answers A, C and D: Microsoft Learn's comparison table states that for Azure roles the 'Scope can be specified at multiple levels (management group, subscription, resource group, resource)' (A), while for Microsoft Entra roles the scope 'can be specified at the tenant level (organization-wide), administrative unit, or on an individual object (for example, a specific application)' (C). The same table lists 'Supports custom roles' for both systems (D). B is wrong because by default the Global Administrator does not have access to Azure resources; access to all subscriptions requires the additional step of setting the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to Yes, which is additional configuration. E is wrong because the relationship does not work in that direction at all: Azure role assignments do not grant access to Microsoft Entra ID, so no Azure role, including Owner at root scope, confers a directory role.
tags: azure rbac,microsoft entra roles,scope,custom roles,administrative unit

sotto_argomento: Interpret access assignments
domanda: Which tasks are excluded from the Contributor built-in role by its NotActions? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Creating a virtual machine in a resource group.
opzione_b: Sharing an Azure Compute Gallery image gallery with another subscription.
opzione_c: Creating an Azure role assignment for another user.
opzione_d: Creating or updating an Azure Blueprints blueprint assignment.
opzione_e: Creating a general-purpose v2 storage account.
spiegazione: Correct answers B, C and D: The official Contributor description states the role 'Grants full access to manage all resources, but does not allow you to assign roles in Azure RBAC, manage assignments in Azure Blueprints, or share image galleries.' These three exclusions map directly to entries in the role's NotActions array: Microsoft.Compute/galleries/share/action (B), Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete which remove roleAssignments/write and /delete (C), and Microsoft.Blueprint/blueprintAssignments/write and /delete (D). A and E are wrong because Contributor's Actions are the wildcard '*', and neither Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write nor Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/write appears in NotActions, so both remain permitted; creating ordinary resources of any type is exactly what Contributor is designed for.

sotto_argomento: Interpret access assignments
domanda: A new administrator is assigned the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID. The administrator has no Azure role assignments on any subscription. Which statement correctly describes the administrator's access?
opzione_a: The administrator automatically has the Owner role on every subscription in the tenant.
opzione_b: The administrator can manage Microsoft Entra resources such as users and groups, but has no access to Azure resources such as virtual machines by default.
opzione_c: The administrator automatically has the Reader role on every subscription in the tenant.
opzione_d: The administrator can manage Azure resources only after a subscription Owner assigns them the Contributor role at the root management group.
spiegazione: Correct answer B: Microsoft Entra ID and Azure resources are secured independently of one another. Microsoft Entra role assignments do not grant access to Azure resources, and Azure role assignments do not grant access to Microsoft Entra ID. Microsoft Learn states explicitly that 'by default, the Global Administrator doesn't have access to Azure resources.' A and C are wrong because no Azure RBAC role is implicitly granted by holding a Microsoft Entra role; the two systems do not overlap by default. D is wrong on two counts: no third party is required, because a Global Administrator can self-service by setting the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to Yes, and that elevation grants the User Access Administrator role at root scope, not Contributor.
tags: microsoft entra id,global administrator,azure rbac,directory roles,scope

sotto_argomento: Interpret access assignments
domanda: Fabrikam organizes its Azure estate as follows. A management group named mg-prod contains a subscription named sub-01. The sub-01 subscription contains two resource groups, rg-web and rg-data. A Microsoft Entra group named G1 is assigned the Reader role at the mg-prod scope and the Contributor role at the rg-web scope. A deployment stack manages the resources in rg-web and was created with a deny settings mode of DenyDelete, applying to All Principals with no excluded principals and no excluded actions. User1 is a member of G1. Select the correct option for each drop-down.
opzione_a: User1's effective access to a storage account in rg-data: [No access | Read only | Read and write | Full control including delete]
opzione_b: User1 can create a new virtual machine in rg-web: [Yes | No]
opzione_c: User1 can delete a resource that is managed by the deployment stack in rg-web: [Yes | No]
opzione_d: If User1 is also assigned the Owner role at the sub-01 scope, User1 can delete a resource that is managed by the deployment stack in rg-web: [Yes | No]
spiegazione: Drop-down 1 - Read only: Lower levels inherit role permissions from higher levels, so the Reader assignment at mg-prod inherits to sub-01 and to rg-data. Role assignments are transitive for groups, so User1 receives G1's permissions. The Contributor assignment applies only at the rg-web scope and does not reach rg-data, and the deny assignment is scoped to rg-web. User1 therefore has Reader only in rg-data. (Note that Reader is a control plane role: User1 could see the storage account but not read the blob data, because control plane access is not inherited to the data plane.) Drop-down 2 - Yes: Azure RBAC is additive, so at rg-web User1's effective permissions are the sum of Reader (inherited from mg-prod) and Contributor (assigned at rg-web), which is effectively Contributor. Contributor's Actions are *, so User1 can create a virtual machine. The deny settings mode is DenyDelete, which prohibits delete operations only - it does not block write operations. Drop-down 3 - No: Specifying deny settings when creating a deployment stack causes Azure to create a deny assignment owned by the deployment stack. A deny assignment 'blocks users from performing specific Azure resource actions even if a role assignment grants them access,' and Azure Resource Manager evaluates deny assignments before role assignments: 'If a deny assignment applies, access is blocked. Otherwise, evaluation continues.' The deny assignment targets All Principals with no excluded principals, so User1 is blocked from deleting managed resources despite holding Contributor.
