This matters for compliance and data residency, and control plane operations for the group are routed through that location. Wrong: b - the documentation explicitly says the resources in a resource group can be located in different regions than the resource group (using the same location is only a recommendation). Wrong: c - billing rates are determined by the region of each individual resource and its meters, not by the resource group's location; a resource group is not a billing construct. Wrong: d - a resource group location does not create replication or disaster recovery for the resources it contains; ARM only fails over control plane requests for the resource group's metadata to a secondary region, which is not the same as replicating the resources.
tags: resource group, region, metadata, azure resource manager, governance

sotto_argomento: Manage resource groups
domanda: Your team is consolidating resources into a new resource group. Which resource type CANNOT be moved to a different resource group?
opzione_a: An Azure Storage account
opzione_b: A network security group
opzione_c: An Azure key vault
opzione_d: An Azure application gateway
spiegazione: Correct: d. In the Azure resource types for move operations reference, Microsoft.Network/applicationGateways is listed as No for resource group move, No for subscription move, and No for region move. An application gateway must be re-created in the target resource group instead. Wrong: a - Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts supports both resource group and subscription moves. Wrong: b - Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups is listed as Yes for resource group move, Yes for subscription move, and even supports region move via Azure Resource Mover. Wrong: c - Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults is listed as Yes for both resource group and subscription moves (region move is not supported, but the question asks about a resource group move).
tags: move resources, move support, application gateway, resource group, limitations

sotto_argomento: Manage subscriptions
domanda:
Contoso is divesting a business unit. A pay-as-you-go subscription named Sub-BU must be handed over to the acquiring company, whose Azure account lives in a different Microsoft Entra tenant. In the Azure portal, an administrator opens the subscription, selects Transfer billing ownership, enters the recipient's email address, and selects the 'Move subscription tenant' option before sending the request. Evaluate each of the following statements:
1. Because 'Move subscription tenant' is selected, all existing Azure role assignments that grant access to resources in Sub-BU are permanently removed when the transfer completes.
2. The transfer request remains valid indefinitely until the recipient accepts or declines it.
3. Any user who holds the Owner role on Sub-BU can initiate the transfer of billing ownership.
opzione_a: Because 'Move subscription tenant' is selected, all existing Azure role assignments that grant access to resources in Sub-BU are permanently removed when the transfer completes.
opzione_b: The transfer request remains valid indefinitely until the recipient accepts or declines it.
opzione_c: Any user who holds the Owner role on Sub-BU can initiate the transfer of billing ownership.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. Microsoft Learn warns that if you choose to move the subscription to the new account's Microsoft Entra tenant, all Azure role assignments to access resources in the subscription are permanently removed, and only the user in the new account who accepts the transfer request will have access to manage the resources. The alternative is to clear the 'Move subscription tenant' option, which transfers billing ownership while maintaining existing Azure role assignments. Statement 2 - No. The documentation states that only one transfer request is active at a time and that a transfer request is valid for 15 days, after which it expires. Statement 3 - No. This conflates billing administration with Azure RBAC. The documentation states that only the account administrator of an account can transfer ownership of a subscription. The Owner role is an Azure RBAC role that controls access to resources in the subscription; it does not confer billing ownership rights. (For a Microsoft Azure plan subscription, you instead need to be an owner or contributor on the invoice section to which the subscription is billed.)
tags: subscription transfer, billing ownership, account administrator, entra tenant, rbac, pay-as-you-go

sotto_argomento: Manage user and group properties
domanda: Woodgrove Bank has a Microsoft Entra ID P1 tenant containing a security group named Helpdesk-Team. The group was created with Membership type set to Dynamic User and a rule of user.jobTitle -eq "Helpdesk Analyst". You must assign the Helpdesk Administrator Microsoft Entra role to the group so that all of its members inherit the role. You sign in as a Privileged Role Administrator, but the group does not appear as an available option when you try to assign the role. You must resolve the issue while keeping the number of administrative steps to a minimum. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create a new security group, set "Microsoft Entra roles can be assigned to the group" to Yes, set the Membership type to Assigned, add the analysts as members, and assign the Helpdesk Administrator role to the new group.
opzione_b: Edit the properties of Helpdesk-Team and set the isAssignableToRole property to true by using Microsoft Graph PowerShell.
opzione_c: Change the Membership type of Helpdesk-Team from Dynamic User to Assigned, and then assign the Helpdesk Administrator role to the group.
opzione_d: Add Helpdesk-Team as a nested member of a new role-assignable security group, and then assign the Helpdesk Administrator role to the parent group.
spiegazione: Correct (a): To assign a Microsoft Entra role to a group, the group must have been created with isAssignableToRole set to true (the "Microsoft Entra roles can be assigned to the group" option). Microsoft Learn states this property can only be set on new groups, that it is immutable, that you can't make an existing group a role-assignable group, and that the membership type for role-assignable groups must be Assigned and can't be a dynamic group. Creating a new group with both settings correct is therefore the only supported path, and it requires at least the Privileged Role Administrator role, which you already have. In the portal, enabling the option automatically selects Assigned as the Membership type. Wrong (b): The isAssignableToRole property can only be set on new groups and is immutable once the group is created, so this fails regardless of the tool used. Wrong (c): Changing the membership type to Assigned does not make the group role-assignable. The group still has isAssignableToRole set to false and that value cannot be changed after creation. Wrong (d): Group nesting isn't supported for role-assignable groups; Learn states a group can't be added as a member of a role-assignable group.
tags: microsoft entra id,role-assignable group,isassignabletorole,dynamic membership,privileged role administrator,troubleshooting

sotto_argomento: Manage user and group properties
domanda: Your security team is reviewing the design constraints of role-assignable Microsoft Entra groups before rolling them out. Which statements about role-assignable groups are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: The membership type of a role-assignable group must be Assigned.
opzione_b: The isAssignableToRole property can be enabled on an existing group that was created without it.
opzione_c: You must be assigned at least the Privileged Role Administrator role to create a role-assignable group.
opzione_d: A group cannot be added as a member of a role-assignable group.
opzione_e: A maximum of 5,000 role-assignable groups can be created in a single tenant.
spiegazione: Correct (a): Microsoft Learn states the membership type for role-assignable groups must be Assigned and can't be a Microsoft Entra dynamic group, because automated population of dynamic membership groups could lead to an unwanted account being added to the group and thus assigned the role. Correct (c): Learn states you must be assigned at least the Privileged Role Administrator role to create a role-assignable group. Correct (d): Group nesting isn't supported; a group can't be added as a member of a role-assignable group. Wrong (b): The isAssignableToRole property can only be set on new groups and is immutable. Learn explicitly states you can't make an existing group a role-assignable group. Wrong (e): The documented limit is a maximum of 500 role-assignable groups in a single Microsoft Entra organization, not 5,000. Note also that the feature requires a Microsoft Entra ID P1 license, that a role-assignable group can be either a security group or a Microsoft 365 group, and that Microsoft Graph requires the RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory permission (Group.ReadWrite.All is not sufficient) to manage the membership of such a group.

sotto_argomento: Manage user and group properties
domanda: Contoso has an existing Microsoft Entra security group named Sales-All. The group was created with the Membership type set to Assigned, and the option "Microsoft Entra roles can be assigned to the group" was left set to No. You sign in as a Groups Administrator. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. 1) You can change the membership type of Sales-All from Assigned to Dynamic User. 2) After Sales-All is changed to Dynamic User, you can still manually add a specific user to the group from the Members page. 3) You can change the group type of Sales-All from Security to Microsoft 365.
opzione_a: You can change the membership type of Sales-All from Assigned to Dynamic User.
opzione_b: After Sales-All is changed to Dynamic User, you can still manually add a specific user to the group from the Members page.
opzione_c: You can change the group type of Sales-All from Security to Microsoft 365.
spiegazione: Statement 1 = Yes: On the group's Properties page you can edit the group name, description, and Membership type. Microsoft Learn states the membership type can be changed and that it is locked only if the "Microsoft Entra roles can be assigned to the group" option was enabled, which is not the case here. The Groups Administrator role is sufficient to edit group settings. Statement 2 = No: Learn explicitly states that you can't manually add or remove a member of a dynamic membership group. Membership is determined solely by evaluating the membership rule against user or device attributes. Statement 3 = No: Learn explicitly states that you can't change the type of a group after it's been created. To change the Group type you must delete the group and create a new one.
tags: microsoft entra id,groups,membership type,group type,dynamic membership,group properties

sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda: Litware, Inc. uses an Azure key vault named KV1 that is configured with the Azure role-based access control permission model. For each requirement, select the built-in role that grants the required access with the fewest permissions. Select the appropriate option in each drop-down list.
opzione_a: An application must read the values of secrets stored in KV1: [Key Vault Contributor | Key Vault Reader | Key Vault Secrets User]
opzione_b: An auditor must view the names and metadata of the certificates, keys and secrets in KV1, without reading any sensitive values: [Key Vault Administrator | Key Vault Reader | Key Vault Secrets Officer]
opzione_c: An operations team must create and delete key vault resources, without gaining access to keys, secrets or certificates: [Key Vault Contributor | Key Vault Administrator | Key Vault Certificates Officer]
opzione_d: A team lead must create a CanNotDelete lock on the resource group that contains KV1: [Contributor | Reader | User Access Administrator]
risposta_corretta: Key Vault Secrets User,Key Vault Reader,Key Vault Contributor,User Access Administrator
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - Key Vault Secrets User: this role is defined as 'Read secret contents including secret portion of a certificate with private key' and is the minimal data plane role for reading secret values. Key Vault Contributor is a control plane role that Microsoft Learn notes 'does not allow access to keys, secrets and certificates'. Key Vault Reader cannot read sensitive values. Dropdown 2 - Key Vault Reader: 'Read metadata of key vaults and its certificates, keys, and secrets. Cannot read sensitive values such as secret contents or key material', which matches the auditor requirement precisely. Key Vault Administrator performs all data plane operations and would expose the values. Key Vault Secrets Officer can perform any action on secrets, also exceeding the requirement. Dropdown 3 - Key Vault Contributor: it is the control plane role for managing key vault resources and explicitly grants no data access. Key Vault Administrator is the opposite: it performs all data plane operations but cannot manage key vault resources. Key Vault Certificates Officer is a data plane role scoped to certificates. Dropdown 4 - User Access Administrator: creating management locks requires Microsoft.Authorization/* or Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* actions, which Owner and User Access Administrator provide. Contributor is wrong because Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write is in its NotActions, and Reader grants no write actions at all.
tags: key vault,rbac permission model,data plane,key vault contributor,resource locks

sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda: Contoso Ltd. is standardizing on least-privileged built-in Azure roles. For each requirement, select the appropriate built-in role. Select the appropriate option in each drop-down list.
opzione_a: Create and manage virtual machines, without being able to reconfigure the virtual network they connect to: [Contributor | Virtual Machine Contributor | Virtual Machine Administrator Login]
opzione_b: Sign in to a Windows virtual machine with administrator privileges by using a Microsoft Entra identity: [Virtual Machine Contributor | Virtual Machine Administrator Login | Owner]
opzione_c: Read blob data in a storage account by using Microsoft Entra credentials rather than account keys: [Storage Account Contributor | Reader | Storage Blob Data Reader]
opzione_d: Assign Azure roles to other users at a resource group, and also manage Azure Policy assignments there: [Contributor | Network Contributor | User Access Administrator]
risposta_corretta: Virtual Machine Contributor,Virtual Machine Administrator Login,Storage Blob Data Reader,User Access Administrator
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - Virtual Machine Contributor: the role 'Lets you manage virtual machines, but not access to them, and not the virtual network or storage account they're connected to', which matches the requirement exactly. Contributor is wrong because its wildcard would also permit reconfiguring the virtual network. Virtual Machine Administrator Login is wrong because it grants guest sign-in, not VM management. Dropdown 2 - Virtual Machine Administrator Login: guest OS sign-in is a data plane capability, and this role grants administrator sign-in. Virtual Machine Contributor is wrong because it explicitly excludes access to the VMs themselves, and Owner is wrong because its control plane wildcard does not include guest sign-in data actions. Dropdown 3 - Storage Blob Data Reader: only a role with blob DataActions permits reading blob data with a Microsoft Entra identity, since control plane access is not inherited into the data plane. Storage Account Contributor is a control plane role for managing the account, and Reader grants only */read on the control plane. Dropdown 4 - User Access Administrator: it holds the broad Microsoft.Authorization/* wildcard, which covers both role assignments and policy assignments. Contributor is wrong because Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write is in its NotActions. Network Contributor is wrong because it manages networks and does not let you control who has access.
tags: least privilege,virtual machine contributor,storage blob data reader,user access administrator,service-specific roles

sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda:
An administrator named Admin1 is assigned the Global Administrator role in your Microsoft Entra tenant. Admin1 has no Azure role assignments on any management group, subscription, resource group, or resource. The tenant contains three subscriptions. Evaluate each of the following statements. Does each statement evaluate to Yes?
1. Before any elevation, Admin1 can view all of the virtual machines in all three subscriptions.
2. If Admin1 sets the Access management for Azure resources toggle to Yes, Admin1 is assigned the User Access Administrator role at root scope (/).
3. Setting the Access management for Azure resources toggle to Yes elevates access for every user who is assigned the Global Administrator role.
opzione_a: Before any elevation, Admin1 can view all of the virtual machines in all three subscriptions.
opzione_b: If Admin1 sets the Access management for Azure resources toggle to Yes, Admin1 is assigned the User Access Administrator role at root scope (/).
opzione_c: Setting the Access management for Azure resources toggle to Yes elevates access for every user who is assigned the Global Administrator role.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No: Microsoft Entra ID and Azure resources are secured independently. Microsoft Entra role assignments do not grant access to Azure resources, and Microsoft Learn states that 'by default, the Global Administrator doesn't have access to Azure resources.' Without an Azure role assignment, Admin1 cannot view the virtual machines. Statement 2 is Yes: 'When you set the toggle to Yes, you are assigned the User Access Administrator role in Azure RBAC at root scope (/)', which grants permission to assign roles in all Azure subscriptions and management groups associated with the tenant. Statement 3 is No: Microsoft Learn states 'This setting is not a global property and applies only to the currently signed in user. You can't elevate access for all members of the Global Administrator role.' Each Global Administrator must elevate individually, and because it is a per-user setting, the same user must set the toggle back to No to remove the elevated access.
tags: elevate access,global administrator,user access administrator,root scope,microsoft entra id

sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda: Your security team wants a delegated administrator who can assign Azure roles to other users at a resource group, and who can read resource properties, but who must not be able to control access by any other mechanism such as Azure Policy. Which built-in role meets the requirement with the fewest permissions?
opzione_a: Owner
opzione_b: User Access Administrator
opzione_c: Role Based Access Control Administrator
opzione_d: Resource Policy Contributor
spiegazione: Correct answer C: The Role Based Access Control Administrator role is described as 'Manage access to Azure resources by assigning roles using Azure RBAC. This role does not allow you to manage access using other ways, such as Azure Policy.' Its Actions are limited to Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete, */read and Microsoft.Support/*, which is exactly the requested capability and nothing more. B is wrong because User Access Administrator holds the much broader Microsoft.Authorization/* wildcard, which also covers policy assignments, deny assignments and locks, so it exceeds the requirement. A is wrong because Owner grants full access to manage all resources in addition to assigning roles, which is far more than needed. D is wrong because Resource Policy Contributor manages Azure Policy definitions and assignments; it does not grant the ability to create Azure role assignments.
tags: rbac administrator,user access administrator,least privilege,role assignment,built-in roles

sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda: A support engineer is assigned the Virtual Machine Contributor role on a resource group that contains several Windows virtual machines. The engineer can resize and restart the VMs from the Azure portal, but cannot sign in to the guest operating system with administrative rights using their Microsoft Entra credentials. Which built-in role should you additionally assign?
opzione_a: Virtual Machine Administrator Login
opzione_b: Virtual Machine User Login
opzione_c: Desktop Virtualization User
opzione_d: Owner
spiegazione: Correct answer A: Virtual Machine Contributor 'Lets you manage virtual machines, but not access to them, and not the virtual network or storage account they're connected to.' Managing a VM is a control plane capability; signing in to the guest OS with a Microsoft Entra identity is a data plane capability delivered by the Virtual Machine Administrator Login role, which grants administrator sign-in rights. B is wrong because Virtual Machine User Login grants sign-in as a regular user without administrator privileges, which does not meet the stated requirement. C is wrong because Desktop Virtualization User applies to Azure Virtual Desktop application groups, not to signing in to a standalone VM. D is wrong because Owner is a control plane wildcard role; like Contributor it does not include the guest sign-in data actions, so it would not fix the problem and would also be a large over-grant.
tags: virtual machine contributor,virtual machine administrator login,data plane,compute roles,sign-in

sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda: In the Azure portal, a Global Administrator browses to Microsoft Entra ID > Properties and sets the Access management for Azure resources toggle to Yes. Which role assignment is created as a result?
opzione_a: The Owner role at the scope of each subscription in the tenant.
opzione_b: The User Access Administrator role at root scope (/).
opzione_c: The Role Based Access Control Administrator role at the root management group.
opzione_d: The Contributor role at root scope (/).
spiegazione: Correct answer B: Microsoft Learn states that when you elevate your access, 'you are assigned the User Access Administrator role in Azure at root scope (/)', which allows you to view all resources and assign access in any subscription or management group in the tenant. A is wrong because Owner is never granted by the toggle; the elevation deliberately grants an access-management role rather than full resource control. C is wrong on both the role and the scope: the role granted is User Access Administrator, and the scope is root ('/'), which sits above the root management group. D is wrong because Contributor cannot assign roles at all, which would defeat the purpose of the elevation (regaining the ability to grant access). Note the elevation is a per-user setting and should be set back to No once the required changes are made.
tags: elevate access,global administrator,user access administrator,root scope,azure rbac

sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda: A platform team member named Priya must be able to assign and remove Azure role assignments for other users on a resource group named rg-shared. Priya must not be able to create or modify Azure Policy assignments, and she must not be able to manage the resources in rg-shared. You must follow the principle of least privilege and use a built-in role. Which role should you assign to Priya at the rg-shared scope?
opzione_a: Owner
opzione_b: Contributor
opzione_c: User Access Administrator
opzione_d: Role Based Access Control Administrator
spiegazione: Correct: d. The Role Based Access Control Administrator role is described as 'Manage access to Azure resources by assigning roles using Azure RBAC. This role does not allow you to manage access using other ways, such as Azure Policy.' Its Actions are exactly Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete, */read, and Microsoft.Support/*, which lets Priya add and remove role assignments and read resources, but not write to resources or to policy assignments. Wrong: a. Owner has Actions of * with no NotActions, granting full management of all resources plus role assignment - far more than required. Wrong: b. Contributor's NotActions include Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete, so Contributor explicitly cannot assign roles; it also grants full resource management, which is not wanted. Wrong: c. User Access Administrator's Actions are */read, Microsoft.Authorization/*, and Microsoft.Support/*. The Microsoft.Authorization/* wildcard includes Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/*, so it would let Priya create and modify Azure Policy assignments, breaking the stated requirement and least privilege.
tags: azure rbac,built-in roles,role based access control administrator,user access administrator,least privilege,delegation

sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda: An onboarding pipeline that grants developers access to resources in a large Azure subscription starts failing with the error: No more role assignments can be created (code: RoleAssignmentLimitExceeded). Investigation shows that the subscription has accumulated thousands of individual role assignments, many of them granting the same built-in role to different users at the same resource group scope. Which action resolves the problem?
opzione_a: Open an Azure support request to increase the role assignment limit for the subscription.
opzione_b: Add the developers to Microsoft Entra groups and replace the individual role assignments with a single role assignment for each group at the same scope.
opzione_c: Create the remaining role assignments at resource scope instead of resource group scope, because only role assignments at subscription and resource group scopes count toward the limit.
opzione_d: Convert the redundant role assignments into deny assignments, which are not counted against the role assignment limit.
spiegazione: Correct: b. Azure supports up to 4000 role assignments per subscription, and the documented Solution 1 is to 'Replace principal-based role assignments with group-based role assignments': add principals to groups and assign roles to the groups instead. This works because role assignments are transitive for groups, so every member inherits the permissions from the single group assignment, collapsing many assignments into one. Wrong: a. Microsoft Learn states explicitly: 'The 4000 role assignments limit per subscription is fixed and cannot be increased.' A support request cannot raise it. Wrong: c. The limit 'includes role assignments at the subscription, resource group, and resource scopes,' so moving assignments to resource scope does not help. (Only management group scope assignments are excluded from the per-subscription limit, and those are governed by a separate limit of 500 per management group.) Wrong: d. You can't directly create deny assignments - they're created and managed by Azure - and deny assignments block access rather than grant it, so they cannot replace role assignments that are meant to give developers access.

sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda: Contoso Ltd. has 12 Azure subscriptions that are all direct children of a management group named mg-contoso-prod. The tenant also contains other subscriptions that are outside mg-contoso-prod. The security team must grant the Reader role to a Microsoft Entra group named SecOps-Auditors for all 12 subscriptions, and for those subscriptions only, by creating a single role assignment. At which scope should you create the role assignment?
opzione_a: The mg-contoso-prod management group
opzione_b: Each of the 12 subscriptions individually
opzione_c: The Tenant Root Group management group
opzione_d: The Microsoft Entra tenant
spiegazione: Correct: a. Azure RBAC supports four scope levels - management group, subscription, resource group, and resource - structured in a parent-child relationship, and lower levels inherit role permissions from higher levels. A single Reader assignment on mg-contoso-prod inherits to every subscription under it, which is exactly the 12 target subscriptions and nothing else. Wrong: b. Assigning Reader on each subscription produces the required access but creates 12 role assignments, not the single assignment the requirement specifies. Wrong: c. The Tenant Root Group is a valid scope and would be one assignment, but everything in the directory folds up to the root management group, so the assignment would also grant Reader on the subscriptions outside mg-contoso-prod, violating the 'those subscriptions only' requirement. Wrong: d. The Microsoft Entra tenant is not an Azure RBAC scope. Microsoft Entra ID and Azure resources are secured independently; Microsoft Entra role assignments do not grant access to Azure resources.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: A storage account named storage1 is configured as follows: the network rule set default action is Deny; a virtual network rule grants access to Subnet1 of VNet1, which has the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint enabled; and the exception that allows Azure services on the trusted services list to access the account is enabled. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true. 1) A virtual machine in Subnet1 that also meets the storage account's authorization requirements can read blob data in storage1. 2) Adding an IP network rule for 10.20.0.0/16 will grant access to an on-premises network that uses that address space internally. 3) An administrator working from an unlisted public IP address is blocked by the firewall when listing the containers of storage1 in the Azure portal.
opzione_a: A virtual machine in Subnet1 that also meets the storage account's authorization requirements can read blob data in storage1.
opzione_b: Adding an IP network rule for 10.20.0.0/16 will grant access to an on-premises network that uses that address space internally.
opzione_c: An administrator working from an unlisted public IP address is blocked by the firewall when listing the containers of storage1 in the Azure portal.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: the virtual network rule for Subnet1, combined with the required Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on that subnet, permits the traffic through the firewall. Microsoft Learn is explicit that clients making requests from allowed sources must also meet the storage account's authorization requirements, which the statement stipulates, so the request succeeds. Statement 2 - No: 10.20.0.0/16 is an RFC 1918 private range and is rejected outright, since IP network rules are allowed only for public internet IP addresses. On-premises access requires the public or NAT IP addresses that the network presents to the internet. Statement 3 - No: Azure Storage firewall rules apply only to data plane operations; control plane operations are not subject to the restrictions specified in firewall rules. Listing containers from the Azure portal is performed through the control plane and succeeds unless blocked by another mechanism, whereas reading blob data from a tool such as Azure Storage Explorer would be controlled by the firewall.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: For a general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1, an administrator sets Public network access to Disabled and creates a private endpoint in Subnet1 with the target sub-resource set to blob. Applications in Subnet1 can now read blobs successfully, but a virtual machine in Subnet1 fails to mount an Azure file share hosted in storage1 over SMB. What should you do to resolve the failure?
opzione_a: Create an additional private endpoint for storage1 and set its target sub-resource to file.
opzione_b: Add a virtual network rule for Subnet1 to the storage account firewall.
opzione_c: Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on Subnet1.
opzione_d: Change Public network access to Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses.
spiegazione: Correct: a separate private endpoint is required for each storage resource you need to access. Blobs, Data Lake Storage, Files, Queues, Tables, and Static Websites are each defined as a distinct target sub-resource, so a blob private endpoint provides no connectivity to the file endpoint. Private endpoints support all protocols the account supports, including SMB. Wrong - virtual network rule: storage firewall rules only govern access through the public endpoint. With public network access disabled the public endpoint is unavailable, and a virtual network rule would neither be used nor fix file access. Wrong - Microsoft.Storage service endpoint: service endpoints reach the service's public endpoint, which is disabled on this account, so this does not restore file access. Wrong - Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses: re-opening the public endpoint would contradict the design and would still require a virtual network rule; the documented solution for the private-access design is a file-targeted private endpoint.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: A storage account named storage1 and a virtual network named VNet1 are both deployed in the West Europe region. You must allow blob access only from Subnet1 in VNet1 and from a small set of on-premises public IP addresses, and block everything else that arrives on the public endpoint. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Public network access setting on storage1: [Enabled from all networks | Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses | Disabled]
opzione_b: Service endpoint to enable on Subnet1: [Microsoft.Storage | Microsoft.Storage.Global | Microsoft.Network]
opzione_c: Maximum number of virtual network rules supported per storage account: [100 | 200 | 400]
risposta_corretta: Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses,Microsoft.Storage,400
spiegazione: Public network access: "Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses" is the setting that keeps the public endpoint reachable only for the networks, IP ranges, and resource instances you explicitly allow; in the API this corresponds to a defaultAction of Deny. "Enabled from all networks" is the permissive default and would allow the traffic you must block. "Disabled" would block the on-premises IP addresses too, because it permits traffic only through a private endpoint. Service endpoint: Microsoft.Storage is correct because it provides connectivity to storage accounts in the same region as the virtual network, and VNet1 and storage1 are both in West Europe. Microsoft.Storage.Global is the cross-region endpoint and is unnecessary here; only one of the two can be associated with a subnet. Microsoft.Network is not a storage service endpoint. Maximum virtual network rules: Microsoft Learn documents that you can add up to 400 virtual network rules per storage account; 100 and 200 are not the documented limits.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: Storage account storage1 has a firewall with the default action set to Deny and a single IP network rule that permits the public IP address of a virtual machine named VM1. VM1 resides in Subnet1 of VNet1 and has been reaching blob data successfully for months. After a network engineer enables the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on Subnet1, VM1 immediately begins receiving HTTP 403 errors when it calls the blob endpoint. What is the MOST likely cause?
opzione_a: Enabling the service endpoint switched the source address of the traffic to a private virtual network address, so the existing IP network rule no longer matches.
opzione_b: Enabling the service endpoint automatically regenerated the account access keys, invalidating the connection string used by VM1.
opzione_c: Enabling the service endpoint set the storage account's Public network access property to Disabled.
opzione_d: Enabling the service endpoint requires the storage account and the virtual network to be in different regions, and they are in the same region.
spiegazione: Correct: with a service endpoint enabled, traffic from the subnet stops using a public IP address and uses the private virtual network address as the source IP instead. Microsoft Learn states explicitly that IP network rules permitting traffic from those subnets no longer have an effect. The fix is to add a virtual network rule for Subnet1. Wrong - key regeneration: enabling a service endpoint is a networking operation and has no effect on account access keys; a bad key would also produce an authorization failure signature, not a firewall denial. Wrong - Public network access set to Disabled: enabling a service endpoint on a subnet does not modify the storage account's public network access setting; that is a separate, explicit configuration on the account. Wrong - different regions: the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint provides connectivity to storage accounts in the same region as the virtual network, so same-region placement is the normal, supported scenario, not an error.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: You must provide clients in a virtual network with private connectivity to the Azure file shares hosted in a general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1, using Azure Private Link and the default private DNS integration. Select the appropriate option for each item.
opzione_a: Target sub-resource of the private endpoint: [blob | file | dfs]
opzione_b: Recommended private DNS zone name: [privatelink.file.core.windows.net | privatelink.blob.core.windows.net | file.privatelink.core.windows.net]
opzione_c: Endpoint that clients in the virtual network should use in their connection string: [the privatelink subdomain URL | the standard storage account endpoint URL | the private endpoint IP address]
spiegazione: Target sub-resource: a separate private endpoint is required for each storage resource, and the File service maps to the target sub-resource named file. The blob sub-resource targets Blob Storage, and dfs targets Data Lake Storage; neither provides access to file shares. Private DNS zone: the documented recommended zone name for the File service is privatelink.file.core.windows.net. privatelink.blob.core.windows.net is the zone for the Blob service, and file.privatelink.core.windows.net inverts the label order and is not a valid zone name. Connection string: Microsoft Learn states that clients should use the same connection string they would use otherwise and explicitly warns not to connect using the privatelink subdomain URL. DNS resolution transparently routes the standard endpoint name to the private endpoint's IP address from inside the virtual network, and taking a dependency on a hard-coded IP address is discouraged.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: As part of a design review, you must document the constraints that apply to IP network rules on an Azure Storage account. Which of the following statements are accurate? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Address ranges reserved for private networks by RFC 1918 cannot be used in an IP network rule.
opzione_b: Ranges that use a /31 or /32 prefix size are not supported and must instead be configured as individual IP address rules.
opzione_c: IPv6 address ranges can be configured as IP network rules.
opzione_d: IP network rules have no effect on requests that originate from the same Azure region as the storage account.
opzione_e: A storage account supports a maximum of 100 IP network rules.
spiegazione: Correct - RFC 1918 ranges: IP network rules are allowed only for public internet IP addresses; private ranges beginning with 10, 172.16 through 172.31, and 192.168 are rejected. Correct - /31 and /32: Microsoft Learn states that small address ranges using /31 or /32 prefix sizes are not supported and that such ranges must be configured using individual IP address rules. Correct - same-region requests: the documentation states that IP network rules cannot restrict access to clients in the same Azure region as the storage account and have no effect on same-region requests, because those services communicate using private Azure IP addresses; virtual network rules must be used instead. Wrong - IPv6: only IPv4 addresses are supported for the configuration of storage firewall rules. Wrong - 100 rules: the documented limit is 400 IP network rules per storage account, which matches the 400 virtual network rules per account limit.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: A storage account named storage1 has its firewall default action set to Deny. You must permit traffic from several internet-facing locations by adding IP network rules. Which value will Azure REJECT when you attempt to add it as an IP network rule?
spiegazione: Correct: 192.168.10.0/24 falls inside the private address space defined by RFC 1918. Azure Storage IP network rules are allowed only for public internet IP addresses, and ranges reserved for private networks (addresses starting with 10, 172.16 through 172.31, and 192.168) are not accepted. Wrong - 52.239.0.0/16: this is a routable public CIDR range and is accepted. Wrong - 203.0.113.45: individual public IP addresses are explicitly supported; the documentation shows rules in the form of a single address such as 16.17.18.19. Wrong - 198.51.100.0/24: a public range expressed in valid CIDR notation, in the documented form 16.17.18.0/24, and it is not one of the unsupported /31 or /32 prefix sizes, so it is accepted. Correction: the rationale for 198.51.100.0/24 previously described the prefix as "larger than /31", which inverts prefix-length terminology; it now states the range is accepted because it is not a /31 or /32.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: VNet1 is deployed in the West Europe region and contains a subnet named Subnet1. A storage account named storage1 is deployed in the North Europe region. You must create a virtual network rule that grants Subnet1 access to storage1 through the storage firewall. Which service endpoint resource must you enable on Subnet1?
opzione_a: Microsoft.Storage
opzione_b: Microsoft.Storage.Global
opzione_c: Microsoft.Network
opzione_d: Microsoft.AzureActiveDirectory
spiegazione: Correct: the Azure Storage cross-region service endpoint, resource name Microsoft.Storage.Global, provides connectivity to storage accounts in any region, which is what this cross-region scenario requires. Wrong - Microsoft.Storage: the standard Azure Storage service endpoint provides connectivity only to storage accounts in the same region as the virtual network, so it does not cover a North Europe account from a West Europe virtual network. Note that only one of these two endpoint types can be associated with a subnet at a time. Wrong - Microsoft.Network: this is not a service endpoint resource for Azure Storage; it is the resource provider name that identifies Azure networking services on the trusted services list. Wrong - Microsoft.AzureActiveDirectory: this tag exists only to support service endpoints for Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 and is unrelated to securing a general-purpose storage account.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: You plan to enable the exception named "Allow Azure services on the trusted services list to access this storage account" on a firewall-protected storage account. Which of the following are documented as trusted Azure services whose resources, when registered in the same Microsoft Entra tenant, can be granted access through this exception? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Azure Backup (Microsoft.RecoveryServices)
opzione_b: Azure Monitor (Microsoft.Insights)
opzione_c: Azure Cosmos DB (Microsoft.DocumentDB)
opzione_d: Azure networking services (Microsoft.Network)
opzione_e: Azure Virtual Desktop (Microsoft.DesktopVirtualization)
spiegazione: Correct - Azure Backup (Microsoft.RecoveryServices): it is listed as trusted so it can run backups and restores of unmanaged disks in IaaS virtual machines; this is not required for managed disks, which Azure already manages. Correct - Azure Monitor (Microsoft.Insights): it is listed as trusted so it can write monitoring data such as resource logs and Microsoft Entra sign-in and audit logs to a secured storage account. Correct - Azure networking services (Microsoft.Network): it is listed as trusted so services such as Azure Network Watcher and Azure Traffic Manager can store and analyze network traffic logs. Wrong - Azure Cosmos DB (Microsoft.DocumentDB): it does not appear on the trusted access list for storage network security. Wrong - Azure Virtual Desktop (Microsoft.DesktopVirtualization): it does not appear on the trusted access list for storage network security.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: Contoso connects its datacenter to Azure by using ExpressRoute with Microsoft peering. On-premises servers, which use the 10.10.0.0/16 address space internally, must read blob data from a storage account whose firewall default action is Deny. What should you configure?
opzione_a: An IP network rule that contains the NAT IP addresses used for Microsoft peering.
opzione_b: An IP network rule that contains 10.10.0.0/16.
opzione_c: The Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on the GatewaySubnet of the connected virtual network.
opzione_d: The exception that allows Azure services on the trusted services list to access the storage account.
spiegazione: Correct: when you use ExpressRoute with Microsoft peering, you must identify the NAT IP addresses used for that peering, which are provided either by the service provider or by the customer, and allow those public IP addresses in the storage account's IP network rules. Wrong - 10.10.0.0/16: this is an RFC 1918 private range, and IP network rules are allowed only for public internet IP addresses; Azure rejects addresses starting with 10, 172.16-172.31, and 192.168. Wrong - service endpoint on GatewaySubnet: Microsoft Learn states that endpoints are enabled on subnets in Azure virtual networks and cannot be used for traffic from on-premises services to Azure services. Wrong - trusted services exception: that exception is for first-party Azure services operating outside your network boundary, not for a customer's on-premises servers.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: Using an Azure Resource Manager template, a colleague deploys a storage account named storage1 together with one virtual network rule and two IP network rules. After the deployment completes, clients from arbitrary public IP addresses that are not listed in any rule can still read blob data in storage1. Which change will enforce the intended restriction?
opzione_a: Set the defaultAction property of the network rule set to Deny.
opzione_b: Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on every subnet referenced by the rules.
opzione_c: Regenerate both account access keys for storage1.
opzione_d: Enable the exception that allows Azure services on the trusted services list to access storage1.
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft Learn states plainly that network rules have no effect unless the default action is set to Deny. By default a storage account accepts connections from clients on any network, so the rules are inert until defaultAction is Deny. Wrong - service endpoint on subnets: service endpoints are required for virtual network rules to function, but they do nothing to block unlisted public clients while defaultAction remains Allow. Wrong - regenerate access keys: key rotation changes the credentials but does not restrict which networks may reach the public endpoint; firewall behaviour is independent of authorization. Wrong - trusted services exception: this widens access for specific Azure services rather than restricting it, and it also has no effect while the default action is Allow.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda: The account archivedata is a standard general-purpose v2 storage account configured for locally redundant storage (LRS). It contains blobs in the archive tier. You must reconfigure the account for geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) by adding zone-redundancy first, without copying the data to a new storage account. Arrange the required actions in the correct order.
opzione_a: Rehydrate all blobs in the archive tier to an online tier
opzione_b: Perform a conversion from ZRS to GZRS
opzione_c: Wait at least 72 hours for background processes to complete
opzione_d: Initiate a customer-initiated conversion from LRS to ZRS
opzione_e: Verify that the storage account's region supports zone-redundant storage
spiegazione: Correct order: (1) Verify that the account's region supports zone-redundant storage - Microsoft directs you to make sure the region where your storage account is located supports all of the desired replication settings before converting, and attempting a zonal conversion in an unsupported region generates an error. (2) Rehydrate all archived blobs to an online tier, because the archive tier isn't supported for ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS accounts; to convert an LRS, GRS, or RA-GRS account to a zone-redundant option you must first move archived blobs to the hot, cool, or cold tier. (3) Initiate the customer-initiated conversion from LRS to ZRS, which adds zone-redundancy and can be started from the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell, or the Azure CLI. (4) Wait at least 72 hours, because after a zone-redundancy conversion you must wait that long before changing the redundancy setting of the account again so background processes can complete. (5) Perform the ZRS to GZRS change, which adds geo-redundancy and completes the two-step path. This ordering matters: verification precedes work, the archive blocker must clear before any zonal conversion is attempted, and the mandatory 72-hour hold falls between the two redundancy changes, not before them.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda:
The account sales-gpv2 is a standard general-purpose v2 storage account configured for locally redundant storage (LRS). It is located in a region that supports availability zones and has a paired region. The account contains no blobs in the archive tier, does not have NFSv3 enabled, and has never been failed over. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true.

1. You can change the account from LRS to GRS by using the Azure portal.
2. You can change the account from LRS to GZRS in a single operation by using the Azure portal.
3. You can change the account from LRS to ZRS by initiating a customer-initiated conversion.
opzione_a: You can change the account from LRS to GRS by using the Azure portal.
opzione_b: You can change the account from LRS to GZRS in a single operation by using the Azure portal.
opzione_c: You can change the account from LRS to ZRS by initiating a customer-initiated conversion.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: Adding geo-redundancy is a change you make directly with the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell, or the Azure CLI. The migration table shows LRS to GRS/RA-GRS as a direct change on the Redundancy blade under Data management. Note that adding geo-redundancy incurs a one-time egress charge because the entire account is replicated to the secondary region. Statement 2 - No: A direct LRS to GZRS conversion isn't supported. Any change that involves zone-redundancy requires a conversion and must be performed separately from the geo-redundancy change, so the account must go through a two-step process - either LRS to ZRS then ZRS to GZRS, or LRS to GRS then GRS to GZRS. Statement 3 - Yes: Adding zone-redundancy to a standard general-purpose v2 account is a conversion, and customers in most regions can start a customer-initiated conversion and monitor its progress from the Azure portal, with Azure PowerShell (Start-AzStorageAccountMigration -TargetSku), or with the Azure CLI (az storage account migration start). Microsoft recommends customer-initiated conversion over a support-initiated conversion whenever possible. The scenario rules out the usual blockers, such as archived blobs, NFSv3, and a prior failover.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda: You are preparing a reference card that summarizes the durability targets Microsoft publishes for Azure Storage redundancy options, together with how many availability zones zone-redundant storage uses. Select the correct value for each item.
opzione_a: Durability of objects over a given year for LRS: [at least 99.9% | at least 99.999999999% (11 nines) | at least 99.99999999999999% (16 nines)]
opzione_b: Durability of objects over a given year for ZRS: [11 nines | 12 nines | 16 nines]
opzione_c: Durability of objects over a given year for GZRS: [11 nines | 12 nines | 16 nines]
opzione_d: Number of availability zones across which ZRS replicates data in the primary region: [two | three or more | six]
risposta_corretta: at least 99.999999999% (11 nines),12 nines,16 nines,three or more
spiegazione: Correct selections: LRS replicates data within a single physical datacenter in the primary region and provides at least 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability of objects over a given year. ZRS copies data synchronously across three or more Azure availability zones in the primary region and offers durability of at least 99.9999999999% (12 nines). GZRS combines ZRS in the primary region with asynchronous replication to a secondary region and is designed to provide at least 99.99999999999999% (16 nines) durability - the same target as GRS, because within the secondary region data is always replicated synchronously using LRS. Why the other choices are wrong: 'At least 99.9%' is the availability target for read and write requests, not a durability figure, and is a common confusion between the availability and durability rows of the redundancy summary table. Assigning 11 or 12 nines to GZRS understates it by ignoring the secondary region, while assigning 16 nines to ZRS overstates it, since ZRS alone does not protect against a regional disaster. 'Two' zones is wrong because a ZRS write returns successfully only after data is written to all replicas across the three availability zones; 'six' is not a documented figure.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda: The account fin-prod is a standard general-purpose v2 storage account configured for LRS. It resides in a region that supports availability zones and has a paired region, contains no archived blobs, and has never been failed over. You must reconfigure it for RA-GZRS using the fewest possible redundancy change operations, without copying data to a new account. Select the correct option for each item.
opzione_a: Minimum number of redundancy change operations required: [one | two | three]
opzione_b: First operation: [LRS to RA-GRS | LRS to RA-GZRS | LRS to GZRS]
opzione_c: Second operation: [RA-GRS to RA-GZRS | RA-GRS to ZRS | none required]
opzione_d: Minimum time you must wait after a zone-redundancy conversion before changing the redundancy setting again: [24 hours | 72 hours | 7 days]
risposta_corretta: two,LRS to RA-GRS,RA-GRS to RA-GZRS,72 hours
spiegazione: Correct selections: Geo-redundancy and read-access can be changed together, but any change that also involves zone-redundancy requires a conversion and must be performed separately, so two operations are the minimum. The first operation switches LRS to RA-GRS using the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell, or the Azure CLI - the migration table shows this as a direct change from LRS to GRS/RA-GRS. The second operation is the zone-redundancy conversion RA-GRS to RA-GZRS, which the FAQ lists explicitly among supported zonal conversions. After a zone-redundancy conversion you must wait at least 72 hours before changing the redundancy setting of the account again, so that background processes can complete and account consistency and integrity are preserved. Why the other choices are wrong: 'One' operation is impossible because a direct LRS to GZRS conversion isn't supported, and 'three' is more than the minimum. Choosing 'LRS to RA-GZRS' or 'LRS to GZRS' as the first step repeats that unsupported single-hop change. 'RA-GRS to ZRS' would strip the geo-redundancy the first step just added, and 'none required' contradicts the two-step requirement. '24 hours' and '7 days' are not the documented interval.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda: Following a prolonged outage, an administrator initiated a customer-managed (unplanned) failover of a general-purpose v2 storage account that had been configured for GRS. The failover completed successfully. Management now wants the account protected against the loss of a single availability zone in the new primary region. What must you do?
opzione_a: Perform a manual migration of the data to a new zone-redundant storage account
opzione_b: Initiate a customer-initiated conversion from LRS to ZRS on the existing account
opzione_c: Re-enable GRS on the account, and then convert it to GZRS
opzione_d: Fail the account back to the original primary region, and then convert it to GZRS
spiegazione: Correct: A customer-managed unplanned failover automatically converts the storage account to locally redundant storage (LRS) in the new primary region. Microsoft explicitly states that conversion to ZRS or GZRS for an LRS account resulting from a failover isn't supported, and that you must instead perform a manual migration to add zone-redundancy. A manual migration copies the data to a new account with the desired redundancy using a tool such as AzCopy. Why the others are wrong: Initiating an LRS to ZRS conversion is exactly the blocked operation - the FAQ also lists 'account is failed over' as a conflicting scenario for zonal conversions. Re-enabling GRS and then converting to GZRS still requires the zonal conversion step, which remains unsupported on an account that reached LRS through a failover; re-enabling geo-redundancy only restores the geo aspect. Failing back to the original primary region does not help either, because after an unplanned failover the copy of the data in the original primary region is deleted and geo-redundancy is lost; the failed-over account remains ineligible for a zonal conversion.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda: A trading platform stores small objects in a premium block blob storage account to obtain consistently low write latency. The risk team now requires that the data also be replicated to a second, geographically distant region. What should you tell the risk team?
opzione_a: Enable RA-GRS on the existing account from the Redundancy blade in the Azure portal
opzione_b: Premium block blob accounts support only LRS and ZRS, so geo-redundancy cannot be configured on this account type
opzione_c: Open a support request so that Microsoft can perform a support-initiated conversion of the account to GZRS
opzione_d: Convert the account to GZRS by running Start-AzStorageAccountMigration with the -TargetSku parameter
spiegazione: Correct: The premium block blobs account type supports only LRS and ZRS. Geo-redundant options (GRS, RA-GRS, GZRS, RA-GZRS) are not available for this account type, which is why the disaster recovery documentation also states that storage accounts supporting premium block blobs don't currently support geo-redundancy and cannot be failed over. Meeting the requirement means copying data to a separate account in another region, not changing the SKU. Why the others are wrong: Enabling RA-GRS from the Redundancy blade works for standard general-purpose v2 accounts, but the geo-redundant SKUs are simply not offered for premium block blob accounts. A support-initiated conversion cannot create a redundancy option that the account type does not support - and the migration guidance shows premium block blob accounts as supporting neither portal-based nor support-request conversions, only manual migration. Start-AzStorageAccountMigration performs a zone-redundancy conversion (for example LRS to ZRS) on supported account types; it cannot add geo-redundancy, and premium block blob accounts do not support conversion at all.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda:
An application team owns a standard general-purpose v2 storage account named webassets that is configured for read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS). The account stores block blobs. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true.

1. After a customer-managed (unplanned) failover completes, the account is automatically configured as RA-GRS in the new primary region.
2. The secondary read endpoint for Blob Storage is https://webassets-secondary.blob.core.windows.net.
3. Blobs in this account can be moved to the archive tier.
opzione_a: After a customer-managed (unplanned) failover completes, the account is automatically configured as RA-GRS in the new primary region.
opzione_b: The secondary read endpoint for Blob Storage is https://webassets-secondary.blob.core.windows.net.
opzione_c: Blobs in this account can be moved to the archive tier.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: Initiating a customer-managed unplanned failover automatically converts the storage account to locally redundant storage (LRS) in the new primary region and deletes the storage account in the original primary region, so geo-redundancy is lost rather than retained. You can re-enable GRS or RA-GRS afterward, but re-replicating the data to the new secondary region incurs a charge. This is the key contrast with a customer-managed planned failover, after which geo-redundancy is retained and the account is converted to GRS. Statement 2 - Yes: When read access to the secondary is enabled, the secondary endpoint appends the suffix -secondary to the account name. If the primary blob endpoint is webassets.blob.core.windows.net, the secondary endpoint is webassets-secondary.blob.core.windows.net, and the account access keys are the same for both endpoints. Statement 3 - Yes: Only storage accounts configured for LRS, GRS, or RA-GRS support moving blobs to the archive tier. Because this account is RA-GRS, archiving is supported; it would not be supported if the account were ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda: A general-purpose v2 storage account is configured for read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS) and contains several thousand blobs in the archive tier. A new resiliency standard requires the account to be reconfigured for read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS). You want to keep the existing account. What must you do before the conversion can succeed?
opzione_a: Rehydrate all archived blobs to an online tier
opzione_b: Change the account's default access tier to Cool
opzione_c: Disable soft delete for blobs on the account
opzione_d: Enable the change feed on the account
spiegazione: Correct: The archive tier is supported only for LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS accounts - it isn't supported for ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS accounts. To change the redundancy configuration of an account that contains archived blobs to a zone-redundant option, you must first rehydrate all archived blobs to the hot, cool, or cold tier. The FAQ likewise lists archive data as a conflicting scenario that generates errors during a zonal conversion. Why the others are wrong: Changing the default access tier to Cool only sets the tier inferred by newly uploaded blobs that have no explicit tier; it does nothing to the blobs already sitting in the archive tier, which are the actual blocker. Disabling blob soft delete is unrelated to redundancy conversions - soft delete is a data protection feature and is not listed among the conflicting features for zonal conversions. Enabling the change feed makes matters worse rather than better: the FAQ lists object replication and similar features as conflicting, and change feed is explicitly unsupported for customer-managed planned failover.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda: You are reviewing several pending redundancy changes and must identify the ones that cannot be handled by a conversion and therefore require a manual migration. Which three scenarios require a manual migration? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Moving a storage account and its data to a different Azure region
opzione_b: Changing the redundancy of a premium block blob storage account
opzione_c: Changing a standard general-purpose v2 account from LRS to GRS
opzione_d: Adding zone-redundancy to an account that became LRS as the result of a customer-managed unplanned failover
opzione_e: Changing a standard general-purpose v2 account from GRS to GZRS
spiegazione: Correct answers: Microsoft states you must perform a manual migration if you want to migrate your storage account to a different region, or if your storage account is a block blob account - the migration support table confirms premium block blob accounts support neither portal-based nor support-request conversions, only manual migration. Separately, conversion to ZRS or GZRS for an LRS account resulting from a failover isn't supported, and the documentation directs you to perform a manual migration to add zone-redundancy instead. Why the others are wrong: Changing a standard general-purpose v2 account from LRS to GRS is a geo change that you make directly with the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell (Set-AzStorageAccount -SkuName), or the Azure CLI (az storage account update --sku); no manual migration is involved. Changing a general-purpose v2 account from GRS to GZRS is a zone-redundancy conversion, listed in the FAQ among supported zonal conversions and performed as a single conversion on the existing account.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda: A standard general-purpose v2 storage account named contosodata is currently configured for locally redundant storage (LRS) in a region that supports availability zones and has a paired region. You must reconfigure the account for geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) without copying the data to a new account. Which approach works?
opzione_a: Set the redundancy directly to GZRS in a single operation on the Redundancy blade
opzione_b: Convert LRS to GRS, and then convert GRS to GZRS
opzione_c: Convert LRS to RA-GRS, and then convert RA-GRS to ZRS
opzione_d: Fail the account over to the secondary region, and then set the redundancy to GZRS
spiegazione: Correct: A direct LRS to GZRS conversion isn't supported. The change requires a two-step process, which can be completed either as LRS to ZRS followed by ZRS to GZRS, or as LRS to GRS followed by GRS to GZRS. Adding geo-redundancy (LRS to GRS) is done with the portal, PowerShell, or the CLI, and adding zone-redundancy (GRS to GZRS) is a conversion; both steps preserve the account and its data. Why the others are wrong: Setting GZRS in a single operation fails because any change that involves zone-redundancy requires a conversion and must be performed separately from the geo-redundancy change - the two aspects cannot be altered in one operation. Converting LRS to RA-GRS and then RA-GRS to ZRS ends at ZRS, which has no geo-redundancy at all, so it does not meet the requirement. Account failover is a disaster recovery mechanism, not a migration tool; it requires an account that is already geo-redundant, and an unplanned failover would actually leave the account as LRS in the new primary region.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda: You are standardizing on zone-redundant storage (ZRS) wherever the account type allows it. Which three storage account types support ZRS? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Standard general-purpose v2
opzione_b: Premium block blobs
opzione_c: Premium file shares
opzione_d: Standard general-purpose v1
opzione_e: Legacy Blob Storage (BlobStorage)
spiegazione: Correct answers: The storage account overview lists ZRS as a supported redundancy option for standard general-purpose v2, premium block blobs, and premium file shares. Standard general-purpose v2 is the recommended account type for most scenarios and supports the full range of options (LRS, ZRS, GRS, RA-GRS, GZRS, RA-GZRS); premium block blobs and premium file shares each support LRS and ZRS only, with no geo-redundant options. Note that ZRS availability also varies by region, since the region must support availability zones. Why the others are wrong: Standard general-purpose v1 is a legacy account type that supports only LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS; the redundancy summary lists it under 'Legacy' for LRS and GRS/RA-GRS and shows N/A for ZRS and GZRS. A GPv1 account must be upgraded to GPv2 before a ZRS conversion is possible. Legacy Blob Storage (BlobStorage) accounts likewise support only LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS, and Microsoft recommends upgrading them to general-purpose v2.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda: Your change advisory board asks what the impact of a redundancy conversion will be on a general-purpose v2 storage account. Which three statements accurately describe a conversion? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: No data is lost during the conversion, and there is no loss of durability
opzione_b: Access keys, shared access signatures, and service endpoints remain unchanged
opzione_c: The storage account must be re-created in a different region to complete the conversion
opzione_d: An account with a hierarchical namespace enabled might experience a pause of less than 30 seconds
opzione_e: Client applications must be reconfigured to use new service endpoints after the conversion
spiegazione: Correct answers: During a conversion you can access data in your storage account with no loss of durability and no data is lost, and the Azure Storage SLA is maintained throughout. Service endpoints, access keys, shared access signatures, and other account options remain unchanged after the migration. Accounts without a hierarchical namespace experience no interruption to availability, while HNS-enabled accounts might experience a brief pause lasting less than 30 seconds, after which requests complete automatically. Why the others are wrong: Re-creating the account in a different region describes a manual migration, which is the alternative you choose when a conversion isn't supported or when you need to move regions - a conversion operates in place on the existing account. Reconfiguring clients to use new endpoints is unnecessary precisely because the endpoints do not change; that step would be required only after a manual migration to a new account name.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage redundancy
domanda: A colleague asks you to document the durability target that Microsoft publishes for locally redundant storage (LRS). Over a given year, what is the minimum durability of objects that LRS is designed to provide?
opzione_a: At least 99.9% (3 nines)
opzione_b: At least 99.999999999% (11 nines)
opzione_c: At least 99.9999999999% (12 nines)
spiegazione: Correct: LRS replicates data within a single physical datacenter in the primary region and is designed to provide at least 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability of objects over a given year. Why the others are wrong: 'At least 99.9%' is an availability figure for read/write requests, not a durability figure - it is the availability SLA target for hot-tier data, so it is a classic confusion between the availability and durability columns of the redundancy summary table. '12 nines' (99.9999999999%) is the durability target for zone-redundant storage (ZRS), which replicates synchronously across three or more availability zones and therefore earns a higher target than LRS. '16 nines' (99.99999999999999%) is the durability target for the geo-redundant options GRS/RA-GRS and GZRS/RA-GZRS, which add asynchronous replication to a secondary region hundreds of miles away.

sotto_argomento: Configure blob lifecycle management
domanda:
Northwind stores contract documents as block blobs in a general-purpose v2 storage account. Compliance requires that every change to a contract be retained, and that superseded copies be purged automatically 180 days after they were first written. Neither blob versioning nor any lifecycle management policy is currently configured on the account.

You need to implement the requirement by using the Azure portal.

Drag the four actions into the correct order.
opzione_a: In the rule's blob subtype configuration, select Previous versions and add a Delete action with daysAfterCreationGreaterThan set to 180.
opzione_b: On the Data protection blade of the storage account, select Enable versioning for blobs.
opzione_c: Save the policy, then allow up to 24 hours for the change to take effect and for the first policy run to start.
opzione_d: On the Lifecycle management blade, add a rule and set the blob type filter to Block blobs.
spiegazione:
Correct order: b, d, a, c.

1. Enable versioning for blobs on the Data protection blade (b). Versioning must exist before a rule can act on previous versions. Once enabled, every write operation to a blob creates a new version, so the superseded copies the rule will later delete only start accumulating from this point. Blobs created before versioning was enabled do not have a version ID.

2. Add a lifecycle management rule and set the blob type filter to Block blobs (d). The blobTypes filter is a required element of every rule and must be set before the actions can be defined; it accepts blockBlob or appendBlob.

3. Configure the Delete action under Previous versions with daysAfterCreationGreaterThan set to 180 (a). Rules for previous versions use the creation time of that version when the blob was first written, which is exactly what the compliance requirement specifies, so daysAfterCreationGreaterThan is the correct run condition.

4. Save the policy and wait (c). Microsoft Learn states that when you add or edit the rules of a lifecycle policy, it can take up to 24 hours for changes to go into effect and for the first execution to start, so this step is necessarily last.

A common error is reversing steps 1 and 2: creating the lifecycle rule first leaves nothing for the Previous versions action to target, because no versions are being generated yet. Note also that enabling the "Delete versions after" option directly on the Data protection blade would auto-create a lifecycle rule, but it doesn't provide the block-blob filtering shown here.
tags: blob storage,lifecycle management,blob versioning,delete previous versions,azure portal,policy execution

sotto_argomento: Configure blob lifecycle management
domanda:
A general-purpose v2 storage account has blob versioning enabled. Auditors require that previous versions of block blobs be permanently removed 90 days after the version itself was first written, while the current version of each blob remains untouched. You are building the lifecycle management rule that implements this.

Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: blobTypes filter value to specify: [blockBlob | appendBlob | pageBlob]
opzione_b: Section of the rule definition that the Delete action must be placed under: [baseBlob | snapshot | version]
opzione_c: Run condition to pair with the Delete action: [daysAfterModificationGreaterThan | daysAfterCreationGreaterThan | daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan]
spiegazione:
Dropdown 1 - blockBlob: The blobTypes filter is required and accepts only blockBlob or appendBlob. The requirement names block blobs, so blockBlob is correct. pageBlob isn't a valid blobTypes value at all, and appendBlob would not match the target data.

Dropdown 2 - version: A policy can operate on current versions, previous versions, and snapshots. Placing the Delete action under version targets previous versions only, leaving the current version untouched as required. Putting it under baseBlob would delete the current version, and snapshot targets manually created snapshots rather than versions.

Dropdown 3 - daysAfterCreationGreaterThan: Microsoft Learn states that rules for previous versions use the creation time of that version when the blob was first written, not when the version became a previous version, and that daysAfterCreationGreaterThan applies to actions on the current version, the previous version, or a snapshot. daysAfterModificationGreaterThan applies only to actions on a current version. daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan applies only to tierToArchive actions, not to Delete.

Note that a lifecycle policy will not delete the current version of a blob until any previous versions or snapshots associated with it have been deleted.

sotto_argomento: Configure blob lifecycle management
domanda:
A storage account has a lifecycle management policy whose only rule applies a tierToArchive action to block blobs when daysAfterModificationGreaterThan is 365. An engineer rehydrates several archived blobs to the Hot tier by calling Set Blob Tier because a project restarted. Within 24 hours, every rehydrated blob is back in the Archive tier, even though the engineer is actively reading them.

You need to prevent the policy from returning rehydrated blobs to the Archive tier for 30 days after rehydration, while keeping the existing archiving behavior for all other blobs.

What should you do?
opzione_a: Add the daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan condition set to 30 to the tierToArchive action.
opzione_b: Increase daysAfterModificationGreaterThan on the tierToArchive action from 365 to 395.
opzione_c: Enable last access time tracking and replace daysAfterModificationGreaterThan with daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan set to 30 on the tierToArchive action.
opzione_d: Add the enableAutoTierToHotFromCool action to the rule.
spiegazione:
Correct: Rehydrating a blob does not update its last modified time, so the blob still satisfies daysAfterModificationGreaterThan and the policy re-archives it. Microsoft Learn documents daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan as the condition that specifies the minimum number of days a rehydrated blob is kept in an online tier before being returned to Archive, and it applies only to tierToArchive actions. Setting it to 30 gives exactly the required 30-day grace period.

Why the others are wrong:
- Raising daysAfterModificationGreaterThan to 395 only delays archiving for blobs modified less than 395 days ago. The rehydrated blobs were last modified far longer ago, so they would still be re-archived on the next run.
