- daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan is a valid condition, but it changes the archiving criteria for every blob the rule matches, which violates the requirement to keep the existing behavior for other blobs. Learn specifically prescribes daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan for the rehydration scenario.
- enableAutoTierToHotFromCool moves blobs from Cool to Hot when accessed. It requires the daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan condition and does nothing for blobs being tiered to Archive.

sotto_argomento: Configure blob lifecycle management
domanda:
Before rolling out lifecycle management policies across several general-purpose v2 storage accounts, you must brief the operations team on the documented constraints of the feature.

Which three statements are accurate? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A lifecycle management policy can rehydrate blobs from the Archive tier to the Hot tier when a matching rule is evaluated.
opzione_b: If a rule applies the prefixMatch filter, it can define up to 10 case-sensitive prefixes.
opzione_c: A single lifecycle management policy can define up to 100 rules.
opzione_d: Tiering actions such as tierToCool are supported for append blobs and page blobs in a general-purpose v2 account.
opzione_e: The delete action of a lifecycle management policy has no effect on a blob that is in an immutable container.
spiegazione:
Correct answers:
- Microsoft Learn states that each rule can define up to 10 case-sensitive prefixes when the prefixMatch filter is applied. The same limit of 10 conditions applies to the blobIndexMatch filter.
- The rules array requires at least one rule and you can define up to 100 rules in a policy.
- The delete action won't work with any blob in an immutable container, because a time-based retention policy or legal hold allows objects to be created and read but not modified or deleted.

Why the others are wrong:
- Lifecycle management policies explicitly cannot be used to rehydrate blobs to an online tier. Rehydration must be performed with Set Blob Tier or Copy Blob.
- Tiering is allowed only on block blobs, not on append or page blobs, and tiering isn't supported at all in a premium block blob storage account. The blobTypes filter itself accepts only blockBlob or appendBlob, and append blobs can be targeted only by actions such as delete.

sotto_argomento: Configure blob versioning
domanda:
A general-purpose v2 storage account named fabrikamdocs has blob versioning enabled and blob soft delete enabled with a 7-day retention period. The account does not have a hierarchical namespace and has no object replication policies.

Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true for this configuration.

1. When an application overwrites a block blob with Put Block List, a new version is created and no soft-deleted snapshot is created.
2. If an administrator calls Delete Blob and specifies the version ID of a previous version, that version is soft-deleted and is permanently removed after 7 days.
3. If you disable blob versioning on fabrikamdocs, the versions that already exist are deleted from the storage account.
opzione_a: When an application overwrites a block blob with Put Block List, a new version is created and no soft-deleted snapshot is created.
opzione_b: If an administrator calls Delete Blob and specifies the version ID of a previous version, that version is soft-deleted and is permanently removed after 7 days.
opzione_c: If you disable blob versioning on fabrikamdocs, the versions that already exist are deleted from the storage account.
spiegazione:
Statement 1 - Yes: Microsoft Learn states that if blob versioning and blob soft delete are both enabled, overwriting a blob automatically creates a new previous version that reflects the blob's state before the write operation, and no soft-deleted snapshots are created. The new version isn't soft-deleted and isn't removed when the soft-delete retention period expires. Put Block List is one of the write operations that triggers version creation.

Statement 2 - Yes: To delete a previous version you call Delete Blob and specify the version ID. Soft delete offers additional protection for blob versions: the deleted version becomes soft-deleted and is preserved until the soft delete retention period elapses, at which point it's permanently deleted. Note that deleting a previous version requires the Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/deleteBlobVersion/action data action, granted by Storage Blob Data Owner.

Statement 3 - No: Disabling blob versioning doesn't delete existing blobs, versions, or snapshots. Existing versions remain accessible and can still be read, listed, or deleted by version ID; only new version creation stops. (Object replication relies on versioning, so any object replication policies would have to be deleted before versioning could be disabled, but the account has none.)
tags: blob storage,blob versioning,soft delete,delete blob version,disable versioning

sotto_argomento: Configure blob versioning
domanda:
A general-purpose v2 storage account has blob versioning enabled and blob soft delete enabled with a 7-day retention period. The account does not have a hierarchical namespace. An application calls Delete Blob against a blob named catalog.json without specifying a version ID. Users now report that catalog.json returns 404 Not Found.

You need to make the most recent state of catalog.json available again at its original blob name.

What should you do?
opzione_a: Call Undelete Blob on catalog.json, which promotes the most recent previous version back to the current version.
opzione_b: Call Copy Blob to copy the most recent previous version of catalog.json over the blob name, creating a new current version.
opzione_c: Use container soft delete to restore the parent container within the 7-day retention period.
opzione_d: Call Set Blob Tier on the most recent previous version of catalog.json and specify the Hot tier.
spiegazione:
Correct: When versioning and soft delete are both enabled and you delete a blob without a version ID, the current version simply becomes a previous version and there is no longer a current version. All previous versions persist and are not soft-deleted. Microsoft Learn states that to restore the current version you must promote a previous version by copying it with Copy Blob, which creates a new current version.

Why the others are wrong:
- Undelete Blob restores soft-deleted versions or snapshots but explicitly does not restore the current version. In this scenario no version was soft-deleted at all, so Undelete Blob would have no useful effect.
- Container soft delete restores whole containers. The container here was never deleted, and Learn warns that container soft delete cannot be used to restore an individual blob when the parent container still exists.
- Set Blob Tier only changes the access tier of a version. It does not promote a previous version to be the current version, so catalog.json would still return 404.
tags: blob storage,blob versioning,soft delete,undelete blob,copy blob,promote version

sotto_argomento: Configure identity-based access for Azure Files
domanda: Contoso stores FSLogix profile containers on an SMB Azure file share. The session hosts are Microsoft Entra joined Windows 11 multi-session VMs with no line of sight to the on-premises domain controllers. All users are hybrid identities synced from AD DS to Microsoft Entra ID. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Identity source to enable on the storage account: [On-premises AD DS | Microsoft Entra Domain Services | Microsoft Entra Kerberos]
opzione_b: Number of identity sources that can be enabled on the storage account: [One | Two | Unlimited]
opzione_c: Role that grants read, write, and delete access on files and directories at the share level: [Storage File Data SMB Share Reader | Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor | Storage Blob Data Contributor]
opzione_d: Mechanism that enforces directory-level and file-level permissions: [Azure RBAC role assignments | Windows ACLs | Stored access policies]
risposta_corretta: Microsoft Entra Kerberos,One,Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor,Windows ACLs
spiegazione: Microsoft Entra Kerberos is the documented choice when clients lack unimpeded connectivity to AD DS or when storing FSLogix profiles on Azure file shares for Microsoft Entra joined VMs; it requires clients to be Microsoft Entra joined or Microsoft Entra hybrid joined, which the session hosts are. On-premises AD DS would require connectivity to a domain controller, and Microsoft Entra Domain Services requires the client to be domain joined to the managed domain. You can use only one identity source for file access authentication per storage account, and it applies to all shares in the account; if another source is already enabled you must disable it first. Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor grants read, write, and delete access on files and directories; Storage File Data SMB Share Reader grants read only, and Storage Blob Data Contributor applies to Blob Storage, not to SMB file shares. Below the share, access is enforced with Windows ACLs (also called NTFS permissions) on directories and files; Azure RBAC operates at the share level, and stored access policies relate to service SAS tokens, not to SMB identity-based access.
tags: azure files,microsoft entra kerberos,share-level permissions,windows acls,fslogix,hotspot

sotto_argomento: Configure identity-based access for Azure Files
domanda: Litware runs Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts that are Microsoft Entra joined and have no network connectivity to the company's on-premises domain controllers. User accounts originate in on-premises AD DS and are synced to Microsoft Entra ID with Microsoft Entra Connect Sync. You must let these users authenticate to an SMB Azure file share by using their existing credentials. Which identity source should you enable on the storage account?
opzione_a: On-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)
opzione_b: Microsoft Entra Domain Services
opzione_c: Microsoft Entra Kerberos
opzione_d: Shared Key authorization with the storage account key
spiegazione: Microsoft Entra Kerberos lets Microsoft Entra ID issue the Kerberos tickets used to reach the share over SMB, so end users can access Azure file shares without network connectivity to domain controllers. The documented guidance is to choose Microsoft Entra Kerberos when clients lack unimpeded connectivity to AD DS or when storing FSLogix profiles on Azure file shares for Microsoft Entra joined VMs, and the clients must be Microsoft Entra joined or Microsoft Entra hybrid joined. On-premises AD DS is wrong because it requires clients to be domain joined or to have uninterrupted connectivity to a domain controller. Microsoft Entra Domain Services is wrong because Kerberos authentication requires the client to be domain joined to the Domain Services managed domain; Microsoft Entra joined session hosts do not meet that requirement. Shared Key authorization uses the storage account key and is not identity-based authentication; it cannot enforce per-user permissions.
tags: azure files,microsoft entra kerberos,smb,identity-based authentication,azure virtual desktop

sotto_argomento: Configure identity-based access for Azure Files
domanda: Which statements about identity-based authentication for Azure Files are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: You can use only one identity source for file access authentication per storage account, and it applies to all file shares in that account.
opzione_b: Identity-based authentication is supported for both SMB file shares and NFS file shares.
opzione_c: Share-level permissions are granted by assigning built-in Azure RBAC roles such as Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor.
opzione_d: Directory-level and file-level permissions are enforced through Windows access control lists (ACLs).
opzione_e: Microsoft Entra Domain Services authentication requires that clients be Microsoft Entra joined.
spiegazione: You can enable only one identity source (on-premises AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services, or Microsoft Entra Kerberos) per storage account, and the setting applies to every file share in the account. Share-level access is granted through built-in Azure RBAC roles such as Storage File Data SMB Share Reader, Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor, and Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor. Granular access below the share is enforced with Windows ACLs on directories and files, just as on a Windows file server. Option B is wrong: Azure Files doesn't currently support identity-based authentication for NFS file shares; the feature applies to SMB shares only. Option E is wrong: for Microsoft Entra Domain Services, Kerberos authentication requires the client to be domain joined to the Domain Services managed domain, not Microsoft Entra joined; being Microsoft Entra joined is a requirement of Microsoft Entra Kerberos instead.

sotto_argomento: Configure object replication
domanda: You must configure object replication between two existing general-purpose v2 storage accounts by using the Az.Storage PowerShell module. Neither account currently has any containers, blob versioning, or change feed configured. Place the four actions in the correct order.
opzione_a: Create the replication policy on the destination account by calling Set-AzStorageObjectReplicationPolicy with a policy ID of default.
opzione_b: Enable blob versioning on both accounts and enable change feed on the source account by calling Update-AzStorageBlobServiceProperty.
opzione_c: Create the same replication policy on the source account by using the policy ID returned from the destination account.
opzione_d: Create the source and destination containers by calling New-AzStorageContainer.
spiegazione: The documented PowerShell sequence is: (1) B - enable the prerequisites first, because blob versioning is required on both the source and the destination account and change feed is required on the source account before a policy can be created. (2) D - create the source and destination containers, because both containers must already exist before they can be named in a replication rule. (3) A - create the replication policy on the destination account, setting the policy ID to the string value default so that Azure Storage generates the real policy ID and the rule IDs for you. (4) C - create the same policy on the source account using the policy ID that was returned for the destination account. The policy ID on the source and destination accounts must be identical for replication to take place, which is why the destination must be configured first. Note that this ordering applies to PowerShell, Azure CLI, and the resource provider APIs. In the Azure portal you configure the policy only on the source account, and the portal automatically creates the matching policy on the destination account for you.
tags: object replication, az powershell, policy id, replication policy, configuration order

sotto_argomento: Configure object replication
domanda:
Fabrikam has two general-purpose v2 storage accounts: storage1 in East US (subscription A) and storage2 in West Europe (subscription B). Both accounts belong to the same Microsoft Entra tenant. Blob versioning is enabled on both accounts and change feed is enabled on storage1. An object replication policy replicates one container pair from storage1 to storage2, and the copy scope of the rule is left at its default value. The source container already contained 500 block blobs when the policy was created.

Evaluate each of the following statements:
1. The 500 block blobs that existed in the source container before the policy was created are replicated to the destination container.
2. You can disable blob versioning on storage1 while the replication policy is still in effect.
3. If a replicated blob in the source container is later moved to the archive tier, object replication of that blob fails.
opzione_a: The 500 block blobs that existed in the source container before the policy was created are replicated to the destination container.
opzione_b: You can disable blob versioning on storage1 while the replication policy is still in effect.
opzione_c: If a replicated blob in the source container is later moved to the archive tier, object replication of that blob fails.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: the default copy scope copies only new objects. After a replication rule is created, preexisting blobs are ignored and only new block blobs added after the rule was created are copied. To include the 500 existing blobs, the rule would have to be configured to copy everything, or to use a custom copy scope with a minimum creation time that predates them. Statement 2 - No: if a storage account has object replication policies in effect, you cannot disable blob versioning for that account. You must delete any object replication policies on the account before you can disable versioning. Statement 3 - Yes: object replication is supported when the source and destination accounts are in any online tier (hot, cool, or cold) and the tiers may differ, but object replication fails if a blob in either the source or the destination account is moved to the archive tier. Rehydrating an archived blob does not by itself trigger replication; replication is triggered only when the blob data is updated again after rehydration.
tags: object replication, copy scope, blob versioning, archive tier, troubleshooting

sotto_argomento: Configure object replication
domanda: An object replication policy replicates block blobs from a source container to a destination container. Both storage accounts are general-purpose v2 accounts encrypted with customer-managed keys, and both accounts are online in the hot tier. Most blobs replicate successfully, but a subset of blobs consistently reports a replication status of failure in the source account. Investigation shows that a line-of-business application writes exactly that subset of blobs by supplying an encryption key on each Put Blob request. What is the most likely cause of the failures?
opzione_a: The destination account uses customer-managed keys, which are not supported by object replication.
opzione_b: Blobs in the source account that are encrypted with a customer-provided key cannot be replicated by object replication.
opzione_c: The change feed retention period on the source account expired before the blobs could be replicated.
opzione_d: Blob versioning was never enabled on the destination account, so those blobs have no version to replicate.
spiegazione: Correct: Supplying an encryption key on the request is the customer-provided key (CPK) scenario. Object replication is not supported for blobs in the source account that are encrypted with a customer-provided key, and the documentation lists CPK-encrypted source blobs as an explicit cause of replication failure. Option A is wrong because object replication is fully supported for accounts encrypted with either Microsoft-managed keys or customer-managed keys; only customer-provided keys break it, and the similarity of the names is the trap here. Option C is wrong because change feed retention is not a documented cause of replication failure, and it would not selectively affect only the blobs written by one application. Option D is wrong because blob versioning is a hard prerequisite on both the source and the destination account: without it the replication policy could not have been created at all, and no blobs would replicate rather than just a subset.
tags: object replication, customer-provided key, replication status, troubleshooting, encryption

sotto_argomento: Configure object replication
domanda: An object replication policy is active between a source container named archive-src and a destination container named archive-dst. A developer uses the Azure portal to upload a new blob directly into archive-dst. What is the result?
opzione_a: The upload succeeds, and the blob is replicated back to the source container on the next replication cycle.
opzione_b: The upload succeeds, but the blob is deleted the next time the replication policy runs.
opzione_c: The upload fails with error code 409 (Conflict).
opzione_d: The upload fails with error code 403 (Forbidden).
spiegazione: Correct: After a replication policy is created, write operations to the destination container are not permitted, and any attempt to write fails with error code 409 (Conflict). To write to the destination container you must first disable replication, either by deleting the rule for that container or by removing the entire replication policy. Read and delete operations against the destination container are still permitted while the policy is active. Option A is wrong because object replication is strictly one-way from source to destination; there is no write-back path. Option B is wrong because the write never succeeds in the first place, so there is nothing for a later cycle to remove. Option D is wrong because 403 (Forbidden) is the error returned in a different scenario, for example when a customer-managed key has been revoked or an encryption scope has been disabled, not when writing to a replication destination.
tags: object replication, destination container, 409 conflict, replication rules, blob storage

sotto_argomento: Configure object replication
domanda: An administrator opens the Object replication blade of a general-purpose v2 storage account and selects Create replication rules to replicate data to a second general-purpose v2 account. Select the correct value for each statement about the default object replication behaviour.
opzione_a: Feature that must be enabled on the source account but not on the destination account: [Blob versioning | Change feed | Blob soft delete]
opzione_b: Default copy scope applied to a new replication rule: [Only new objects | Everything | Custom]
opzione_c: Blob types that object replication copies: [Block blobs only | Block and append blobs | Block append and page blobs]
opzione_d: Maximum number of destination accounts for a single source account: [1 | 2 | 10]
risposta_corretta: Change feed,Only new objects,Block blobs only,2
spiegazione: Change feed: change feed must be enabled on the source account only, because Azure Storage periodically inspects the source account's change feed to find operations to replicate. Blob versioning is required on both accounts, and blob soft delete is not a prerequisite, so neither is the correct answer for a source-only requirement. Only new objects: after you create a replication rule, preexisting blobs are ignored and only new block blobs added after the rule is created are copied by default. Everything and Custom are valid copy scope choices you can select by using the change link, but they are not the default. Block blobs only: object replication supports block blobs only; append blobs and page blobs are not supported. 2: a source account can replicate to no more than two destination accounts, with one policy per destination account, so 1 understates and 10 overstates the documented limit.
tags: object replication, copy scope, change feed, block blobs, azure portal

sotto_argomento: Configure object replication
domanda: Contoso plans to use object replication to asynchronously copy block blobs from a general-purpose v2 storage account named storageeast to a general-purpose v2 storage account named storagewest. Before the replication policy can be created, which storage features must be enabled?
opzione_a: Change feed on both the source and destination accounts, and blob versioning on the source account only.
opzione_b: Blob versioning on both the source and destination accounts, and change feed on the source account.
opzione_c: Blob versioning on the source account only, and blob soft delete on the destination account.
opzione_d: Point-in-time restore on the source account, and change feed on the destination account.
spiegazione: Correct: Object replication has exactly two feature prerequisites. Blob versioning must be enabled on BOTH the source and the destination account, and change feed must be enabled on the SOURCE account. Azure Storage reads the source account's change feed to discover write and delete operations, and versioning is what allows the current version and any previous versions to be replicated. Option A inverts the requirement: change feed is needed only on the source, not on both, and versioning on the source alone is not sufficient. Option C is wrong because versioning is required on both accounts, and blob soft delete is not a prerequisite for object replication at all. Option D is wrong because point-in-time restore is a separate data-protection feature that is not required by object replication, and change feed is required on the source rather than the destination.
tags: object replication, blob versioning, change feed, blob storage, prerequisites

sotto_argomento: Configure object replication
domanda: You are designing an object replication topology for block blob data. Which of the following statements about object replication are true? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: The source and destination storage accounts can reside in different regions and in different subscriptions.
opzione_b: A single source account can replicate to a maximum of two destination accounts, with one policy per destination account.
opzione_c: Object replication copies block blobs, append blobs, and page blobs.
opzione_d: Object replication is supported for storage accounts that have a hierarchical namespace enabled.
opzione_e: Snapshots of a blob in the source account are not replicated to the destination account.
spiegazione: Correct: (A) The source and destination accounts may be in the same region or in different regions, and in the same subscription or in different subscriptions; they may even reside in different Microsoft Entra tenants if cross-tenant replication is allowed. (B) A source account can replicate to no more than two destination accounts, with one policy for each destination, and an account can likewise serve as the destination for no more than two replication policies. (E) Object replication does not support blob snapshots, so any snapshots on a source blob are not replicated. Incorrect: (C) Object replication supports block blobs only; append blobs and page blobs are not supported. (D) Object replication is not yet supported in accounts that have a hierarchical namespace enabled, and blobs uploaded through Data Lake Storage APIs are not replicated.
tags: object replication, replication policies, block blobs, hierarchical namespace, snapshots

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda: Your team is designing a data protection plan that relies on Azure Files share snapshots. Which statements about share snapshots are correct? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Share snapshots are incremental: only the data that changed since the most recent share snapshot is stored
opzione_b: Deleting a file share also deletes all of the share snapshots that were taken of it
opzione_c: You can retain a share snapshot for up to 10 years
opzione_d: You can copy an entire share snapshot to a different storage account in a single operation
opzione_e: The space consumed by share snapshots counts toward the maximum size limit of the file share
spiegazione: Option a is correct: snapshots are incremental, so only content changed since the previous snapshot is saved, which reduces both snapshot creation time and storage cost. Option b is correct: snapshots persist until you explicitly delete them or until the file share is deleted; you cannot delete a share and keep its snapshots, because the delete workflow removes them automatically. Option c is correct: Microsoft documents that you can retain share snapshots for up to 10 years (with a limit of 200 snapshots per share). Option d is incorrect: you cannot copy a whole share snapshot to another storage account; you must copy the data file by file by using AzCopy or a similar mechanism. Option e is incorrect: snapshots do not count toward the maximum share size limit, and there is no limit on the total space that snapshots of a share can consume, although storage account limits still apply.
tags: azure files, share snapshots, incremental, retention, limits

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda: Soft delete for file shares is enabled on storage account sa1 with a 90-day retention period. A test file share named 'temp01' was deleted this morning and is now listed in a soft deleted state. Because 'temp01' contained confidential test data, you must remove it permanently today, without waiting for the retention period to expire. Which sequence of actions achieves this?
opzione_a: Undelete 'temp01', disable soft delete on the storage account, and then delete 'temp01' again
opzione_b: Change the soft delete retention period on sa1 to 1 day and wait until the following day
opzione_c: Delete the storage account sa1 and then re-create it with the same name
opzione_d: Apply a CanNotDelete lock to sa1 and then purge the share from the Snapshots blade
spiegazione: Microsoft documents exactly this procedure: to permanently delete a file share that is in a soft deleted state before its expiry time, you must undelete the share, disable soft delete, and then delete the share again (you can re-enable soft delete afterwards to protect the other shares). Option b is wrong: shares deleted before a retention period update expire based on the retention period that was configured when the data was deleted, so lowering the setting to 1 day does not shorten the existing 90-day clock for 'temp01'. Option c is wrong: deleting and re-creating a storage account is destructive to every other share in it and is not the documented method. Option d is wrong: a CanNotDelete lock prevents deletion rather than enabling it, and in fact locks must be removed before snapshots or shares can be deleted; the Snapshots blade has no purge action for soft deleted shares.
tags: azure files, soft delete, undelete, permanent delete, retention

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda: Storage account sa1 hosts several SMB file shares used by different departments. Management asks you to protect the shares against accidental deletion by an administrator, and to keep any deleted share recoverable for the longest period that Azure Files supports. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Level at which soft delete for file shares is configured: [An individual file share | The file service (all file shares in the storage account) | A resource lock on the resource group]
opzione_b: Retention period to configure: [7 days | 90 days | 365 days]
opzione_c: Soft delete can recover an individual file that a user deleted from inside a share: [Yes | No]
opzione_d: Feature to add if individual deleted files must also be recoverable: [Share snapshots | Object replication | Blob versioning]
risposta_corretta: The file service (all file shares in the storage account),365 days,No,Share snapshots
spiegazione: Soft delete for file shares is enabled at the storage account (file service) level, so the setting applies to every file share in the account; it is not a per-share property. The supported retention range is 1 to 365 days, so 365 days is the longest period available (7 days is only the default for new accounts). Soft delete works at the file share level only: undeleting a share restores the share and all of its contents including snapshots, but it cannot recover a single file deleted from within a live share. To recover individual files, Microsoft directs you to share snapshots or Azure file share backup. Object replication and blob versioning are Blob Storage features and do not apply to Azure Files at all. A resource lock is a valid complementary control against deletion but is not where soft delete is configured.
tags: azure files, soft delete, file service, retention, share snapshots

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda:
Storage account sa1 is a StorageV2 account that contains an SMB file share named 'legal'. Soft delete for file shares is enabled on sa1 with a retention period of 14 days, and the 'legal' share currently has 12 share snapshots. Three days ago, a user permanently deleted an important document from inside the 'legal' share; the share itself was never deleted. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is correct.
1. Soft delete allows you to undelete the individual document that the user removed from the 'legal' share.
2. If an administrator deletes the entire 'legal' share and you undelete it within 14 days, the share is restored together with its 12 share snapshots.
3. If you now change the soft delete retention period on sa1 to 30 days, any share that was already deleted before you made the change will be retained for 30 days from its deletion.
opzione_a: Soft delete allows you to undelete the individual document that the user removed from the 'legal' share.
opzione_b: If an administrator deletes the entire 'legal' share and you undelete it within 14 days, the share is restored together with its 12 share snapshots.
opzione_c: If you now change the soft delete retention period on sa1 to 30 days, any share that was already deleted before you made the change will be retained for 30 days from its deletion.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No: soft delete only works at the file share level. It protects against deleting an entire share, not against deletion or modification of individual files inside a live share. To recover a single file, you would use a share snapshot or Azure file share backup. Statement 2 is Yes: Microsoft documents that when you undelete a file share, the file share and all of its contents, including snapshots, are restored to their state prior to deletion. Statement 3 is No: the retention period clock starts when the file share is deleted, and shares deleted before a retention period update expire based on the retention period that was configured at the time that data was deleted. Changing the setting to 30 days affects only shares deleted after the change.
tags: azure files, soft delete, share snapshots, retention, undelete

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda: A scheduled script has been creating share snapshots of the SMB file share 'projects' every hour for several weeks. The script now fails whenever it tries to create a new snapshot, although the share is well below its provisioned size. What should you do to allow new snapshots to be created?
opzione_a: Increase the quota of the 'projects' file share
opzione_b: Delete some of the existing share snapshots
opzione_c: Enable the large file shares feature on the storage account
opzione_d: Move the 'projects' share to the SSD (premium) media tier
spiegazione: Azure Files supports a maximum of 200 share snapshots per file share. After that limit is reached, new snapshot creation fails until older snapshots are deleted, which matches the symptom of an hourly job failing after several weeks. Increasing the share quota is wrong: snapshots do not count toward the maximum size limit of the share, and the stem already states the share is below its provisioned size. Enabling large file shares is wrong: that legacy setting only allowed pay-as-you-go shares to grow beyond 5 TiB; it has no effect on the snapshot count limit. Moving to the SSD (premium) tier is wrong: the 200-snapshot limit applies to every classic file share regardless of media tier, and a share cannot be moved between media tiers in place anyway.
tags: azure files, share snapshots, limits, 200 snapshots

sotto_argomento: Configure snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files
domanda: A compliance team asks you to configure soft delete for the file shares in storage account sa1 so that an accidentally deleted share stays recoverable for as long as Azure Files allows. What is the maximum retention period you can configure?
opzione_a: 7 days
opzione_b: 30 days
opzione_c: 365 days
opzione_d: 3,650 days
spiegazione: Soft delete for Azure file shares supports any retention period between 1 and 365 days, so 365 days is the maximum. 7 days is wrong: that is the default retention period applied to new storage accounts, not the maximum. 30 days is wrong: 30 days is a common default in other Azure services (for example, Recovery Services vault retention) but it is not a limit in Azure Files soft delete. 3,650 days is wrong: 10 years is the maximum period for which you can retain a share snapshot, not a soft delete retention value.
tags: azure files, soft delete, retention, data protection

sotto_argomento: Configure soft delete for blobs and containers
domanda:
You are documenting the behavior of blob soft delete for a general-purpose v2 storage account that does not have a hierarchical namespace.

Which three statements are accurate? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: The soft delete retention period can be set to any value between 1 and 365 days.
opzione_b: Blob soft delete does not protect against deletion of the storage account; an Azure Resource Manager lock on the account resource is required for that.
opzione_c: Data in a page blob that is overwritten by the Put Page operation can be recovered by using blob soft delete.
opzione_d: Soft-deleted data is billed at the same rate as active data.
opzione_e: Shortening the retention period causes objects that were already soft-deleted to expire sooner, based on the new value.
spiegazione:
Correct answers:
- The retention period for soft-deleted objects is specified as a value between 1 and 365 days, exactly as documented on Microsoft Learn.
- Learn states plainly that blob soft delete does not protect against the deletion of a storage account and recommends configuring a lock on the storage account resource for that scenario.
- All soft-deleted data is billed at the same rate as active data; you are only relieved of the charge once the object is permanently deleted after the retention period elapses.

Why the others are wrong:
- Put Page is explicitly listed as "no change" in the soft delete protection matrix. Page blob data that is overwritten or cleared with Put Page isn't saved and isn't recoverable, which is why soft delete cannot undo writes made by an Azure VM to an unmanaged disk.
- An updated retention period applies only to data deleted after the change. Any data deleted before the change remains subject to the retention period that was in effect at the time it was deleted, and attempting to delete a soft-deleted object doesn't affect its expiry time.
tags: blob storage,blob soft delete,retention period,put page,billing,resource lock

sotto_argomento: Configure soft delete for blobs and containers
domanda:
A general-purpose v2 storage account named contosodata7 does not have a hierarchical namespace. Blob soft delete is enabled with a retention period of 14 days. Container soft delete is not enabled, and blob versioning is not enabled.

Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true for this configuration.

1. If a user calls Delete Container on a container in contosodata7, the container and its blobs can be restored within 14 days.
2. If an application overwrites an existing block blob by calling Put Blob, a soft-deleted snapshot capturing the blob's state prior to the write is created automatically.
3. If a user deletes the contosodata7 storage account resource, the blobs it contained can be recovered within 14 days.
opzione_a: If a user calls Delete Container on a container in contosodata7, the container and its blobs can be restored within 14 days.
opzione_b: If an application overwrites an existing block blob by calling Put Blob, a soft-deleted snapshot capturing the blob's state prior to the write is created automatically.
opzione_c: If a user deletes the contosodata7 storage account resource, the blobs it contained can be recovered within 14 days.
spiegazione:
Statement 1 - No: Blob soft delete protects an individual blob, snapshot, or version. The protection matrix on Microsoft Learn lists Delete Container as "No change. Blobs in the deleted container aren't recoverable." Restoring a deleted container requires container soft delete, which is not enabled here.

Statement 2 - Yes: When blob soft delete is enabled on an account without a hierarchical namespace, overwriting a blob with Put Blob, Put Block List, or Copy Blob automatically creates a soft-deleted snapshot of the blob's state prior to the write operation. That snapshot is permanently deleted when the 14-day retention period expires. This behavior applies because versioning is not enabled; with versioning enabled a new version would be created instead.

Statement 3 - No: Learn states explicitly that blob soft delete does not protect against the deletion of a storage account, and that containers and blobs in a deleted account aren't recoverable. To protect the account itself you must configure an Azure Resource Manager lock on the storage account resource.
tags: blob storage,blob soft delete,soft-deleted snapshot,delete container,storage account deletion

sotto_argomento: Configure soft delete for blobs and containers
domanda:
During a cleanup script test, a developer accidentally ran a Delete Container operation against a container named prod-invoices in a general-purpose v2 storage account. The container and all of its blobs disappeared. Management asks you to make sure that a future accidental container deletion can be reversed for at least 30 days.

What should you configure on the storage account?
opzione_a: Container soft delete with a 30-day retention period
opzione_b: Blob soft delete with a 30-day retention period
opzione_c: Blob versioning, and keep all versions
opzione_d: A CanNotDelete Azure Resource Manager lock on the storage account resource
spiegazione:
Correct: Container soft delete is the only in-account feature that retains a deleted container so that it can be recovered with the Restore Container operation. The retention period is configurable between 1 and 365 days, so 30 days is valid. When a container is restored, its blobs and any versions and snapshots are restored with it.

Why the others are wrong:
- Blob soft delete protects only an individual blob, snapshot, or version. Microsoft Learn is explicit that when a container is deleted, the blobs inside it are not recoverable through blob soft delete.
- Blob versioning cannot help you recover from the accidental deletion of a container or a storage account; it only preserves previous versions of blobs whose parent container still exists.
- An ARM lock on the storage account prevents deletion of the account resource, not of containers created within it, because container deletion is a data-plane operation. It also provides no way to recover a container that was already deleted.
tags: blob storage,container soft delete,data protection,restore container

sotto_argomento: Configure soft delete for blobs and containers
domanda:
You are reviewing the Data protection blade of a general-purpose v2 storage account and must record the configurable boundaries of the soft delete features for a design document.

Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Minimum retention period that can be configured for blob soft delete: [1 day | 7 days | 14 days]
opzione_b: Maximum retention period that can be configured for container soft delete: [90 days | 365 days | 3,650 days]
opzione_c: Default retention period for container soft delete: [1 day | 7 days | 30 days]
spiegazione:
Dropdown 1 - 1 day: When you enable blob soft delete you specify a retention period for deleted objects of between 1 and 365 days, so 1 day is the minimum you can configure. 7 days is only the minimum retention period that Microsoft recommends, not a hard floor, and 14 days is not a boundary of the feature.

Dropdown 2 - 365 days: Container soft delete uses the same 1 to 365 day range as blob soft delete, so 365 days is the maximum. 90 days is the Cold tier minimum retention period, not a soft delete boundary, and 3,650 days is not a valid soft delete value.

Dropdown 3 - 7 days: Microsoft Learn states that the default retention period for container soft delete is seven days and recommends a minimum of seven days, increasing it as needed based on data volume and how long it may take to detect a data-loss event.
tags: blob storage,blob soft delete,container soft delete,retention period,data protection

sotto_argomento: Configure storage account encryption
domanda: You are preparing to protect a storage account with a customer-managed key held in an Azure key vault. Select the correct value for each requirement.
opzione_a: Key type and key sizes supported for storage account encryption: [RSA 2048/3072/4096 | EC-P256/EC-P384 | AES-128/AES-256]
opzione_b: Minimum key permissions the managed identity needs on the key: [get + wrapKey + unwrapKey | get + list + create | sign + verify + decrypt]
opzione_c: Managed identity type required when you configure customer-managed keys at the time you create the storage account: [System-assigned | User-assigned | Either type]
opzione_d: Configuration that makes Azure Storage pick up new key versions automatically: [Omit the key version | Specify the full key version URI | Assign the Key Vault Contributor role]
risposta_corretta: RSA 2048/3072/4096,get + wrapKey + unwrapKey,User-assigned,Omit the key version
spiegazione: RSA 2048/3072/4096: Azure Storage encryption supports RSA and RSA-HSM keys of sizes 2048, 3072, and 4096. EC keys are not supported, and AES is the symmetric algorithm used for the data itself rather than a key type you can place in the vault for this purpose. get + wrapKey + unwrapKey: the managed identity associated with the storage account must have at minimum the wrapKey, unwrapKey, and get permissions, because Azure Storage wraps the account encryption key with the customer-managed key and must unwrap it for read and write operations. get + list + create and sign + verify + decrypt are real Key Vault key permissions but they are not the ones required here. User-assigned: when you configure customer-managed keys at the time that you create a storage account, you must use a user-assigned managed identity, because a system-assigned identity does not exist until the account has been created and therefore cannot be granted key permissions in advance. Only when you configure customer-managed keys on an existing storage account can you use either a user-assigned or a system-assigned managed identity. Omit the key version: to automatically update to a new key version, omit the key version when you enable encryption with customer-managed keys. Azure Storage then checks the key vault daily for a new version and uses the latest one. Specifying the full key version URI pins the account to that version and forces manual updates, and a Key Vault rotation policy rotates the key in the vault but does not by itself change how the storage account references the key.
tags: customer-managed keys, managed identity, key rotation, key vault, storage encryption

sotto_argomento: Configure storage account encryption
domanda:
A general-purpose v2 storage account named storage2 is configured to use a customer-managed key stored in a key vault named kv1. The key vault and the storage account are in the same Microsoft Entra tenant. Access to the key is authorized through the system-assigned managed identity of storage2, and the customer-managed key configuration was saved without specifying a key version. The storage account was created by using the Azure portal with default settings and hosts blob, file, queue, and table data.

Evaluate each of the following statements:
1. If an administrator disables the key in kv1, client requests to read blob data from storage2 fail with error code 403 (Forbidden).
2. Data stored in the Queue and Table services of storage2 is automatically protected by the customer-managed key.
3. After a new version of the key is created in kv1, you must manually update storage2 to reference the new key version URI.
opzione_a: If an administrator disables the key in kv1, client requests to read blob data from storage2 fail with error code 403 (Forbidden).
opzione_b: Data stored in the Queue and Table services of storage2 is automatically protected by the customer-managed key.
opzione_c: After a new version of the key is created in kv1, you must manually update storage2 to reference the new key version URI.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: disabling the key in the key vault is the documented way to revoke access to a storage account that uses customer-managed keys. After the key has been disabled, clients cannot call operations that read from or write to a resource or its metadata, and those operations fail with error code 403 (Forbidden) for all users, including Get Blob. Restoring access to the key restores the operations. Statement 2 - No: data stored in Queue and Table storage is not automatically protected by a customer-managed key when customer-managed keys are enabled for the storage account. Queue and table protection can only be configured at the time that you create the storage account, which was not done here. By contrast, data in Blob storage and Azure Files is always protected by the customer-managed key once it is configured for the account. Statement 3 - No: because the key version was omitted when customer-managed keys were configured, Azure Storage checks the key vault daily for a new version of the key and automatically uses the latest version. Manual updating of the key version URI is required only when a specific key version was explicitly pinned in the configuration. Because the check happens only once per day, you should wait 24 hours after rotating a key before disabling the older version.
tags: customer-managed keys, key revocation, queues and tables, key version, storage encryption

sotto_argomento: Configure storage account encryption
domanda: A regulator requires that all existing and future data in a general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1 be encrypted twice, once at the service level and once at the infrastructure level, with two different algorithms and two different keys. The account was created 18 months ago without infrastructure encryption and currently holds 4 TB of blob data. What should you do?
opzione_a: On the Encryption blade of storage1, set Enable infrastructure encryption to Enabled.
opzione_b: Create a new general-purpose v2 storage account with infrastructure encryption enabled and migrate the data from storage1 to the new account.
opzione_c: Configure a customer-managed key for storage1 and add a second key in the key vault to act as the infrastructure-level key.
opzione_d: Create an encryption scope on storage1 with infrastructure encryption enabled and apply it to the existing containers.
spiegazione: Correct: To enable infrastructure encryption for a storage account, you must configure the account to use infrastructure encryption at the time that you create the account. Infrastructure encryption cannot be enabled or disabled after the account has been created, so the only way to satisfy the requirement for the existing 4 TB is to create a new account (general-purpose v2, premium block blob, premium page blob, or premium file shares) with infrastructure encryption enabled and migrate the data. Option A is wrong because the portal exposes Enable infrastructure encryption on the Encryption tab only while creating the account; on an existing account the Encryption blade lets you verify the setting but not change it. Option C is wrong because customer-managed keys apply to service-level encryption only. Infrastructure-level encryption always relies on Microsoft-managed keys and always uses a separate key, so you cannot supply your own second key. Option D is wrong on two counts: a default encryption scope must be specified for a container at the time the container is created, so it cannot be applied to existing containers, and even if new containers were created, applying a scope does not re-encrypt the 4 TB of data that already exists.
tags: infrastructure encryption, double encryption, storage encryption, account creation, compliance

sotto_argomento: Configure storage account encryption
domanda: A multitenant SaaS application stores each customer's blobs in the same storage account and uses encryption scopes to create secure boundaries between them. Which statements about encryption scopes are true? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: An encryption scope can be protected with either a Microsoft-managed key or a customer-managed key stored in Azure Key Vault.
opzione_b: The infrastructure encryption setting for an encryption scope cannot be changed after the scope is created.
opzione_c: A default encryption scope can be assigned to a container at any time after the container has been created.
opzione_d: An encryption scope can be deleted from the storage account when it is no longer needed.
opzione_e: If infrastructure encryption is enabled at the account level, every encryption scope created in that account automatically uses infrastructure encryption.
spiegazione: Correct: (A) When you define an encryption scope you can specify whether it is protected with a Microsoft-managed key or with a customer-managed key in Azure Key Vault, and different scopes in the same account can use different key types. You can also switch a scope between the two key types at any time. (B) The infrastructure encryption setting for an encryption scope cannot be changed after the scope is created; if the account does not already have infrastructure encryption, you can only opt in for a scope at the time you create that scope. (E) If infrastructure encryption is enabled for an account, then any encryption scope created on that account automatically uses infrastructure encryption. Incorrect: (C) A default encryption scope must be specified for a container at the time that the container is created; it cannot be added to an existing container afterwards. (D) It is not possible to delete an encryption scope. You can only disable it, after which read and write operations that use the scope fail with HTTP 403 (Forbidden). Note also that an enabled scope is billed for a minimum of 30 days.
tags: encryption scopes, infrastructure encryption, customer-managed keys, blob storage, multitenant

sotto_argomento: Configure storage account encryption
domanda: A security auditor asks you to describe how data at rest is protected in a general-purpose v2 storage account that was created five minutes ago and has not been modified since. Which statement is accurate?
opzione_a: Data is automatically encrypted with 256-bit AES encryption, and Azure Storage encryption cannot be disabled.
opzione_b: Data is encrypted only after an administrator turns on Azure Storage Service Encryption from the Encryption blade of the account.
opzione_c: Data is encrypted with 128-bit AES encryption by default, and you can upgrade the account to 256-bit AES encryption.
opzione_d: Only blob and file data is encrypted by default; queue and table data must be protected by using client-side encryption.
spiegazione: Correct: Azure Storage uses service-side encryption to automatically encrypt data when it is persisted to the cloud. Data is encrypted and decrypted transparently using 256-bit AES encryption, it is FIPS 140-2 compliant, encryption is enabled for all storage accounts, and Azure Storage encryption cannot be disabled. There is no additional cost. Option B is wrong because encryption is on by default and there is no switch to enable or disable it; the Encryption blade lets you choose the key management model (Microsoft-managed versus customer-managed keys), not whether encryption occurs. Option C is wrong because the cipher strength is 256-bit AES from the start and is not configurable. Option D is wrong because all Azure Storage resources are encrypted, including blobs, disks, files, queues, and tables, and all object metadata is encrypted as well; client-side encryption is an optional additional capability, not a requirement for queues and tables.
tags: storage encryption, encryption at rest, aes-256, microsoft-managed keys, sse

sotto_argomento: Configure storage account encryption
domanda: Your compliance team requires that an existing general-purpose v2 storage account be encrypted with a customer-managed key that your organization stores in Azure Key Vault. Which configuration must be in place on the key vault before you can enable customer-managed keys on the storage account?
opzione_a: Soft delete and purge protection must both be enabled on the key vault.
opzione_b: The key vault must use the vault access policy permission model rather than Azure RBAC.
opzione_c: The key vault must reside in the same region and the same subscription as the storage account.
opzione_d: The key vault must contain an elliptic curve (EC) key of at least 256 bits.
spiegazione: Correct: The key vault or managed HSM that stores the customer-managed key must have both soft delete and purge protection enabled. This prevents a deleted or purged key from permanently orphaning the data that its wrapped account encryption key protects. Option B is wrong because the documented requirement is simply that the managed identity be granted the get, wrapKey, and unwrapKey permissions on the key; the permission model itself is not dictated. Option C is wrong because the documentation explicitly states that the storage account and the key vault or managed HSM can be in different Microsoft Entra tenants, regions, and subscriptions. Option D is wrong because Azure Storage encryption supports RSA and RSA-HSM keys of sizes 2048, 3072, and 4096 only; elliptic curve keys are not supported for storage account encryption.
tags: customer-managed keys, azure key vault, soft delete, purge protection, storage encryption

sotto_argomento: Configure storage tiers
domanda:
Your organization keeps long-term backups in the Archive tier of a GRS general-purpose v2 storage account. You are preparing a runbook that describes how operators retrieve archived data during an incident.

Which three statements about blob rehydration are accurate? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A standard-priority rehydration request might take up to 15 hours to complete for objects under 10 GB in size.
opzione_b: While a standard-priority rehydration is pending, you can raise the rehydration priority to High, but you cannot lower a pending High-priority request back to Standard.
opzione_c: After a Set Blob Tier rehydration request is initiated, you can cancel it while it's still in progress.
opzione_d: Starting with service version 2021-02-12, you can rehydrate an archived blob by copying it to a different storage account, as long as the destination account is in the same region as the source account.
opzione_e: A blob snapshot or a previous version that is in the Archive tier can be rehydrated directly to the Hot tier by calling Set Blob Tier on it.
spiegazione:
Correct answers:
- Microsoft Learn defines standard priority as processed in the order received, possibly taking up to 15 hours to complete for objects under 10 GB. High priority might complete in less than one hour for objects under 10 GB.
- Learn states that while a standard-priority rehydration is pending you can update the setting to High to rehydrate the blob more quickly, and that the rehydration priority setting can't be lowered from High to Standard for a pending operation.
- Before service version 2021-02-12 rehydration by copy was supported only within the same storage account. From 2021-02-12 onward you can copy to a different storage account provided it's in the same region, which lets you segregate production and backup data.

Why the others are wrong:
- Once a Set Blob Tier request is initiated, it can't be canceled. During the operation the blob's access tier continues to show as archived until rehydration completes.
- Snapshots and previous versions cannot be rehydrated back to an online tier directly. To access data from an archived snapshot or previous version, you must copy it to a new blob in an online tier with the Copy Blob operation.
tags: blob storage,archive tier,rehydration priority,set blob tier,copy blob,snapshots

sotto_argomento: Configure storage tiers
domanda:
Fabrikam must retain diagnostic exports in a general-purpose v2 storage account that is configured for geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS). The exports are read only two or three times a year, but each read must return the first byte within milliseconds. Fabrikam wants the lowest possible storage capacity cost that still meets the latency requirement, and new blobs uploaded to the account must land in that tier automatically without the upload code specifying a tier.

Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Access tier to apply to the export blobs: [Cool | Cold | Archive]
opzione_b: Minimum recommended retention period before an early deletion penalty applies to those blobs: [30 days | 90 days | 180 days]
opzione_c: Default account access tier setting to configure on the storage account: [Cold | Archive | Cannot be configured for this tier]
spiegazione:
Dropdown 1 - Cold: The Cold tier is an online tier optimized for data that is rarely accessed but still requires fast retrieval, with lower storage costs than Cool. Cool also meets the millisecond latency requirement but costs more to store, so Cold is the lowest-cost option that qualifies. Archive is wrong twice over: it's an offline tier with retrieval latency measured in hours, and it isn't supported on GZRS accounts at all.

Dropdown 2 - 90 days: Data in the Cold tier should be stored for a minimum of 90 days or a prorated early deletion charge applies. 30 days is the Cool tier minimum and 180 days is the Archive tier minimum.

Dropdown 3 - Cold: The default account access tier setting determines the online tier in which a new blob is created when the upload doesn't specify one, and it can be set to Hot, Cool, or Cold. Setting it to Cold satisfies the requirement that new blobs land in the correct tier automatically. The Archive tier is explicitly not supported as the default access tier for a storage account, and the setting is certainly configurable for Cold, so the third option is incorrect.
tags: blob storage,access tiers,cold tier,default access tier,gzrs,early deletion

sotto_argomento: Configure storage tiers
domanda:
A legal team needs to analyze a 6-GB block blob named case4471.vhdx that was moved to the Archive tier 40 days ago. The blob must be readable in an online tier, but your manager insists that the operation must not trigger the 180-day early deletion fee on the archived data.

Which action should you perform?
opzione_a: Call Set Blob Tier on case4471.vhdx and specify the Hot tier with a high rehydrate priority.
opzione_b: Call Copy Blob to copy case4471.vhdx to a new blob name in the Hot tier, leaving the source blob in the Archive tier.
opzione_c: Add a lifecycle management rule with a tierToCool action and daysAfterModificationGreaterThan set to 0.
opzione_d: Create a snapshot of case4471.vhdx and call Set Blob Tier on the snapshot to move it to the Hot tier.
spiegazione:
Correct: Copying an archived blob to a new blob in an online tier leaves the source blob unmodified in the Archive tier, so the early deletion fee is never assessed. Microsoft Learn recommends Copy Blob for exactly this reason and notes the copy must target a different blob name or a different container. You are billed for data read transactions, data retrieval, and capacity for both blobs.

Why the others are wrong:
- Set Blob Tier changes the tier of the archived blob itself. Because only 40 of the required 180 days have elapsed, this incurs an early deletion fee equivalent to the remaining 140 days.
- Lifecycle management policies cannot be used to rehydrate blobs from the Archive tier to an online tier at all, so the rule would have no effect on the archived blob.
- Snapshots aren't supported for blobs in the Archive tier, so the snapshot cannot be created. Learn also states that snapshots and previous versions cannot be rehydrated directly.
tags: blob storage,archive tier,rehydration,copy blob,early deletion penalty

sotto_argomento: Configure storage tiers
domanda:
A storage administrator reports a problem with a general-purpose v2 storage account named contosoarchive1 that is configured for geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS). When she selects a block blob in a container and opens the Change tier pane, only Hot, Cool, and Cold are offered. Attempts to set the Archive tier by using Az PowerShell also fail.

What is the reason that the Archive tier is unavailable?
opzione_a: The Archive tier is supported only for storage accounts that are configured for LRS, GRS, or RA-GRS.
opzione_b: The Archive tier can be assigned only as the default account access tier and never on an individual blob.
opzione_c: A blob must first be moved to the Cold tier and remain there for 90 days before it is eligible for the Archive tier.
opzione_d: Blob versioning must be disabled on the storage account before any blob can be moved to the Archive tier.
spiegazione:
Correct: Only storage accounts configured for LRS, GRS, or RA-GRS support moving blobs to the Archive tier. Microsoft Learn explicitly states that the Archive tier isn't supported for ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS accounts, which is why the option is unavailable on a GZRS account.

Why the others are wrong:
- The reverse is true: Archive is set per blob and is explicitly NOT supported as the default account access tier (only Hot, Cool, or Cold can be the account default).
- There is no requirement to stage a blob through the Cold tier. Set Blob Tier can move a blob directly from Hot to Archive; the tier-change matrix on Learn lists Hot to archive as a supported transition.
- Blob versioning has no bearing on Archive eligibility. Versions of a block blob can themselves be moved to the Archive tier with Set Blob Tier.

sotto_argomento: Configure storage tiers
domanda:
Contoso archives quarterly compliance exports in a general-purpose v2 storage account. The exports are rarely read, but when auditors request one it must be returned in milliseconds, so the operations team moves the export blobs to the Cold access tier. You must document the number of days a blob must remain in the Cold tier before it can be deleted or moved to another tier without incurring an early deletion penalty.

What is the minimum recommended data retention period for the Cold tier?
opzione_a: 30 days
opzione_b: 90 days
opzione_c: 180 days
opzione_d: 365 days
spiegazione:
Correct: 90 days. Microsoft Learn states that data in the Cold tier should be stored for a minimum of 90 days; if a blob is deleted, overwritten, or moved to a different tier before 90 days elapse, a prorated early deletion charge applies.

Why the others are wrong:
- 30 days is the minimum recommended retention period for the Cool tier, not the Cold tier. This is the classic confusion between the two adjacent online tiers.
- 180 days is the minimum retention period for the Archive tier, which is an offline tier.
- 365 days is not a retention period for any access tier. It is the maximum retention period you can configure for blob or container soft delete, which is an unrelated data protection feature.
tags: blob storage,access tiers,cold tier,early deletion,minimum retention

sotto_argomento: Configure stored access policies
domanda: Case study: Fabrikam operates storage account fabstor1, which holds a blob container named exports. Three internal applications authorize to fabstor1 by using key1, and they run continuously. An external partner was given a service SAS for exports that references a stored access policy named partner-read; the policy grants Read and List and expires in six months. Fabrikam's security team reports that the partner's SAS URI was leaked in a shared mailbox. You must block the partner's access immediately, and the three internal applications must continue running without any change or outage. What should you do?
opzione_a: Regenerate key1 and key2 on fabstor1.
opzione_b: Delete the stored access policy named partner-read from the exports container.
opzione_c: Configure a SAS expiration policy on fabstor1 with an upper limit of one hour and the Block action.
opzione_d: Set the AllowSharedKeyAccess property of fabstor1 to false to disallow Shared Key authorization.
spiegazione: Deleting the stored access policy revokes every SAS bound to it immediately, because Azure Storage can no longer locate the policy named in the signedIdentifier field and denies the request. It affects only the partner's token, so the three internal applications that authorize with key1 are untouched. This is precisely why Microsoft recommends using a stored access policy with a service SAS: it lets you revoke permissions without regenerating the account keys. Regenerating key1 and key2 would revoke the partner's SAS, but it would also cause all three internal applications to fail authorization until they are updated with a new key, which violates the no-outage requirement. A SAS expiration policy only constrains the validity interval of newly created signatures; the Block action denies out-of-policy tokens going forward but is an account-wide control that would also affect signatures the internal applications create, and it is not the targeted revocation mechanism for a policy-bound SAS. Disallowing Shared Key authorization would break the partner's SAS but would simultaneously break all three internal applications that rely on key1. Note that when re-creating a policy later you should use a different signed identifier, because re-creating a policy with exactly the same name would make the leaked SAS valid again.
tags: stored access policy,revocation,service sas,shared key,case study

sotto_argomento: Configure stored access policies
domanda: A service SAS for a blob container references a stored access policy that has the signed identifier reports-read. You must revoke every SAS token bound to that policy while leaving the storage account access keys untouched. Which actions achieve the goal? Each correct answer presents a complete solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Delete the stored access policy named reports-read from the container.
opzione_b: Modify the stored access policy so that its expiry time is a value in the past.
opzione_c: Replace the stored access policy with one that uses a different signed identifier.
opzione_d: Change the container's public access level to Private (no anonymous access).
opzione_e: Add a signedIp (sip) restriction to the SAS tokens that were already distributed.
spiegazione: Deleting the stored access policy revokes the SAS, because Azure Storage can no longer locate the policy named in the signedIdentifier field and denies the request. Changing the expiry time to a value in the past causes any associated signatures to expire. Renaming the policy by changing the signed identifier breaks the association between the existing signatures and the policy, which also revokes them. All three take effect immediately for every SAS bound to the policy, and none of them require regenerating the account keys. Changing the container's public access level is wrong because that setting governs anonymous access only; a SAS is authorized by its signature and keeps working. Adding a signedIp value to tokens that were already distributed is wrong because a SAS token is immutable once signed: altering any field invalidates the signature, and you cannot modify a copy that is already in someone else's hands.

sotto_argomento: Configure stored access policies
domanda: Your security team requires that any delegated access token issued for a blob container can be revoked at any time without regenerating the storage account access keys, because dozens of internal applications depend on those keys. Which approach meets the requirement?
opzione_a: Issue an account SAS and reduce the expiry time to one hour.
opzione_b: Issue a service SAS that references a stored access policy defined on the container.
opzione_c: Issue an ad hoc service SAS and rely on a near-term expiry time.
opzione_d: Enable a SAS expiration policy on the storage account with the Block action.
spiegazione: Stored access policies give you the option to revoke permissions for a service SAS without having to regenerate the storage account keys: you can delete the policy, change its signed identifier, or move its expiry time into the past, and the change immediately affects every SAS associated with it. An account SAS cannot reference a stored access policy (stored access policies are not supported for account SAS or user delegation SAS), so a short expiry is the only control and it does not provide revocation. An ad hoc service SAS with a near-term expiry is a good mitigation but still cannot be revoked without regenerating the key. A SAS expiration policy with Block enforces an upper limit on the validity interval for newly created signatures; it is not a per-token revocation mechanism and would not selectively revoke one partner's token.

sotto_argomento: Configure stored access policies
domanda: Storage account sa1 contains a blob container named data. A stored access policy named policy1 is defined on data, and several service SAS tokens were issued that reference policy1 through the signedIdentifier (si) field. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true. 1) Deleting policy1 immediately revokes every service SAS token that references it. 2) You can specify the expiry time on policy1 and also specify a different expiry time on the SAS token, so that the value on the token overrides the policy. 3) You can associate an account SAS with policy1 so that the account SAS can also be revoked by deleting the policy.
opzione_a: Deleting policy1 immediately revokes every service SAS token that references it.
opzione_b: You can specify the expiry time on policy1 and also specify a different expiry time on the SAS token, so that the value on the token overrides the policy.
opzione_c: You can associate an account SAS with policy1 so that the account SAS can also be revoked by deleting the policy.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes: deleting or modifying the stored access policy immediately affects all shared access signatures associated with it, and if Azure Storage can't locate the policy named in the signature, the client can't access the resource. Statement 2 is No: you must specify the start time, expiry time, and permissions either entirely on the SAS token or entirely on the stored access policy; you can't specify the same parameter in both places, and signedExpiry and signedPermissions must be omitted from the URI if they are set in the associated policy. There is no override behaviour. Statement 3 is No: stored access policies are not supported for an account SAS (nor for a user delegation SAS); an account SAS must always be an ad hoc SAS, and the only way to revoke it immediately is to regenerate the account key that signed it.
tags: stored access policy,service sas,account sas,revocation,signed identifier

sotto_argomento: Configure stored access policies
domanda: Which statements correctly describe stored access policies in Azure Storage? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: A stored access policy can be defined on a blob container, a file share, a queue, or a table.
opzione_b: A maximum of five stored access policies can be set on a container at one time.
opzione_c: A stored access policy can be associated with an account SAS to enable revocation of that account SAS.
opzione_d: Creating or updating a stored access policy can take up to 30 seconds to take effect, and requests can fail with status code 403 during that interval.
opzione_e: Associating a user delegation SAS with a stored access policy extends the maximum validity of the SAS beyond seven days.
spiegazione: Blob containers, file shares, queues, and tables all support stored access policies. The documented limit is five access policies per container, table, queue, or share at one time; exceeding it returns status code 400 (Bad Request). When you create or update a policy, the change might take up to 30 seconds to take effect, and during that interval requests made with an associated SAS might fail with status code 403 (Forbidden). Option C is wrong: stored access policies are explicitly not supported for an account SAS, which must always be an ad hoc SAS. Option E is wrong for two reasons: stored access policies are not supported for a user delegation SAS either, and a user delegation SAS has a hard maximum expiry interval of seven days that nothing can extend.
tags: stored access policy,limits,account sas,user delegation sas,propagation

sotto_argomento: Configure stored access policies
domanda: While planning delegated access to a blob container, you decide to group your service SAS tokens under stored access policies. What is the maximum number of stored access policies that you can set on a single container at one time?
spiegazione: You can set a maximum of five access policies on a container, table, queue, or share at one time; each SignedIdentifier element with its unique Id corresponds to one policy. Attempting to set more than five at once causes the service to return status code 400 (Bad Request). 1 is wrong: multiple policies per container are explicitly supported. 10 and 50 are wrong: they are plausible-looking but incorrect limits; the documented limit is five per resource.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a container
domanda:
You are creating a blob container in the Azure portal to hold web server logs. The New container pane rejects the name you type.

Which container name is valid?
opzione_a: Archive-Logs
opzione_b: ab
opzione_c: archive-logs-2026
opzione_d: archive_logs
spiegazione:
Correct: archive-logs-2026 satisfies every rule. Microsoft Learn states that a container name must be lowercase, must start with a letter or number, may contain only letters, numbers, and the dash (-) character, and must be between 3 and 63 characters long.

Why the others are wrong:
- Archive-Logs contains uppercase letters. Container names must be all lowercase.
- ab is only 2 characters. The minimum length is 3 characters.
- archive_logs uses an underscore. Only letters, numbers, and the dash character are permitted.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda:
Case study: Fabrikam runs a Windows Server 2019 file server named FS1 in its Boston datacenter. FS1 hosts departmental shares on D:, a directly attached 1.5 TiB NTFS volume that is now 95 percent full. Most of the data has not been opened in over a year, but users must still be able to browse it. Fabrikam wants to centralize the file data in an Azure file share, stop purchasing additional disks for FS1, and keep Boston users accessing their data at LAN speed through the existing UNC paths and NTFS permissions. Fabrikam's ISP blocks outbound TCP port 445 and this cannot be changed. Fabrikam has no ExpressRoute circuit and does not want to deploy a site-to-site VPN.

Which solution meets Fabrikam's requirements?
opzione_a: On FS1, mount the Azure file share with net use, then re-share the mounted drive to Boston users over SMB
