opzione_b: Install the Azure File Sync agent on FS1, register FS1 with a Storage Sync Service, create a sync group whose cloud endpoint is the Azure file share and whose server endpoint is D:\, and enable cloud tiering on the server endpoint
opzione_c: Migrate the data to an NFS Azure file share and mount it on FS1, then re-share it to Boston users over SMB
opzione_d: Create a private endpoint for the storage account and have Boston users map a drive directly to the Azure file share
spiegazione: Azure File Sync is the solution Microsoft recommends for exactly this scenario. It turns FS1 into a fast local cache of the Azure file share: the namespace and hot files stay on D: while cloud tiering replaces cool file content with reparse points, freeing local capacity so no new disks are needed. Users keep the existing UNC paths and Windows ACLs, which Azure File Sync preserves. Critically, the agent communicates with the Storage Sync Service and the Azure file share over HTTPS on port 443, so a blocked outbound port 445 is not an obstacle. Option a is wrong: mounting the share with net use is an SMB client operation that requires outbound TCP 445, which the ISP blocks. Option c is wrong: NFS Azure file shares are not supported on Windows clients, and NFS shares are not reachable over an unrestricted public endpoint. Option d is wrong: a private endpoint gives the storage account a private IP inside an Azure virtual network, but Boston clients would still need a VPN or ExpressRoute to reach that address, and they would still need port 445 for SMB, both of which the scenario excludes.
tags: azure file sync, cloud tiering, port 445, sync group, server endpoint, hybrid file server

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: A Linux-based analytics workload running on VMs in VNet1 must store data on an Azure file share that is mounted with NFS 4.1. The share must not be reachable from the public internet, and the mount target must keep a static IP address inside VNet1. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Storage account kind and SKU: [StorageV2 with Standard_LRS | FileStorage with Premium_LRS | FileStorage with Premium_GRS]
opzione_b: Protocol to select when you create the file share: [SMB | NFS]
opzione_c: TCP port the Linux clients must be able to reach: [443 | 445 | 2049]
opzione_d: Network configuration to use: [Enable access from all networks on the public endpoint | Create a private endpoint for the storage account in VNet1 | Add an IP address rule for the VM public IPs]
risposta_corretta: FileStorage with Premium_LRS,NFS,2049,Create a private endpoint for the storage account in VNet1
spiegazione: NFS Azure file shares require the SSD (premium) media tier, which means the FileStorage account kind, and only LRS or ZRS redundancy is supported, so FileStorage with Premium_LRS is correct. Premium_GRS is not a valid option because geo-redundancy is not available for NFS shares. StorageV2 with Standard_LRS places shares on the HDD (standard) tier, which does not support NFS. An individual Azure file share supports either SMB or NFS but never both, so NFS must be selected at share creation time. NFS uses TCP 2049 (445 is SMB and 443 is FileREST/HTTPS). NFS shares are never accessible over an unrestricted public endpoint; you must use a private endpoint or a service endpoint. Because the requirement calls for a static IP address, a private endpoint is the correct choice, as service endpoints do not guarantee a stable underlying IP. IP address rules are not supported for NFS Azure file shares.
tags: azure files, nfs, private endpoint, port 2049, filestorage, premium

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: During a hybrid file server rollout, you are adding a server endpoint for E:\Departments on a registered Windows Server 2022 instance. Volume E: is a 500 GiB directly attached NTFS volume formatted with a 4 KiB cluster size. The business requires that at least 20 percent of volume E: always remains free, and that files not accessed for 30 days are moved to the cloud to free local capacity. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Volume free space policy to configure: [10% | 20% | 80%]
opzione_b: Date policy to configure: [7 days | 30 days | 365 days]
opzione_c: Smallest file size that cloud tiering will tier on this volume: [4 KiB | 8 KiB | 64 KiB]
opzione_d: Policy that takes precedence when both are configured: [Date policy | Volume free space policy]
spiegazione: The volume free space policy specifies the percentage of the volume that Azure File Sync keeps free, so requiring at least 20 percent free means setting the policy to 20%. The date policy tiers cool files that have not been accessed (read or written) for the specified number of days, so 30 days matches the requirement. The minimum file size eligible for cloud tiering is calculated as 2x the volume cluster size, with an absolute floor of 8 KiB. On a 4 KiB cluster the calculation gives 8 KiB, so 8 KiB is correct; 4 KiB is below the documented absolute minimum, and 64 KiB would be the threshold for a 32 KiB cluster size. When both policies are configured, the volume free space policy takes precedence: Azure File Sync tiers files as needed to reach the free space target regardless of recent access, so the date policy cannot prevent that tiering.
tags: azure file sync, cloud tiering, volume free space policy, date policy, cluster size, minimum tier size

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: FS1 is a Windows Server 2022 file server with an Azure File Sync server endpoint on D:\Data. Cloud tiering is enabled on the server endpoint. The operations team backs up D:\Data by using a third-party file-level backup agent installed on FS1. During a restore test, several recovered files turn out to contain only reparse-point stubs rather than real data. You must give the team a supported way to back up this data set with an on-premises backup product. What should you recommend?
opzione_a: Perform the backups from another server in the same sync group that has cloud tiering disabled
opzione_b: Enable bare-metal restore for FS1 so that tiered files are captured in the system image
opzione_c: Set the volume free space policy on FS1 to 99 percent so that all files are tiered before each backup runs
opzione_d: Configure the backup agent to skip any file that has the offline attribute set
spiegazione: Microsoft states that you should not use solutions that directly back up a server endpoint or a VM containing a server endpoint when cloud tiering is enabled, because tiered files are backed up as stubs. If you prefer an on-premises backup solution, perform the backups on a server in the sync group that has cloud tiering disabled so that the full data set is present locally. Option b is wrong: bare-metal restore, VM restore, and system restore are explicitly not supported when cloud tiering is enabled and can cause unexpected results. Option c is wrong: tiering more files makes the problem worse, since even more files would be backed up as stubs. Option d is wrong: skipping offline files would silently exclude the tiered data from the backup, producing an incomplete backup rather than a usable one.
tags: azure file sync, cloud tiering, backup, tiered files, reparse point

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: You plan to create an Azure File Sync server endpoint with cloud tiering enabled on a new Windows Server 2022 file server. Which requirements must be met for this configuration to be supported? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: The path used by the server endpoint must be on a directly attached volume that is formatted with NTFS
opzione_b: The server endpoint path must not be on the Windows system volume
opzione_c: The Azure file share used as the cloud endpoint must use the NFS protocol
opzione_d: The volume must be formatted with ReFS so that the StorageSync.sys filter can create reparse points
opzione_e: The Windows Server instance must be registered with a Storage Sync Service before you can add the server endpoint
spiegazione: Option a is correct: Azure File Sync is supported only on directly attached NTFS volumes. Option b is correct: cloud tiering is explicitly not supported on the Windows system volume. Option e is correct: server endpoints represent paths on registered servers, so you must install the agent and register the server with a Storage Sync Service before you can create a server endpoint in a sync group. Option c is incorrect and is the classic misconception: Azure File Sync supports only SMB Azure file shares. NFS shares (and file shares created with the Microsoft.FileShares resource provider, which are NFS only) are not supported as cloud endpoints. Option d is incorrect: ReFS, FAT, FAT32, and other file systems are not supported; only NTFS is, and it is NTFS that stores the cloud tiering reparse points.
tags: azure file sync, cloud tiering, server endpoint, ntfs, system volume, prerequisites

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: SyncGroup1 belongs to Storage Sync Service SSS1 and uses the Azure file share 'projects' as its cloud endpoint. A server endpoint on FS1 already syncs D:\Projects with that cloud endpoint. A second file server, FS2, must now serve exactly the same 'projects' data set to a different office. What should you do?
opzione_a: Add a server endpoint on FS2 to SyncGroup1
opzione_b: Create SyncGroup2 in SSS1, set its cloud endpoint to the 'projects' share, and add a server endpoint on FS2
opzione_c: Add a second cloud endpoint to SyncGroup1 that points to the 'projects' share, and add a server endpoint on FS2
opzione_d: Register FS2 with a second Storage Sync Service and create a sync group there that uses the 'projects' share
spiegazione: A sync group contains exactly one cloud endpoint (the Azure file share) and one or more server endpoints, and all endpoints in the sync group stay in sync with each other. To have FS2 serve the same data, you simply add another server endpoint on FS2 to the existing SyncGroup1. Option b is wrong: a sync group cannot use a cloud endpoint (Azure file share) that is already configured in another sync group. Option c is wrong: a sync group supports only a single cloud endpoint, so you cannot add a second one. Option d is wrong for two reasons: the 'projects' share is already a cloud endpoint in SyncGroup1 and cannot be reused in another sync group, and a server or cluster can be registered with only one Storage Sync Service at a time.
tags: azure file sync, sync group, cloud endpoint, server endpoint, topology

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: On an Azure File Sync server endpoint, cloud tiering is enabled with a volume free space policy of 20 percent and a date policy of 60 days. An administrator observes that files accessed only two days ago are being tiered to the cloud. Which statement explains this behavior?
opzione_a: The volume free space policy takes precedence over the date policy, so files are tiered as needed to reach the free space target regardless of how recently they were accessed
opzione_b: The date policy takes precedence, so the volume free space policy is ignored whenever a date policy is configured
opzione_c: When both policies are configured, Azure File Sync tiers only files that satisfy both policies at the same time
opzione_d: Cloud tiering ignores both policies during the first 60 days after the server endpoint is created
spiegazione: Microsoft documents that the volume free space policy takes precedence over the date policy: Azure File Sync tiers files as needed to reach the configured free space target, even if those files were accessed recently, selecting the coolest files first based on the heatmap. Option b is wrong: the precedence is the opposite, and the volume free space policy is never ignored. Option c is wrong: the policies are not evaluated as an AND condition; either policy on its own can cause a file to be tiered. Option d is wrong: no such grace period exists. Cloud tiering evaluates policy compliance approximately every 60 minutes, and during initial upload the volume free space policy still applies in low disk space mode.
tags: azure file sync, cloud tiering, volume free space policy, date policy

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda:
Storage Sync Service SSS1 is deployed in the East US region. A Windows Server 2022 file server named FS1 is registered with SSS1. SyncGroup1 in SSS1 has a cloud endpoint that points to the SMB Azure file share 'share1' and a server endpoint for D:\Data on FS1 with cloud tiering enabled. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is correct.
1. You can add a server endpoint for C:\Windows\Shares on FS1 to SyncGroup1 and enable cloud tiering on it.
2. If you upload a file directly into 'share1' by using the Azure portal, Azure File Sync might take up to 24 hours to detect the change and sync it to FS1, because the change detection job for a cloud endpoint runs only once every 24 hours.
3. You can additionally register FS1 with a second Storage Sync Service named SSS2 so that E:\Archive can sync to an Azure file share managed by SSS2.
opzione_a: You can add a server endpoint for C:\Windows\Shares on FS1 to SyncGroup1 and enable cloud tiering on it.
opzione_b: If you upload a file directly into 'share1' by using the Azure portal, Azure File Sync might take up to 24 hours to detect the change and sync it to FS1, because the change detection job for a cloud endpoint runs only once every 24 hours.
opzione_c: You can additionally register FS1 with a second Storage Sync Service named SSS2 so that E:\Archive can sync to an Azure file share managed by SSS2.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No: cloud tiering is explicitly not supported on the Windows system volume, and C:\Windows\Shares is on the system volume. Statement 2 is Yes: changes made directly to a cloud endpoint (the Azure file share) must be discovered by an Azure File Sync change detection job, and that job starts only once every 24 hours. Changes made on a server endpoint are detected immediately by the FileSyncSvc.exe service instead. Statement 3 is No: a server or cluster can be registered with only one Storage Sync Service at a time. After registration, FS1 can participate in multiple sync groups, but only within SSS1; to use SSS2 you would first have to unregister FS1 from SSS1.
tags: azure file sync, storage sync service, registered server, cloud tiering, system volume, change detection

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: A development team needs an Azure file share that Linux VMs will mount by using the NFS 4.1 protocol. Which storage account configuration supports this requirement?
opzione_a: A StorageV2 (general-purpose v2) account with the Standard_LRS SKU
opzione_b: A FileStorage account with the Premium_LRS SKU
opzione_c: A StorageV2 (general-purpose v2) account with the Standard_GRS SKU
opzione_d: A BlockBlobStorage account with the Premium_ZRS SKU
spiegazione: NFS Azure file shares are available only on the SSD (premium) media tier, which requires the FileStorage storage account kind, and only LRS or ZRS redundancy is supported. A FileStorage account with Premium_LRS therefore meets the requirement. StorageV2 with Standard_LRS is wrong: pay-as-you-go StorageV2 accounts place file shares on the HDD (standard) media tier, which does not support NFS. StorageV2 with Standard_GRS is wrong for the same reason, and geo-redundancy is not even available for NFS shares because NFS requires SSD storage. BlockBlobStorage is wrong: that account kind hosts only blob containers and cannot contain file shares at all.
tags: azure files, nfs, filestorage, premium, ssd, redundancy

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a file share in Azure Files
domanda: Users in a branch office must map a drive letter to an SMB Azure file share hosted at contososa.file.core.windows.net. The branch firewall currently denies all outbound traffic that is not explicitly allowed. Which outbound TCP port must you permit so that the SMB mount succeeds?
opzione_a: TCP 443
opzione_b: TCP 445
opzione_c: TCP 2049
opzione_d: TCP 3389
spiegazione: SMB access to an Azure file share requires TCP port 445 to the storage account endpoint; this is the single most common cause of mount failures because many organizations and ISPs block outbound 445. TCP 443 is wrong: it is the port used by the FileREST/HTTPS protocol (portal, AzCopy, SDKs) and by the Azure File Sync agent, not by an SMB drive mapping. TCP 2049 is wrong: that is the port used by NFS Azure file shares, and NFS shares cannot be mounted from Windows clients. TCP 3389 is wrong: that is RDP, which has nothing to do with mounting a file share.
tags: azure files, smb, port 445, mount, connectivity

sotto_argomento: Create and configure storage accounts
domanda: A media company is designing storage for an application that requires enterprise-grade Azure file shares over both SMB and NFS, consistently low latency, and resilience to the loss of a single availability zone within the primary region. Select the correct option for each item.
opzione_a: Storage account type to create: [Standard general-purpose v2 | Premium block blobs | Premium file shares]
opzione_b: Performance tier of this account type: [Standard | Premium]
opzione_c: Most resilient redundancy option supported by this account type: [ZRS | GZRS | RA-GZRS]
opzione_d: Read access to a secondary region for Azure Files: [Supported | Not supported]
spiegazione: Correct selections: The premium file shares account type is the premium storage account type for file shares only and is the type Microsoft names when you need a storage account that supports both SMB and NFS file shares. It is a premium performance account, and premium performance storage accounts use solid-state drives (SSDs) to deliver low latency and high throughput. Premium file shares support LRS and ZRS only, so ZRS is the most resilient option available and it satisfies the requirement to survive the loss of one availability zone - Microsoft also recommends ZRS for Azure Files because no remounting of shares is required if a zone becomes unavailable. Finally, Azure Files doesn't support read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS) or read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS). Why the other choices are wrong: Standard general-purpose v2 supports Azure Files but not NFS shares, and Premium block blobs hosts no file shares at all. Selecting Standard for the performance tier contradicts both the account type and the low-latency requirement. GZRS and RA-GZRS are not offered for premium file share accounts, which have no geo-redundant options.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure storage accounts
domanda: While scripting the deployment of a new Azure Storage account, you must generate a name that Azure will accept. Which naming requirement must the generated name satisfy?
opzione_a: Between 3 and 24 characters, containing only lowercase letters and numbers, and unique across all of Azure
opzione_b: Between 3 and 63 characters, containing lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens, and unique within the resource group
opzione_c: Between 1 and 80 characters, containing letters, numbers, hyphens, and underscores, and unique within the subscription
opzione_d: Between 5 and 50 characters, containing only lowercase letters, and unique within the region
spiegazione: Correct: Storage account names must be between 3 and 24 characters in length, can contain only numbers and lowercase letters, and must be unique within Azure. Global uniqueness is required because the account name becomes the subdomain of the public service endpoint, for example https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net. Why the others are wrong: '3 to 63 characters with hyphens, unique within the resource group' describes blob container naming rules (containers do allow hyphens and are scoped to the account), not storage account naming - hyphens are never valid in a storage account name. '1 to 80 characters with hyphens and underscores, unique within the subscription' is close to the generic Azure resource-group naming rule and wrongly scopes uniqueness to the subscription. '5 to 50 characters, unique within the region' invents a limit that does not exist; regional uniqueness would be insufficient because the DNS namespace is global.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure storage accounts
domanda: An engineering team needs a storage account that can host both Server Message Block (SMB) and Network File System (NFS) file shares for a latency-sensitive application. Which type of storage account should you create?
opzione_a: Standard general-purpose v2
opzione_b: Premium block blobs
opzione_c: Premium file shares
opzione_d: Premium page blobs
spiegazione: Correct: The premium file shares account type is the premium storage account type for Azure Files only, and Microsoft explicitly directs you to it when you want a storage account that supports both SMB and NFS file shares. It is recommended for enterprise or high-performance scale applications and uses SSDs for low latency and high throughput. Why the others are wrong: Standard general-purpose v2 does support Azure Files, but the account overview states that if you want support for NFS in Azure Files you must use the premium file shares account type - so it fails the NFS requirement. Premium block blobs supports only Blob Storage (block blobs and append blobs); it hosts no file shares at all and is aimed at high transaction rates and small objects. Premium page blobs supports page blobs only, which back disk-style workloads rather than SMB or NFS file shares.

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: You must generate one account SAS for storage account sa1 that allows a reporting application to enumerate every container in the account, list the blobs inside those containers, and download blob content. The application must not be able to create, overwrite, or delete anything, and it must not reach the Queue, Table, or File endpoints. Select the appropriate value for each SAS query parameter.
opzione_a: SignedServices (ss): [b | bf | bqtf]
opzione_b: SignedResourceTypes (srt): [o | co | sco]
opzione_c: SignedPermissions (sp): [r | rl | rwl]
opzione_d: SignedProtocol (spr): [http | https | http only]
spiegazione: SignedServices must be b (Blob) only, because the application must not reach Azure Files, Queue, or Table; bf would add the Azure Files endpoint and bqtf would add all four. SignedResourceTypes must be sco: List Containers is a service-level API and requires the Service (s) resource type, List Blobs is a container-level API and requires Container (c), and Get Blob is an object-level API and requires Object (o). Using o alone or co would omit the resource type needed for List Containers. SignedPermissions must be rl: Read (r) is required for Get Blob and List (l) is required for both List Containers and List Blobs. r alone omits the List permission, and rwl adds Write, which would let the application create and overwrite blobs and containers, violating the requirement. SignedProtocol should be https so that only HTTPS requests are accepted; the default of https,http would also permit HTTP, and HTTP only is never a permitted value for spr.

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A service principal named app1 is assigned the Storage Blob Data Reader role, scoped to a single blob container in storage account sa1. When app1 calls Get User Delegation Key, the call fails. You must allow app1 to create user delegation SAS tokens while granting the fewest additional permissions. What should you do?
opzione_a: Assign the Storage Blob Delegator role to app1 at the scope of the storage account.
opzione_b: Assign the Storage Account Contributor role to app1 at the scope of the storage account.
opzione_c: Assign the Storage Blob Data Reader role to app1 at the scope of the subscription.
opzione_d: Assign the Reader role to app1 at the scope of the resource group.
spiegazione: The Get User Delegation Key operation acts at the level of the storage account, so the generateUserDelegationKey action must be granted at the storage account, resource group, or subscription scope. When a principal already has a data-access role scoped to a container, Microsoft's documented guidance is to additionally assign a delegator role such as Storage Blob Delegator at the account, resource group, or subscription scope. Storage Account Contributor also includes the action but grants broad management permissions over the account, including access to the account keys, so it violates least privilege. Re-assigning Storage Blob Data Reader at subscription scope would work technically but grants read access to blob data across every storage account in the subscription, which is far more than required. The Reader role grants no data actions and does not include the generateUserDelegationKey action, so the call would still fail.
tags: user delegation sas,storage blob delegator,rbac,scope,least privilege

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A monitoring tool must be able to call List Containers, read and set Blob service properties, create and delete containers, and also read messages from queues in the same storage account. You must delegate this access with a single signature and without granting the tool an account key permanently. Which type of SAS must you generate?
opzione_a: A service SAS scoped to a container (sr=c)
opzione_b: An account SAS
opzione_c: A user delegation SAS scoped to the container
opzione_d: A service SAS that references a stored access policy
spiegazione: Only an account SAS can delegate access to service-level operations such as Get/Set Service Properties, Get Service Stats, and List Containers, and only an account SAS can span more than one storage service (for example Blob and Queue) in a single signature. It also permits create and delete operations on containers and queues. A service SAS scoped to a container is wrong: a service SAS delegates access to a resource in only one service and explicitly cannot create, delete, or list containers, nor read or write container metadata and properties. A user delegation SAS scoped to a container is wrong: it is scoped to a single service resource and cannot cover both blob service-level operations and queue messages with one token. A service SAS that references a stored access policy is still a service SAS and inherits the same restrictions on service-level and container-management operations.

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A web API signs in with a managed identity and issues user delegation SAS tokens to its clients so that they can download blobs directly from storage account sa1. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true. 1) The API can create the user delegation SAS tokens without ever retrieving a storage account access key. 2) Calling the Revoke User Delegation Keys operation invalidates every user delegation SAS that was signed with the revoked key. 3) If you configure a SAS expiration policy on sa1 with an upper limit of 30 days, a user delegation SAS issued afterwards can be valid for up to 30 days.
opzione_a: The API can create the user delegation SAS tokens without ever retrieving a storage account access key.
opzione_b: Calling the Revoke User Delegation Keys operation invalidates every user delegation SAS that was signed with the revoked key.
opzione_c: If you configure a SAS expiration policy on sa1 with an upper limit of 30 days, a user delegation SAS issued afterwards can be valid for up to 30 days.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes: a user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key obtained from Microsoft Entra ID through the Get User Delegation Key operation, so the account key is never needed. The managed identity must simply hold a role that includes the generateUserDelegationKey action, such as Storage Blob Delegator, at the storage account, resource group, or subscription scope. Statement 2 is Yes: when you revoke the user delegation key, any shared access signatures that rely on that key become invalid, and this is documented as the quickest way to revoke a user delegation SAS. Statement 3 is No: a user delegation SAS has a maximum expiry interval of 7 days regardless of the SAS expiration policy, and if the policy is set to a value greater than 7 days it has no effect on a user delegation SAS.
tags: user delegation sas,revoke user delegation keys,sas expiration policy,seven days,managed identity

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A third-party auditing tool must call Get Blob Service Stats and List Containers against storage account sa1, and it must also read messages from a queue in the same account. Your policy forbids giving the vendor an account key permanently, but the vendor's tool cannot use Microsoft Entra ID. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown to describe the resulting design.
opzione_a: SAS type to issue: [Service SAS | Account SAS | User delegation SAS]
opzione_b: Credential used to sign the token: [Storage account key | User delegation key | Managed identity certificate]
opzione_c: Supported with a stored access policy: [Yes | No]
opzione_d: Fastest way to immediately revoke the issued token: [Delete the stored access policy | Regenerate the storage account key | Call Revoke User Delegation Keys]
risposta_corretta: Account SAS,Storage account key,No,Regenerate the storage account key
spiegazione: Only an account SAS can delegate service-level operations such as Get Service Stats and List Containers and can span more than one service (Blob and Queue) in a single token, so a service SAS is insufficient and a user delegation SAS is ruled out because the tool cannot authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID. An account SAS is secured with a storage account key (Shared Key authorization), not with a user delegation key or a certificate. Stored access policies are explicitly not supported for an account SAS, so the token must be an ad hoc SAS: deleting a stored access policy is therefore not an option, and Revoke User Delegation Keys applies only to user delegation SAS. Because there is no policy to delete, regenerating the account key that signed the token is the only way to immediately revoke it.

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A contractor accidentally posted an ad hoc service SAS URI for a blob in a public ticketing system. The SAS was signed with key1, does not reference any stored access policy, and is valid for another 20 days. You must invalidate the token immediately. What should you do?
opzione_a: Regenerate the storage account access key that was used to sign the SAS.
opzione_b: Create a stored access policy on the container with an expiry time in the past.
opzione_c: Set the public access level of the container to Private (no anonymous access).
opzione_d: Configure a SAS expiration policy on the storage account and set the expiration action to Log.
spiegazione: Regenerating the account key that was used to create the signature is the only way to immediately revoke an ad hoc SAS, because the signature is validated against that key. Creating a stored access policy afterwards has no effect: the already-issued token does not carry a signedIdentifier (si) value, so it is not bound to any policy. Changing the container public access level only controls anonymous access; a SAS is authorized by its signature and continues to work. A SAS expiration policy with the Log action only warns the creator and writes a SasExpiryStatus entry to the logs when an out-of-policy SAS is used; it does not block or revoke tokens that were already issued.

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A developer asks you which kind of shared access signature (SAS) can be created without the application ever holding a storage account access key. Which SAS type is secured with Microsoft Entra credentials instead of the account key?
opzione_a: Account SAS
opzione_b: Service SAS
opzione_c: User delegation SAS
opzione_d: Service SAS that references a stored access policy
spiegazione: A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key that is obtained from Microsoft Entra ID by calling Get User Delegation Key, so the application never needs the storage account key. Microsoft recommends this type for superior security. Account SAS is wrong because it is signed with the storage account key (Shared Key). Service SAS is wrong for the same reason: it is also signed with the account key. A service SAS that references a stored access policy is still a service SAS and is still signed with the account key; the stored access policy only adds server-side control over the constraints, it does not change the signing credential.
tags: sas,user delegation sas,microsoft entra id,storage,shared key

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: An application requests a user delegation key by calling the Get User Delegation Key operation and then uses that key to sign multiple user delegation SAS tokens. What is the maximum period for which the user delegation key can be valid?
opzione_a: 1 hour
opzione_b: 24 hours
opzione_c: 7 days
opzione_d: 90 days
spiegazione: You can specify that a user delegation key is valid for a period of up to seven days. The signedKeyExpiryTime (ske) value may be a maximum of seven days from the start time of the SAS, and a user delegation SAS therefore has a maximum expiry interval of 7 days regardless of any SAS expiration policy. 1 hour is wrong: it is the legacy limit for a service SAS that used a REST version prior to 2012-02-12 and did not reference a stored access policy. 24 hours and 90 days are wrong: they are not documented limits for the user delegation key.
tags: user delegation sas,user delegation key,expiry,seven days

sotto_argomento: Manage access keys
domanda: Your governance team requires that the access keys of every storage account be rotated at least every 90 days, and that non-compliant accounts be reported centrally. You plan to configure a key expiration policy with the Az PowerShell module and to monitor compliance with a built-in policy definition. Select the appropriate option for each item.
opzione_a: Set-AzStorageAccount parameter used to define the policy: [-KeyExpirationPeriodInDay | -KeyRotationPeriodInDays | -KeyPolicy]
opzione_b: Prerequisite before the policy can be created on a legacy account: [Both access keys must be rotated at least once | Shared Key authorization must be disallowed | A private endpoint must exist]
opzione_c: Built-in Azure Policy definition used to report non-compliance: [Storage account keys should not be expired | Storage accounts should prevent shared key access | Storage accounts should restrict network access]
risposta_corretta: -KeyExpirationPeriodInDay,Both access keys must be rotated at least once,Storage account keys should not be expired
spiegazione: Parameter: Set-AzStorageAccount uses -KeyExpirationPeriodInDay, set to the interval in days until the key should be rotated; the same parameter is available on New-AzStorageAccount, and the Azure CLI equivalent is --key-exp-days. -KeyRotationPeriodInDays is not a valid parameter name, and KeyPolicy is the read-only property you inspect to verify the policy, not a parameter you set. Prerequisite: the KeyCreationTime property indicates when the keys were created or last rotated, and older accounts can have a null value. If KeyCreationTime is null for either key, the expiration policy cannot be created until both keys are rotated. Disallowing Shared Key and creating a private endpoint are unrelated to this prerequisite. Policy definition: "Storage account keys should not be expired" is the built-in definition documented for monitoring whether keys have been rotated within the recommended interval. "Storage accounts should prevent shared key access" governs the AllowSharedKeyAccess property instead, and "Storage accounts should restrict network access" targets firewall configuration.

sotto_argomento: Manage access keys
domanda: To satisfy a compliance requirement, you set the AllowSharedKeyAccess property of a storage account to false. Which outcomes result from this change? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Requests that present an account SAS are denied.
opzione_b: Requests that present a service SAS are denied.
opzione_c: Requests that present a user delegation SAS to Blob Storage are still permitted.
opzione_d: Requests that are authorized with Microsoft Entra ID are denied.
opzione_e: The two account access keys are deleted from the storage account.
spiegazione: Correct - account SAS denied: an account SAS is authorized with Shared Key, so when AllowSharedKeyAccess is false the request is denied for all Azure Storage services and fails with error code 403 (Forbidden). Correct - service SAS denied: a service SAS is likewise signed with the account key and is therefore denied for all Azure Storage services. Correct - user delegation SAS permitted: a user delegation SAS is authorized with Microsoft Entra ID rather than the account key, so the request is permitted; Microsoft recommends it where Microsoft Entra authorization is otherwise unavailable. Wrong - Microsoft Entra requests denied: the entire purpose of the setting is to force clients onto Microsoft Entra ID; only secured requests authorized with Microsoft Entra ID will succeed. Wrong - keys deleted: the property only causes Azure Storage to reject requests authorized with the keys. The keys continue to exist and can still be listed or regenerated by users holding the relevant permissions.

sotto_argomento: Manage access keys
domanda: A storage account named storage1 was created several years ago and has never had its keys rotated. In the Azure portal, you open Security + networking > Access keys for storage1 and find that the Set rotation reminder button is greyed out, so you cannot create a key expiration policy. What must you do first?
opzione_a: Regenerate each of the two account access keys at least once.
opzione_b: Assign yourself the Storage Account Key Operator Service Role at the subscription scope.
opzione_c: Set the AllowSharedKeyAccess property of storage1 to true.
opzione_d: Upgrade storage1 from general-purpose v1 to general-purpose v2.
spiegazione: Correct: the KeyCreationTime property records when the keys were created or last rotated, and older accounts can have a null value because it was never set. A key expiration policy cannot be created while KeyCreationTime is null, so you must rotate each key at least once. Microsoft Learn notes that if Set rotation reminder is greyed out, you need to rotate your keys. Wrong - Storage Account Key Operator Service Role: the button is greyed out because of the null KeyCreationTime, not a permissions gap; if you can see the Access keys blade you already hold listkeys. Wrong - AllowSharedKeyAccess set to true: this property controls whether Shared Key authorization is accepted for data requests; it is not a prerequisite for a key expiration policy, and the property is permissive when null or true anyway. Wrong - upgrade to general-purpose v2: key expiration policies are not gated on the account kind; the blocker is the unset KeyCreationTime.

sotto_argomento: Manage access keys
domanda: Company policy requires that the access keys of a storage account named storage1 be rotated manually every 90 days without any interruption to the application that consumes them. The application currently uses the primary access key (key1) in its connection strings, and Azure Key Vault is not in use. Arrange the four actions in the correct order to perform the documented manual key rotation procedure.
opzione_a: Regenerate the secondary access key (key2).
opzione_b: Update the connection strings in the application code to reference the secondary access key (key2).
opzione_c: Update the connection strings in the application code to reference the newly regenerated primary access key (key1).
opzione_d: Regenerate the primary access key (key1).
spiegazione: The documented manual rotation procedure is: first update the connection strings in your application code to reference the secondary access key, which keeps the application working while key1 is replaced; then regenerate the primary access key; then update the connection strings in your code to reference the new primary access key; and finally regenerate the secondary access key in the same manner. Two keys are assigned specifically so that the application maintains access to Azure Storage throughout the process. Regenerating a key before moving the application off it would break the application, which is why option d cannot come first. Microsoft also recommends using only one of the keys across all applications at the same time, because mixing key1 in some places and key2 in others makes it impossible to rotate without an application losing access.

sotto_argomento: Manage access keys
domanda: Following a suspected credential leak, you regenerate the primary access key (key1) of a storage account. Several partner applications that consume shared access signatures immediately start failing with authorization errors. Which type of shared access signature continues to work after an account access key is regenerated?
opzione_a: An account SAS
opzione_b: A service SAS that is associated with a stored access policy
opzione_c: A user delegation SAS
opzione_d: A service SAS that specifies an allowed IP address range
spiegazione: Correct: a user delegation SAS is secured with Microsoft Entra credentials rather than the account key, so it is not affected by key rotation. Microsoft Learn states that rotating or regenerating access keys revokes SAS tokens generated based on that key, and that user delegation SAS tokens are the exception. Wrong - account SAS: it is signed with the account key, so regenerating that key revokes it and new tokens must be issued. Wrong - service SAS with a stored access policy: the stored access policy only centralizes constraints and revocation; the token is still signed with the account key and is therefore revoked by rotation. Wrong - service SAS with an allowed IP range: an IP constraint restricts where the token may be used but does not change how it is signed; it is still key-signed and is revoked.

sotto_argomento: Manage access keys
domanda: An application stores a connection string that references the primary access key (key1) of a storage account named storage1. In response to a security incident, an administrator runs New-AzStorageAccountKey with -KeyName key1 against storage1. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true. 1) Partners that were issued an account SAS signed with key1 must be issued new SAS tokens. 2) An application that uses a user delegation SAS to read blob data in storage1 is unaffected by the operation. 3) The operation also invalidates the secondary access key (key2), so any client using key2 loses access.
opzione_a: Partners that were issued an account SAS signed with key1 must be issued new SAS tokens.
opzione_b: An application that uses a user delegation SAS to read blob data in storage1 is unaffected by the operation.
opzione_c: The operation also invalidates the secondary access key (key2), so any client using key2 loses access.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: rotating or regenerating an access key revokes the shared access signatures that were generated based on that key. Microsoft Learn states that after access key rotation you must regenerate account and service SAS tokens to avoid disruptions to applications. Statement 2 - Yes: a user delegation SAS is secured with Microsoft Entra credentials rather than the account key, and Microsoft Learn confirms that user delegation SAS tokens aren't affected by key rotation. Statement 3 - No: a storage account is issued two independent 512-bit keys precisely so that one can be regenerated while the other continues to serve traffic. New-AzStorageAccountKey regenerates only the key named in -KeyName, which is why the documented rotation procedure moves applications to key2 before regenerating key1.

sotto_argomento: Manage access keys
domanda: A member of your security operations team must be able to list and regenerate the access keys of a storage account named storage1. The user must NOT be able to modify any other property of the storage account and must not receive any Microsoft Entra ID-based access to blob data. Following the principle of least privilege, which built-in Azure role should you assign?
opzione_a: Storage Account Contributor
opzione_b: Storage Blob Data Owner
opzione_c: Storage Account Key Operator Service Role
opzione_d: Reader
spiegazione: Correct: the Storage Account Key Operator Service Role includes Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listkeys/action and Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/regeneratekey/action, which are exactly the permissions required to view and rotate account access keys, and nothing more. Wrong - Storage Account Contributor: it does include listkeys, but it also grants Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/write, allowing the user to change any storage account property, which violates the least-privilege requirement. Wrong - Storage Blob Data Owner: this is a data-plane role that grants Microsoft Entra ID-based access to blob data; it does not grant listkeys or regeneratekey. Wrong - Reader: it can view the storage account resource but does not include listkeys/action, so the keys cannot be retrieved or regenerated.

sotto_argomento: Manage data by using Azure Storage Explorer and AzCopy
domanda: Your team uses AzCopy v10 for scripted transfers and Azure Storage Explorer for ad hoc browsing of blob data. Select the correct value for each statement.
opzione_a: Authorization credentials that AzCopy accepts for the storage service: [Microsoft Entra ID or a SAS token | Storage account key or a SAS token | Microsoft Entra ID or a storage account key]
opzione_b: Least privileged built-in role for downloading blobs with AzCopy by using a user identity: [Storage Blob Data Reader | Reader | Storage Account Contributor]
opzione_c: Values that the azcopy sync command compares by default: [File names and last modified timestamps | MD5 hashes | File sizes only]
opzione_d: Storage Explorer method for attaching a single blob container when you have data-layer access but no management-layer access: [Sign in using Microsoft Entra ID | Account name and key | Local storage emulator]
risposta_corretta: Microsoft Entra ID or a SAS token,Storage Blob Data Reader,File names and last modified timestamps,Sign in using Microsoft Entra ID
spiegazione: Microsoft Entra ID or a SAS token: AzCopy accepts credentials either by using Microsoft Entra ID (user identity, managed identity, or service principal) or by appending a SAS token to each source or destination URL. AzCopy does not take a storage account key, which rules out the two options that include one. Storage Blob Data Reader: for download operations against Blob Storage the documented role is Storage Blob Data Reader; upload operations require Storage Blob Data Contributor or Storage Blob Data Owner. Reader and Storage Account Contributor are control-plane roles that do not grant access to blob data. File names and last modified timestamps: by default the sync command compares file names and last modified timestamps. You can override that behaviour to use MD5 hashes instead by using the --compare-hash flag, so MD5 hashes is the opt-in behaviour rather than the default. Because last modified times are critical when --compare-hash is not used, the machine running sync should have an accurate system clock. Sign in using Microsoft Entra ID: Microsoft Entra ID is the preferred option if you have data layer access to your resource but no management layer access, and Storage Explorer supports it when attaching blob containers, Data Lake Storage containers and directories, and queues. Account name and key is not offered when attaching an individual blob container (it applies to attaching a whole storage account), and the local storage emulator connects to Azurite or the Azure Storage Emulator rather than to a real container.
tags: azcopy, azure storage explorer, sas token, microsoft entra id, azcopy sync

sotto_argomento: Manage data by using Azure Storage Explorer and AzCopy
domanda: A nightly unattended job on a Windows server must make a blob container an exact mirror of the local folder C:\\data. Files that are added or changed locally must be uploaded, and blobs whose corresponding local files were deleted must be removed from the container. The job runs from a scheduled task, so no interactive prompt can be answered. Which AzCopy v10 command should you run?
opzione_a: azcopy sync 'C:\\data' 'https://contoso.blob.core.windows.net/mycontainer' --recursive --delete-destination=true
opzione_b: azcopy sync 'C:\\data' 'https://contoso.blob.core.windows.net/mycontainer' --recursive --delete-destination=prompt
opzione_c: azcopy copy 'C:\\data' 'https://contoso.blob.core.windows.net/mycontainer' --recursive --overwrite=ifSourceNewer
opzione_d: azcopy copy 'C:\\data' 'https://contoso.blob.core.windows.net/mycontainer' --recursive --delete-destination=true
spiegazione: Correct: The sync command replicates the source location to the destination location, comparing file names and last modified timestamps by default. Setting the --delete-destination flag to true makes AzCopy delete files in the destination that no longer exist in the source, and it does so without providing a prompt, which is what an unattended scheduled task requires. Option B is wrong because the prompt value makes AzCopy ask for confirmation before each deletion, which will stall a job that has no interactive console. Option C is wrong because the copy command never removes objects from the destination; --overwrite=ifSourceNewer only controls whether an existing destination object is replaced, so blobs for deleted local files would remain. (Microsoft does recommend copy with --overwrite=ifSourceNewer over sync when you do not need deletions, because copy consumes less memory and incurs less billing cost.) Option D is wrong because --delete-destination is an option of the sync command, not of the copy command. As a safeguard, enable blob soft delete before you use --delete-destination=true or prompt.
tags: azcopy, azcopy sync, delete-destination, blob storage, data transfer

sotto_argomento: Manage data by using Azure Storage Explorer and AzCopy
domanda: A user is assigned the Owner role scoped to a storage account named contoso. The user runs azcopy login, signs in successfully with their Microsoft Entra ID credentials, and then runs azcopy copy to upload files to a blob container in contoso. The upload fails with an authorization error. You must resolve the failure while continuing to use Microsoft Entra ID authorization. What should you do?
opzione_a: Assign the Storage Blob Data Contributor role to the user, scoped to the storage account.
opzione_b: Assign the Storage Account Contributor role to the user, scoped to the storage account.
opzione_c: Assign the Reader role to the user, scoped to the subscription that contains the storage account.
opzione_d: Regenerate key1 for the storage account and rerun azcopy login.
spiegazione: Correct: As the documentation states, an owner of a storage account is not automatically assigned permissions to access the data. Owner is a control-plane (Azure Resource Manager) role; it does not grant data-plane access when AzCopy presents a Microsoft Entra ID OAuth token. For upload operations against Blob Storage the user needs Storage Blob Data Contributor or Storage Blob Data Owner. (Role assignments can take up to five minutes to propagate.) Option B is wrong because Storage Account Contributor is likewise a control-plane role that manages the account resource but grants no access to blob data over Microsoft Entra ID. Option C is wrong because Reader is a control-plane role and grants no data access whatsoever, and it is even weaker than the Owner role the user already holds. Option D is wrong because regenerating an account key is irrelevant to Microsoft Entra ID authorization; account keys are a different authorization mechanism, and azcopy login obtains an OAuth token that has nothing to do with the account keys.
tags: azcopy, microsoft entra id, storage blob data contributor, rbac, data plane

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Disk Encryption
domanda: An administrator at Fabrikam compares the encryption options available for Azure managed disks before documenting a standard for the organization. Select the appropriate option for each statement.
opzione_a: Encrypts the temporary disk and the OS and data disk caches at rest: [Server-side encryption with platform-managed keys | Encryption at host | Double encryption at rest]
opzione_b: Encrypts disks from inside the guest operating system by using BitLocker or DM-Crypt: [Azure Disk Encryption | Encryption at host | Confidential disk encryption]
opzione_c: Is always enabled for managed disks and automatically encrypts OS and data disks at rest: [Azure Disk Encryption | Server-side encryption | Encryption at host]
opzione_d: Resource required to use a customer-managed key for a managed disk: [A disk encryption set | A key encryption key configured on the virtual machine | A storage account customer-managed key]
risposta_corretta: Encryption at host,Azure Disk Encryption,Server-side encryption,A disk encryption set
spiegazione: Encryption at host is correct for the first statement because it's the option that ensures all temp disks and disk caches are encrypted at rest and flow encrypted to the storage clusters; server-side encryption explicitly doesn't encrypt temp disks or disk caches, and double encryption at rest only adds a second infrastructure-layer pass over persisted disks, snapshots, and images. Azure Disk Encryption is correct for the second statement because ADE encrypts the OS and data disks inside the VM by using the DM-Crypt feature of Linux or the BitLocker feature of Windows; encryption at host runs on the Azure host and doesn't use the VM's CPU, and confidential disk encryption binds keys to the VM's virtual TPM rather than using BitLocker or DM-Crypt. Server-side encryption is correct for the third statement because Azure Disk Storage server-side encryption is always enabled and automatically encrypts data on managed OS and data disks when it persists them; ADE and encryption at host are both opt-in. A disk encryption set is correct for the fourth statement because the disk encryption set is the resource that references the key vault and key and is associated with disks to enable customer-managed keys; a key encryption key is an ADE concept configured with Key Vault rather than on the VM, and a storage account customer-managed key applies to Azure Storage accounts, not managed disks.
tags: sse, encryption at host, azure disk encryption, disk encryption set, bitlocker, dm-crypt

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Disk Encryption
domanda: An existing Azure virtual machine named VM1 has never had Azure Disk Encryption enabled and uses a VM size that supports encryption at host. You need to enable encryption at host on VM1 and encrypt the OS and data disk caches by using a customer-managed key. No key vault, key, or disk encryption set exists yet, and the feature has never been used in the subscription. Which five actions should you perform in sequence?
opzione_a: Deallocate VM1.
opzione_b: Register the EncryptionAtHost feature for the Microsoft.Compute resource provider in the subscription and confirm that the registration state is Registered.
opzione_c: Create a disk encryption set that references the key, and grant the disk encryption set permissions to the key vault.
opzione_d: Create a key vault with soft delete and purge protection enabled, and generate an RSA key in the key vault.
opzione_e: On the Disks pane of VM1, set Encryption at host to Yes, select the customer-managed key, save the change, and start VM1.
spiegazione: The correct sequence is B, D, C, A, E. B comes first because Microsoft states that you must enable the EncryptionAtHost feature for your subscription before you can use encryption at host for a VM or a virtual machine scale set, using Register-AzProviderFeature or az feature register against the Microsoft.Compute namespace, and you must confirm the registration state is Registered before trying the feature. D comes next because the key vault and key must exist before the disk encryption set can reference them, and soft delete and purge protection are mandatory when using a key vault for encrypting managed disks. C follows because the disk encryption set is created against an existing key vault and key, and it gets a system-assigned managed identity that must then be granted permissions on the key vault before any disk can be associated with it. A precedes E because existing VMs must be deallocated and reallocated in order to be encrypted. E is last: encryption at host is selected on the VM's Disks pane along with the customer-managed key, after which the VM is started. Note that the disk encryption set, VM, disks, and snapshots must all be in the same region and subscription, although the key vault itself may be in a different subscription in the same region.
tags: encryption at host, disk encryption set, key vault, feature registration, customer-managed keys

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Disk Encryption
domanda: The security team at Fabrikam issues a new standard for Azure virtual machines. The temporary disk and the OS and data disk caches must be encrypted at rest, data must flow encrypted between compute and storage, and the encryption must not consume the virtual machine's CPU. Which encryption option meets the requirements?
opzione_a: Server-side encryption with customer-managed keys
opzione_b: Encryption at host
opzione_c: Azure Disk Encryption
opzione_d: Double encryption at rest
spiegazione: Encryption at host is correct: the encryption starts on the Azure server hosting the VM, which is where the temporary disk and the OS/data disk caches are stored. All that data is encrypted at rest and flows encrypted to the Storage service, and Microsoft states that encryption at host doesn't use your VM's CPU and doesn't impact VM performance. Server-side encryption with customer-managed keys is wrong because SSE, whether with platform-managed or customer-managed keys, doesn't encrypt temp disks or disk caches and doesn't encrypt the data flow between compute and storage. Azure Disk Encryption is wrong because although it does encrypt the temp disk and caches, it runs BitLocker or DM-Crypt inside the guest, so it does use the VM's CPU; ADE is also scheduled for retirement on September 15, 2028, and Microsoft directs new VMs to encryption at host. Double encryption at rest is wrong because it adds a second infrastructure-layer encryption pass to persisted OS and data disks, snapshots, and images only; it doesn't address temp disks, caches, or the compute-to-storage data flow.
tags: encryption at host, azure disk encryption, sse, temp disk, disk cache, end-to-end encryption

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Disk Encryption
domanda: A virtual machine named VM1 was protected with Azure Disk Encryption last year. The encryption has since been disabled on VM1, and the disks are now encrypted only by platform-managed server-side encryption. As part of a migration away from Azure Disk Encryption, you must enable encryption at host for the workload that runs on VM1. What should you do?
opzione_a: Deallocate VM1, and then select Encryption at host on the Disks pane of VM1.
opzione_b: Register the EncryptionAtHost feature for the subscription, and then restart VM1.
opzione_c: Deploy a new virtual machine with encryption at host enabled and move the workload to it, because encryption at host can't be enabled on VM1.
opzione_d: Enable double encryption at rest on the disks of VM1.
spiegazione: Deploying a new VM is correct: a documented restriction of encryption at host is that it can't be enabled on virtual machines or virtual machine scale sets that currently or ever had Azure Disk Encryption enabled. Because VM1 had ADE enabled in the past, the restriction applies permanently to VM1 even though ADE was later disabled, so the workload must move to a new VM. Deallocating VM1 and selecting Encryption at host is wrong because, although existing VMs must indeed be deallocated and reallocated to be encrypted, the deallocation doesn't lift the prior-ADE restriction. Registering the feature and restarting is wrong on two counts: feature registration is a required subscription-level prerequisite but doesn't override the prior-ADE restriction, and a restart is insufficient because the VM must be deallocated and reallocated. Enabling double encryption at rest is wrong because it's a different feature that adds a second encryption layer to persisted disks; it doesn't encrypt the temp disk or caches and doesn't satisfy the requirement to enable encryption at host.
tags: encryption at host, azure disk encryption, ade migration, restrictions, deallocate

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Disk Encryption
domanda: You plan to implement server-side encryption with customer-managed keys for the managed disks of several Azure virtual machines by using a disk encryption set. Which requirements must be met? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: The key vault must have soft delete and purge protection enabled.
opzione_b: The key vault must be in the same region as the disk encryption set.
opzione_c: The key must be an RSA key with a size of 2,048 bits, 3,072 bits, or 4,096 bits.
opzione_d: The key vault must be in the same subscription as the disk encryption set.
opzione_e: The managed disks must already be encrypted with Azure Disk Encryption.
spiegazione: Options A, B, and C are correct. A is correct because Microsoft states that when creating the key vault instance you must enable soft delete and purge protection, and that these settings are mandatory when using a key vault for encrypting managed disks. B is correct because managed disks and the key vault or managed HSM must be in the same Azure region, and the key vault must be in the same region as the disk encryption set. C is correct because only software and HSM RSA keys of sizes 2,048-bit, 3,072-bit, and 4,096-bit are supported; no other key types or sizes are. D is wrong because Azure key vaults may be used from a different subscription as long as they're in the same region as the disk encryption set; they can even be in a different Microsoft Entra tenant when cross-tenant customer-managed keys are configured. E is wrong because it's the opposite of the documented restriction: managed disks currently or previously encrypted using Azure Disk Encryption can't be encrypted using customer-managed keys.
tags: customer-managed keys, disk encryption set, key vault, soft delete, purge protection, sse

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure backup for an App Service
domanda: An app named app3 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Premium v3 tier. Corporate policy requires that scheduled custom backups of app3 be written to a storage account named sa1. On sa1, public network access is denied and only selected virtual networks are allowed. You must configure the scheduled custom backups so that they succeed. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create a private endpoint for app3 and set public network access for app3 to Disabled.
opzione_b: Enable virtual network integration for app3, grant the integration subnet access on sa1, and select the option to back up and restore over virtual network integration.
opzione_c: Assign a system-assigned managed identity to app3 and grant the identity the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on sa1.
opzione_d: Configure automatic backups for app3 and set sa1 as the backup destination.
spiegazione: Correct: Custom backups can target a firewall-protected storage account only when the app is integrated with a virtual network (or hosted in an App Service Environment v3), the storage account allows access from that virtual network, and the backup/restore over virtual network integration option is selected on the custom backup configuration. Why the others are wrong: A private endpoint on app3 controls inbound access to the app itself; it does nothing for the app's outbound call to the storage account. Managed identity authentication is not supported for App Service backup and restore, which requires a storage account that supports SAS-based authorization, so granting the identity an RBAC role does not enable the backup. Automatic backups require no configuration and are stored on the platform in the same datacenter as the App Service; you cannot point them at your own storage account, and they are not supported over a virtual network.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure backup for an App Service
domanda: A junior administrator is preparing a backup plan for several App Service apps and asks you to confirm the platform behavior of App Service backups. Select the correct value for each statement.
opzione_a: Minimum App Service plan tier that supports backup and restore: [Free (F1) | Shared (D1) | Basic (B1)]
opzione_b: Maximum size of an automatic backup: [10 GB | 30 GB | 100 GB]
opzione_c: Maximum size of a custom backup: [4 GB | 10 GB | 30 GB]
opzione_d: Retention period of automatic backups: [7 days | 30 days | 90 days]
spiegazione: Correct: Backup and restore is supported in the Basic, Standard, Premium, and Isolated tiers; the Free and Shared tiers do not support it, and in the Basic tier you can back up and restore only the production slot. Automatic backups have a backup size of 30 GB, are created hourly, and are retained for 30 days; the retention schedule is not configurable. Custom backups have a maximum size of 10 GB, of which up to 4 GB can be a linked database, which is why 4 GB is a plausible but incorrect value for the total custom backup size. 100 GB and 7/90 days are not documented App Service backup values.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure certificates and Transport Layer Security (TLS) for an App Service
domanda: A web app named app1 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Standard tier. The custom domain www.contoso.com is mapped to app1 by using an A record at the domain registrar. To meet a compliance requirement for a dedicated certificate and a dedicated IP address, an administrator changes the existing binding for www.contoso.com from SNI SSL to IP-based SSL. Shortly afterward, users report that https://www.contoso.com returns an error, although https://app1.azurewebsites.net still works. What should you do to restore access?
opzione_a: Set the minimum inbound TLS version of app1 to 1.2 in the general settings of the app.
opzione_b: Update the A record at the domain registrar so that it points to the new dedicated inbound IP address that is shown on the app's Custom domains page.
opzione_c: Delete the IP-based SSL binding, recreate it as an SNI SSL binding, and add a TXT record named asuid for the domain.
opzione_d: Add a CNAME record for www that points to sni.app1.azurewebsites.net.
spiegazione: Correct: By default an app uses a shared public inbound IP address. When you bind a certificate by using IP-based SSL, App Service allocates a new, dedicated inbound IP address to the app. Any A record that pointed at the old shared address is now stale, so you must copy the new dedicated address from the app's Custom domains page and remap the A record to it. Why the others are wrong: Changing the minimum TLS version affects which TLS protocol versions clients may negotiate; it does not fix a name-resolution problem and 1.2 is already the default. Recreating the binding as SNI SSL would work around the issue but abandons the dedicated-IP compliance requirement, and the asuid TXT record is used for domain-ownership verification when adding the domain, not for restoring a binding. Adding a CNAME to sni.app1.azurewebsites.net is the remap step required when an SNI SSL binding exists on <app-name>.azurewebsites.net; it is not the remap for IP-based SSL, and a CNAME cannot be combined with the existing A-record mapping here.
tags: app service,ip based ssl,sni ssl,tls binding,dns,a record

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure certificates and Transport Layer Security (TLS) for an App Service
domanda: Fabrikam hosts a web app named app1 in an App Service plan that uses the Standard tier. The security team wants to secure several custom domains by using free App Service managed certificates instead of purchasing certificates. Which domain CANNOT be secured by a free App Service managed certificate?
opzione_a: www.fabrikam.com, mapped with a CNAME record that points directly to app1.azurewebsites.net
opzione_b: fabrikam.com, mapped with an A record that points to the app's inbound IP address
opzione_c: *.fabrikam.com, mapped with a CNAME record that points directly to app1.azurewebsites.net
opzione_d: shop.fabrikam.com, mapped with a CNAME record that points directly to app1.azurewebsites.net
spiegazione: Correct: *.fabrikam.com is a wildcard domain. The free App Service managed certificate explicitly does not support wildcard certificates, so this domain must be secured with an uploaded private certificate, an App Service certificate, or a certificate imported from Azure Key Vault. Why the others are wrong: www.fabrikam.com and shop.fabrikam.com are subdomains, which are supported as long as the CNAME record maps directly to <app-name>.azurewebsites.net (mapping to an intermediate CNAME value would block issuance and renewal, but that is not the case here). fabrikam.com is an apex/root domain, which is supported provided it has an A record pointing to the web app's IP address, the app has no IP restrictions that block internet reachability, and the root domain is not integrated with Azure Traffic Manager.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure deployment slots
domanda: An app named app9 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Standard tier and has a production slot and a staging slot. After the last swap, the operations team reports three findings: the Application Insights connection string that was configured only in staging is now live in production; the custom domain shop.contoso.com stayed on the production slot; and the virtual network integration configured on staging did not follow the content into production. No swap-behavior override app settings are configured. Select the correct option for each statement.
opzione_a: To keep APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING with each slot during a swap, you must: [Mark the setting as a deployment slot setting in both slots | Add the app setting WEBSITE_OVERRIDE_PRESERVE_DEFAULT_STICKY_SLOT_SETTINGS with a value of 0 to both slots | Store the value in Azure Key Vault and reference it from both slots]
opzione_b: Custom domain names during a swap are: [Swapped | Not swapped | Swapped only when HTTPS Only is disabled]
opzione_c: Virtual network integration during a swap is: [Swapped | Not swapped | Swapped only in the Premium v3 and Isolated v2 tiers]
opzione_d: To validate the staging slot with the production slot's settings applied before completing the swap, use: [Swap with preview | Auto swap | Traffic routing with the x-ms-routing-name query parameter]
risposta_corretta: Mark the setting as a deployment slot setting in both slots,Not swapped,Not swapped,Swap with preview
spiegazione: Correct: App settings are swapped by default, so an instrumentation or connection-string app setting follows the content into production unless it is marked as a deployment slot setting (slotSetting) in the slots. The override app setting WEBSITE_OVERRIDE_PRESERVE_DEFAULT_STICKY_SLOT_SETTINGS=0 only reverts the default sticky behavior of protocol settings, IP restrictions, Always On, diagnostic log settings, and CORS; it does not make an app setting slot specific. A Key Vault reference changes where the secret is stored, not whether the setting swaps. Custom domain names and virtual network integration are both on the documented list of settings that are not swapped, in every tier. Swap with preview performs the first phase of the swap, applying the target slot's slot-specific settings to the source slot and pausing so you can validate before completing; auto swap promotes automatically with no validation pause, and x-ms-routing-name traffic routing sends a share of live users to a slot rather than validating a pending swap.
tags: app service,deployment slots,swap with preview,sticky settings,custom domain,vnet integration

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure deployment slots
domanda: An app named app4 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Standard tier and has a deployment slot named staging. A connection string named SqlDb is defined in both slots: the production slot points to a production database and the staging slot points to a test database. After the release team swaps staging into production, the production site begins writing to the test database. You must ensure that each slot keeps its own SqlDb value after future swaps, while application content continues to swap normally. What should you do?
opzione_a: Add the app setting WEBSITE_OVERRIDE_PRESERVE_DEFAULT_STICKY_SLOT_SETTINGS with a value of 0 to both slots.
opzione_b: In each slot, edit the SqlDb connection string and select Deployment slot setting.
opzione_c: Use swap with preview instead of a direct swap when promoting the staging slot.
opzione_d: Enable auto swap on the staging slot and set the target slot to production.
spiegazione: Correct: Connection strings are swapped by default. Marking the SqlDb connection string as a deployment slot setting (the slotSetting property, or --slot-settings in the Azure CLI) makes it slot specific, so each slot keeps its own value while the app content still swaps. Why the others are wrong: WEBSITE_OVERRIDE_PRESERVE_DEFAULT_STICKY_SLOT_SETTINGS=0 reverts the platform's default sticky behavior for protocol settings, IP restrictions, Always On, diagnostic log settings, and CORS; it applies to those marked settings only and would make them swappable, which is the opposite of the goal and does not affect connection strings. Swap with preview only pauses the swap so you can validate the source slot with the target slot's settings applied; it does not change which settings are swapped. Auto swap automates the promotion, but the connection string would still swap.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure deployment slots
domanda: An app named app6 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Premium v3 tier and has a deployment slot named staging. Before a release, an engineer must document which configuration elements stay with the slot rather than follow the content when the two slots are swapped. No app setting or connection string has been marked as a deployment slot setting, and no swap-behavior override app settings are configured. Which configuration elements are NOT swapped? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: App settings
opzione_b: Custom domain names
opzione_c: Managed identities
opzione_d: Connection strings
opzione_e: Virtual network integration
spiegazione: Correct: Custom domain names, managed identities, and virtual network integration are all documented as settings that are not swapped; they stay with the slot. The same list also includes publishing endpoints, non-public certificates and TLS/SSL settings, protocol settings such as HTTPS Only and TLS version, scale settings, WebJobs schedulers, IP restrictions, Always On, diagnostic log settings, CORS, and settings ending with _EXTENSION_VERSION. Why the others are wrong: App settings and connection strings are swapped by default and follow the content across a swap. They stay with the slot only when you explicitly select Deployment slot setting for them (the slotSetting property), which the scenario states has not been done.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure networking settings for an App Service
domanda: Litware runs an internal line-of-business app named app5 in an App Service plan that uses the Premium v3 tier. App5 must be reachable only from virtual machines in a hub-and-spoke topology and from the on-premises datacenter, which connects to the hub virtual network over ExpressRoute private peering. App5 must not be reachable from the public internet. Which networking feature should you configure?
opzione_a: Regional virtual network integration with outbound internet traffic routing enabled
opzione_b: An access restriction rule that is based on a service endpoint for the virtual machine subnet
opzione_c: A private endpoint for app5, and public network access set to Disabled
opzione_d: Hybrid Connections
spiegazione: Correct: A private endpoint gives app5 a network interface with a private IP address from your virtual network, so clients in peered virtual networks and on-premises clients connected over ExpressRoute private peering can reach the app privately. Disabling public network access removes the default public entry point and completes the isolation. Why the others are wrong: Virtual network integration is an outbound-only feature. It lets the app call resources in the virtual network but explicitly does not grant inbound private access to the app, and routing all outbound traffic does not change that. A service endpoint based access restriction limits the public endpoint to selected Azure subnets, but the app keeps a public endpoint and on-premises clients arriving over ExpressRoute are not covered by a service endpoint rule. Hybrid Connections provide outbound access from the app to a TCP endpoint on-premises; they do not publish the app privately.
tags: app service,private endpoint,vnet integration,private site access,expressroute

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure networking settings for an App Service
domanda: Contoso deploys a web app named app7 to an App Service plan that uses the Premium v3 tier. App7 must connect to an Azure SQL database that is exposed only through a private endpoint in a virtual network named vnet1. In addition, app7 itself must be reachable only from clients inside vnet1 and must reject all traffic from the public internet. Which actions should you perform? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Enable regional virtual network integration for app7 by using a subnet in vnet1 that is delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms.
