opzione_b: Create a private endpoint for app7 in vnet1 and set public network access for app7 to Disabled.
opzione_c: Link the privatelink.database.windows.net private DNS zone to vnet1 so that app7 resolves the database to its private endpoint address.
opzione_d: Create the private endpoint for app7 in the same subnet that is used for virtual network integration.
opzione_e: Add an access restriction rule to app7 that allows the AzureCloud service tag and set the unmatched rule action to Deny.
spiegazione: Correct: Virtual network integration on a delegated subnet gives app7 outbound access into vnet1, which is what lets it reach the database's private endpoint. A private endpoint for app7 plus public network access set to Disabled provides inbound private-only access and eliminates public exposure. Linking the privatelink.database.windows.net private DNS zone to vnet1 ensures the app's DNS lookup for the database resolves to the private IP address; without private DNS resolution the app would resolve the public name and the connection would fail. Why the others are wrong: The virtual network integration feature cannot use the same subnet as the private endpoint, so option D is unsupported. The AzureCloud service tag covers the public IP ranges of Azure services worldwide, which is far broader than vnet1 and would not restrict access to vnet1 clients; access restriction rules are also not evaluated for traffic arriving through a private endpoint.
tags: app service,private endpoint,vnet integration,private dns zone,subnet delegation

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure networking settings for an App Service
domanda: A web app named app10 runs in an App Service plan named plan1 that uses the Premium v3 tier. Regional virtual network integration is enabled for app10 by using a subnet named Subnet1 in a virtual network named vnet1. Evaluate each of the following statements about this configuration and indicate whether it is true. 1) Regional virtual network integration allows virtual machines in vnet1 to reach app10 by using a private IP address. 2) Subnet1 must be delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms and cannot be shared with resources of other types. 3) Plan1 can have virtual network integration with up to two subnets, but app10 can use only one virtual network integration at a time.
opzione_a: Regional virtual network integration allows virtual machines in vnet1 to reach app10 by using a private IP address.
opzione_b: Subnet1 must be delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms and cannot be shared with resources of other types.
opzione_c: Plan1 can have virtual network integration with up to two subnets, but app10 can use only one virtual network integration at a time.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No: virtual network integration is used only to make outbound calls from the app into the virtual network. It gives the app access to resources in the virtual network but does not grant inbound private access to the app; for inbound private access you must use a private endpoint. Statement 2 is Yes: virtual network integration depends on a dedicated subnet that is delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms, and the integration subnet cannot be shared with other resource types (an orphaned Microsoft.Web/serverFarms delegation is precisely what blocks subnet reuse after an app is deleted without disconnecting). Statement 3 is Yes: the feature supports two virtual interfaces per worker, which means an App Service plan can integrate with up to two subnets/virtual networks, while any single app can have only one virtual network integration at a given time.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda:
Case study: Litware, Inc. runs a public e-commerce site in an App Service plan named ASP-Prod that uses the Premium v3 (P1v3) pricing tier in the West Europe region. ASP-Prod hosts three web apps. During weekday business hours the traffic is steady and two instances are sufficient. However, every Friday from 18:00 to 23:00 Litware runs a flash-sale event that drives a large but entirely predictable traffic spike, and the apps must already have extra capacity in place when the event starts rather than adding instances only after the load arrives. Outside business hours, traffic is minimal and Litware wants to minimize cost. The operations team wants a single, native configuration on ASP-Prod and does not want to rely on reactive metric thresholds alone.

What should you configure?
opzione_a: An autoscale setting with a single default profile that contains a Percentage CPU scale-out rule, with instance limits of minimum 2 and maximum 30.
opzione_b: Enable automatic scaling on ASP-Prod, set Maximum burst to 30, and set Always ready instances to 2 for each app.
opzione_c: An autoscale setting that contains a recurrence profile scheduled for Fridays from 18:00 to 23:00 with higher instance limits, in addition to the default profile that has lower instance limits.
opzione_d: Scale up ASP-Prod to the Isolated v2 tier and manually set the instance count to 20.
spiegazione: Option c is correct. Microsoft Learn documents the recurrence profile as the autoscale profile type used for a day or set of days of the week, and states that autoscale evaluates profiles in the order fixed-date, recurring, then default, using the first suitable profile found. A recurrence profile for Fridays 18:00-23:00 with raised instance limits therefore takes effect on schedule and provisions capacity before the predictable spike arrives, while the default profile keeps limits - and cost - low the rest of the time. Autoscale supports up to 20 profiles per setting, and it is available on Standard and up, so a Premium v3 plan qualifies. Option a is wrong because a single metric-based default profile is purely reactive: instances are only added after CPU has already risen for the rule's duration, which conflicts with the requirement to have capacity in place when the event starts and with the requirement not to rely on metric thresholds alone. Option b is wrong because automatic scaling is traffic-based only - Learn explicitly states it has no schedule-based scaling and advises using autoscale instead if you need time-based scaling. It is also reactive, so it does not pre-provision for a known event window. Option d is wrong because it is manual and permanent: 20 Isolated v2 instances would run continuously regardless of load, which is the opposite of minimizing cost, and it requires an App Service Environment plus a separately charged virtual network.
tags: app service, autoscale, recurrence profile, scheduled scaling, premium v3, cost optimization, azure monitor

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda:
An autoscale setting named AS1 targets an App Service plan named ASP1 that uses the Premium v3 tier. AS1 contains only a default profile with the following configuration:
- Instance limits: minimum = 2, maximum = 10, default = 5
- Scale-out rule: metric Percentage CPU, time aggregation Average, duration 10 minutes, operator GreaterThan, threshold 75, action Increase count by 2, cool down 5 minutes
- Scale-in rule: metric Percentage CPU, time aggregation Average, duration 10 minutes, operator LessThan, threshold 25, action Decrease count by 1, cool down 5 minutes
ASP1 is currently running 2 instances. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: When the scale-out rule is triggered for the first time, the instance count becomes: [3 | 4 | 10]
opzione_b: If autoscale cannot read the Percentage CPU metric, autoscale: [takes no action | scales out to 5 instances | scales in to 2 instances]
opzione_c: If average CPU drops to 10 percent and stays there, the instance count becomes: [0 | 1 | 2]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1: 4. The scale-out rule's scaleAction is Increase count by 2, so the new capacity is 2 + 2 = 4, which is within the maximum of 10. It is not 3 (that would be an increase of 1) and it is not 10 (autoscale does not jump to the maximum instance limit; the maximum is only a ceiling). Dropdown 2: scales out to 5 instances. Microsoft Learn describes the capacity.default element as follows: if there's a problem reading the resource metric and the current capacity is below the default, autoscale scales out to the default to ensure the availability of the resource. Current capacity is 2, which is below the default of 5, so autoscale scales out to 5. (If the current capacity were already higher than the default, autoscale would not scale in.) Dropdown 3: 2. The scale-in rule is triggered because average CPU of 10 is less than the threshold of 25, and the action would decrease the count by 1 to 1 instance. However, capacity.minimum ensures that autoscale doesn't scale the resource below the configured minimum, which is 2. The count therefore remains at 2. It is never 0, because a minimum of 2 is enforced.
tags: app service, autoscale, default capacity, instance limits, scale in, azure monitor, autoscale profile

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda: The autoscale setting for an App Service plan contains a single default profile with two scale-in rules. Rule3 decreases the instance count by 1 when the average CPU percentage is less than 25. Rule4 decreases the instance count by 1 when the HTTP queue length is less than 10. The plan is running 6 instances with a minimum instance limit of 2. During an autoscale evaluation, no scale-out rules are triggered, average CPU is 15 percent, and the HTTP queue length is 40. What happens?
opzione_a: Autoscale scales in by 1 instance to 5 instances because Rule3 is triggered.
opzione_b: No scale-in action occurs, because autoscale only scales in when every scale-in rule in the profile is triggered.
opzione_c: Autoscale scales in to the minimum of 2 instances because the profile's scale-in rules take precedence over the current capacity.
opzione_d: Autoscale scales in by 2 instances to 4 instances, applying both scale-in rules cumulatively.
spiegazione: Option b is correct. Microsoft Learn states that if no scale-out rules are triggered, autoscale evaluates the scale-in rules, and that autoscale only scales in if all the scale-in rules are triggered. Rule3 is satisfied (CPU 15 is less than 25) but Rule4 is not (HTTP queue length is 40, which is not less than 10), so the AND condition is not met and no scale-in occurs. Option a is wrong because it applies the OR behaviour that governs scale-out rules to scale-in rules; scale-out uses OR and takes the highest resulting capacity, while scale-in uses AND. Option c is wrong because the minimum instance limit is a floor that prevents autoscale from scaling below 2 instances - it is never a scale-in target, and no scale-in is triggered here anyway. Option d is wrong on two counts: the scale-in condition is not met, and even when multiple scale-in rules do trigger, autoscale does not add their actions together; it scales in by as little as possible, choosing the result that yields the highest capacity, to protect service availability.
tags: app service, autoscale, scale in rules, autoscale evaluation, azure monitor, flapping

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda: An autoscale setting is applied to an App Service plan that uses the Premium v3 tier. The default profile has instance limits of minimum 2, maximum 10, and default 3. The profile contains two scale-out rules: Rule1 increases the instance count by 2 when the average CPU percentage is greater than 70, and Rule2 increases the instance count by 5 when the average memory percentage is greater than 80. The plan is currently running 3 instances when both Rule1 and Rule2 are triggered during the same autoscale evaluation. How many instances will the plan run after the scale action completes?
spiegazione: 8 is correct. Microsoft Learn documents that after autoscale selects a profile, it evaluates all scale-out rules in that profile. If more than one scale-out rule is triggered, autoscale calculates the new capacity determined by the scaleAction of each rule and scales to the highest specified capacity to ensure service availability. Rule1 yields 3 + 2 = 5 instances and Rule2 yields 3 + 5 = 8 instances; autoscale takes the higher value, 8, which is within the maximum of 10. Option a (3) is wrong because it assumes the rules cancel each other out or that autoscale requires all scale-out rules to agree; that AND behaviour applies to scale-in rules, where autoscale only scales in if all scale-in rules are triggered. Option b (5) is wrong because it applies only Rule1, but autoscale does not pick the first or the smallest scale-out result. Option d (10) is wrong because autoscale does not jump to the maximum instance limit when rules trigger - the maximum is a ceiling that prevents scaling beyond 10, not a target.
tags: app service, autoscale, scale out rules, autoscale evaluation, azure monitor, instance limits

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda: You plan to enable automatic scaling (not rule-based autoscale) for a set of web apps in Azure App Service. Which statements about automatic scaling are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Automatic scaling is available only on Premium v2, Premium v3, and Premium v4 plans.
opzione_b: Automatic scaling requires you to define metric rules based on CPU and memory thresholds.
opzione_c: For a Premium v3 plan, the Maximum burst value can be set to as many as 30 instances.
opzione_d: The Always ready instances setting specifies the minimum number of instances for a web app.
opzione_e: Automatic scaling supports scaling deployment slot traffic.
spiegazione: Options a, c and d are correct. The scale-out options table on Microsoft Learn lists the available tiers for automatic scaling as Premium v2 - v4 (compared with Basic and up for manual scaling and Standard and up for autoscale). Learn states that for Premium v2, v3 and v4 plans you can specify a Maximum burst of up to 30 instances, and that the maximum burst number must be equal to or greater than the number of workers specified for the plan. The app-level Always ready instances setting specifies the minimum number of instances; if load exceeds that minimum, additional instances are added up to the plan's Maximum burst value. Option b is wrong because that describes autoscale, not automatic scaling: automatic scaling is traffic-based and has no rule-based or schedule-based scaling - Learn advises using autoscale instead if you need CPU-, memory- or time-based scaling. Option e is wrong because Learn explicitly notes that automatic scaling is not supported for deployment slot traffic.
tags: app service, automatic scaling, maximum burst, always ready instances, prewarmed instances, premium v3

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda: A web app named App1 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Basic (B2) pricing tier. The operations team must configure rules that automatically add instances when the average CPU percentage exceeds a threshold and remove instances when CPU drops. You need to make the smallest change that enables this capability. What should you do?
opzione_a: Enable automatic scaling on the existing Basic plan and set Maximum burst to 10.
opzione_b: Scale out the existing Basic plan manually to 3 instances.
opzione_c: Scale up the App Service plan to the Standard tier.
opzione_d: Scale up the App Service plan to the Premium v3 tier.
spiegazione: Scaling up to the Standard tier is correct. The App Service scale-out options table on Microsoft Learn shows that manual scaling is available on Basic and up, rule-based autoscale is available on Standard and up, and automatic scaling is available on Premium v2 through v4. Metric-based scale rules therefore require at minimum the Standard tier, and Standard is the smallest change from Basic. Option a is wrong on two counts: automatic scaling is not available on Basic plans, and automatic scaling is traffic-based rather than rule-based - it explicitly does not use CPU or memory rules. Option b is wrong because manual scaling only fixes a static instance count; it provides no rules and no automatic reaction to CPU. Option d is wrong because although Premium v3 does support autoscale, it is a larger and more expensive change than necessary; the requirement is the smallest change.
tags: app service, autoscale, scale rules, standard tier, scale up, automatic scaling

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda: Fabrikam hosts a web app in an App Service plan that currently uses the Basic (B2) pricing tier. The operations team has two new requirements: the plan must support metric-based autoscale rules, and the app must support five deployment slots for staged releases. You will scale the plan up to the lowest pricing tier that satisfies both requirements. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Lowest pricing tier that satisfies both requirements: [Basic (B2) | Standard (S2) | Premium v3 (P1v3)]
opzione_b: Maximum number of instances that tier can scale out to: [3 | 10 | 30]
opzione_c: Maximum number of deployment slots per app that tier supports: [0 | 5 | 20]
spiegazione: Standard (S2) is the lowest tier that satisfies both requirements. Rule-based autoscale is available on Standard and up, and deployment slots require the Standard, Premium or Isolated tier - the Basic tier supports no deployment slots and no autoscale rules. Premium v3 would satisfy both requirements as well, but it is not the lowest such tier. The Standard tier scale-out maximum is 10 dedicated instances (Basic is 3, Premium v2-v4 is 30, Isolated is 100). The Standard tier supports 5 deployment slots per app (Free, Shared and Basic support none; Premium v1-v4 and Isolated support 20). Note that because Standard supports exactly 5 slots, this plan is at the documented limit - Learn warns that an app with more than five slots cannot be scaled down to the Standard tier.
tags: app service, app service plan, standard tier, deployment slots, autoscale, scale out limits

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create a virtual machine
domanda:
A virtual machine named VM2 is a Generation 1 VM that was deployed from an Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS Marketplace image. VM2 uses the Standard_A4_v2 size and is protected by Azure Backup with a Standard backup policy. You plan to upgrade VM2 to Generation 2 with Trusted launch. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether each one is correct.
1. You must change the size of VM2 to a size family that supports Trusted launch before you perform the upgrade.
2. You must migrate the Azure Backup protection for VM2 from the Standard policy to the Enhanced policy before you perform the upgrade.
3. After the upgrade completes, you can return VM2 to its original Generation 1 configuration by setting its security type to Standard.
opzione_a: You must change the size of VM2 to a size family that supports Trusted launch before you perform the upgrade.
opzione_b: You must migrate the Azure Backup protection for VM2 from the Standard policy to the Enhanced policy before you perform the upgrade.
opzione_c: After the upgrade completes, you can return VM2 to its original Generation 1 configuration by setting its security type to Standard.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. The A-family is listed as a size family that does not support Generation 2 VMs and is explicitly listed as not supported for Trusted launch. Learn's unsupported Gen1 configurations section states that the upgrade is not supported for a VM configured with a size not listed under Trusted launch supported size families, and gives the workaround: update the VM size to a Trusted launch supported VM size family (for example, a D-family size). Statement 2 - Yes. The prerequisites state that Azure Backup, if enabled, must be configured with the Enhanced backup policy, because the Trusted launch security type can't be enabled for VMs configured with Standard policy backup protection; existing backups can be migrated from Standard to Enhanced. Statement 3 - No. Learn states that a VM once upgraded to Trusted launch can't be rolled back to Gen1 configuration and must be fully recovered using the backup taken before the upgrade. Setting the security type to Standard only rolls the VM back to a Gen2 (non-Trusted launch) configuration, not to Generation 1 - and even that is a one-way operation. Note that as an endorsed Ubuntu Marketplace image, VM2's guest volume already has the GPT layout and EFI system partition, so no MBR-to-GPT conversion is needed.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create a virtual machine
domanda: A Generation 1 virtual machine named FS1 runs Windows Server 2022 on a Standard_D8s_v4 size and is protected by Azure Backup. You plan to upgrade FS1 to Generation 2 with Trusted launch. Which actions must you perform to satisfy the documented prerequisites? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Convert the guest OS volume from an MBR disk layout to a GPT disk layout and add an EFI system partition
opzione_b: Deallocate FS1 to complete the upgrade
opzione_c: Migrate the Azure Backup protection for FS1 from the Standard policy to the Enhanced policy
opzione_d: Convert the OS disk of FS1 to an Ultra Disk
opzione_e: Resize FS1 to a Standard_A8_v2 size before starting the upgrade
spiegazione: Correct: a, b, c. Learn states that Generation 2 VMs require a guest OS volume with a GPT disk layout and an EFI system partition, and that Gen1 Windows volumes are mostly MBR without that partition, so you run MBR2GPT.exe (/validate then /convert with /allowFullOS) before the upgrade (a). The upgrade procedure requires the VM to be deallocated to complete - the portal prompts to confirm deallocation, and the PowerShell and CLI flows begin with Stop-AzVM / az vm deallocate (b). The prerequisites also state that Azure Backup, if enabled, must be configured with the Enhanced backup policy, because Trusted launch can't be enabled for VMs protected by a Standard policy (c). Why the others are wrong: d is wrong because the OS disk type is irrelevant to the Gen1-to-Trusted launch upgrade; Gen2 supports Ultra Disk but it is not a prerequisite. e is wrong and is in fact counterproductive: the A-family does not support Generation 2 VMs at all and is listed as unsupported for Trusted launch, so resizing to Standard_A8_v2 would block the upgrade. Standard_D8s_v4 is already a supported D-family size, so no resize is needed.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create a virtual machine
domanda: You are creating a new Azure virtual machine from a Windows Server 2022 Marketplace image. The virtual machine must boot with UEFI, have Secure Boot and vTPM enabled, and use an operating system disk of 3 TiB. The virtual machine will use the Standard_D4s_v5 size. Select the appropriate value for each setting.
opzione_a: VM generation required: [Generation 1 | Generation 2]
opzione_b: Security type to select: [Standard | Trusted launch]
opzione_c: Additional Azure charge for the security type: [None | Per vCPU per hour | Per vTPM per month]
opzione_d: Maximum supported OS disk size for this VM: [2 TiB | 4 TiB | 64 TiB]
spiegazione: Correct: Generation 2, Trusted launch, None, 4 TiB. Generation 2 is required because only Gen2 VMs use the UEFI boot architecture and only Gen2 supports an OS disk larger than 2 TiB; Generation 1 fails both requirements. Trusted launch is the security type that delivers Secure Boot and vTPM on Gen2 VMs - the Generation 2 comparison table shows Secure Boot and vTPM in Azure are available 'with trusted launch', and Standard provides neither. Learn states that Trusted launch doesn't increase existing VM pricing costs, so there is no per-vCPU or per-vTPM surcharge; the other two choices are invented billing models. The Gen2 FAQ states you can increase the OS disk size up to a recommended maximum of 4 TiB and that OS disk sizes larger than 4 TiB are not supported, so 4 TiB is the ceiling - 2 TiB is the Generation 1 limit and 64 TiB corresponds to large data disk sizes, not OS disks. Standard_D4s_v5 is a D-family size, which is listed as supported for both Generation 2 and Trusted launch.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create a virtual machine
domanda: Contoso runs an existing Generation 1 virtual machine named APP1 that hosts Windows Server 2019 on a Standard_D4s_v3 size. A new security baseline requires that APP1 boot with Secure Boot and expose a vTPM. Which approach is supported by Azure?
opzione_a: Upgrade APP1 to Generation 2 by changing its security type to Trusted launch
opzione_b: Upgrade APP1 to Generation 2 only, and then enable Secure Boot and vTPM as a separate step
opzione_c: Set the Hyper-V generation property of APP1's existing OS disk to V2 while the VM is running
opzione_d: No upgrade path exists; you must rebuild APP1 from a Generation 2 Marketplace image
spiegazione: Correct: a. Learn states that Azure Virtual Machines supports upgrading Generation 1 VMs to Generation 2 by upgrading to the Trusted launch security type, which combines Secure Boot, vTPM, and boot integrity monitoring. Windows Server 2019 and the D-family are both on the supported lists, so APP1 qualifies (after the guest OS volume is converted from MBR to GPT). Why the others are wrong: b is wrong because the documentation explicitly states that upgrading Gen1 VMs to Gen2 without enabling Trusted launch is not supported - Trusted launch is the upgrade path, not an optional follow-up. c is wrong because the HyperVGeneration property can only be set to V2 when creating a managed disk from an uploaded Gen2 VHD; it is not a live property you can flip on an existing running VM's OS disk. d is wrong because a supported in-place upgrade path does exist, so a full rebuild is unnecessary.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create a virtual machine
domanda: A finance workload requires an Azure virtual machine whose operating system disk is 3 TiB. You must select the correct configuration at deployment time. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create the VM as Generation 1 and expand the OS disk to 3 TiB after deployment
opzione_b: Create the VM as Generation 2 and expand the OS disk to 3 TiB
opzione_c: Create the VM as Generation 1 and change the OS disk to an Ultra Disk, because generation does not affect OS disk size
opzione_d: The requirement cannot be met, because Azure OS disks are limited to 2 TiB for every VM
spiegazione: Correct: b. The Generation 1 vs. Generation 2 capabilities table shows that an OS disk larger than 2 TiB is supported only on Generation 2 VMs. Learn states that by default OS disks are smaller than 2 TiB, and you can increase the disk size up to a recommended maximum of 4 TiB (sizes larger than 4 TiB are not supported), so 3 TiB is achievable on Gen2. Why the others are wrong: a is wrong because a Generation 1 VM cannot have an OS disk larger than 2 TiB, no matter how it is expanded afterwards. c is wrong because the OS disk size ceiling is a function of the VM generation, not the disk SKU; Gen2 does support Ultra Disk, but switching disk type does not lift the Gen1 2 TiB OS disk limit. d is wrong because the 2 TiB ceiling applies only to Generation 1; Gen2 supports OS disks up to a recommended maximum of 4 TiB.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: Registry acr1 must be reachable only from a virtual network named vnet1. You plan to create a private endpoint for acr1 in vnet1, integrate it with a private DNS zone so that clients keep using the acr1.azurecr.io name, and then set Public network access to Disabled on the Networking blade. Your CI pipeline currently runs az acr build against acr1 from a hosted agent on the internet. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Minimum pricing plan required for the private endpoint: [Basic | Standard | Premium]
opzione_b: Private DNS zone that must resolve the registry FQDN: [privatelink.azurecr.io | privatelink.registry.azure.com | acr.privatelink.core.windows.net]
opzione_c: Effect on az acr build from the hosted agent after public network access is disabled: [It continues to work unchanged | It fails unless you use a dedicated agent pool or allow the regional AzureContainerRegistry service tag IPs | It works only if the admin user is enabled]
risposta_corretta: Premium,privatelink.azurecr.io,It fails unless you use a dedicated agent pool or allow the regional AzureContainerRegistry service tag IPs
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - Premium: private link with private endpoints is available in the Premium container registry service tier, with a maximum of 200 private endpoints. Basic and Standard are marked N/A for private link in the SKU feature matrix. Dropdown 2 - privatelink.azurecr.io: to override the default DNS resolution for an Azure container registry with a private zone, the zone must be named privatelink.azurecr.io; the portal likewise offers (New) privatelink.azurecr.io during private endpoint creation. The other two names are invented and would never be queried, because the registry FQDN resolves through a CNAME to <registry>.privatelink.azurecr.io. Dropdown 3 - it fails: Microsoft Learn explicitly notes that if you disable public network access, az acr build commands no longer work, because Tasks reserve a set of public IPs in each region for outbound requests. The documented options are to assign a dedicated agent pool (a Premium feature) or to add the regional AzureContainerRegistry service tag IPv4 ranges to the firewall access rules. 'Continues to work unchanged' contradicts the documentation, and enabling the admin user changes only authentication, not network reachability. Note that creating a private endpoint also automatically enables dedicated data endpoints, so plan for one private IP for the global endpoint plus one per geo-replica for the data endpoints.
tags: acr,private endpoint,private link,privatelink.azurecr.io,public network access,az acr build

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: A Docker-enabled Linux virtual machine named vm1 is configured with a user-assigned managed identity named id1. The VM must pull images from a registry named acr1 without any credentials being stored on the VM. The registry uses the RBAC Registry Permissions role assignment mode. Select the appropriate option to complete each step.
opzione_a: Role to assign to id1, scoped to acr1: [AcrPull | AcrPush | Contributor]
opzione_b: Command to run on vm1 to sign in to the Azure CLI: [az login --identity --username <id1 resource ID> | az login --service-principal --username <appId> --password <secret> | az acr credential show --name acr1]
opzione_c: Command to run next on vm1 to authenticate to the registry: [az acr login --name acr1 | az acr update --name acr1 --admin-enabled true | az acr token create --name acr1 --repository nginx content/read]
risposta_corretta: AcrPull,az login --identity --username <id1 resource ID>,az acr login --name acr1
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - AcrPull: for a non-ABAC registry, the managed identity article says to assign AcrPull, which provides pull permissions only, scoped to the registry resource ID. AcrPush would additionally allow pushing, and Contributor is a control plane role that would let the identity reconfigure or delete the registry - both exceed what a pull-only workload needs. Dropdown 2 - az login --identity --username <id1 resource ID>: this is the documented way to sign the Azure CLI in with a user-assigned managed identity on the VM (a system-assigned identity would use az login --identity with no username). az login --service-principal requires a secret to be stored on the VM, which the requirement forbids, and az acr credential show retrieves the admin account credentials - also a stored credential, and it does not sign anyone in. Dropdown 3 - az acr login --name acr1: after az login, the CLI reuses the Microsoft Entra token it created to authenticate the session with the registry, and subsequent docker pull commands need no credentials. Keep in mind the token az acr login uses is valid for 3 hours. az acr update --admin-enabled true enables the admin account, which is the credential-based approach being avoided, and az acr token create creates a non-Microsoft Entra repository-scoped token, which again means managing a secret.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda:
From Azure Cloud Shell, you must copy container images into a registry named acrprod by using az acr import. The sources include a public registry, an Azure container registry in another Microsoft Entra tenant, and an Azure container registry in your own tenant that has public network access disabled. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true.
1. A local Docker Engine installation is required for az acr import to copy the images.
2. You can import an image from an Azure container registry in a different Microsoft Entra tenant by specifying the source registry's login server name together with credentials that allow pull access to it.
3. To import from a source Azure container registry that has public network access disabled, you specify the source registry by its resource ID with the --registry parameter.
opzione_a: A local Docker Engine installation is required for az acr import to copy the images.
opzione_b: You can import an image from an Azure container registry in a different Microsoft Entra tenant by specifying the source registry's login server name together with credentials that allow pull access to it.
opzione_c: To import from a source Azure container registry that has public network access disabled, you specify the source registry by its resource ID with the --registry parameter.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: importing images to an Azure container registry is done through Azure APIs without using Docker commands. Microsoft Learn lists as a benefit that if your client environment doesn't need a local Docker installation, you can import any container image regardless of the supported OS type - which is precisely why the command works from Azure Cloud Shell. Statement 2 - Yes: to import images from a registry in a different Microsoft Entra tenant, you specify the source registry by login server name and provide credentials that enable pull access, for example the appId and password of a service principal that has AcrPull (or Container Registry Repository Reader on an ABAC-enabled registry) on the source, a non-Microsoft Entra repository-scoped token, or an access token passed as the password. Be aware that cross-tenant import isn't supported over a public-access-disabled registry. Statement 3 - Yes: when public access to the source registry is disabled, you supply the resource ID of the source registry with the --registry parameter and the --source parameter then specifies only the repository and tag, not the login server name. Also remember that a network-restricted registry must allow access by trusted services to bypass the network, otherwise the import fails; that setting is enabled by default.
tags: acr,az acr import,cross-tenant,resource id,trusted services,cloud shell

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda:
A registry named acr1 uses the Standard pricing plan, and its admin user account is currently enabled. All developers share the admin credentials to run docker login. Your team is reviewing how clients authenticate to acr1. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true.
1. Disabling the admin account and having developers authenticate with az acr login means their registry access is governed by Azure RBAC role assignments.
2. The Microsoft Entra token that az acr login places in the Docker configuration file remains valid for 30 days.
3. Anonymous pull access can be enabled on acr1 without changing the registry's pricing plan.
opzione_a: Disabling the admin account and having developers authenticate with az acr login means their registry access is governed by Azure RBAC role assignments.
opzione_b: The Microsoft Entra token that az acr login places in the Docker configuration file remains valid for 30 days.
opzione_c: Anonymous pull access can be enabled on acr1 without changing the registry's pricing plan.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: the authentication options table shows that individual Microsoft Entra identity sign-in via az acr login supports Azure RBAC, whereas the admin user row shows 'No, always pull and push access'. Using az acr login with Azure identities enables Azure role-based access control, so each developer can be granted only the roles they need (for example AcrPull or AcrPush). This is why Microsoft recommends individual identities for users and service principals or managed identities for headless scenarios instead of the shared admin account. Statement 2 - No: Microsoft Learn states that for registry access, the token that az acr login uses is valid for 3 hours, so you should always sign in to the registry before running a docker command and re-run az acr login to refresh an expired token. 30 days is not a documented ACR token lifetime (1 year is the default expiry of a service principal password, which is a different thing). Statement 3 - Yes: the SKU features and limits table marks anonymous pull access as N/A for Basic but Supported for both Standard and Premium. Because acr1 already uses Standard, the feature can be turned on with no plan change. Note that this statement is about technical feasibility, not about whether anonymous pull is advisable for a private registry.
tags: acr,authentication,admin account,az acr login,token lifetime,anonymous pull

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: A build server has the Azure CLI installed but has no Docker Engine and cannot run Docker commands. You must copy the multi-architecture nginx:latest image from Docker Hub into an Azure container registry named acrprod, and every architecture listed in the image manifest list must be copied. Which command should you run?
opzione_a: az acr build --registry acrprod --image nginx:v1 .
opzione_b: az acr import --name acrprod --source docker.io/library/nginx:latest --image nginx:v1
opzione_c: docker pull nginx:latest, then docker tag and docker push acrprod.azurecr.io/nginx:v1
opzione_d: az acr repository show --name acrprod --repository nginx
spiegazione: Correct: az acr import copies images into a registry by using Azure APIs without any Docker commands, so no local Docker installation is needed, and Microsoft Learn states that when you import a multi-architecture image such as an official Docker image, images for all architectures and platforms specified in the manifest list are copied. Because hello-world and nginx are official Docker Hub images, the source path includes the default library repository, as in docker.io/library/nginx:latest. Option a is wrong: az acr build runs a quick task that builds an image from a Dockerfile and a source context - it is for building, not for copying an existing image from another registry. Option c is wrong: it is the classic pull/tag/push workaround, which requires a working Docker Engine that the build server does not have, and a plain docker pull retrieves only the single architecture matching the client platform rather than the whole manifest list. Option d is wrong: az acr repository show only displays the attributes of a repository that already exists in the registry; it copies nothing.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: You are documenting which Azure Container Registry capabilities justify the cost of the Premium pricing plan for your organization. Which three features are available only in the Premium plan? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Geo-replication
opzione_b: Content trust (Docker Content Trust)
opzione_c: Customer-managed keys
opzione_d: Zone redundancy (availability zones)
opzione_e: Anonymous pull access
spiegazione: Correct: geo-replication, content trust, and customer-managed keys are all marked Supported for Premium only and N/A for Basic and Standard in the Azure Container Registry SKU features and limits table. Geo-replication gives high availability by managing a single registry across multiple regions; content trust implements the Docker Content Trust model for pushing and pulling signed images; customer-managed keys let you encrypt registry content with your own key. Option d is wrong: the SKU table lists availability zones as Supported for Basic, Standard, and Premium, and the article states that all SKUs have zone redundancy enabled by default in supported regions - it is not a Premium differentiator. Option e is wrong: anonymous pull access is N/A for Basic but Supported for both Standard and Premium, so it is not Premium-only. Other genuinely Premium-only capabilities not listed here include private link with private endpoints, dedicated data endpoints, connected registries, retention policy for untagged manifests, and dedicated agent pools for Tasks.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: Your team maintains several application images that are built FROM a common base image stored in the same Azure container registry. Whenever the base image is patched and pushed again, every dependent application image must be rebuilt automatically, with no manual command and no dependency on a developer workstation. What should you configure?
opzione_a: An Azure Container Registry task that uses a base image update trigger
opzione_b: A registry webhook that calls an Azure function, which then runs docker build on a virtual machine
opzione_c: A quick task that is started with az acr build each time the base image changes
opzione_d: An Azure Container Registry task that uses a timer trigger scheduled to run every night
spiegazione: Correct: ACR Tasks can track an application image's dependency on a base image at build time. When the updated base image is pushed to your registry, or updated in a public repo such as Docker Hub, the task automatically rebuilds any application image based on it - this is the documented way to automate OS and framework patching without manually tracking every dependent image. Option b is wrong: it is an unnecessary custom solution that reintroduces a build host to maintain and duplicates a capability ACR Tasks already provides natively. Option c is wrong: a quick task (az acr build) is an on-demand, manually invoked build for the inner-loop development cycle; something or someone still has to notice the base image changed and run the command, which the requirement forbids. Option d is wrong: a timer trigger runs the task on a fixed schedule regardless of whether the base image changed, so rebuilds are delayed until the next scheduled run and happen even when nothing was patched - it does not react to the base image update itself.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: A colleague is reviewing the Access keys blade of an Azure container registry and asks you about the admin user account. Which statement accurately describes the admin user account of an Azure container registry?
opzione_a: The admin account is enabled by default on every new registry.
opzione_b: The admin account provides two passwords, and either password can be used with the docker login command.
opzione_c: You can assign the AcrPull role to the admin account so that it is limited to pull-only access.
opzione_d: The admin account issues a separate credential set for each user who signs in to the registry.
spiegazione: Correct: the admin account has two passwords, both of which can be regenerated, and you can pass the admin username with either password to docker login. Having two passwords lets you keep connectivity through one password while you rotate the other. Option a is wrong: Microsoft Learn states that each container registry includes an admin user account that is disabled by default; you must explicitly enable it (for example, az acr update -n <acrName> --admin-enabled true, or the Admin user check box under Settings > Access keys). Option c is wrong: the admin account is not integrated with Microsoft Entra ID and therefore has no Azure RBAC role assignments - the authentication options table shows 'No, always pull and push access' for it, so it can never be reduced to pull-only. Option d is wrong: there is a single admin account per registry and it is designed for a single user, mainly for testing; all users who authenticate with it appear as the same identity, which is why Microsoft advises against sharing it among multiple users.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: An Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster named aks1 must pull container images from an existing registry named acrshared, which uses the Basic plan and the RBAC Registry Permissions role assignment mode. The solution must not require an image pull secret in the cluster and must grant the smallest set of permissions possible. What should you do?
opzione_a: Run az aks update --name aks1 --resource-group rg1 --attach-acr acrshared.
opzione_b: Enable the admin user on acrshared and create a Kubernetes secret from the admin username and password.
opzione_c: Assign the AcrPush role to the kubelet managed identity of aks1 on acrshared.
opzione_d: Assign the Reader role to the control plane managed identity of aks1 on acrshared.
spiegazione: Correct: az aks update --attach-acr configures the AKS-to-ACR integration, which assigns the AcrPull role to the Microsoft Entra managed identity associated with the cluster's agent pool (the kubelet identity). Microsoft Learn presents this as the automatic authentication mechanism between AKS and ACR, so no image pull secret is needed, and AcrPull is pull-only. Any ACR plan works - the article's own example creates the registry with --sku basic. Option b is wrong: it uses the shared admin account in an image pull secret, which is the credential-based approach Microsoft explicitly steers away from (image pull secrets are for private external registries), and the admin account always carries push and pull access. Option c is wrong in the role, not the identity: AcrPush would work for pulling but grants push as well, exceeding least privilege. Option d is wrong on both counts: images are pulled by the kubelet identity, not the control plane identity, and Reader is a control plane role that grants no data plane pull permission.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: A Linux virtual machine named vm1 runs a containerized workload and has a system-assigned managed identity. The identity must be able to pull container images from a registry named acr1, but it must not be able to push images, delete images, or change the registry configuration. The registry uses the RBAC Registry Permissions role assignment mode. You must apply the principle of least privilege. Which role should you assign, and at which scope?
opzione_a: AcrPull, scoped to acr1
opzione_b: Reader, scoped to acr1
opzione_c: AcrPush, scoped to acr1
opzione_d: AcrPull, scoped to the subscription that contains acr1
spiegazione: Correct: AcrPull scoped to acr1. For registries in the RBAC Registry Permissions mode, Microsoft Learn recommends AcrPull for identities that only need to pull images and artifacts; it grants data plane read-only access with no control plane or write permissions. Assigning it directly on the registry resource limits the identity to exactly one registry. Option b is wrong: Reader is a control plane role that lets you view the registry resource and its configuration, but it grants no data plane permission, so docker pull still fails. Option c is wrong: AcrPush grants push in addition to pull, which exceeds what the workload needs and violates least privilege. Option d is wrong for the scope, not the role: assigning AcrPull at the subscription lets the VM pull from every registry in that subscription now and in the future, which is broader than required. Azure RBAC assignments are inherited downward, so the narrowest scope that satisfies the requirement is the registry itself.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: An existing Azure container registry named acr1 uses the Premium pricing plan and is geo-replicated to the West Europe and East US regions. The registry stores 60 GiB of images. To reduce cost, you open Settings > Properties in the Azure portal and try to change the pricing plan to Standard, but the operation fails. What should you do first?
opzione_a: Delete the geo-replicas in West Europe and East US, and then change the pricing plan.
opzione_b: Disable the admin user account on acr1, and then change the pricing plan.
opzione_c: Reduce the registry's storage consumption below the 100 GiB that is included with the Standard plan.
opzione_d: Delete acr1 and recreate it with the Standard plan, because a registry's pricing plan cannot be changed after creation.
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft Learn states that when you move from Premium to a lower plan, features specific to Premium are disabled, and in some cases you must remove the related resources first - you must delete any geo-replications or connected registries before you can switch from Premium to Standard or Basic. Geo-replication is a Premium-only feature, so the replicas block the downgrade. Option b is wrong: the admin account is available in every plan and is unrelated to changing the pricing plan. Option c is wrong on two counts: 100 GiB is the storage included in the Standard daily rate, not a cap - additional storage is simply billed per GiB up to the plan's storage limit, and the Standard storage limit is 40 TiB, so 60 GiB is nowhere near a blocker. Option d is wrong: a registry's plan can be changed at any time in the portal, with az acr update --sku, or with Update-AzContainerRegistry, and the change causes no downtime or impact on registry operations.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: You are planning automated image builds by using Azure Container Registry tasks. Which three events can automatically trigger a task run? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: A commit to a GitHub repository that is configured as the task's source code context
opzione_b: An update to the base image that the task's image is built from
opzione_c: A timer schedule defined on the task
opzione_d: A docker pull of an image from the registry
opzione_e: A change to the registry's pricing plan
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft Learn describes exactly these three categories of automatically triggered tasks. Source code update triggers fire when code is committed, or a pull request is made or updated, in a public or private Git repository in GitHub or Azure DevOps (the commit trigger is enabled by default; the pull request trigger is not). Base image update triggers rebuild application images when their base image is pushed to your registry or updated in a public repo such as Docker Hub. Timer triggers run a task on a defined schedule. Option d is wrong: pulling an image is a data plane read operation - it can raise a registry webhook event to notify an external service, but it is not a task trigger. Option e is wrong: changing the pricing plan is a control plane configuration change; it causes no downtime and does not start a task run. Note that source code triggers require a personal access token so the task can create the webhook in the Git repo.
tags: acr,acr tasks,triggers,commit trigger,base image update,timer trigger

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: Contoso plans to deploy a new Azure container registry. The registry must replicate its images to three Azure regions from a single login server, and it must be reachable only through a private endpoint in a virtual network. Which pricing plan must you select when you create the registry?
opzione_a: Basic
opzione_b: Standard
opzione_c: Premium
opzione_d: Standard, with zone redundancy enabled
spiegazione: Correct: Premium. The Azure Container Registry SKU feature matrix lists both geo-replication and private link with private endpoints as supported only in the Premium plan. A single Premium registry replicated to several regions still exposes one global login server (myregistry.azurecr.io), which is exactly what the scenario requires. Basic is wrong: it is the cost-optimized entry point for developers and supports neither geo-replication nor private endpoints. Standard is wrong: it raises included storage and image throughput over Basic but the SKU table marks geo-replication and private link as N/A for Standard. 'Standard with zone redundancy enabled' is wrong because it confuses two different capabilities: zone redundancy protects against a zonal outage inside one region and is supported on all three plans, so enabling it does not add geo-replication or private endpoint support to a Standard registry.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: You are sizing Azure container registries for several teams and need to compare the plans. Select the correct value for each statement based on the Azure Container Registry service tier features and limits.
opzione_a: Storage included in the daily rate for a Standard registry: [10 GiB | 100 GiB | 500 GiB]
opzione_b: Maximum number of webhooks for a Basic registry: [2 | 10 | 500]
opzione_c: Storage limit for a Premium registry: [40 TiB | 100 TiB | 500 TiB]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - 100 GiB: the SKU features and limits table lists included storage as 10 GiB for Basic, 100 GiB for Standard, and 500 GiB for Premium. This is the storage included in the daily rate; you can use additional storage up to the plan's storage limit at an extra daily per-GiB rate, so 10 GiB (Basic) and 500 GiB (Premium) are the values for the other two plans. Dropdown 2 - 2: the webhook limit is 2 for Basic, 10 for Standard, and 500 for Premium, so 10 and 500 belong to the other plans. Dropdown 3 - 100 TiB: the storage limit is 40 TiB for both Basic and Standard and 100 TiB for Premium; 40 TiB is the Basic/Standard limit, and 500 TiB does not appear in the table at all (500 GiB is Premium's included storage, which is a different figure). You can check a registry's current consumption against these limits on the registry Overview page in the portal, or with az acr show-usage.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy a resource by using an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: Resource group RG1 contains a storage account named storage1, a virtual network named vnet1, and a virtual machine named vm1. An ARM template named Template1 defines only two resources: storage1, with a different SKU than the one currently deployed, and a network interface named nic1 that does not yet exist. Template1 is deployed to RG1. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true. 1) If Template1 is deployed by using incremental mode, vnet1 is deleted from RG1. 2) If Template1 is deployed by using complete mode, vm1 is deleted from RG1. 3) If Template1 is deployed by using incremental mode, nic1 is created in RG1.
opzione_a: If Template1 is deployed by using incremental mode, vnet1 is deleted from RG1.
opzione_b: If Template1 is deployed by using complete mode, vm1 is deleted from RG1.
opzione_c: If Template1 is deployed by using incremental mode, nic1 is created in RG1.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No. In incremental mode, "Resource Manager leaves unchanged resources that exist in the resource group but aren't specified in the template." vnet1 is not in Template1, so incremental mode leaves it untouched. Deletion of resources absent from the template is the behaviour of complete mode, not incremental mode. Statement 2 - Yes. In complete mode, "Resource Manager deletes resources that exist in the resource group but aren't specified in the template." vm1 exists in RG1 and is not defined in Template1, so it is deleted. Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines is a parent resource type, and parent resources are automatically deleted when not in a template deployed in complete mode. Statement 3 - Yes. "For both modes, Resource Manager tries to create all resources specified in the template." Incremental mode adds resources that are in the template to the resource group, so nic1 is created. Incremental never means "only update, never create." Note also that storage1 would be updated to the new SKU in either mode, since changing a SKU is a property change rather than a change of location or type.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy a resource by using an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: An administrator intends to decommission several resources in a resource group named RG-Legacy by deploying a trimmed-down ARM template in complete mode. The deployment reports success, but every resource that was expected to be removed still exists. The template is a root-level template deployed at resource group scope, and the resources in question all support complete mode deletion. What is the most likely cause?
opzione_a: A CanNotDelete lock is applied to the resource group.
opzione_b: The administrator was assigned the Contributor role instead of the Owner role at the resource group scope.
opzione_c: The template's contentVersion value was not incremented before the deployment.
opzione_d: An Azure Policy assignment with the Deny effect is applied to the resource group.
spiegazione: Correct: A CanNotDelete lock on the resource group. Learn states directly: "If the resource group is locked, complete mode doesn't delete the resources." The deployment still succeeds for the resources defined in the template, which matches the observed behaviour of a successful deployment with no deletions. Why the others are wrong: (b) Contributor grants full management access to resources including delete permissions; it only withholds the ability to grant RBAC access and manage assignments. Insufficient permissions would also surface as a failed or unauthorized deployment, not a silent success. (c) contentVersion is free-form documentation metadata. Resource Manager does not compare it between deployments and never changes behaviour based on it. (d) A Deny policy assignment blocks the creation or update of non-compliant resources; it does not prevent deletion, and a policy denial would cause the deployment to fail rather than report success. Microsoft recommends running the what-if operation before any complete mode deployment to preview exactly which resources will be deleted.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy a resource by using an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: A DevOps pipeline deploys a root ARM template that includes a linked template through a Microsoft.Resources/deployments resource. To clean up resources that are no longer defined, an engineer sets "mode": "Complete" in the properties of the linked deployment resource. Which statement correctly describes the outcome?
opzione_a: The linked deployment deletes any resource in the resource group that is not defined in the linked template.
opzione_b: Complete mode is supported only for root-level templates; for linked or nested templates you must use incremental mode.
opzione_c: The linked deployment deletes resources that are not defined in the linked template across every resource group in the subscription.
opzione_d: Complete mode works in a linked template only when the template uses the subscriptionDeploymentTemplate.json schema.
spiegazione: Correct: Complete mode is supported only for root-level templates. Learn states: "Only root-level templates support the complete deployment mode. For linked or nested templates, you must use incremental mode." The mode set on a nested deployment resource cannot be Complete. Why the others are wrong: (a) describes what the engineer intends, but the platform does not honour complete mode at the nested level, so no cleanup deletion occurs from the linked deployment. (c) is wrong on two counts: complete mode never spans a whole subscription, and when a template deploys to more than one resource group only resources in the resource group named in the deployment operation are eligible for deletion; resources in secondary resource groups aren't deleted. (d) inverts the facts. Subscription-level deployments don't support complete mode at all, so the subscription schema would make complete mode less available, not more. Microsoft's current guidance is to use deployment stacks when deletions are required, as complete mode is being gradually deprecated.
tags: arm template,complete mode,linked template,nested template,deployment modes

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy a resource by using an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: Your organization is documenting the constraints of complete deployment mode before allowing its use in production pipelines. Which statements about complete mode are correct? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Subscription-level deployments don't support complete mode.
opzione_b: Only root-level templates support complete mode; linked and nested templates must use incremental mode.
opzione_c: Complete mode can be selected when deploying a custom template from the Azure portal.
opzione_d: If the target resource group is locked, complete mode doesn't delete the resources.
opzione_e: In a template that deploys to more than one resource group, resources in the secondary resource groups are also eligible for deletion.
spiegazione: Correct answers: a, b and d. (a) Learn states: "Subscription level deployments don't support complete mode." Complete mode applies only at resource group scope. (b) "Only root-level templates support the complete deployment mode. For linked or nested templates, you must use incremental mode." (d) "If the resource group is locked, complete mode doesn't delete the resources." Why the others are wrong: (c) is false. Learn states "Currently, the portal doesn't support complete mode." You must use Azure PowerShell (-Mode Complete), Azure CLI (--mode Complete) or the REST API. (e) is false and inverts the documented rule: "If you deploy to more than one resource group in a template, resources in the resource group specified in the deployment operation are eligible to be deleted. Resources in the secondary resource groups aren't deleted." Note that Microsoft now recommends deployment stacks for deletion scenarios, since complete mode is being gradually deprecated.
tags: arm template,complete mode,deployment modes,resource lock,portal,subscription deployment

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy a resource by using an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: Which of the following statements accurately describe incremental deployment mode for ARM templates and Bicep files? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Resources that exist in the resource group but aren't specified in the template are left unchanged.
opzione_b: When an existing resource is redeployed, properties that aren't included in the template are reset to their default values.
opzione_c: It is the mode that Resource Manager uses when no mode is specified on the deployment operation.
opzione_d: Resources that exist in the resource group but aren't specified in the template are deleted.
opzione_e: Changing the location of an existing resource in the template relocates that resource during redeployment.
spiegazione: Correct answers: a, b and c. (a) Learn states that in incremental mode "Resource Manager leaves unchanged resources that exist in the resource group but aren't specified in the template." (b) "When redeploying an existing resource in incremental mode, all properties are reapplied. The properties aren't incrementally added... Properties that aren't included in the template are reset to the default values." The resource definition always contains the final state of the resource and cannot express a partial update. (c) "The default mode is incremental." Why the others are wrong: (d) describes complete mode, not incremental mode. This is the defining difference between the two modes and the most common confusion on this topic. (e) is false. For both modes, "If you try to update the location or type of an existing resource, the deployment fails with an error." You must instead deploy a new resource with the location or type that you need.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy a resource by using an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: Resource group RG1 currently contains three resources named ResourceA, ResourceB and ResourceC. An ARM template named Template1 defines ResourceA, ResourceB and ResourceD. Template1 is deployed to RG1 by using complete mode. Which resources exist in RG1 after the deployment succeeds?
opzione_a: ResourceA, ResourceB and ResourceD only
opzione_b: ResourceA, ResourceB, ResourceC and ResourceD
opzione_c: ResourceA and ResourceB only
opzione_d: ResourceD only
spiegazione: Correct: ResourceA, ResourceB and ResourceD only. In complete mode, Resource Manager deletes resources that exist in the resource group but aren't specified in the template. ResourceC is not in Template1, so it is deleted. ResourceA and ResourceB are in the template and are redeployed/updated, and ResourceD is created because Resource Manager still tries to create all resources specified in the template in both modes. Why the others are wrong: (b) is the result of an incremental deployment: incremental leaves ResourceC unchanged, so all four would remain. This is the classic distractor. (c) incorrectly assumes complete mode also skips resources that are new in the template; complete mode still creates ResourceD. (d) incorrectly assumes complete mode deletes and recreates everything from scratch. Existing resources whose settings are unchanged have no operation taken against them; they are not deleted and recreated.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy a resource by using an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: A release engineer at Contoso deploys an ARM template to a resource group by running New-AzResourceGroupDeployment without including the -Mode parameter. Which deployment mode does Azure Resource Manager use for this deployment?
opzione_a: Complete
opzione_b: Incremental
opzione_c: Validate
opzione_d: Complete, but only if the template defines every resource that already exists in the resource group
spiegazione: Correct: Incremental. The Learn documentation states plainly that "The default mode is incremental." When -Mode is omitted, Resource Manager adds or updates the resources defined in the template and leaves untouched any resource that exists in the resource group but is not in the template. Why the others are wrong: (a) Complete is never the default; it must be requested explicitly with -Mode Complete (PowerShell) or --mode Complete (Azure CLI), because it deletes resources that are absent from the template. (c) Validate is not a deployment mode. Validation is a separate operation (Test-AzResourceGroupDeployment / az deployment group validate); the only two deployment modes are Incremental and Complete. (d) This describes a conditional behaviour that does not exist. Mode selection is an explicit parameter of the deployment operation and is never inferred from the template contents.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: You are hardening the rolling upgrade policy of a Virtual Machine Scale Set that hosts a production API across three availability zones. The Application Health extension is already reporting health. Which configuration actions correctly achieve their stated goal? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Set maxBatchInstancePercent to 10 so that no more than 10 percent of the instances are upgraded in a single batch.
opzione_b: Set maxUnhealthyInstancePercent to 20 so that the rolling upgrade stops if more than 20 percent of the instances in the scale set report as unhealthy.
opzione_c: Enable MaxSurge so that new instances that use the latest model are created and marked healthy before instances that use the old model are deleted.
opzione_d: Enable cross-zone upgrade so that the rolling upgrade guarantees that only one availability zone is upgraded at a time.
opzione_e: Set pauseTimeBetweenBatches to PT0S so that the scale set verifies that every instance in a batch is healthy before starting the next batch.
spiegazione: Correct answers a, b and c. maxBatchInstancePercent specifies how many of the total instances you want upgraded at one time; Learn's example states that a batch size of 20 percent with 10 instances produces batches of two instances, so setting it to 10 correctly caps each batch at 10 percent. maxUnhealthyInstancePercent specifies the total number of instances allowed to be marked unhealthy before and during the rolling upgrade; Learn's example states that with a value of 20 and a scale set of 10 instances, the rolling upgrade stops if more than two instances report unhealthy. MaxSurge is documented as creating new instances in batches using the latest scale model and, once the batch is successfully created and marked healthy, deleting instances in batches matching the old model, which improves service uptime during upgrades. Why the others are wrong: enable cross-zone upgrade does the opposite of the stated goal. Learn states it allows the scale set to ignore availability zone boundaries when determining batches, essentially treating a zone-spanning deployment as a regional (nonzonal) one; it does not confine an upgrade to one zone at a time. Setting pauseTimeBetweenBatches to PT0S does not verify health at all - the setting only specifies how long the scale set waits between finishing one batch and starting the next, and PT0S means no wait. Batch health gating is governed by maxUnhealthyInstancePercent and maxUnhealthyUpgradedInstancePercent instead.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda:
A Virtual Machine Scale Set named vmss-batch uses autoscale and has the OldestVM scale-in policy configured on the scale set model. The oldest instance in the scale set is running a long batch job that must not be interrupted, so you set the protectFromScaleIn property to true on that instance and leave protectFromScaleSetActions unset. You need to evaluate the resulting behaviour. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
1. When autoscale triggers a scale-in, the protected instance is skipped even though it is the oldest virtual machine in the scale set.
2. An administrator can still delete the protected instance manually at any time.
3. Setting protectFromScaleIn also prevents the instance from being upgraded when the scale set model changes.
opzione_a: When autoscale triggers a scale-in, the protected instance is skipped even though it is the oldest virtual machine in the scale set.
opzione_b: An administrator can still delete the protected instance manually at any time.
opzione_c: Setting protectFromScaleIn also prevents the instance from being upgraded when the scale set model changes.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes. Learn states that a protected virtual machine is not deleted through a scale-in action regardless of the scale-in policy applied, and gives exactly this example: if VM_0 (the oldest VM in the scale set) is protected from scale-in and the scale set has the OldestVM policy enabled, VM_0 is not considered for being scaled in even though it is the oldest VM. Statement 2 is Yes. Learn states that for protect from scale-in, user-initiated instance operations, including instance delete, are not blocked, and that a protected virtual machine can be manually deleted by the user at any time regardless of the scale-in policy enabled on the scale set. Instance protection guards against autoscale-initiated scale-in, not against deliberate administrator action. Statement 3 is No. Learn states that protectFromScaleIn protects the instance only from autoscale-initiated scale-in, and that operations initiated on the scale set (upgrade, reimage, deallocate, and so on) are not blocked. Blocking scale set operations such as upgrade requires the separate protectFromScaleSetActions property, which was left unset here. Note that protectFromScaleSetActions also implies protection from autoscale-initiated scale-in, and you cannot specify protectFromScaleIn as false while setting protectFromScaleSetActions to true.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: You are authoring an autoscale rule for a Virtual Machine Scale Set in an Azure Resource Manager template. The rule must meet the following requirements. The Percentage CPU metric must be sampled and averaged once every minute. Each time autoscale runs, it must evaluate the metrics collected over the preceding 10 minutes. When the threshold is exceeded, the scale set must add instances. After a scale action completes, no further scale action may occur for 10 minutes. Select the appropriate value for each setting.
opzione_a: metricTrigger.timeGrain: [PT1M | PT10M | PT30M]
opzione_b: metricTrigger.timeWindow: [PT1M | PT10M | PT1H]
opzione_c: scaleAction.direction: [Increase | Decrease | None]
opzione_d: scaleAction.cooldown: [PT2M | PT5M | PT10M]
spiegazione: timeGrain = PT1M. Learn defines timeGrain as the metric sampling duration, and states that timeGrain = 'PT1M' means the metrics are aggregated every 1 minute by using the aggregation method specified in the statistic element, which matches the requirement to sample and average once per minute. PT10M and PT30M would sample every 10 or 30 minutes and do not meet the requirement. timeWindow = PT10M. Learn defines timeWindow as the amount of time to look back for metrics, and states that timeWindow = 'PT10M' means that every time autoscale runs, it queries metrics for the past 10 minutes. PT1M would look back only one minute and would react to transient spikes; PT1H would look back an hour. direction = Increase. Learn states that the scaleAction direction is 'Increase' to scale out, or 'Decrease' to scale in; adding instances therefore requires Increase. Decrease would remove instances and None is not a valid documented direction value. cooldown = PT10M. Learn defines cooldown as the amount of time to wait after a scale operation before scaling again, giving the example that cooldown = 'PT10M' means autoscale does not attempt to scale again for another 10 minutes. PT2M and PT5M would permit another scale action after only 2 or 5 minutes, which violates the requirement.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: Contoso must choose an orchestration mode for a new Virtual Machine Scale Set. Which capabilities are supported by Flexible orchestration but NOT supported by Uniform orchestration? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Protecting the scale set instances by using Azure Backup.
opzione_b: Adding an existing standalone Azure virtual machine to the scale set.
opzione_c: Running Spot priority instances and Regular priority instances in the same scale set.
opzione_d: Performing image-based automatic OS image upgrades on the instances.
opzione_e: Scaling the instance count automatically based on host metric thresholds.
spiegazione: Correct answers a, b and c. Azure Backup: the Learn comparison table lists Azure Backup as supported for Flexible orchestration and not supported for Uniform orchestration, because Uniform instances are scale-set-specific VMs (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachineScaleSets/virtualMachines) that are not compatible with Azure Backup or Azure Site Recovery, whereas Flexible instances are standard IaaS VMs. Adding an existing VM: the table row 'Add/remove existing VM to the group' is Yes for Flexible and No for Uniform, since Uniform can only manage VMs implicitly created from its configuration model. Mixing Spot and Regular: Learn states that Flexible supports both Spot and Regular priority instances in the same scale set, while for Uniform 'instances must either be all Spot or all Regular'. Why the others are wrong: automatic OS image upgrades are the reverse of the requirement - Learn lists Automatic OS Updates as Yes for Uniform and No for Flexible, and image-based automatic OS upgrades appear in the list of parameters not supported with Flexible orchestration. Metrics-based autoscale is supported by both modes: the Learn table shows automatic scaling (manual, metrics based, schedule based) as Yes for Flexible and Yes for Uniform, so it does not differentiate them.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: Northwind runs a production API on a Virtual Machine Scale Set that uses Flexible orchestration. You configure a rolling upgrade policy so that model changes roll out in batches. Which additional component must you configure so that the scale set can monitor application health during the rolling upgrade?
opzione_a: An Azure Load Balancer health probe attached to the backend pool.
opzione_b: The Application Health extension on the scale set instances.
opzione_c: An Azure Monitor Agent deployment with a data collection rule that collects performance counters.
opzione_d: An availability test in Application Insights that targets the API endpoint.
spiegazione: Correct: the Application Health extension. Microsoft Learn states that when using a rolling upgrade policy on Virtual Machine Scale Sets with Flexible orchestration, the scale set must also use the Application Health extension to monitor application health.
