Rolling upgrades depend on per-instance health signals to decide whether a batch succeeded and whether to continue, pause, or stop the upgrade. Why the others are wrong: a load balancer health probe is a valid health source only for Uniform orchestration, where Learn says the scale set must have a health probe or use the Application Health extension. For Flexible orchestration, application health via a Standard Load Balancer health probe is explicitly listed as an unsupported parameter, and the guidance is to use the Application Health extension on instances instead. The Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule gathers telemetry into a Log Analytics workspace for monitoring and alerting, but it does not report instance health to the scale set orchestrator and cannot gate a rolling upgrade. An Application Insights availability test monitors endpoint reachability from outside Azure and produces alerts, but it likewise provides no per-instance health signal to the scale set.
tags: vmss,rolling upgrade,application health extension,flexible orchestration,upgrade policy

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: A scale set named vmss-app was created in Uniform orchestration mode six months ago. The operations team now requires that the individual instances be protected by Azure Backup, which Uniform orchestration does not support. You must meet the requirement with the supported approach. What should you do?
opzione_a: Run az vmss update and set the orchestration mode of vmss-app to Flexible.
opzione_b: Create a new scale set that uses Flexible orchestration mode and redeploy the workload to it.
opzione_c: Set the singlePlacementGroup property of vmss-app to false and register the instances with a Recovery Services vault.
opzione_d: Increase the platformFaultDomainCount of vmss-app to 5 and enable the Azure Backup extension on each instance.
spiegazione: Correct: recreate the scale set in Flexible orchestration mode. Microsoft Learn states explicitly that the orchestration mode is defined when you create the scale set and cannot be changed or updated later. Because the Azure Backup comparison table shows Azure Backup as supported for Flexible orchestration and not supported for Uniform orchestration, the only way to meet the requirement is to deploy a new scale set in Flexible mode and move the workload. Why the others are wrong: az vmss update cannot change the orchestration mode; the mode is immutable after creation, so this command cannot satisfy the requirement. Changing singlePlacementGroup only controls whether a Uniform scale set spans one or multiple placement groups (affecting the 0-100 versus 0-1,000 instance range); it has no bearing on Azure Backup support, which is blocked because Uniform instances are scale-set-specific VMs rather than standard IaaS VMs. Changing platformFaultDomainCount only controls fault domain spreading and likewise does not make Uniform instances compatible with Azure Backup; there is no Azure Backup extension that works around this limitation.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: An engineer creates a Virtual Machine Scale Set by using an Azure Resource Manager template that does not include an upgradePolicy property. Several weeks later, the template is edited to reference a newer image version and is redeployed to the same scale set. What happens to the VM instances that already exist in the scale set?
opzione_a: All existing instances are brought down at the same time and upgraded to the new image immediately.
opzione_b: Existing instances are upgraded in batches of 20 percent, with a health check between each batch.
opzione_c: Existing instances are not changed until you manually upgrade them; only instances added afterwards use the new model.
opzione_d: The redeployment fails because the upgradePolicy property is required when the image reference changes.
spiegazione: Correct: existing instances are unchanged until manually upgraded. Microsoft Learn states that if you do not explicitly set the upgrade policy mode, it defaults to manual. With a manual upgrade policy mode, nothing happens automatically to the existing virtual machines when changes occur to the scale set model, and new instances added to the scale set use the most up-to-date model available. The administrator must explicitly trigger an upgrade on the existing instances. Why the others are wrong: bringing all instances down at once describes the automatic upgrade policy mode, where the scale set makes no guarantees about the order of virtual machines being brought down and might take down all VMs at the same time; that is not the default. Upgrading in batches describes the rolling upgrade policy mode, which must be explicitly selected and additionally requires application health monitoring; 20 percent is the default maxBatchInstancePercent of the rolling upgrade policy, but rolling mode is not the default mode. The deployment does not fail: upgradePolicy is optional, and omitting it simply yields the manual default.
tags: vmss,upgrade policy,manual upgrade,scale set model,arm template

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: A zone-spanning Virtual Machine Scale Set is deployed across three availability zones and has the OldestVM scale-in policy configured. The instances are currently distributed as follows. Zone 1 contains instance IDs 3, 4, 5 and 10. Zone 2 contains instance IDs 2, 6, 9 and 11. Zone 3 contains instance IDs 1, 7 and 8. Lower instance IDs correspond to older virtual machines, and no instance is protected. Autoscale triggers a scale-in of one instance. Which instance does the scale set delete?
opzione_a: Instance 1, because it is the oldest virtual machine in the entire scale set.
opzione_b: Instance 2, because it is the oldest virtual machine in the zones that are over-provisioned.
opzione_c: Instance 3, because it is the oldest virtual machine in Zone 1.
opzione_d: Instance 11, because it has the highest instance ID in the scale set.
spiegazione: Correct: instance 2. Microsoft Learn documents that the OldestVM policy deletes the oldest created VM after first balancing VMs across availability zones for zone-spanning scale sets. Zone 1 and Zone 2 each hold four instances while Zone 3 holds three, so the scale set is unbalanced and the deletion candidate must come from Zone 1 or Zone 2. Across those two zones the oldest VM is instance 2 in Zone 2, so instance 2 is deleted. This matches the worked example in the Learn documentation. Why the others are wrong: instance 1 is indeed the oldest VM in the scale set, but it sits in Zone 3, which already has the fewest instances; deleting it would worsen the zone imbalance, and zone balancing takes precedence over the scale-in policy. Instance 3 is the oldest VM in Zone 1 and is a valid zone candidate, but instance 2 is older than instance 3, so the OldestVM policy selects instance 2 from among the two eligible zones. Instance 11 is the newest VM; deleting it would be the behaviour of the NewestVM scale-in policy, not OldestVM, and the highest instance ID rule belongs to the Default policy.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: Fabrikam plans to run a stateless web tier on a Virtual Machine Scale Set that uses Flexible orchestration. The instances will be deployed from an image version stored in an Azure Compute Gallery. What is the maximum number of VM instances that the scale set can contain?
spiegazione: Correct: 1,000. Microsoft Learn states that you can add up to 1,000 VMs to a scale set in Flexible orchestration mode, and the comparison table lists a maximum instance count (with fault domain guarantees) of 1,000 for Flexible orchestration. Scale sets support up to 1,000 instances for standard marketplace images and for custom images published through the Azure Compute Gallery. Why the others are wrong: 100 is the maximum instance count with fault domain guarantees for Uniform orchestration, and is also the range limit (0-100 VMs) when a Uniform scale set uses a single placement group (singlePlacementGroup = true) - it is not the Flexible limit. 200 is the maximum number of VMs in an availability set, a different availability construct, and is also the Flexible limit only in the narrow case of VM sizes that do not support memory preserving updates combined with fixed spreading. 600 is the instance limit that applies when a scale set is created from a managed image rather than a marketplace or Azure Compute Gallery image, so it does not apply to this Compute Gallery deployment.
tags: vmss,flexible orchestration,scale set limits,instance count,azure compute gallery

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: A single autoscale profile that targets a Virtual Machine Scale Set contains two scale-in rules. The first triggers when the average Percentage CPU is less than 30 percent. The second triggers when the average Network In is less than 500,000 bytes. During the evaluation window the average Percentage CPU is 22 percent, but Network In remains far above its threshold. No scale-out rule is triggered, and the current instance count is above the profile minimum. What does autoscale do?
opzione_a: It scales in, because at least one scale-in rule was triggered.
opzione_b: It does not scale in, because autoscale scales in only when all of the scale-in rules in the profile are triggered.
opzione_c: It scales in, but only by the smaller of the two instance counts calculated by the rules.
opzione_d: It scales out to the profile default instance count, because the rule set is in conflict.
spiegazione: Correct: no scale-in occurs. Microsoft Learn states that autoscale scales out if any scale-out rule is met, but scales in only when all scale-in rules are met. Because the Network In scale-in rule is not triggered, the AND condition across scale-in rules fails and the instance count is left unchanged. This asymmetry is deliberate and biased toward availability. Why the others are wrong: the any-rule-is-enough behaviour applies to scale-out rules (direction Increase), not to scale-in rules, so a single triggered scale-in rule is insufficient. Choosing the smaller calculated count describes nothing in the documented algorithm; in fact, when all scale-in rules do trigger, Learn states autoscale scales in by as little as possible, resulting in the highest of the calculated instance counts, not the smallest. Autoscale does not scale out to the default instance count here: the default capacity is used only when there is a problem reading the resource metric, and metrics are being read successfully in this scenario.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set
domanda: An autoscale setting that targets a Virtual Machine Scale Set contains three profiles: a fixed-date profile that covers a product launch on 20 November, a recurrence profile that covers weekday business hours, and a default profile. On Friday 20 November at 10:00 local time, all three profiles are applicable. Which profile does the autoscale engine execute?
opzione_a: The default profile, because it always acts as the fallback and overrides scheduled profiles.
opzione_b: The recurrence profile, because weekday business hours are more specific than a single date.
opzione_c: The fixed-date profile, because fixed-date profiles are evaluated first and the first suitable profile is used.
opzione_d: All three profiles, because autoscale merges the rules and uses the highest maximum capacity.
spiegazione: Correct: the fixed-date profile. Microsoft Learn states that each time the autoscale service runs, profiles are evaluated in the order fixed-date profiles, then recurring profiles, then the default profile, and the first suitable profile that is found is used. Because 20 November at 10:00 falls inside the fixed-date window, that profile matches first and is the one executed. Why the others are wrong: the default profile runs only when no other applicable profile exists for the current date and time; it is last in the evaluation order, not an override. The recurrence profile is second in the evaluation order and is only selected when no fixed-date profile applies; the engine does not rank profiles by how specific they appear. Autoscale does not merge profiles: Learn states that each time the autoscale engine runs, it executes one profile, so capacity limits and rules are never combined across profiles.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy resources by using an Azure Resource Manager template or a Bicep file
domanda: Contoso stores its infrastructure as Bicep files. An engineer must run several deployments from a workstation that has both the Azure CLI and Az PowerShell installed. Select the correct option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Cmdlet that deploys main.bicep when the file sets targetScope = 'subscription': [New-AzSubscriptionDeployment | New-AzResourceGroupDeployment | New-AzManagementGroupDeployment]
opzione_b: Azure CLI command that deploys main.bicep to an existing resource group: [az deployment group create | az deployment sub create | az group deployment create]
opzione_c: Switch that is mandatory for a subscription-scope deployment: [--location | --resource-group | --mode]
opzione_d: Deployment history name when main.bicep is deployed without specifying a deployment name: [main | A generated GUID | The name of the resource group]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1: To deploy at the subscription scope with Azure PowerShell you use New-AzSubscriptionDeployment, which is an alias of the New-AzDeployment cmdlet. New-AzResourceGroupDeployment targets the resource group scope and New-AzManagementGroupDeployment targets a management group. Dropdown 2: az deployment group create is the current command for resource group scope deployments. az deployment sub create targets the subscription scope, and az group deployment create is the retired command replaced by az deployment group create. Dropdown 3: Subscription, management group, and tenant deployments must all provide a location, because the deployment location determines where the deployment data is stored; it is separate from the location of the resources being deployed. --resource-group is not valid at the subscription scope, and --mode is optional and defaults to Incremental. Dropdown 4: If you do not provide a name for the deployment, its name becomes the name of the Bicep file, so deploying main.bicep produces a deployment named main. A GUID is generated for an unnamed MODULE (nested deployment), not for the top-level deployment.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy resources by using an Azure Resource Manager template or a Bicep file
domanda: You have a Bicep file named storage.bicep that deploys a storage account. You must deploy it to a new resource group named RG-App in the East US region by using the Azure CLI, supply the parameter values from a Bicep parameters file, and confirm what the deployment will change before it runs. Which five actions should you perform in sequence?
opzione_a: Run az group create --name RG-App --location eastus
opzione_b: Run az login and set the subscription context by using az account set
opzione_c: Run az deployment group create --name AppDeploy --resource-group RG-App --parameters storage.bicepparam
opzione_d: Create storage.bicepparam containing a using './storage.bicep' statement and the parameter values
opzione_e: Run az deployment group what-if --resource-group RG-App --parameters storage.bicepparam
spiegazione: Correct order: b, a, d, e, c. You must first authenticate with az login and select the correct subscription with az account set. Next, because you are deploying to a resource group that does not exist, you create it with az group create; a resource group scope deployment cannot create its own target resource group. Then you author storage.bicepparam; the using statement inside the file points at storage.bicep and supplies the parameter values. You then run the what-if operation to preview the changes the file will make and to validate it for errors. Finally you run az deployment group create. Note that when you pass a .bicepparam file to --parameters, you must not also pass --template-file, because the using statement already identifies the template; supplying both raises the error 'Only a .bicep file is allowed with a .bicepparam file'. The same applies to the what-if command, which has identical permission and input requirements to the deployment command.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy resources by using an Azure Resource Manager template or a Bicep file
domanda: During a clean-up project, an engineer maintains a Bicep file with targetScope = 'subscription' that assigns policies and creates resource groups. Obsolete policy assignments that were created outside the file still exist, and the engineer proposes running az deployment sub create with --mode Complete so that Resource Manager removes them. You must explain why this approach will not work and what to do instead. What should you tell the engineer?
opzione_a: Complete mode works at the subscription scope only after all resource locks in the subscription are removed.
opzione_b: Complete mode is supported only from the Azure portal, so the deployment must be re-run from the Template deployment blade.
opzione_c: Complete mode requires the what-if operation to be run first with --confirm-with-what-if; otherwise Resource Manager silently falls back to incremental mode.
opzione_d: Subscription-level deployments do not support complete mode; use deployment stacks to delete resources that are no longer defined.
spiegazione: Correct: d. Subscription level deployments do not support complete mode. Microsoft's guidance is that complete mode is being gradually deprecated and that deployment stacks are the supported way to perform resource deletions with Bicep files or ARM templates. Wrong: a. Locks are relevant to complete mode only at the resource group scope, where a locked resource group prevents complete mode from deleting resources. Removing locks does not make complete mode available at the subscription scope. Wrong: b. The reverse is true: the portal currently does not support complete mode, so it is not an alternative path. Wrong: c. What-if is strongly recommended before any complete mode deployment because it shows what will be deleted, but it is not a prerequisite, and Resource Manager never silently downgrades a requested mode.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy resources by using an Azure Resource Manager template or a Bicep file
domanda: A Bicep file named main.bicep begins with the line targetScope = 'subscription' and declares a Microsoft.Resources/resourceGroups resource. You must deploy the file by using the Azure CLI. Which command should you run?
opzione_a: az deployment group create --resource-group RG1 --template-file main.bicep
opzione_b: az deployment sub create --location centralus --template-file main.bicep
opzione_c: az deployment sub create --template-file main.bicep
opzione_d: az deployment mg create --location centralus --template-file main.bicep
spiegazione: Correct: b. A Bicep file whose targetScope is 'subscription' is deployed with az deployment sub create, and subscription-level deployments require a --location value. The deployment location is where the deployment metadata is stored and is separate from the location of the resources being deployed. Wrong: a. az deployment group create targets the resource group scope. It cannot deploy a file whose targetScope is 'subscription', and a resource group cannot be created from inside a resource group scoped deployment. Wrong: c. The command is the right one, but --location is mandatory for subscription-level deployments; omitting it makes the command fail. Wrong: d. az deployment mg create targets the management group scope and requires targetScope = 'managementGroup' in the file.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and availability sets
domanda: You are producing a one-page reference card that summarizes the Azure Virtual Machines high-availability options for your operations team. Select the correct value for each item.
opzione_a: Maximum fault domains in an availability set: [2 | 3 | 20]
opzione_b: Maximum update domains in an availability set: [5 | 20 | 100]
opzione_c: SLA for two or more VMs across two or more availability zones: [99.9% | 99.95% | 99.99%]
opzione_d: SLA for two or more VMs in a single availability set: [99.9% | 99.95% | 99.99%]
spiegazione: Fault domains: each availability set can have up to 3 fault domains, which group VMs that share a common power source and network switch; 2 is the frequent portal default and 20 is the update domain maximum, so both are distractors. Update domains: each availability set can have up to 20 update domains, which group VMs that can be restarted at the same time during planned maintenance; 5 is a common default and 100 is not a valid value. Availability zone SLA: two or more VMs spread across two or more availability zones in the same region qualify for the highest VM uptime tier of 99.99%, because each zone has a distinct power source, network, and cooling. Availability set SLA: two or more VMs in an availability set meet the 99.95% Azure SLA - lower than zones because an availability set is still susceptible to shared infrastructure failures such as a datacenter-level network outage that spans multiple fault domains. 99.9% is the single-instance premium SSD / ultra disk figure and applies to neither multi-instance configuration.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and availability sets
domanda: A virtual machine named VM1 was deployed as a zonal VM into availability zone 1 of the East US region. Capacity planning now requires VM1's workload to run in availability zone 3 of the same region. You must minimize administrative effort while meeting the requirement. What should you do?
opzione_a: Stop VM1, change the Availability zone property on the VM blade, and start VM1.
opzione_b: Deploy a new zonal virtual machine in availability zone 3 and migrate the workload to it.
opzione_c: Add VM1 to an availability set that spans availability zones 1 and 3.
opzione_d: Use Azure Resource Mover to move VM1 between availability zones.
spiegazione: Correct: zonal VMs can't be moved to a different availability zone. Microsoft states you must deploy a new zonal VM in the desired zone instead. Option A is wrong because the availability zone is fixed at creation and there is no editable zone property that lets you relocate an existing zonal VM; the Availability + scaling blade only exposes a regional-to-zonal move for nonzonal VMs. Option C is wrong on two counts: an availability set is a regional construct that does not span availability zones, and you can't add an existing VM to an availability set after creation. Option D is wrong because Azure Resource Mover moves resources across Azure regions; the regional-to-zonal workflow it powers applies to nonzonal (regional) single-instance VMs, not to relocating an already-zonal VM to another zone.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and availability sets
domanda: An availability set named AS1 exists in the East US region. AS1 was created with a platform fault domain count of 2 and a platform update domain count of 5, and it currently contains two virtual machines named VM1 and VM2. A third virtual machine named VM3 already exists in the same region and resource group but is not a member of any availability set. Evaluate each of the following proposed statements and determine whether it is correct. 1) You can reconfigure AS1 to use 3 fault domains without re-creating the availability set. 2) You can add the existing VM3 to AS1 so that AS1 contains three virtual machines. 3) Running VM1 and VM2 inside AS1 qualifies the workload for the 99.95% Azure SLA.
opzione_a: You can reconfigure AS1 to use 3 fault domains without re-creating the availability set.
opzione_b: You can add the existing VM3 to AS1 so that AS1 contains three virtual machines.
opzione_c: Running VM1 and VM2 inside AS1 qualifies the workload for the 99.95% Azure SLA.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No. Each availability set can have up to 3 fault domains and 20 update domains, but these settings can't be changed after the availability set is created. To use 3 fault domains you must create a new availability set with that fault domain count and deploy the VMs into it. Statement 2 - No. VMs must be created within the availability set so that Azure can distribute them correctly across the hardware; you can't add an existing VM to an availability set after it's created. VM3 would have to be redeployed as a member of AS1. Statement 3 - Yes. Using two or more VMs in an availability set helps keep applications highly available and meets the 99.95% Azure SLA. There's no extra cost for the availability set itself; you only pay for each VM instance.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and availability sets
domanda: You are designing a Virtual Machine Scale Set for a quorum-based service in a region that supports availability zones. The design must meet the following requirements. Instances must be spread across zones 1, 2 and 3. Within each zone, Azure must spread the instances across as many fault domains as possible. Any scaling operation that would leave the zones unevenly populated must be blocked, even when a zone is unavailable. When autoscale scales in, the scale set must remove the most recently created virtual machine from an over-provisioned zone. Select the appropriate value for each setting.
opzione_a: Availability zone configuration: [Regional (nonzonal) | Zonal (single zone) | Zone spanning]
opzione_b: platformFaultDomainCount: [1 | 3 | 5]
opzione_c: zoneBalance: [true | false]
opzione_d: scaleInPolicy rules: [Default | NewestVM | OldestVM]
spiegazione: Availability zone configuration = Zone spanning. Learn states that a zone spanning scale set spreads instances across all selected zones ('zones': ['1','2','3']) and is the recommended model, meeting the 99.99 percent SLA. Zonal places all instances in a single zone and regional (nonzonal) provides no guarantee of balance or spread across zones, so neither satisfies the requirement. platformFaultDomainCount = 1. Learn states that max spreading is platformFaultDomainCount = 1, and that with max spreading the scale set spreads your VMs across as many fault domains as possible within each zone; Microsoft recommends max spreading for most workloads. 5 is fixed spreading across exactly five fault domains, and fixed spreading with 2 or 3 fault domains is supported for regional (nonzonal) deployments only and is invalid for zone-spanning scale sets, which must use 1 or 5. zoneBalance = true. Learn states you can specify strict zone balance by setting 'zoneBalance': 'true', and that with strict zone balancing the scale set must be balanced at all times and any scaling operation that would result in an unbalanced scale set is blocked, even if one or more zones are down. false selects the default best-effort mode, which deliberately permits a temporary imbalance when a single zone is unavailable and therefore does not meet the requirement. scaleInPolicy rules = NewestVM. Learn states the NewestVM policy deletes the newest, or most recently created, virtual machine in the scale set after balancing VMs across availability zones. Default balances across zones and fault domains and then deletes the VM with the highest instance ID, while OldestVM deletes the oldest VM; neither targets the most recently created VM by creation time.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and availability sets
domanda: A regional (nonzonal) Virtual Machine Scale Set named vmss-web contains 5 instances in a region that supports availability zones. You must convert vmss-web into a zone-spanning scale set that ends with 5 instances spread across zones 1, 2 and 3, while keeping the workload available throughout. Which four actions should you perform in sequence? Move the appropriate actions from the list to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
opzione_a: Reduce the capacity of the scale set to 5 so that Azure removes the original nonzonal instances.
opzione_b: Verify that platformFaultDomainCount is set to 1 or 5 and that the VM size and disk types are available in all three zones.
opzione_c: Update the zones parameter on the scale set to ["1","2","3"].
opzione_d: Increase the capacity of the scale set to 10 so that 5 new zonal instances are created.
opzione_e: Change the orchestration mode of the scale set from Uniform to Flexible.
spiegazione: Correct order: b, c, d, a. Learn documents that expanding to a zone-spanning scale set is done in three steps - prepare for zone expansion, update the zones parameter on the scale set, then add new zonal instances and remove original instances - and the manual balancing procedure expands the last step into a scale out followed by a scale in. Step b (prepare) comes first because Learn requires validating that the configuration is valid for zonal and zone-spanning scale sets: platformFaultDomainCount must be set to 1 or 5, since fixed spreading with 2 or 3 fault domains is not supported for zonal and zone-spanning scale sets, and you must check quota and that the VM size and disk types are available in the desired zones. Step c updates the zones parameter, which is supported with API version 2023-03-01 or greater. Step d scales out: Learn's worked example for a nonzonal scale set with 5 instances states you should set the capacity to 10 (5 + 5) so the new instances are created across the zones while old instances remain where they are. Step a scales in to 5, and Learn states the platform always prefers removing the nonzonal instances first, then follows the scale set's scale-in policy, leaving 5 zonal instances spread across the zones. Why option e is not used: it is a distractor. Learn states that the orchestration mode is defined when you create the scale set and cannot be changed or updated later, so this action is impossible and is not required for zone expansion in either orchestration mode.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and availability sets
domanda:
A zone-spanning Virtual Machine Scale Set is deployed across availability zones 1, 2 and 3 and uses the default zone balance mode. Following a recent incident, zone 1 contains 1 VM, zone 2 contains 3 VMs, and zone 3 contains 3 VMs. All instances were created successfully and are running. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
1. The scale set is currently considered unbalanced.
2. If zone 2 and zone 3 both become unavailable, the scale set can still scale out by adding instances to zone 1.
3. Adding another availability zone to the scale set automatically redistributes the existing VM instances into the new zone.
opzione_a: The scale set is currently considered unbalanced.
opzione_b: If zone 2 and zone 3 both become unavailable, the scale set can still scale out by adding instances to zone 1.
opzione_c: Adding another availability zone to the scale set automatically redistributes the existing VM instances into the new zone.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes. Learn states that a scale set is considered balanced if each zone has the same number of VMs plus or minus 1 VM. Here zone 1 has 2 fewer VMs than zones 2 and 3, which exceeds the allowed threshold of plus or minus 1 VM. This is the exact scenario in Learn's Example 3 (1 VM in zone 1, 3 VMs in zone 2, 3 VMs in zone 3), which the documentation labels unbalanced. Statement 2 is No. With best-effort zone balancing, which is the default mode, Learn states that if one zone is unavailable the scale set attempts to scale out into the zones that are still available and allows a temporary imbalance, but that this imbalance is only permitted when a single zone is unavailable. It further states that if two or more zones are unavailable, the scale set cannot proceed with scaling operations and any scaling operations are blocked. Because two zones are down, scale-out is blocked. Statement 3 is No. Learn states that when you add availability zones to an existing scale set, existing VMs remain unchanged and do not get moved or redistributed, and that adding a zone does not trigger a rebalancing operation. Zone balancing only happens during scale-out operations when new instances are added, and zone balance does not replace existing instances; rebalancing must be performed manually by scaling out and then scaling in.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Export a deployment as an Azure Resource Manager template or convert an Azure Resource Manager template to a Bicep file
domanda: A resource group named RG1 was built entirely through the Azure portal. You must capture its current configuration as a Bicep file that your team can refine and commit to source control. You plan to use the Azure CLI and the Bicep CLI on your workstation. Which four actions should you perform in sequence?
opzione_a: Run az bicep decompile --file main.json
opzione_b: Run az group export --name RG1 > main.json
opzione_c: Review the generated main.bicep, fix the reported warnings, and rename the autogenerated symbolic names
opzione_d: Run az login and select the target subscription by using az account set
spiegazione: Correct order: d, b, a, c. First you sign in with az login and, because the workstation has access to multiple subscriptions, select the correct one with az account set; otherwise az group export runs against the wrong context. Second, az group export --name RG1 > main.json writes the resource group's current state as an ARM JSON template, since the Azure CLI cannot export Bicep directly. Third, az bicep decompile --file main.json converts that JSON to main.bicep in the same directory. Fourth, you review the result: decompilation is a best-effort conversion with no guaranteed mapping from JSON to Bicep, so you might need to fix warnings and errors, and exported templates typically carry autogenerated symbolic names and variable names that should be renamed before the file is fit for reuse. The decompile step cannot precede the export step because main.json does not exist yet, and reviewing the Bicep file is only possible once it has been generated.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Export a deployment as an Azure Resource Manager template or convert an Azure Resource Manager template to a Bicep file
domanda: Before adopting the Export template feature as part of your infrastructure-as-code migration, you must document its constraints for the team. Which of the following statements about exporting templates are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Exporting a resource group that contains more than 200 resources fails with the error 'Export template is not supported for resource groups more than 200 resources'.
opzione_b: The export template feature does not support exporting Azure Data Factory resources.
opzione_c: Exporting from the deployment history returns an ARM JSON template only; it cannot produce a Bicep file directly.
opzione_d: Exported templates are guaranteed to be production ready and can be redeployed without modification.
opzione_e: The Azure CLI can export a resource group directly as a Bicep file by using az group export --output bicep.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft documents a limit of 200 resources for the resource group you create the exported template for, and returns exactly that error message when the limit is exceeded. Correct: b. The export template feature explicitly does not support exporting Azure Data Factory resources; you must instead use the copy or clone a data factory guidance. Correct: c. The Save from history option supports exporting only ARM JSON templates. To get Bicep from a historical deployment you export the JSON and then decompile it. Wrong: d. The opposite is documented: export is not guaranteed to succeed and is not a reliable way to turn pre-existing resources into production-usable templates. Most exported templates require adjustments before they can be deployed. Wrong: e. Bicep files can currently be exported only from the Azure portal. The Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell export ARM JSON, which you then pass to the decompile command.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Export a deployment as an Azure Resource Manager template or convert an Azure Resource Manager template to a Bicep file
domanda: To reproduce a production environment in a test subscription, an administrator selects a resource group that contains a Windows virtual machine, chooses Export template in the Azure portal, and downloads the ARM JSON template with Include parameters selected. When the template is deployed to the test subscription, the deployment fails because the local administrator password required by the virtual machine is not defined anywhere in the template. What is the most likely cause, and how should the administrator resolve it?
opzione_a: Some password parameters can be missing from exported templates; the administrator must consult the template reference and add the missing parameters manually.
opzione_b: Include parameters was misused; clearing that option makes Resource Manager generate the password parameter automatically.
opzione_c: The password was exported as an encrypted secureString value, but it can only be decrypted in the source subscription.
opzione_d: The administrator should export the template from the resource group's deployment history instead, because that option includes the original password value.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft documents this explicitly as a limitation of the export feature: some password parameters might be missing from exported templates. You must check the template reference and manually add these parameters before the exported template can be used to deploy resources. Wrong: b. Include parameters controls whether the autogenerated template parameters are emitted at all; clearing it means you author your own parameters, so it removes parameters rather than adding a missing password parameter. Wrong: c. Azure never returns secure values through the export API. Secure parameter values are not saved to the deployment history and are not exported in any form, encrypted or otherwise. Wrong: d. Exporting from history returns an exact copy of the template that was used for the deployment, but secure parameter VALUES are still not stored in the deployment history, so this does not supply the password.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Export a deployment as an Azure Resource Manager template or convert an Azure Resource Manager template to a Bicep file
domanda:
Contoso has built its Azure estate manually over several years and now wants the existing configuration captured as Bicep files in a Git repository. An engineer investigates the export and decompile tooling and makes the following three claims. Evaluate each claim and indicate whether it is correct.

1. Selecting a deployment in the resource group's deployment history in the Azure portal and choosing Template lets you download the deployment as a Bicep file.
2. Running az group export --name RG1 > main.json and then az bicep decompile --file main.json produces a file named main.bicep.
3. Converting an ARM JSON template to Bicep and then building it back to JSON always reproduces the original JSON syntax exactly.
opzione_a: Selecting a deployment in the resource group's deployment history in the Azure portal and choosing Template lets you download the deployment as a Bicep file.
opzione_b: Running az group export --name RG1 > main.json and then az bicep decompile --file main.json produces a file named main.bicep.
opzione_c: Converting an ARM JSON template to Bicep and then building it back to JSON always reproduces the original JSON syntax exactly.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No. The Save from history option supports exporting only ARM JSON templates. It retrieves an exact copy of the template used for that deployment, and you must decompile the JSON afterwards if you want Bicep. Bicep files can be exported only from a resource group or an individual resource, and only from the Azure portal. Statement 2 is Yes. This is the documented export-and-convert workflow: az group export writes the resource group's ARM JSON to main.json, and az bicep decompile --file main.json creates main.bicep in the same directory as main.json. Statement 3 is No. The decompile and build commands produce templates that are functionally equivalent, but they might not be identical in implementation. Converting a template from JSON to Bicep and back to JSON can produce a template with different syntax than the original, although the deployed result is the same.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Interpret an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: A junior engineer is learning to read Bicep files and asks you to confirm the purpose of several language elements. Select the correct answer for each statement.
opzione_a: Keyword used to declare a value that is supplied when the deployment runs: [param | var | output]
opzione_b: Keyword used to declare a value that is calculated inside the file to simplify a complex expression: [param | var | resource]
opzione_c: Decorator that marks a value so it isn't saved to the deployment history or logged: [@description | @secure | @allowed]
opzione_d: Keyword used to reuse code from another Bicep file within the current deployment: [resource | module | output]
spiegazione: Correct selections: param, var, @secure, module. (a) param declares parameters, which Learn describes as values "that need to vary for different deployments" and that can be supplied at deployment time, optionally with a default value (for example, param storageSKU string = 'Standard_LRS'). output returns values from the deployment rather than accepting them. (b) var declares a variable: "To make your Bicep file more readable, encapsulate complex expressions in a variable" (for example, var uniqueStorageName = '${storagePrefix}${uniqueString(resourceGroup().id)}'). resource declares a resource to deploy, not a computed value. (c) The @secure decorator "Marks the parameter as secure. The value for a secure parameter isn't saved to the deployment history and isn't logged." @description supplies documentation text only and has no security effect, and @allowed restricts a parameter to a set of predefined values but does not hide it. (d) module links to another Bicep file so its resources are deployed as part of the current deployment. resource declares a single resource inline, and output returns a value after deployment.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Interpret an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: An ARM JSON template that does not use symbolic names deploys an Azure CDN endpoint and a web app. The endpoint must read the first host name of the web app into its originHostHeader property, and the endpoint must be deployed only after the web app. The template author wants to rely on an implicit dependency instead of adding a dependsOn entry. Which expression must be used for originHostHeader?
opzione_a: "[reference(variables('webAppName')).hostNames[0]]"
opzione_b: "[reference(resourceId('Microsoft.Web/sites', variables('webAppName'))).hostNames[0]]"
opzione_c: "[resourceId('Microsoft.Web/sites', variables('webAppName'))]"
opzione_d: "[variables('webAppName')]"
spiegazione: Correct: reference(variables('webAppName')).hostNames[0]. The reference and list* functions implicitly declare that one resource depends on another, but Learn adds a critical qualifier: "To enforce an implicit dependency, refer to the resource by name, not resource ID. If you pass the resource ID into the reference or list functions, an implicit reference isn't created." Passing the bare name creates the implicit dependency and returns the runtime state of the web app. Why the others are wrong: (b) is syntactically valid and returns the same host name, but because the resource ID is passed into reference() instead of the name, no implicit dependency is created and the endpoint could be deployed before the web app exists. This is the key distinction being tested. (c) resourceId is a pure string-construction function evaluated at compile time. It never contacts the resource provider, never returns runtime state, and creates no dependency at all; it also returns an ID, not a host name. (d) returns the variable's literal string value, not the web app's host name, and creates no dependency.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Interpret an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: A Bicep file declares a storage account with the symbolic name storage. It also declares a file service resource of type Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/fileServices that sets parent: storage, and a separate resource that reads exampleDnsZone.properties.nameServers from a DNS zone declared in the same file. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true. 1) The file service resource must include an explicit dependsOn entry that targets the storage account so that it is deployed after the storage account. 2) The resource that reads exampleDnsZone.properties.nameServers has an implicit dependency on the DNS zone. 3) Resources in the file that have no dependency relationship with each other are deployed in parallel.
opzione_a: The file service resource must include an explicit dependsOn entry that targets the storage account so that it is deployed after the storage account.
opzione_b: The resource that reads exampleDnsZone.properties.nameServers has an implicit dependency on the DNS zone.
opzione_c: Resources in the file that have no dependency relationship with each other are deployed in parallel.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No. In Bicep, "A resource that includes the parent property has an implicit dependency on the parent resource." The parent: storage assignment is enough to guarantee ordering, and Learn is explicit that "When an implicit dependency exists, don't add an explicit dependency." This is a genuine difference from ARM JSON, where "An implicit deployment dependency isn't automatically created between a child resource and the parent resource" and dependsOn must be set. Statement 2 - Yes. "An implicit dependency is created when one resource declaration references another resource in the same deployment." Reading a property through the symbolic name exampleDnsZone creates that dependency automatically, with no dependsOn required. Statement 3 - Yes. "Azure Resource Manager evaluates the dependencies between resources, and deploys them in their dependent order. When resources aren't dependent on each other, Resource Manager deploys them in parallel." This is why Learn warns that setting unnecessary dependencies slows deployment time.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Interpret an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: Your team is authoring a minimal ARM JSON template and needs to know which top-level elements must be present. For each element, select whether it is required or optional in an ARM template.
opzione_a: $schema: [Required | Optional]
opzione_b: contentVersion: [Required | Optional]
opzione_c: parameters: [Required | Optional]
opzione_d: resources: [Required | Optional]
spiegazione: Correct selections: Required, Required, Optional, Required. Per the ARM template structure reference: $schema is Required and specifies the location of the JSON schema file that describes the version of the template language (for resource group deployments in Visual Studio Code, https://schema.management.azure.com/schemas/2019-04-01/deploymentTemplate.json#). contentVersion is Required; you can provide any value such as 1.0.0.0 and use it to document significant changes to your template. parameters is Optional; it holds values provided when the deployment is executed, and a template that hardcodes everything needs no parameters. resources is Required; it defines the resource types that are deployed or updated. The other top-level elements (languageVersion, apiProfile, definitions, variables, functions and outputs) are all optional as well, which is why parameters being optional is easy to get wrong when you assume every element you commonly see must be mandatory.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Interpret an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: An ARM template deploys four resources into a single resource group. The template defines the following dependsOn relationships: vm1 depends on nic1; nic1 depends on vnet1; vnet1 depends on nsg1; and nsg1 declares no dependencies. Arrange the four resources in the order in which Azure Resource Manager deploys them, from first to last.
opzione_a: nic1
opzione_b: vm1
opzione_c: nsg1
opzione_d: vnet1
spiegazione: Correct order: nsg1, vnet1, nic1, vm1. "Azure Resource Manager evaluates the dependencies between resources, and deploys them in their dependent order." The dependsOn element "enables you to define one resource as a dependent on one or more resources," and a resource is deployed only after everything listed in its dependsOn array has been deployed. Resolving the chain: nsg1 has no dependencies, so it is deployed first. vnet1 depends on nsg1, so it follows. nic1 depends on vnet1, so it is third. vm1 depends on nic1, so it is last. Because this is a linear chain rather than a set of independent branches, no two resources can be deployed in parallel here; if the dependencies were removed, Resource Manager would deploy the independent resources concurrently. Note that Resource Manager identifies circular dependencies during template validation, so a chain that looped back on itself would fail validation before any resource was deployed.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Interpret an ARM template or Bicep file
domanda: Before splitting a very large ARM template into linked templates, an architect reviews the documented limits for a single template. Select the correct limit for each template section.
opzione_a: Maximum number of parameters in a template: [64 | 256 | 800]
opzione_b: Maximum number of variables in a template: [64 | 256 | 800]
opzione_c: Maximum number of resources in a template: [64 | 256 | 800]
opzione_d: Maximum number of outputs in a template: [64 | 256 | 800]
spiegazione: Correct selections: 256, 256, 800, 64. The ARM template structure and syntax reference states each of these limits explicitly: "You're limited to 256 parameters in a template. You can reduce the number of parameters by using objects that contain multiple properties." "You're limited to 256 variables in a template." "You're limited to 800 resources in a template." "You're limited to 64 outputs in a template." The distractors are the real limits from the neighbouring sections, so mixing them up is the realistic failure mode: answering 800 for parameters or 256 for outputs are both plausible-sounding but wrong. Note that the 800-resource limit is per template and can be worked around with linked or nested templates and copy loops, and that using an object parameter is Microsoft's documented technique for staying under the 256-parameter cap.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage sizing and scaling for containers, including Azure Container Instances and Azure Container Apps
domanda: A container app named worker1 pulls messages from an on-premises message broker over an outbound connection. Ingress is disabled for worker1, no scale rule is defined, and the minimum replica count is left at its default value. After deployment, worker1 processes messages for a short time and then stops processing permanently, and the revision shows a running status of Scale to 0. You must ensure that worker1 keeps processing messages. The solution must not enable ingress. What should you do?
opzione_a: Set the minimum number of replicas for the revision to 1.
opzione_b: Add an HTTP scale rule with the concurrent requests threshold set to 1.
opzione_c: Change the revision mode of worker1 from Single to Multiple.
opzione_d: Increase the maximum number of replicas for the revision from 10 to 30.
spiegazione: The default minimum replica count per revision is 0 and the default maximum is 10. Microsoft Learn warns that you must create a scale rule or set minReplicas to 1 or more if you do not enable ingress, because with ingress disabled and neither a minimum replica count nor a custom scale rule defined, the container app scales to zero and has no way of starting back up. Setting the minimum replicas to 1 guarantees that an instance of the revision is always running. Option b is incorrect because an HTTP scale rule scales on the number of concurrent HTTP requests to the revision; with ingress disabled, no inbound HTTP requests can reach worker1, so the rule can never trigger a scale-out from zero. Option c is incorrect because the revision mode only controls how many revisions can be active simultaneously and how traffic is split between them; it does not affect replica scaling. Option d is incorrect because the maximum replica count only caps scale-out; the app is stuck at zero replicas, and raising the ceiling never causes the first replica to be created.
tags: azure container apps,scaling,scale to zero,min replicas,keda,ingress disabled,troubleshooting

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage sizing and scaling for containers, including Azure Container Instances and Azure Container Apps
domanda: While designing the autoscale configuration for a set of container apps, you need to identify the trigger types that Azure Container Apps supports for scale rules. Which triggers can you use? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: The number of concurrent HTTP requests to the revision
opzione_b: The number of concurrent TCP connections to the revision
opzione_c: The number of messages in an Azure Service Bus queue
opzione_d: The disk IOPS consumed by the replica's ephemeral storage
opzione_e: A vertical resize of the replica's CPU and memory when memory pressure exceeds a threshold
spiegazione: Azure Container Apps implements scaling with KEDA and supports three categories of triggers: HTTP, based on the number of concurrent HTTP requests to the revision; TCP, based on the number of concurrent TCP connections to the revision; and custom, based on custom metrics such as CPU and memory or supported event-driven data sources including Azure Service Bus, Azure Event Hubs, Apache Kafka, and Redis. Options a, b, and c match those categories, with the Service Bus queue length implemented as a custom KEDA scaler. Option d is incorrect because disk IOPS on ephemeral storage is not a documented Container Apps trigger category or supported event source. Option e is incorrect because it describes vertical scaling, which the scaling documentation lists explicitly as a known limitation: vertical scaling is not supported. Container Apps scales horizontally by adding and removing replicas.
tags: azure container apps,keda,scale rules,http scaling,tcp scaling,custom scaler,azure service bus,vertical scaling

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage sizing and scaling for containers, including Azure Container Instances and Azure Container Apps
domanda: A junior administrator deploys a container app to a Container Apps environment and accepts every scale-related default, without defining any scale rule and without changing the replica limits. You must document the resulting scale configuration. Select the appropriate option for each setting.
opzione_a: Default minimum number of replicas per revision: [0 | 1 | 3]
opzione_b: Default maximum number of replicas per revision: [10 | 30 | 300]
opzione_c: Trigger used by the default scale rule: [HTTP | CPU | Azure Service Bus]
opzione_d: Default concurrent requests threshold for an HTTP scale rule: [1 | 10 | 100]
spiegazione: The Container Apps scale limits table gives a default of 0 for the minimum number of replicas per revision and a default of 10 for the maximum number of replicas per revision; the maximum value configurable for either limit is 1,000. When you do not create a scale rule, the documented default scale rule uses an HTTP trigger with min replicas 0 and max replicas 10, which is why HTTP is correct rather than CPU or Azure Service Bus (both of those are available only as custom KEDA rules that you must define yourself). The concurrentRequests property of an HTTP scale rule has a default value of 10 and a minimum value of 1: when the number of concurrent HTTP requests exceeds this value, the app adds another replica, up to maxReplicas.
tags: azure container apps,scaling,defaults,min replicas,max replicas,http scale rule,concurrent requests,keda

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine disks
domanda: Contoso deploys a three-node SQL Server failover cluster instance on Azure virtual machines. Each node is deployed to a different availability zone in the same region. All three nodes must simultaneously attach a single managed data disk, and the disk must remain accessible if one availability zone fails. Select the appropriate option for each setting.
opzione_a: Shared data disk configuration: [Standard HDD with LRS | Premium SSD with ZRS | Ultra Disk with LRS]
opzione_b: Minimum maxShares value for the disk: [1 | 3 | 5]
opzione_c: Host caching for the shared disk: [None | ReadOnly | ReadWrite]
opzione_d: Supported encryption for the shared disk: [Azure Disk Encryption | Server-side encryption | Confidential disk encryption]
spiegazione: Premium SSD with ZRS is correct because only Ultra Disks, Premium SSD v2, Premium SSD, and Standard SSD can be used as shared disks, which rules out Standard HDD, and a Premium SSD shared disk can only be shared across availability zones if it uses zone-redundant storage. Ultra Disk with LRS is wrong because shared Ultra Disks can't be shared across availability zones, and ZRS isn't supported for Ultra Disks at all. A maxShares value of 3 is correct because maxShares represents the maximum number of nodes that can simultaneously share the disk, so a three-node cluster requires maxShares=3; a value of 1 would allow only a single node, and 5 exceeds the minimum required. None is correct for host caching because host caching isn't supported for shared disks and isn't available for Premium SSDs with maxShares greater than 1, which rules out ReadOnly and ReadWrite. Server-side encryption is correct because for shared Premium SSD disks only server-side encryption is supported; Azure Disk Encryption isn't currently supported on shared disks, and confidential disk encryption applies to the OS disk of confidential VM sizes, not to a shared cluster data disk.
tags: shared disks, zrs, availability zones, maxshares, host caching, sql fci

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine disks
domanda: An architect evaluates Premium SSD v2 managed disks for a new Azure deployment. Which statements about Premium SSD v2 are true? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: A Premium SSD v2 disk can't be used as an OS disk.
opzione_b: Premium SSD v2 doesn't support host caching.
opzione_c: Premium SSD v2 supports zone-redundant storage (ZRS).
opzione_d: A Premium SSD v2 disk can be configured as a shared disk with a maxShares value of up to 15.
opzione_e: Premium SSD v2 supports double encryption at rest.
spiegazione: Options A, B, and D are correct. A is correct because a documented Premium SSD v2 limitation is that these disks can't be used as an OS disk or with Azure Compute Gallery; the disk type comparison table lists Premium SSD v2 as not usable as an OS disk. B is correct because Premium SSD v2 doesn't support host caching, benefiting instead from its inherently lower latency. D is correct because for Premium SSD v2 shared disks the minimum maxShares value is 1 and the maximum is 15, with no size restrictions on which disks can use which value. C is wrong because ZRS for managed disks is only supported with Premium SSD and Standard SSD; it isn't supported with Premium SSD v2 or Ultra Disks, and shared Premium SSD v2 disks can't be shared across availability zones. E is wrong because double encryption at rest isn't currently supported with either Ultra Disks or Premium SSD v2 disks; in fact, a disk using double encryption must be switched to a single encryption option before it can be converted to Premium SSD v2.
tags: premium ssd v2, shared disks, maxshares, zrs, host caching, double encryption

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine disks
domanda: An incremental backup process running on a virtual machine named VM1 is filling up its data disk. The disk is a Premium SSD that is currently provisioned at 2 TiB and is attached to VM1 with host caching set to ReadOnly. The disk must be expanded to 8 TiB. What must you do?
opzione_a: Expand the disk to 8 TiB from the Azure portal while VM1 remains running.
opzione_b: Deallocate VM1 and detach the disk, and then expand the disk to 8 TiB.
opzione_c: Enable performance plus on the disk, and then expand it to 8 TiB while VM1 remains running.
opzione_d: Change the host caching setting of the disk to None, and then expand it to 8 TiB while VM1 remains running.
spiegazione: Deallocating VM1 and detaching the disk is correct: Microsoft documents that if a Standard HDD, Standard SSD, or Premium SSD is 4 TiB or less, you must deallocate the VM and detach the disk before you expand it beyond 4 TiB. The disk here is 2 TiB (below the threshold) and the target of 8 TiB crosses it, so expand without downtime doesn't apply. Expanding while running is wrong because the expand-without-downtime feature explicitly excludes this 4-TiB boundary case for Premium SSD. Performance plus is wrong because it's a feature that raises the provisioned IOPS and throughput of larger Standard HDD, Standard SSD, and Premium SSD disks; it has no bearing on whether a resize requires deallocation. Changing host caching to None is wrong because the documentation states directly that the host cache setting of your disk doesn't change whether or not you can expand a data disk without deallocating your VM. Note that shrinking a disk is never supported.
tags: expand disk, resize disk, premium ssd, deallocate, host caching, expand without downtime

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine disks
domanda:
A virtual machine named VM1 has a 128-GiB Premium SSD OS disk named osdisk1 and doesn't use Azure Disk Encryption. After a failed application update, you create a snapshot of an earlier backup disk and use it to create a new managed disk named osdisk2. You plan to use the Az PowerShell module to swap the OS disk of VM1 to osdisk2 by running Set-AzVMOSDisk followed by Update-AzVM. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it's correct.
1. osdisk2 must be the same size as osdisk1.
2. osdisk2 must be located in the same resource group as VM1.
3. Because VM1 doesn't use Azure Disk Encryption, osdisk2 must not use Azure Disk Encryption.
opzione_a: osdisk2 must be the same size as osdisk1.
opzione_b: osdisk2 must be located in the same resource group as VM1.
opzione_c: Because VM1 doesn't use Azure Disk Encryption, osdisk2 must not use Azure Disk Encryption.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes: when swapping the OS disk, Microsoft states that both disks must be the same size, and you must also make sure the VM size and storage type are compatible with the disk you want to attach (for example, a Premium SSD disk requires a Premium storage-capable VM size such as a DS-series size). Statement 2 is No: the documentation explicitly says you can use a managed disk in another resource group, as long as it isn't already in use, so osdisk2 doesn't have to be in the same resource group as VM1. Statement 3 is Yes: mixing an unencrypted VM with an encrypted OS disk isn't supported. If the VM doesn't use Azure Disk Encryption, the OS disk being swapped in shouldn't be using Azure Disk Encryption; similarly, if disks use disk encryption sets, both disks must belong to the same disk encryption set. Swapping the OS disk keeps the existing VM resource, so its name and network configuration are preserved rather than recreated.
tags: swap os disk, set-azvmosdisk, update-azvm, snapshots, azure disk encryption, managed disks

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine disks
domanda: To reduce backup storage costs, an administrator schedules hourly incremental snapshots of a 4-TiB Premium SSD data disk. Which statement correctly describes how incremental snapshots of the disk behave?
opzione_a: The first incremental snapshot is a full copy of the disk, and each subsequent snapshot stores only the changes since the previous snapshot.
opzione_b: Every incremental snapshot is a full copy of the disk, but you're billed only for the delta from the previous snapshot.
opzione_c: Incremental snapshots are stored on Premium SSD storage so that they match the storage type of the parent disk.
opzione_d: Incremental snapshots must be restored in sequence, applying each snapshot in order after the first full snapshot.
spiegazione: Option A is correct: Microsoft documents that the first incremental snapshot is a full copy of the disk and subsequent incremental snapshots occupy only the delta changes to the disk since the last snapshot. Option B is wrong because it inverts the behavior: the snapshots themselves store only deltas after the first one, rather than being full copies that are billed as deltas. Option C is wrong because incremental snapshots always use Standard HDD storage irrespective of the storage type of the parent disk; only full snapshots can use Premium SSD storage. Option D is wrong because when you restore a disk from an incremental snapshot the system reconstructs the full disk automatically for that point in time; each incremental snapshot can be used immediately and independently to create a full managed disk or a full snapshot, with no manual chain replay. Note the 500 incremental snapshots per disk limit at any given point in time.
tags: snapshots, incremental snapshots, backup, standard hdd, managed disks

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine disks
domanda: Contoso migrates an on-premises Windows Server Failover Cluster to Azure virtual machines and plans to use a Premium SSD Azure shared disk for the clustered storage. Which statements correctly describe the requirements and behavior of the shared disk? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: The shared disk must be attached as a data disk, because shared disks can't be enabled on OS disks.
opzione_b: Host caching must be set to ReadOnly on every node that mounts the shared disk.
opzione_c: A cluster manager such as Windows Server Failover Cluster is required, and the clustered application arbitrates write access by using SCSI persistent reservations.
opzione_d: The maxShares value can be set or edited only while the disk is detached from all nodes.
opzione_e: Azure Disk Encryption must be enabled on the shared disk to protect the clustered data at rest.
spiegazione: Options A, C, and D are correct. A is correct because for Premium SSD and Standard SSD shared disks Microsoft states that sharing can only be enabled on data disks, not OS disks. C is correct because shared disks require a cluster manager such as WSFC or Pacemaker to handle node communication and write locking, and VMs read or write based on the reservation taken by the clustered application using SCSI Persistent Reservations (SCSI PR). D is correct because the docs note that the maxShares value can only be set or edited when the disk is detached from all nodes. B is wrong because host caching isn't supported for shared disks at all, and host caching isn't available for Premium SSDs with maxShares greater than 1, so ReadOnly can't be configured. E is wrong because for shared Premium SSD and Standard SSD disks only server-side encryption is supported; Azure Disk Encryption isn't currently supported on shared disks.
tags: shared disks, scsi pr, wsfc, maxshares, host caching, server-side encryption

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine disks
domanda:
A virtual machine named VM1 runs in the East US region and uses a size that supports Premium storage. A 1-TiB Standard HDD data disk named disk1 is attached to VM1. The application that runs on VM1 now needs higher and more consistent IOPS, so you're asked to review the options for changing the storage type of disk1. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it's correct.
1. You can change the storage type of disk1 from Standard HDD to Premium SSD while VM1 remains running.
2. You can change the storage type of disk1 at most twice per day.
3. You can change disk1 directly from Standard HDD to an Ultra Disk by updating the SKU of the disk.
opzione_a: You can change the storage type of disk1 from Standard HDD to Premium SSD while VM1 remains running.
opzione_b: You can change the storage type of disk1 at most twice per day.
opzione_c: You can change disk1 directly from Standard HDD to an Ultra Disk by updating the SKU of the disk.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No: converting a managed disk between Standard HDD, Standard SSD, and Premium SSD requires a restart of the virtual machine, and the documented procedures for the portal, Azure PowerShell, and the Azure CLI all stop and deallocate the VM before updating the disk SKU, so the change can't be made while VM1 remains running. Statement 2 is Yes: a documented restriction states that you can only change disk type twice per day. Statement 3 is No: for most cases you can't yet switch from or to an Ultra Disk by changing the SKU. To move to an Ultra Disk you must deploy a new disk from an incremental snapshot of the existing disk, and the logical sector size must be 512. By contrast, you can switch an existing disk directly to a Premium SSD v2 the same way as other disk types, subject to its own limitations.
tags: convert disk type, disk sku, standard hdd, premium ssd, ultra disk, snapshots

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine disks
domanda: Contoso migrates a four-node Windows Server Failover Cluster to Azure virtual machines. The four nodes must simultaneously attach a single Premium SSD managed disk that is configured as a shared disk. You need to identify the smallest Premium SSD disk size that supports the required maxShares value. Which disk size should you choose?
spiegazione: P30 is correct: for Premium SSD shared disks, the maxShares limit is 3 for sizes P1 through P20, 5 for P30, P40, and P50, and 10 for P60, P70, and P80. Four nodes require maxShares=4, so the smallest size that allows it is P30 (limit 5). P15 and P20 are wrong because both fall in the P1-P20 band whose maxShares limit is 3, which is fewer than the four nodes required. P60 is wrong because although its limit of 10 is sufficient, P60 is 8,192 GiB and is not the smallest size that meets the requirement, so it would be needlessly expensive. Note that maxShares can only be set or edited while the disk is detached from all nodes.
tags: shared disks, maxshares, premium ssd, failover cluster, wsfc

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine sizes
domanda:
Case study: Litware, Inc. runs a three-tier application in the West Europe region. The database tier runs on a virtual machine named VM-DB1, which uses the Standard_D8s_v3 size and is a member of an availability set named AS-DB. AS-DB also contains two other virtual machines, VM-DB2 and VM-DB3, which are running. To support a growing workload, Litware must change VM-DB1 to the Standard_E32s_v5 size. An administrator deallocates VM-DB1 and runs az vm list-vm-resize-options for VM-DB1, but Standard_E32s_v5 is not returned. Standard_E32s_v5 is offered in the West Europe region, and Litware's subscription has sufficient vCPU quota. VM-DB1 must remain a member of AS-DB, and the solution must minimize administrative effort.

What should you do?
opzione_a: Deallocate VM-DB2 and VM-DB3 as well, then resize VM-DB1 to Standard_E32s_v5 and start the virtual machines
opzione_b: Remove VM-DB1 from AS-DB, resize VM-DB1 to Standard_E32s_v5, and then add VM-DB1 back to AS-DB
opzione_c: Create a proximity placement group, add AS-DB to the proximity placement group, and then resize VM-DB1
opzione_d: Redeploy VM-DB1 to a different Azure region where Standard_E32s_v5 is available, and then resize the virtual machine
spiegazione: Correct: a. An availability set is pinned to a single hardware cluster, and the resize documentation states that if the new size for a VM in an availability set isn't available on the hardware cluster currently hosting the VM, then you need to deallocate all VMs in the availability set to resize the VM. Deallocating VM-DB1 alone is not enough because VM-DB2 and VM-DB3 keep the availability set anchored to the original cluster. Once every VM in AS-DB is deallocated, Azure can place the set on a cluster that offers Standard_E32s_v5. Learn's sample scripts implement exactly this flow: check the available sizes, and if the desired size is absent, deallocate all VMs in the availability set, resize, and start them again. Why the others are wrong: b is wrong because a virtual machine's availability set membership is fixed at creation - you cannot remove a VM from an availability set and add it back; you would have to delete and recreate the VM, which also violates the minimal-effort requirement. c is wrong because a proximity placement group controls network latency by co-locating resources; it does not make a size available on a cluster, and it cannot be applied to an availability set that has running VMs anyway. d is wrong because Standard_E32s_v5 is already offered in West Europe - the constraint is the current hardware cluster, not the region - and moving regions would be far more effort while breaking the AS-DB membership requirement.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine sizes
domanda: A virtual machine named WEB1 runs Windows Server 2022 and currently uses the Standard_D4ds_v5 size, which includes a local temporary disk. To reduce cost, you plan to move WEB1 to Standard_D4s_v5, a size that has no local temporary disk. What should you do?
opzione_a: Deallocate WEB1 and then change its size to Standard_D4s_v5
opzione_b: Create a snapshot of WEB1's OS disk, create a managed disk from the snapshot, and create a new VM from that disk using Standard_D4s_v5
opzione_c: Detach the temporary disk from WEB1, then resize WEB1 while it is running
opzione_d: Add WEB1 to an availability set, which permits resizing across sizes with and without a local temporary disk
spiegazione: Correct: b. The resize limitations state that resizing between VM sizes that have a local temp disk and VM sizes that have no local temp disk is supported for Linux VMs, but for Windows VMs only two combinations are allowed: local temp disk to local temp disk, and no local temp disk to no local temp disk. Because WEB1 is a Windows VM, the documented workaround is to create a snapshot of the VM, create a disk from the snapshot, and create a VM from the disk with the appropriate size. Why the others are wrong: a is wrong because deallocating does not lift this limitation - it is a Windows guest restriction, not a cluster capacity restriction, so the resize is still blocked. c is wrong because the local temporary disk is host-provided storage tied to the VM size; it is not an attachable resource you can detach, and doing so would not change the supported resize matrix. d is wrong because availability sets govern fault and update domain placement; they grant no exception to the Windows temp-disk resize rule.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine sizes
domanda: A SQL Server database VM must keep 256 GiB of memory, 32 data disks, and 80,000 IOPS of I/O bandwidth, which are the specifications of the Standard_E32s_v5 size. However, the per-core SQL Server licensing cost of 32 vCPUs is unacceptable, and the database engine does not benefit from that many cores. Which VM size should you select to minimize licensing cost while preserving the required specifications?
opzione_a: Standard_E32-8s_v5
opzione_b: Standard_E8s_v5
opzione_c: Standard_E32as_v5
opzione_d: Standard_D32s_v5
spiegazione: Correct: a. Standard_E32-8s_v5 is a constrained vCPU size: Learn's comparison table shows it exposes 8 active vCPUs (24 disabled) while maintaining the 256 GiB of memory, 32 disks, and 80,000 IOPS of the base Standard_E32s_v5. Because per-core licensed products count the available vCPUs, licensing cost drops while the memory and I/O specifications are preserved. Why the others are wrong: b reduces the vCPU count to 8 but also scales memory down proportionally, so it cannot deliver 256 GiB of RAM or the same I/O bandwidth. c is simply the AMD-based variant of the full 32-vCPU size - it still exposes 32 billable vCPUs, so licensing cost is unchanged. d is a general purpose size that exposes 32 vCPUs and provides far less memory than the memory optimized E-family, failing both goals. Note that the Azure VM price for a constrained size remains the same as the original size; the saving comes from software licensing, not from Azure compute charges.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine sizes
domanda: While reviewing capacity, an engineer opens a running virtual machine in the Azure portal, selects Size under Availability + scale, and notices that the required Standard_M64s size is not offered in the list. The engineer has the Contributor role on the subscription, and Standard_M64s is offered in the VM's region. What is the most likely explanation?
opzione_a: The portal only lists sizes available on the hardware cluster currently hosting the running VM; stopping (deallocating) the VM may reveal more sizes
opzione_b: The engineer needs the Virtual Machine Contributor role, because Contributor cannot change a VM size
