opzione_c: Memory optimized sizes such as the M-family can only be selected when the VM is first created
opzione_d: The VM must be moved to a different resource group before larger sizes become selectable
spiegazione: Correct: a. Learn states that deallocation may be required if the new size is not available on the hardware cluster currently hosting the VM, and the portal procedure notes explicitly: 'If your VM is still running and you don't see the size you want in the list, stopping the virtual machine may reveal more sizes.' Deallocating frees the VM from its current cluster so Azure can place it on a cluster that offers the target size. Why the others are wrong: b is wrong because Contributor already includes the write permissions needed to resize a VM; Virtual Machine Contributor is a narrower built-in role, not a superset, and RBAC failures produce an authorization error rather than a filtered size list. c is wrong because M-family VMs can be resized after creation like any other family, subject to cluster availability. d is wrong because resource group membership has no bearing on which hardware cluster hosts a VM or which sizes are offered.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine sizes
domanda:
A virtual machine named VM1 runs Windows Server 2022 and uses the Standard_D2s_v3 size. VM1 is running, is not a member of an availability set, and has a dynamic public IP address. You plan to resize VM1 to Standard_D8s_v3. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether each one is correct.
1. If Standard_D8s_v3 is returned by az vm list-vm-resize-options for VM1, you can resize VM1 without first deallocating it.
2. Resizing VM1 while it is running has no impact on the availability of the workload hosted on VM1.
3. If you deallocate VM1 in order to resize it, VM1 retains its current dynamic public IP address.
opzione_a: If Standard_D8s_v3 is returned by az vm list-vm-resize-options for VM1, you can resize VM1 without first deallocating it.
opzione_b: Resizing VM1 while it is running has no impact on the availability of the workload hosted on VM1.
opzione_c: If you deallocate VM1 in order to resize it, VM1 retains its current dynamic public IP address.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. Learn states the resize process works whether the VM is currently running or has already been deallocated, and that deallocation may be required only if the new size isn't available on the hardware cluster currently hosting the VM. az vm list-vm-resize-options returns the sizes available on that cluster, so if Standard_D8s_v3 appears there, no deallocation is needed. Statement 2 - No. Learn warns that if the virtual machine is currently running, changing its size will cause it to restart, and that resizing should be considered a disruptive operation, especially for stateful workloads. The workload is therefore interrupted. Statement 3 - No. Learn states that deallocating the VM also releases any dynamic IP addresses assigned to the VM. To preserve the address across a deallocation you would need a static IP allocation instead. (The OS and data disks, by contrast, are not affected.)

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine sizes
domanda: While reviewing a deployment template, you find a virtual machine configured with the size Standard_E32-8ads_v5. Using the Azure VM size naming conventions, select the correct interpretation of each element of the size name.
opzione_a: Number of vCPUs available to the VM: [8 | 24 | 32]
opzione_b: The letter a indicates: [AMD-based processor | ARM-based processor | Accelerated networking enabled]
opzione_c: The letter d indicates: [Includes local temporary disk | Double the memory of the base size | Dedicated host required]
opzione_d: The letter s indicates: [Compatible with any Premium SSD type | Standard HDD storage only | Secure Boot enabled]
risposta_corretta: 8,AMD-based processor,Includes local temporary disk,Compatible with any Premium SSD type
spiegazione: Correct: 8, AMD-based processor, Includes local temporary disk, Compatible with any Premium SSD type. The naming convention is [Family] + [Sub-family] + [# of vCPUs] + [Constrained vCPUs] + [Additive Features] + [Version]. In Standard_E32-8ads_v5, 32 is the base size's vCPU count and -8 is the constrained vCPU value, so only 8 vCPUs are available to the VM (the constrained vCPU list confirms Standard_E32-8ads_v5 has 8 active vCPUs on base size E32ads_v5) - 32 is the base count and 24 is the number of disabled vCPUs, not the available count. In the additive features table, a = AMD-based processor (p, not a, denotes an ARM-based processor, and accelerated networking is never encoded in a size name). d = includes local temporary disks. s = compatible with any Premium SSD type; it does not mean Standard HDD, and Secure Boot is a Trusted launch setting that is never expressed in the size name.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine sizes
domanda: Before a maintenance window, you must determine whether a running virtual machine named VM1 in the resource group RG1 can be resized to Standard_D8s_v5 without first deallocating it. Which Azure PowerShell command returns the list of sizes that are available on the hardware cluster currently hosting VM1?
opzione_a: Get-AzVMSize -ResourceGroupName 'RG1' -VMName 'VM1'
opzione_b: Get-AzVMSize -Location 'eastus'
opzione_c: Get-AzVM -ResourceGroupName 'RG1' -Name 'VM1' -Status
opzione_d: Get-AzComputeResourceSku -Location 'eastus'
spiegazione: Correct: a. The resize documentation shows Get-AzVMSize -ResourceGroupName $resourceGroup -VMName $vmName as the command that lists the VM sizes available on the hardware cluster where the VM is hosted. If the target size appears in that output, the VM can be resized without being deallocated (although a running VM will restart). Why the others are wrong: b uses the -Location parameter set, which returns every size offered in the region - not the subset available on the cluster hosting VM1, so it cannot answer the question. c returns the VM's power state and instance view, not a list of candidate sizes. d lists SKUs and their restrictions for a subscription in a region (including zone availability), but again it is region-scoped, not scoped to the VM's current hardware cluster. The Azure CLI equivalent of the correct answer is az vm list-vm-resize-options.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage virtual machine sizes
domanda: Your operations team is drafting a change record for resizing production virtual machines and needs to describe the impact accurately. Which statements about resizing an Azure virtual machine are correct? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Changing the size of a virtual machine while it is running causes the virtual machine to restart
opzione_b: Deallocating a virtual machine releases any dynamic IP addresses that are assigned to it
opzione_c: Resizing a virtual machine deletes the data disks that are attached to it
opzione_d: Deallocation may be required if the new size is not available on the hardware cluster that currently hosts the virtual machine
opzione_e: A virtual machine must always be deallocated before any resize operation can be performed
spiegazione: Correct: a, b, d. Learn warns that if the virtual machine is currently running, changing its size will cause it to restart, which is why resizing is treated as a disruptive operation for stateful workloads (a). It also states that deallocating the VM releases any dynamic IP addresses assigned to the VM (b). And it states that deallocation may be required if the new size isn't available on the hardware cluster currently hosting the VM (d). Why the others are wrong: c is wrong because Learn explicitly notes that the OS and data disks are not affected by deallocation or resizing - the disks are managed resources that persist independently of the VM's compute allocation. e is wrong because the resize process works whether the VM is currently running or has already been deallocated; deallocation is conditional on cluster capability, not universally mandatory.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Map an existing custom DNS name to an App Service
domanda: Wide World Importers hosts a web app named app11 in an App Service plan that uses the Free (F1) tier. You must map the existing custom domain www.wideworldimporters.com to app11, verify ownership of the domain, and secure the domain with a free App Service managed certificate. The DNS zone is managed at a third-party registrar. Drag the actions into the correct order to complete the task with the fewest steps.
opzione_a: In the app's Custom domains page, select Add custom domain, enter www.wideworldimporters.com, and copy the domain verification ID and the required record values.
opzione_b: Scale the App Service plan up from the Free (F1) tier to the Basic (B1) tier.
opzione_c: In the Add custom domain dialog, select Validate, confirm that both records show a green check mark, and then select Add.
opzione_d: At the registrar, create a CNAME record for the www host that points to app11.azurewebsites.net, and a TXT record named asuid.www that contains the domain verification ID.
opzione_e: Create an App Service managed certificate for www.wideworldimporters.com and add the TLS/SSL binding by using SNI SSL.
spiegazione: Correct order: (1) Scale up from Free (F1). Mapping a custom domain requires a paid tier, and a free App Service managed certificate additionally requires Basic, Standard, Premium, or Isolated, so Basic (B1) satisfies both and must come first. (2) Open Add custom domain and enter the fully qualified domain name to obtain the domain verification ID and the record values you need. (3) Create the DNS records at the registrar: for a subdomain, a CNAME for www pointing directly to app11.azurewebsites.net (mapping to an intermediate CNAME value would block managed certificate issuance and renewal) plus a TXT record named asuid.www holding the verification ID. (4) Return to the portal and select Validate, then Add; validation reads the records you just created, so it cannot precede them. (5) Only after the domain is mapped and validated can you create the managed certificate for it and bind it. SNI SSL is the correct binding type here because it needs no dedicated IP address and no further DNS remapping.
tags: app service,custom domain,cname,asuid,managed certificate,sni ssl,scale up

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Map an existing custom DNS name to an App Service
domanda: Adventure Works owns the public DNS zone adventureworks.com, which is hosted at a third-party registrar. You must map both adventureworks.com and www.adventureworks.com to an App Service app named app8, and secure each domain with a free App Service managed certificate. App8 currently runs in an App Service plan that uses the Free (F1) tier. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Record used to map adventureworks.com to app8: [A record | CNAME record | NS record]
opzione_b: Recommended record used to map www.adventureworks.com to app8: [A record | CNAME record | TXT record]
opzione_c: Record used to verify ownership of www.adventureworks.com: [TXT record named asuid.www | TXT record named asuid | CNAME record named asuid.www]
opzione_d: Minimum App Service plan tier required to create the managed certificates: [Free (F1) | Shared (D1) | Basic (B1)]
risposta_corretta: A record,CNAME record,TXT record named asuid.www,Basic (B1)
spiegazione: Correct: A root domain such as adventureworks.com must be mapped with an A record that points to the app's IP address; a CNAME record is not allowed at the zone apex. For a subdomain such as www.adventureworks.com the recommended record is a CNAME that points to the app's default hostname, because the app's inbound IP address can change while the default hostname does not. Domain ownership for a subdomain is verified with a TXT record named asuid.<subdomain>, so asuid.www here; the plain asuid host is used for a root or wildcard domain, and the record must be TXT, not CNAME. Free App Service managed certificates require the App Service plan to be in the Basic, Standard, Premium, or Isolated tier, so the plan must be scaled up from Free (F1); the Shared (D1) tier can host a custom domain but cannot create a managed certificate.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Map an existing custom DNS name to an App Service
domanda: Northwind plans to map the root domain northwind.com to an App Service app named app2. The DNS zone for northwind.com is hosted at a third-party registrar. You must complete the mapping and let App Service verify ownership of the domain. Which set of DNS records should you create at the registrar?
opzione_a: An A record for the @ host that points to the app's IP address, and a TXT record named asuid that contains the domain verification ID
opzione_b: A CNAME record for the @ host that points to app2.azurewebsites.net, and a TXT record named asuid that contains the domain verification ID
opzione_c: An A record for the @ host that points to the app's IP address, and a CNAME record named asuid that points to app2.azurewebsites.net
opzione_d: A CNAME record for the @ host that points to app2.azurewebsites.net, and a TXT record named asuid.www that contains the domain verification ID
spiegazione: Correct: For a root (apex) domain, App Service documents an A record on the @ host that points to the app's IP address, plus a TXT record named asuid that holds the domain verification ID. App Service reads the asuid TXT record to confirm that you own the domain, which protects against subdomain takeover. Why the others are wrong: A CNAME record must not be used for a root domain; RFC 1912 forbids a CNAME coexisting with other records at the zone apex, and the documentation explicitly says not to use CNAME for the root domain. The verification record must be of type TXT, not CNAME, because App Service looks up the verification ID as text. The asuid.<subdomain> form (for example, asuid.www) is used for subdomains such as www.northwind.com; for the root domain the host is simply asuid.
tags: app service,custom domain,apex domain,a record,asuid,txt record

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Modify an existing ARM template
domanda: You are editing an ARM template and must build the resource ID of an authorization rule named auth1, which belongs to a queue named queue1, inside a Service Bus namespace named namespace1. All resources are in the current subscription and resource group. Which expression returns the correct resource ID?
opzione_a: "[resourceId('Microsoft.ServiceBus/namespaces/queues/authorizationRules', 'namespace1/queue1/auth1')]"
opzione_b: "[resourceId('Microsoft.ServiceBus/namespaces/queues/authorizationRules', 'namespace1', 'queue1', 'auth1')]"
opzione_c: "[resourceId('Microsoft.ServiceBus/namespaces', 'namespace1', 'queue1', 'auth1')]"
opzione_d: "[subscriptionResourceId('Microsoft.ServiceBus/namespaces/queues/authorizationRules', 'namespace1', 'queue1', 'auth1')]"
spiegazione: Correct: resourceId with one name argument per type segment. The syntax is resourceId([subscriptionId], [resourceGroupName], resourceType, resourceName1, [resourceName2], ...). Learn instructs: "To get the resource ID for a child resource, pay attention to the number of segments in the resource type. Provide a resource name for each segment of the resource type," and gives this exact pattern as its example. The type has three segments (namespaces/queues/authorizationRules), so three name arguments are required. Why the others are wrong: (a) passes a single slash-delimited string as one name argument. The number of name arguments must match the number of type segments; they are not concatenated into one parameter. (c) uses the parent type Microsoft.ServiceBus/namespaces, which has only one segment, and then supplies three names. The type and the name count do not match, and the type does not identify an authorization rule. (d) subscriptionResourceId is for resources deployed at subscription level, such as policy assignments or role definitions. A Service Bus authorization rule lives in a resource group, so resourceId is the correct function.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Modify an existing ARM template
domanda: A virtual network named VNet1 was deployed from an ARM template and later had a tag named Owner with the value "Team A" added to it in the Azure portal. A colleague edits the original template to change the address prefix, but the template's virtual network resource contains no tags element. The colleague redeploys the template to the same resource group by using incremental mode. What happens to the Owner tag on VNet1?
opzione_a: The Owner tag is removed, because properties that aren't included in the template are reset to their default values.
opzione_b: The Owner tag is preserved, because incremental mode only adds or changes the properties that are specified in the template.
opzione_c: The Owner tag is preserved, because tags are metadata and are never evaluated by Azure Resource Manager during a deployment.
opzione_d: The deployment fails with a conflict error because the deployed resource contains a tag that the template does not declare.
spiegazione: Correct: The Owner tag is removed. Microsoft Learn explicitly calls this out as a common misunderstanding: "When redeploying an existing resource in incremental mode, all properties are reapplied. The properties aren't incrementally added... If you don't specify certain properties, Resource Manager interprets the deployment as overwriting those values. Properties that aren't included in the template are reset to the default values." The resource definition in the template always represents the final state of the resource, not a partial update. Why the others are wrong: (b) is exactly the misconception the documentation warns against. "Incremental" refers to how Resource Manager treats resources not in the template, not properties not in the template. (c) is false; tags are part of the resource definition submitted to the resource provider, and the what-if operation reports removed tags as deletions. (d) is false; there is no conflict error for undeclared tags. The deployment succeeds and silently overwrites the tag collection. To keep the tag, the colleague must add it to the template or specify it inline.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Modify an existing Bicep file
domanda:
You are hardening a Bicep file that deploys a storage platform. The file must meet the following requirements:
- The storageAccountName parameter must accept only values between 3 and 24 characters.
- The adminPassword parameter must never appear in the deployment history.
- The storage module, which is declared with a for expression, must deploy its instances two at a time instead of all at once.
- The environmentName parameter must accept only the values dev, test, or prod.

Select the correct decorator for each requirement.
opzione_a: Constrain storageAccountName to 3-24 characters: [@minLength(3) and @maxLength(24) | @minValue(3) and @maxValue(24) | @allowed([3, 24])]
opzione_b: Keep adminPassword out of the deployment history: [@secure() | @description() | @metadata()]
opzione_c: Deploy the module instances two at a time: [@batchSize(2) | @maxValue(2) | @sealed()]
opzione_d: Restrict environmentName to dev, test, or prod: [@allowed(['dev', 'test', 'prod']) | @discriminator('environmentName') | @sealed()]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1: @minLength and @maxLength set the minimum and maximum length for string and array parameters, and the values are inclusive. @minValue/@maxValue apply only to int parameters, and @allowed lists permitted values rather than a length range. Dropdown 2: @secure() marks the parameter as sensitive so that the value is not saved to the deployment history and is not logged. @description() only supplies help text, and @metadata() attaches arbitrary custom properties with no security effect. Dropdown 3: @batchSize(int) is applied to a resource or module definition that uses a for expression and deploys the instances serially in batches of the given size; the default is fully parallel. @maxValue constrains an int parameter, and @sealed applies to object types to elevate BCP089 from a warning to an error. Dropdown 4: @allowed takes an array of permitted values and the deployment fails validation if another value is passed. @discriminator is used for custom-tagged union data types, and @sealed relates to typo detection on user-defined types.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Modify an existing Bicep file
domanda:
A Bicep file named main.bicep begins with the line targetScope = 'subscription'. A developer is refactoring the file and proposes the following three changes. Evaluate each proposal and indicate whether the statement is correct.

1. You can declare a Microsoft.Resources/resourceGroups resource in main.bicep by using the resource keyword.
2. You can declare a Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts resource in main.bicep by using the resource keyword and target it at a resource group by setting the scope property on that resource.
3. If you omit the name property from a module declaration in main.bicep, the file fails to compile.
opzione_a: You can declare a Microsoft.Resources/resourceGroups resource in main.bicep by using the resource keyword.
opzione_b: You can declare a Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts resource in main.bicep by using the resource keyword and target it at a resource group by setting the scope property on that resource.
opzione_c: If you omit the name property from a module declaration in main.bicep, the file fails to compile.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes. Microsoft.Resources/resourceGroups is one of the resource types supported at the subscription level, and creating resource groups is the canonical use of a subscription-scope Bicep file. Statement 2 is No. In a Bicep file, all resources declared with the resource keyword must be deployed at the same scope as the deployment. A storage account is a resource group scoped resource, so it cannot be declared directly in a subscription-scope file. To deploy resources at a different scope within the same deployment you add a module and set the module's scope property, which triggers a nested deployment. Note that this restriction does not apply to existing resources, which can be referenced at a different scope. Statement 3 is No. The name property of a module is optional. If no name is provided, a GUID is generated as the name for the nested deployment resource. Omitting the name is in fact a documented way to guarantee unique module names when the same module is deployed concurrently to the same scope.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Modify an existing Bicep file
domanda: A colleague submits a pull request that adds several decorators to a Bicep file. You must approve only the usages that compile. Which decorator usages are valid? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: @secure() applied to a parameter of type object.
opzione_b: @maxValue(24) applied to a parameter of type string.
opzione_c: @minLength(1) applied to a parameter of type array.
opzione_d: @batchSize(2) applied to a module declaration that uses a for expression.
opzione_e: @allowed(['dev', 'prod']) applied to an output statement.
spiegazione: Correct: a. The @secure() decorator applies to parameters of type string and object, matching the secureString and secureObject types in ARM templates. Correct: c. @minLength and @maxLength apply to array and string parameters. For arrays the length is the number of items, so @minLength(1) on an array is valid. Correct: d. @batchSize is one of the two decorators available for modules (the other is description), and it can be applied only to a resource or module definition that uses a for expression. It makes the instances deploy serially in batches of the specified size. Wrong: b. @maxValue and @minValue apply only to int parameters. To constrain the length of a string you use @maxLength. This swap is the classic mistake. Wrong: e. The @allowed decorator is only permitted on param statements. To declare that a property must be one of a set of predefined values in a type or output statement, you use union type syntax instead.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Modify an existing Bicep file
domanda:
A Bicep file that deploys a virtual machine declares the following parameter:

param adminPassword string

During a security review, an auditor finds that the value supplied for adminPassword is visible in the deployment history in the Azure portal. You must prevent the value from being logged or displayed, while making the smallest possible change to the file. What should you do?
opzione_a: Add the @description('Sensitive') decorator above the parameter declaration.
opzione_b: Add the @metadata({ secure: true }) decorator above the parameter declaration.
opzione_c: Add the @secure() decorator above the parameter declaration.
opzione_d: Change the parameter type from string to int and pass a hash of the password.
spiegazione: Correct: c. When a parameter is decorated with @secure(), Azure Resource Manager treats the value as sensitive: it is not saved to the deployment history and is not logged or displayed in the portal or in command-line output. @secure() is valid on parameters of type string and object, so it applies here. Wrong: a. @description() only supplies help text that is shown to users in the portal; it has no effect on how the value is stored or logged. Wrong: b. @metadata() attaches arbitrary custom properties for documentation purposes. A property named 'secure' inside @metadata() carries no security semantics and does not mark the parameter as secure. Wrong: d. @secure() is not valid on int parameters, and changing the type would break the VM resource definition, which expects a password string. To pass numbers or arrays securely, you wrap them in a secureObject or serialize them as a secureString.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Modify an existing Bicep file
domanda: Your main.bicep file sets targetScope = 'subscription'. You must extend it so that the resources defined in storage.bicep are created in an existing resource group named RG-Prod, which is in the same subscription. Which property must you add to the module declaration?
opzione_a: targetScope: 'resourceGroup'
opzione_b: params: { resourceGroupName: 'RG-Prod' }
opzione_c: dependsOn: [ resourceGroup('RG-Prod') ]
opzione_d: scope: resourceGroup('RG-Prod')
spiegazione: Correct: d. To deploy a module at a scope that differs from the parent file, set the module's scope property to a valid scope object. The resourceGroup() scope function returns that object for an existing resource group, so scope: resourceGroup('RG-Prod') deploys the module's resources into RG-Prod. Wrong: a. targetScope is a file-level statement that appears once at the top of a Bicep file; it is not a property of a module declaration. Wrong: b. Passing the resource group name as a parameter only supplies a string value to the module; it does not change the scope at which the nested deployment runs, so the resources would still target the subscription and the deployment would fail. Wrong: c. dependsOn only forces ordering between deployments; it has no effect on scope, and a scope function is not a valid dependency target.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Move a virtual machine to another resource group, subscription, or region
domanda: Case study: Fabrikam runs a three-tier application in the East US region under a subscription named Subscription1. The web tier consists of VM1, VM2, and VM3 in an availability set named AS1. The data tier consists of a single virtual machine named VM4, which is protected by Azure Backup in a Recovery Services vault; soft delete is enabled on the vault, and instant restore snapshots are stored in a resource group named AzureBackupRG_eastus_1. Following an acquisition, Fabrikam must move all compute resources to a subscription named Subscription2, which is in the same Microsoft Entra tenant. The workload must remain in East US. Your first attempt to move VM4 to Subscription2 fails. What should you do to enable the move of VM4?
opzione_a: Stop the backup while keeping backup data, delete the Restore Point Collection for VM4 from AzureBackupRG_eastus_1, and if soft delete keeps the restore points, disable soft delete or wait 14 days.
opzione_b: Delete the Recovery Services vault that protects VM4, then move VM4 and re-create the vault in Subscription2.
opzione_c: Convert VM4 from a zonal to a nonzonal configuration, then retry the move.
opzione_d: Move the Recovery Services vault and AzureBackupRG_eastus_1 to Subscription2 first, then move VM4.
spiegazione: Correct: to move virtual machines configured with Azure Backup you must delete the restore point collections (instant recovery snapshots) from the vault - the documented flow is to temporarily stop the backup while keeping backup data, delete the resource of type Restore Point Collection named AzureBackup_<VM name>_########### (by default in AzureBackupRG_<VM location>_1), then move the VM and reconfigure backup. Deleting that resource removes only the instant recovery points, not the backed-up data in the vault. Because soft delete is enabled, Microsoft explicitly states you can't move the VM while those restore points are kept, so you must either disable soft delete or wait 14 days after deleting the restore points. Option B is wrong and destructive: deleting the vault is never the documented remediation, would discard the protected backup data, and is unnecessary because restore points already copied to the vault can be retained and moved. Option C is wrong because the case study never places VM4 in an availability zone, and zonal configuration is not a blocker for a subscription move - a move does not alter the physical region or zone of a resource. Option D is wrong because moving the vault does not clear the instant restore point collections that block the VM move; furthermore, moving a Recovery Services vault has its own separate restrictions and does not address the soft delete condition.
tags: move resources,azure backup,restore point collection,soft delete,subscription

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Move a virtual machine to another resource group, subscription, or region
domanda: Fabrikam is reorganizing its Azure estate. VM1 must be relocated from a resource group named RG1 to a resource group named RG2 in the same subscription and region. Separately, VM2 must be relocated from the East US region to the West Europe region. Select the correct answer for each item.
opzione_a: Tool to relocate VM1 from RG1 to RG2: [Azure Resource Mover | Move-AzResource | Azure Site Recovery]
opzione_b: Tool to relocate VM2 from East US to West Europe: [Azure Resource Mover | Move-AzResource | New-AzAvailabilitySet]
opzione_c: Effect of the RG1-to-RG2 move on the physical location of VM1: [Changes to the target region | Remains unchanged | Becomes zone-redundant]
opzione_d: Maximum time the source and destination resource groups stay locked during a move: [30 minutes | 4 hours | 24 hours]
spiegazione: Item 1: a move between resource groups in the same subscription uses the standard Resource Manager move operation - Move-AzResource in Az PowerShell (or az resource move in the Azure CLI). Azure Resource Mover is scoped to cross-region moves, and Azure Site Recovery is a business continuity and disaster recovery service, not a relocation tool for resource groups. Item 2: Azure Resource Mover is the purpose-built hub for moving resources such as VMs across Azure regions; Move-AzResource cannot change a resource's region, and New-AzAvailabilitySet simply creates an availability set. Item 3: moving a resource only changes its associated resource group and doesn't alter the physical region of the resource - this is the single most-tested fact about resource group moves. It also does not confer any zone redundancy. Item 4: Azure Resource Manager allows a move operation four hours to finish, and both the source and destination resource groups are locked for that period; most moves complete faster and the lock is removed accordingly. During the lock you can't create, delete, or update resources in either resource group, although existing resources keep running.
tags: move resources,azure resource mover,move-azresource,resource group lock,region

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Move a virtual machine to another resource group, subscription, or region
domanda: A cross-subscription move of a virtual machine named VM1 fails immediately with the error code MissingMoveDependentResources. VM1 is attached to a network interface in RG-Network, uses managed disks in RG-Storage, and connects to a virtual network in RG-Network. All resources are in Subscription1 and must end up in Subscription2. What should you do first?
opzione_a: Move the network interface, managed disks, and virtual network into the same resource group as VM1, then move that resource group's resources to Subscription2 in a single operation.
opzione_b: Submit separate move operations for VM1, the network interface, the disks, and the virtual network, in that order.
opzione_c: Register the Microsoft.Compute and Microsoft.Network resource providers in Subscription2.
opzione_d: Create replacement network interfaces, disks, and a virtual network in Subscription2, then move VM1.
spiegazione: Correct: for a move across subscriptions, the resource and its dependent resources must be located in the same resource group and must be moved together. Microsoft describes this as a three-step process - first consolidate the dependent resources into one resource group with a resource-group move, then move that set to the target subscription, then optionally redistribute them in the target subscription. Option B is wrong because splitting the resources across separate move requests reproduces the same MissingMoveDependentResources error; a dependent resource must either already exist in the destination or be included in the same request. Option C is wrong because an unregistered provider raises a different error ('subscription isn't registered for a resource type'), not MissingMoveDependentResources. Option D is wrong because a VM in an existing virtual network can be moved to a new subscription only when the virtual network and all its dependent resources are moved as well - pre-creating replacements does not satisfy the dependency validation for VM1's current NIC and disks.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Move a virtual machine to another resource group, subscription, or region
domanda: As part of a governance review, you must document the hard requirements that Azure Resource Manager enforces before a virtual machine can be moved from one subscription to another. Which of the following are genuine requirements? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: The source and destination subscriptions must exist within the same Microsoft Entra tenant.
opzione_b: The account performing the move must have Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups/moveResources/action on the source resource group.
opzione_c: The destination subscription must be registered for the resource provider of the resource being moved.
opzione_d: The source and destination subscriptions must use the same Azure region.
opzione_e: The source and destination resource groups must have the same name.
spiegazione: Correct answers: (A) the source and destination subscriptions must exist within the same Microsoft Entra tenant; if the tenant IDs differ you must first transfer billing ownership or associate the subscription with the target tenant. (B) the account moving the resources needs at least Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups/moveResources/action at the source resource group (and Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups/write at the destination resource group). (C) the destination subscription must be registered for the resource provider of the resource you're moving, otherwise the move fails with a 'subscription isn't registered for a resource type' error. Incorrect: (D) subscriptions are global containers and are not scoped to a region; a move never changes the physical region of a resource, so region alignment is not a requirement. (E) resource group names are irrelevant to the move; in fact the source and destination resource groups must be different, and naming has no bearing on validation.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Move a virtual machine to another resource group, subscription, or region
domanda: Your team is preparing to move several virtual machines from Subscription1 to Subscription2. Both subscriptions are in the same Microsoft Entra tenant. Which of the following characteristics prevent a virtual machine from being moved to another subscription with the standard Resource Manager move operation? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: The virtual machine was created from a Marketplace resource with a plan attached.
opzione_b: The virtual machine is a member of an availability set and is selected on its own.
opzione_c: The virtual machine uses Standard SSD managed disks for its OS and data disks.
opzione_d: The virtual machine is an Azure Spot (low-priority) virtual machine.
opzione_e: The virtual machine runs in a region that does not support availability zones.
spiegazione: Correct answers: (A) virtual machines created from Marketplace resources with plans attached can't be moved across subscriptions - the documented workaround is to deprovision and redeploy in the target subscription after accepting the Marketplace terms there. (B) virtual machines in an availability set can't be moved individually; the availability set and all of its VMs must move together. (D) low-priority virtual machines and low-priority virtual machine scale sets can't be moved across resource groups or subscriptions. Incorrect: (C) the managed disk tier is irrelevant to move support - Standard SSD, Premium SSD, and Standard HDD managed disks all move with the VM as dependent resources; the disk-related blocker is Azure Disk Encryption, not the disk SKU. (E) availability zone support in the source region has no bearing on a resource group or subscription move, because a move does not change the physical region of the resource.
tags: move resources,move limitations,marketplace plan,spot vm,availability set

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Move a virtual machine to another resource group, subscription, or region
domanda: Litware plans to relocate a workload from the North Europe region to the Sweden Central region and wants to use Azure Resource Mover wherever possible. Which resource types can Azure Resource Mover currently move across regions? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Availability sets
opzione_b: Network security groups
opzione_c: Azure Key Vault vaults
opzione_d: Azure SQL databases and elastic pools
opzione_e: Azure App Service plans
spiegazione: Correct answers: Azure Resource Mover currently supports moving Azure VMs and associated disks, encrypted VMs and disks, NICs, availability sets (A), Azure virtual networks, public IP addresses, network security groups (B), internal and public load balancers, and Azure SQL databases and elastic pools (D) across regions. Incorrect: (C) Azure Key Vault is not in the Resource Mover supported list; relocating a key vault to another region requires the service-specific relocation guidance. (E) Azure App Service plans are likewise not supported by Resource Mover; App Service has its own relocation guidance, and the App Service move limitations article covers only resource group and subscription moves. A useful exam anchor: Resource Mover supports VMs but explicitly does not support Azure Spot VMs, and public IP addresses are moved but their addresses are not retained across regions.
tags: azure resource mover,move region,supported resources,relocation,virtual machines

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Move a virtual machine to another resource group, subscription, or region
domanda: An availability set named AS1 in a resource group named RG1 contains three virtual machines: VM1, VM2, and VM3. A colleague attempts to move only VM1 to a resource group named RG2, and the operation is rejected. What must you do to relocate VM1 to RG2?
opzione_a: Deallocate VM1 and retry the move operation.
opzione_b: Move AS1 together with VM1, VM2, and VM3 in the same move operation.
opzione_c: Delete AS1, move VM1 to RG2, then re-create AS1 in RG2 and add VM1 to it.
opzione_d: Use Azure Resource Mover to move VM1 to RG2.
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft documents that virtual machines in an availability set can't be moved individually. The availability set and every VM it contains must be included in the same move request, which also satisfies the dependent-resource rule that would otherwise raise MissingMoveDependentResources. Option A is wrong because deallocation does not lift this restriction - deallocation only matters for a VM integrated with a key vault for Azure Disk Encryption being moved to another resource group. Option C fails because you can't add an existing VM to an availability set after the VM is created, so VM1 could never rejoin the re-created set. Option D is wrong because Azure Resource Mover is the service for moving resources across Azure regions; a move between resource groups in the same region uses the standard Resource Manager move operation (Move-AzResource / az resource move).
tags: move resources,availability set,resource group,move limitations,virtual machines

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Move a virtual machine to another resource group, subscription, or region
domanda: While moving a virtual machine and its dependent resources from Subscription1 to Subscription2, the validation phase fails with an error stating that the subscription is not registered for a resource type. Both subscriptions belong to the same Microsoft Entra tenant and you have Owner on both. What should you do to resolve the error?
opzione_a: Register the resource provider for the resource type in Subscription2.
opzione_b: Request a quota increase for the virtual machine SKU in Subscription2.
opzione_c: Remove the read-only lock from the destination resource group.
opzione_d: Transfer billing ownership of Subscription2 so that both subscriptions share a billing account.
spiegazione: Correct: the destination subscription must be registered for the resource provider of the resource you are moving. This error commonly appears when the destination subscription has never used that resource type. You fix it with Register-AzResourceProvider -ProviderNamespace <namespace> or az provider register --namespace <namespace>. Option B is wrong because insufficient quota produces a quota/limit error, not a provider-registration error - quota is a separate pre-move check. Option C is wrong because a read-only lock produces a distinct failure indicating the resource can't be moved due to the lock, not a provider registration message. Option D is wrong because billing ownership is irrelevant here; the tenant requirement is already satisfied, and billing transfer only matters when the source and destination subscriptions live in different Microsoft Entra tenants.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Move a virtual machine to another resource group, subscription, or region
domanda: VM1 is a Windows virtual machine that is integrated with a key vault named KV1 to implement Azure Disk Encryption. As part of a billing consolidation, VM1 must be moved from Subscription1 to Subscription2. Both subscriptions are in the same Microsoft Entra tenant. What must you do before the move can succeed?
opzione_a: Deallocate VM1 and leave encryption enabled.
opzione_b: Disable disk encryption on VM1.
opzione_c: Move KV1 to Subscription2 before you move VM1.
opzione_d: Convert VM1 to server-side encryption with a customer-managed key.
spiegazione: Correct: a VM integrated with a key vault for Azure Disk Encryption can be moved to another resource group while in a deallocated state, but to move such a VM to another subscription you must disable encryption first (for example, Disable-AzVMDiskEncryption -ResourceGroupName demoRG -VMName VM1 -VolumeType all). Option A is the classic trap: deallocation is the requirement for a cross-resource-group move, not a cross-subscription move. Option C is wrong because moving the key vault first does not remove the cross-subscription encryption restriction, and it would leave VM1 referencing a vault outside its own subscription. Option D is wrong because the documented remediation is to disable Azure Disk Encryption, not to re-encrypt the disks with a different mechanism; changing the encryption model is a far larger operation and is not what the move limitation calls for.
tags: move resources,azure disk encryption,subscription,key vault,move limitations

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Move a virtual machine to another resource group, subscription, or region
domanda: Northwind Traders has two Azure subscriptions named Subscription1 and Subscription2 that belong to the same Microsoft Entra tenant. A resource group named RG1 in Subscription1 contains a virtual machine named VM1 and its dependent resources. An Azure role assignment for a support engineer is scoped directly to VM1. You plan to relocate the workload to Subscription2. Evaluate each of the following proposed statements and determine whether it is correct. 1) You can move RG1 itself into Subscription2 so that RG1 and everything it contains ends up in Subscription2. 2) The role assignment scoped to VM1 moves with VM1 to the destination resource group. 3) A single move operation can include a maximum of 800 resources.
opzione_a: You can move RG1 itself into Subscription2 so that RG1 and everything it contains ends up in Subscription2.
opzione_b: The role assignment scoped to VM1 moves with VM1 to the destination resource group.
opzione_c: A single move operation can include a maximum of 800 resources.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No. You can't move a resource group to a new subscription. You can move all of the resources in a resource group to a resource group in another subscription, but the resource group object itself stays put, and settings such as tags, role assignments, and policies don't transfer automatically to the destination resource group. Statement 2 - No. If you move a resource with an active Azure role assignment, the role assignment doesn't move and becomes orphaned. You must create the role assignment again after the move; Microsoft recommends removing the orphaned assignment before the move. Statement 3 - Yes. Resource Manager immediately returns an error when there are more than 800 resources in a single operation, and Microsoft recommends separating large moves into different operations because even fewer than 800 resources can fail by timing out.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Apps
domanda: A container app named album-api has a single active revision that serves 100 percent of the traffic. You plan to release an updated container image and gradually phase it in by sending 20 percent of the incoming traffic to the new version while the current version keeps serving the remaining 80 percent. You must perform the release from the Azure portal. Which four actions should you perform in sequence? Arrange the actions in the correct order.
opzione_a: Enter the percentage of traffic to route to each revision so that the combined percentage equals 100 percent, and then select Save.
opzione_b: Open the album-api container app and select Revision management.
opzione_c: Select Create new revision, specify a name suffix and the updated container image, and then select Create.
opzione_d: Select Choose revision mode, select Multiple: Several revisions active simultaneously, and then select Apply.
spiegazione: The documented portal procedure for traffic splitting is: first open the container app and select Revision management, which is the blade where revision mode, revision creation, and traffic weights are managed. Next, because the app is in Single revision mode, select Choose revision mode, select Multiple: Several revisions active simultaneously, and select Apply, then wait for the revision mode to update to Multiple; multiple revision mode is a prerequisite because traffic can only be split between active revisions when that mode is enabled. Then create the new revision by selecting Create new revision, entering a name suffix, and specifying the updated image; this is a revision-scope change that produces a second revision. Finally, mark the revisions as Active and enter the traffic percentage for each revision in the Traffic column, ensuring the combined percentage of all traffic equals 100 percent, and select Save. Setting the weights before a second revision exists would leave nothing to split traffic to, so the weight step must come last.
tags: azure container apps,traffic splitting,revisions,multiple revision mode,azure portal,blue-green,drag drop

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Apps
domanda:
A container app named api1 runs in a Container Apps environment named env1. The app is configured with ingress enabled and set to External, HTTP transport, a target port of 8080, a minimum replica count of 0, a maximum replica count of 10, and the default Single revision mode. No custom scale rule is defined. Evaluate each of the following statements about api1. For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

1. Clients on the internet can reach api1 over HTTPS on port 443 by using the app's fully qualified domain name.
2. If api1 stops receiving requests, it can scale in to zero replicas, and you incur no usage charges while it is scaled to zero.
3. You can split incoming traffic between two revisions of api1 without changing the current revision mode.
opzione_a: Clients on the internet can reach api1 over HTTPS on port 443 by using the app's fully qualified domain name.
opzione_b: If api1 stops receiving requests, it can scale in to zero replicas, and you incur no usage charges while it is scaled to zero.
opzione_c: You can split incoming traffic between two revisions of api1 without changing the current revision mode.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes: with HTTP ingress enabled, a container app exposes ports 80 for HTTP and 443 for HTTPS, receives a fully qualified domain name based on the environment's DNS suffix, and terminates TLS at the ingress point; because ingress is External, the app is exposed through the environment's inbound IP address and can receive traffic from the public internet. The target port of 8080 is the port the container listens on internally and does not change the externally exposed ports. Statement 2 is Yes: the minimum replica count is 0, and the scaling documentation states that you are not billed usage charges if your container app scales to zero. Statement 3 is No: traffic splitting between active revisions requires multiple revision mode. By default, when ingress is enabled, all traffic is routed to the latest deployed revision, and you can split incoming traffic between active revisions only when you enable multiple revision mode; api1 is currently in Single revision mode, so the mode must be changed first.
tags: azure container apps,ingress,external,https,scale to zero,billing,revision mode,traffic splitting

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Apps
domanda: You manage a container app named api1 that runs in multiple revision mode. You need to identify which planned change will cause Azure Container Apps to create a new revision when the app is deployed. Which change creates a new revision?
opzione_a: Changing the traffic split weights between two active revisions
opzione_b: Updating the value of a secret that is referenced by the app
opzione_c: Updating the container image to a new tag
opzione_d: Turning off ingress for the app
spiegazione: A revision-scope change is any change to parameters in the properties.template section of the container app resource, which includes the revision suffix, container configuration and images, and scale rules. Updating the container image to a new tag is therefore a revision-scope change and triggers a new, immutable revision. The other three options are application-scope changes, defined as changes to parameters in the properties.configuration section; they are applied globally to all revisions and do not create a new revision. Option a is incorrect because traffic splitting rules are part of the ingress configuration. Option b is incorrect because secret values are application-scope; note that revisions must be restarted before a container recognizes new secret values, but no new revision is produced. Option d is incorrect because turning ingress on or off is part of the ingress configuration and is likewise application-scope.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Apps
domanda: A microservices solution runs in an Azure Container Apps environment named env1. A container app named web1 serves a web front end and must be reachable from the internet. A container app named orders1 exposes an HTTP API that must be callable only by other container apps in env1 and must not be reachable from the public internet. What should you configure for orders1?
opzione_a: Disable ingress for orders1.
opzione_b: Enable ingress for orders1 and set the ingress traffic type to Internal.
opzione_c: Enable ingress for orders1, set the ingress traffic type to External, and add IP restrictions that deny all public IP address ranges.
opzione_d: Enable ingress for orders1 and configure session affinity so that requests are pinned to replicas inside the environment.
spiegazione: Internal ingress makes an app reachable only from within the same Container Apps environment, such as from other container apps, and the app is not directly accessible from the public internet. That is precisely the requirement for orders1, while web1 keeps External ingress. Option a is incorrect because disabling ingress removes the app's endpoint entirely, so web1 would have no way to call the orders API over HTTP. Option c is incorrect because External ingress exposes the app through the environment's inbound IP address; relying on deny rules to undo that exposure is a fragile workaround, and the documented mechanism for environment-only reachability is Internal ingress. Option d is incorrect because session affinity (sticky sessions) only routes a client's HTTP requests to the same replica; it has no effect on whether the app is exposed publicly.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Apps
domanda: A container app named catalog1 currently has a single active revision that serves production traffic. Your change management policy states that any deployment which creates a new revision requires a change record. You need to identify the changes that can be deployed to catalog1 WITHOUT creating a new revision. Which changes qualify? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Updating the value of a secret stored in the container app
opzione_b: Changing the revision mode from Single to Multiple
opzione_c: Updating the container image reference in the app's template
opzione_d: Adding a KEDA scale rule to the app
opzione_e: Turning off ingress for the app
spiegazione: Application-scope changes are changes to parameters in the properties.configuration section of the container app resource. They are applied globally to all revisions and do not create a new revision. The documented application-scope parameters include secret values, the revision mode, ingress configuration (turning ingress on or off, traffic splitting rules, and labels), credentials for private container registries, and Dapr settings. Options a, b, and e are therefore all application-scope. Options c and d are incorrect because they are revision-scope changes: a revision-scope change is any change to the parameters in the properties.template section, which explicitly includes the revision suffix, container configuration and images, and scale rules for the container application. Both would produce a new, immutable revision on deployment.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Instances
domanda: Contoso must run a nightly data-conversion task in Azure Container Instances. The task runs a script that writes its output files to a share so the files survive after the container stops, and the container must be restarted automatically only if the script exits with a nonzero exit code. During the run, an operator must be able to reach a status page hosted by the container by using a fully qualified domain name that is based on a DNS name label. Select the appropriate option for each setting.
opzione_a: OS type: [Linux | Windows | Windows Server Core]
opzione_b: Restart policy: [Always | Never | OnFailure]
opzione_c: Volume type to mount for the output files: [Azure Files | Azure Blob Storage | Azure NetApp Files]
opzione_d: FQDN suffix produced by the DNS name label: [.azurewebsites.net | .azurecontainer.io | .azurecontainerapps.io]
spiegazione: OS type must be Linux because volume mounting, including Azure Files shares, is one of the features restricted to Linux containers in Azure Container Instances. Restart policy must be OnFailure, because it restarts the containers only when the process executed in the container terminates with a nonzero exit code; Always would restart the container after a successful run, and Never would leave a failed run unretried. The volume type must be Azure Files: to persist state beyond the lifetime of the container, Azure Container Instances can mount an Azure file share created with Azure Files over SMB, and the supported volume types are Azure file share, secret, emptyDir, and cloned git repo. Azure Blob Storage and Azure NetApp Files are not supported volume types for a container group. The FQDN suffix is .azurecontainer.io, because a container instance with a DNS name label is publicly reachable at dns-name-label.region.azurecontainer.io; .azurewebsites.net belongs to Azure App Service and .azurecontainerapps.io belongs to Azure Container Apps environments.
tags: azure container instances,aci,hotspot,os type,restart policy,azure files,dns name label,fqdn

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Instances
domanda: A Linux container group in Azure Container Instances mounts an Azure file share as a volume so that the application can persist log files. A security review requires that no storage account key appear in the container group definition. A colleague proposes assigning a user-assigned managed identity to the container group and using it to mount the file share. How should you respond?
opzione_a: Grant the managed identity the Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role on the share, then remove the storage account key from the volume definition.
opzione_b: Azure Storage does not support SMB mounting of a file share by using a managed identity, so the storage account key is still required for the Azure Files volume.
opzione_c: Add a service endpoint for Azure Storage to the delegated subnet, which allows the mount to authenticate with the managed identity instead of a key.
opzione_d: Change the OS type of the container group to Windows, because managed identity authentication for Azure Files volumes is supported only for Windows containers.
spiegazione: The Azure Files volume documentation for Azure Container Instances states explicitly that Azure Storage does not support SMB mounting of a file share by using a managed identity. Mounting an Azure file share as a volume requires three values: the storage account name, the share name, and the storage account key. Option a is incorrect because the Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role enables identity-based access for supported scenarios such as domain-joined clients, but it does not allow an Azure Container Instances volume mount to authenticate without the key. Option c is incorrect because a service endpoint to Azure Storage only provides network reachability when outbound internet access is blocked in the delegated subnet; it changes network path, not authentication. Option d is incorrect and reverses the actual limitation: Azure Files shares can only be mounted to Linux containers, and the mount requires the container to run as root.
tags: azure container instances,aci,volume mount,azure files,smb,managed identity,storage account key

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Instances
domanda: A development team asks you to deploy a container group to Azure Container Instances that contains an application container and a logging sidecar container. Both containers are built from Windows Server base images. What should you tell the team?
opzione_a: The deployment is supported. Create the container group with the OS type set to Windows and define both containers in the containers array.
opzione_b: Multi-container groups support only Linux containers. For Windows containers, Azure Container Instances supports the deployment of a single container instance only.
opzione_c: The deployment is supported only if the container group is deployed into a delegated subnet of an Azure virtual network.
opzione_d: The deployment is supported only if the two containers are placed in separate container groups that communicate over localhost.
spiegazione: Multi-container groups in Azure Container Instances currently support only Linux containers. For Windows containers, Azure Container Instances supports the deployment of a single container instance only, so an application container plus a logging sidecar in one group requires Linux images. Option a is incorrect because setting the OS type to Windows does not lift the restriction; running multiple containers per container group is one of the features restricted to Linux. Option c is incorrect because virtual network deployment does not enable Windows multi-container groups; it is an unrelated networking capability. Option d is incorrect on two counts: splitting the containers into separate groups defeats the sidecar pattern, and localhost communication works only between container instances inside the same container group, never across groups.
tags: azure container instances,aci,container group,multi-container,windows containers,os type,sidecar

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Instances
domanda: A nightly image-rendering job runs as a single Linux container in Azure Container Instances. The job runs a script that exits when the rendering completes. You must ensure that the container is not restarted after the script completes successfully, but that it is restarted automatically if the script terminates with a nonzero exit code. Which restart policy should you configure for the container group?
opzione_a: Always
opzione_b: Never
opzione_c: OnFailure
opzione_d: UnlessStopped
spiegazione: OnFailure restarts the containers in the group only when the process executed in the container fails, that is, when it terminates with a nonzero exit code. The containers therefore run at least once, and a successful exit leaves the container in the Terminated state, which is exactly the required behavior. Always is incorrect: it is the default policy applied when no restart policy is specified, and it restarts the containers unconditionally, so the container would be restarted even after a successful run. Never is incorrect: the containers run at most once and are never restarted, so a failed rendering script would not be retried. UnlessStopped is incorrect: it is a Docker restart policy value and is not one of the three restart policy settings supported by Azure Container Instances, which are Always, Never, and OnFailure.
tags: azure container instances,aci,restart policy,onfailure,container group,run-once task

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Instances
domanda: Your organization runs workloads in Azure Container Instances and is evaluating whether some of them can be migrated from Linux images to Windows images. You need to identify the capabilities that are currently restricted to Linux containers in Azure Container Instances. Which capabilities are restricted to Linux containers? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Mounting an Azure Files share as a volume in the container group
opzione_b: Running multiple containers in a single container group
opzione_c: Assigning a DNS name label to the container group so that it is reachable by FQDN
opzione_d: Collecting container resource usage metrics with Azure Monitor
opzione_e: Configuring a restart policy of OnFailure for the container group
spiegazione: The Azure Container Instances overview lists the features that are currently restricted to Linux containers: multiple containers per container group, volume mounting (Azure Files, emptyDir, GitRepo, and secret volumes), resource usage metrics with Azure Monitor, and GPU resources (preview). Options a, b, and d map directly to that list. Option c is incorrect because container access through an IP address and a DNS name label that produces an FQDN of the form dns-name-label.region.azurecontainer.io is available for container groups regardless of OS type. Option e is incorrect because the restart policy settings Always, Never, and OnFailure are properties of the container group and apply to both Linux and Windows deployments.
tags: azure container instances,aci,os type,linux containers,windows containers,volume mount,azure monitor metrics

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision an App Service plan
domanda: Contoso is selecting a pricing tier for a new App Service plan that will host an internal line-of-business web app. The app must run on virtual machine instances that are dedicated to Contoso and not shared with other Azure customers. Contoso wants the lowest-cost tier that meets this requirement. Which pricing tier should you select?
opzione_a: Free (F1)
opzione_b: Shared (D1)
opzione_c: Basic (B1)
opzione_d: Standard (S1)
spiegazione: Basic (B1) is correct. Microsoft Learn groups App Service pricing tiers into three compute categories: shared compute (Free, Shared), dedicated compute (Basic, Standard, Premium, PremiumV2, PremiumV3, PremiumV4) and isolated (IsolatedV2). Basic is the lowest tier in the dedicated compute category, where apps run on dedicated Azure VMs and only apps in the same App Service plan share those compute resources. Free (F1) is wrong because the Free tier is shared compute: the app runs on the same VM as other App Service apps, including apps belonging to other customers. Shared (D1) is wrong for the same reason - Shared is the second shared-compute base tier and also places the app on a VM shared with other customers; it only adds a per-app CPU quota and custom domain support. Standard (S1) is wrong not because it fails the requirement (Standard is dedicated compute) but because it is a higher, more expensive tier than Basic, so it is not the lowest-cost tier that satisfies the dedicated-VM requirement.
tags: app service, app service plan, pricing tier, dedicated compute, shared compute, basic tier

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision an App Service plan
domanda: Four web apps are hosted in a single App Service plan named ASP1 that uses the Premium v3 (P1v3) pricing tier. Which statements about this configuration are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: All four apps run on the same VM instances that are configured in ASP1.
opzione_b: Scaling out ASP1 to additional instances affects all four apps.
opzione_c: Each of the four apps can be assigned its own pricing tier within ASP1.
opzione_d: Deployment slots created for the apps run on the same VM instances as ASP1.
opzione_e: The storage limit of the Premium v3 tier applies separately to each of the four apps.
spiegazione: Options a, b and d are correct. Microsoft Learn states that when an app runs, it runs on all the VM instances configured in the App Service plan; if multiple apps are in the same plan, they all share the same VM instances; and if an app has multiple deployment slots, all deployment slots also run on those same VM instances (Learn further notes that an active slot is classified as an active app because it competes for resources in the same plan). All apps in a plan scale together because they share the same underlying compute resources, so scaling the plan - manually or through autoscale - affects every app in it. Option c is wrong because the pricing tier is a property of the App Service plan, not of the individual app; to give an app a different tier you must move it to a separate App Service plan. Option e is wrong because the documented storage limit (250 GB for Premium) is the total content size across all apps in the same App Service plan, not a per-app allowance.
tags: app service, app service plan, shared compute resources, deployment slots, storage limit, premium v3

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision an App Service plan
domanda: App1 is a Windows web app that runs in an App Service plan named ASP1. ASP1 uses the Basic (B1) tier, is deployed to the East US region, and belongs to a resource group named RG1. App1 has no virtual network integration configured. You must move App1 to a different App Service plan. Which plan is a valid target for App1?
opzione_a: ASP2: Windows, Standard (S1), East US, resource group RG1
opzione_b: ASP3: Windows, Standard (S1), East US, resource group RG2
opzione_c: ASP4: Windows, Standard (S1), West US, resource group RG1
opzione_d: ASP5: Linux, Standard (S1), East US, resource group RG1
spiegazione: ASP2 is correct. Microsoft Learn states that you can move an app to another App Service plan only as long as the source plan and the target plan are in the same resource group, the same geographical region, and are of the same OS type. ASP2 matches ASP1 on all three: RG1, East US, and Windows. The pricing tier difference (B1 to S1) is irrelevant - the tiers do not have to match. ASP3 is wrong because it is in a different resource group (RG2). This also breaks the underlying webspace requirement: plans are deployed into a webspace determined by the resource group, region and OS combination, and an app can only move between plans in the same webspace. ASP4 is wrong because it is in a different region (West US); the region of a plan cannot be changed, and running the app elsewhere would require app cloning instead. ASP5 is wrong because it is a Linux plan; Learn explicitly says any change in type, such as Windows to Linux, is not supported.
tags: app service, app service plan, move app, webspace, resource group, operating system

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision an App Service plan
domanda: A prototype web app currently runs in an App Service plan that uses the Free (F1) tier and is reachable only at proto.azurewebsites.net. Marketing now requires the app to respond at www.contoso.com. You must meet the requirement at the lowest possible cost. What should you do first?
opzione_a: Add the custom domain to the app while leaving the plan in the Free (F1) tier.
opzione_b: Scale up the App Service plan to the Shared (D1) tier.
opzione_c: Scale up the App Service plan to the Basic (B1) tier.
opzione_d: Scale up the App Service plan to the Standard (S1) tier.
spiegazione: Scaling up to the Shared (D1) tier is correct. The App Service limits table shows that the Free tier supports 0 custom domains and is restricted to the azurewebsites.net subdomain, while the Shared tier and every higher tier support up to 500 custom domains. The App Service plan overview reinforces this by describing exactly this progression: start on Free, and when you add your custom DNS name to the web app, scale the plan up to the Shared tier. Option a is wrong because a custom DNS name cannot be mapped to an app in the Free tier at all. Options c and d are wrong not because they fail technically - Basic and Standard both support 500 custom domains - but because they are higher-priced tiers than Shared, and the requirement is the lowest possible cost. Note that a TLS/SSL binding for that custom domain would require Basic or higher, but the stated requirement here is only the custom domain mapping.
tags: app service, app service plan, custom domain, free tier, shared tier, scale up

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision an App Service plan
domanda:
An App Service plan named ASP1 uses the Free (F1) pricing tier, is deployed to the East US region, and hosts a single Windows web app named App1. App1 has started to receive unpredictable bursts of traffic and the team also wants to secure a custom domain with a certificate. Evaluate each of the following proposed statements and determine whether each one is achievable in the current configuration.

1. Scaling out ASP1 to three instances will improve App1's availability during traffic bursts.
2. Scaling up ASP1 to the Basic (B1) tier will allow you to configure a TLS/SSL binding for a custom domain on App1.
3. Configuring metric-based autoscale rules on ASP1 will automatically add instances when average CPU exceeds 70 percent.
opzione_a: Scaling out ASP1 to three instances will improve App1's availability during traffic bursts.
opzione_b: Scaling up ASP1 to the Basic (B1) tier will allow you to configure a TLS/SSL binding for a custom domain on App1.
opzione_c: Configuring metric-based autoscale rules on ASP1 will automatically add instances when average CPU exceeds 70 percent.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No. In the Free and Shared tiers an app receives CPU minutes on a shared VM instance and cannot scale out; the documented scale-out limit for both Free and Shared is 1 shared instance. Scaling out is only possible from the Basic tier upward (3 for Basic, 10 for Standard, 30 for Premium v2-v4, 100 for Isolated). Statement 2 is Yes. Microsoft Learn describes exactly this progression: you add a custom DNS name by scaling up to Shared, and when you want to create a TLS binding you scale up to the Basic tier. Basic is therefore sufficient for a TLS/SSL binding on a custom domain. Statement 3 is No. Rule-based autoscale requires the Standard tier or higher, as shown in the App Service scale-out options table (manual = Basic and up, autoscale = Standard and up, automatic scaling = Premium v2-v4). A Free-tier plan cannot have autoscale rules at all, so no CPU rule would ever add instances.
tags: app service, free tier, scale out, tls binding, autoscale, pricing tier features

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: Litware is deploying private endpoints in the Azure public cloud for an Azure Key Vault, an Azure SQL Database logical server, and an Azure App Service web app. The private DNS zone configuration for each private endpoint must be generated automatically, so the recommended zone names must be used. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Private DNS zone for the Key Vault private endpoint (vault subresource): [privatelink.vault.azure.net | privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net | privatelink.keyvault.azure.net]
opzione_b: Private DNS zone for the Azure SQL Database private endpoint (sqlServer subresource): [privatelink.database.windows.net | privatelink.sql.azure.com | privatelink.sqlserver.windows.net]
opzione_c: Private DNS zone for the App Service private endpoint (sites subresource): [privatelink.azurewebsites.net | privatelink.web.core.windows.net | privatelink.appservice.azure.com]
opzione_d: Record type that Azure creates in the private DNS zone for each private endpoint: [A | CNAME | SRV]
spiegazione: For Azure Key Vault (Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults, vault subresource) the recommended private DNS zone in the public cloud is privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net, with vault.azure.net and vaultcore.azure.net as the public DNS zone forwarders; privatelink.vault.azure.net and privatelink.keyvault.azure.net are not recommended zone names and would prevent the private DNS zone configuration from being generated automatically. For Azure SQL Database (Microsoft.Sql/servers, sqlServer subresource) the zone is privatelink.database.windows.net, derived from the public suffix database.windows.net; privatelink.sql.azure.com and privatelink.sqlserver.windows.net do not exist. For Azure Web Apps and Function Apps (Microsoft.Web/sites, sites subresource) the zone is privatelink.azurewebsites.net; privatelink.web.core.windows.net belongs to the storage account static website subresource and privatelink.appservice.azure.com is not a recommended zone. Azure creates an A record in the privatelink zone that maps the resource name to the private endpoint's private IP address - the CNAME is what Azure publishes in the public DNS to redirect resolution into the privatelink namespace, and SRV records are not used by private endpoints.
tags: private dns zone,private endpoint,zone naming,key vault,azure sql,app service

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: VNet1 is linked to a private DNS zone named db.contoso.internal. The DNS servers setting of VNet1 was changed from Default (Azure-provided) to a custom DNS server that runs on a domain controller virtual machine inside VNet1. After the change, virtual machines in VNet1 can no longer resolve records in db.contoso.internal. You must restore resolution while keeping the custom DNS server for Active Directory name resolution. What should you do on the domain controller?
opzione_a: Configure a conditional forwarder for db.contoso.internal that points to 168.63.129.16.
opzione_b: Configure a root hint that points to the four Azure DNS name servers assigned to the private DNS zone.
opzione_c: Create a secondary zone for db.contoso.internal and configure a zone transfer from Azure Private DNS.
