opzione_d: Configure a conditional forwarder for db.contoso.internal that points to the first IP address of the VNet1 address space.
spiegazione: Option A is correct. When you define a custom DNS server on a virtual network, the custom setting overrides the default name resolution order and the system no longer automatically queries the private DNS zones linked to that virtual network. If the custom DNS server is a virtual machine, you must configure a conditional forwarder for the private zone that points to Azure DNS at the well-known virtual IP address 168.63.129.16. (Alternatively, an Azure DNS Private Resolver in a linked virtual network can be used as the forwarding target.) Option B is wrong because Azure Private DNS zones are not resolvable from the public DNS hierarchy and are not served by the public Azure DNS name servers, so root hints cannot reach them. Option C is wrong because Azure Private DNS does not expose zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR); you cannot stand up a secondary copy of a private zone. Option D is wrong because the correct target is the Azure DNS virtual IP 168.63.129.16, not an address derived from the virtual network address space; the first usable addresses of a subnet are reserved by Azure but do not host the recursive resolver.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: The public domain adatum.com is already delegated to Azure DNS and hosted in a public DNS zone. A separate team must manage the subdomain engineering.adatum.com in its own zone. You plan to create the child zone and the delegation manually, without using the Child zone option in the Azure portal, and then confirm that the delegation resolves. Arrange the actions in the correct order.
opzione_a: In the adatum.com zone, add an NS record set named engineering that contains the name server entries of the child zone.
opzione_b: Create a public DNS zone named engineering.adatum.com in Azure DNS.
opzione_c: Copy the name server names listed in the engineering.adatum.com zone.
opzione_d: Run nslookup www.engineering.adatum.com and confirm that the expected address is returned.
opzione_e: In the engineering.adatum.com zone, create an A record named www that resolves to 10.10.10.10.
spiegazione: The correct order is B, C, A, E, D. First create the child zone engineering.adatum.com in Azure DNS - the parent adatum.com must already exist and already be delegated to Azure DNS, which the scenario states. Creating the child zone causes Azure DNS to assign name servers to it and to populate the authoritative NS record set at the child zone apex, so those name server names can only be copied after the zone exists (C). Next, add an NS record set named engineering to the parent adatum.com zone containing those name server entries (A); setting up the NS records for a child zone in the parent zone is what performs the delegation, and it cannot be done before the child name servers are known. Then create a test record such as the www A record inside the child zone (E) - a record must exist before it can be looked up. Finally, validate the delegation with nslookup for www.engineering.adatum.com (D), which should return a non-authoritative answer of 10.10.10.10. Placing the NS record set before the child zone exists, or testing before the test record is created, produces a delegation that cannot be verified.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: You administer the public DNS zone northwind.com in Azure DNS and must document how record sets behave in the zone. Select the appropriate option to complete each statement.
opzione_a: Maximum number of records that a single CNAME record set can contain: [1 | 20 | 400]
opzione_b: Record type that must be used to publish Sender Policy Framework information: [SPF | TXT | CAA]
opzione_c: Record type used to specify which certificate authorities may issue certificates for the domain: [CAA | CNAME | TLSA]
opzione_d: Record set type that can be created at the zone apex to reference a Traffic Manager profile: [CNAME | A alias | NS]
spiegazione: The DNS standards do not permit multiple records with the same name for the SOA and CNAME types, so a CNAME record set can contain only a single record. The value 20 is the general limit on records per record set in a public zone, and 400 is the limit for TXT records per record set - neither applies to CNAME. SPF information must be published using the TXT record type: RFC 7208 deprecated the dedicated SPF record type, and Azure DNS does not support it; when a zone file is imported, SPF-type records are converted to TXT. CAA is the record type that lets domain owners declare which certificate authorities are authorized to issue certificates, using the flags, tag (issue, issuewild, iodef), and value properties; CNAME is an aliasing record and TLSA associates a TLS certificate or public key with a name and requires DNSSEC. Finally, a CNAME cannot exist at the zone apex, and the apex NS record set is reserved and managed by Azure DNS, so an A record set qualified as an alias record set is the supported way to point the apex at a Traffic Manager profile.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: A private endpoint is deployed in VNet1 for a storage account, and the private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net contains the correct A record and is linked to VNet1. Virtual machines in VNet1 resolve the storage account FQDN to the private IP address as expected. Virtual machines in VNet2, which is peered with VNet1 and uses the default Azure-provided DNS settings, still resolve the FQDN to the public IP address of the storage account. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create a virtual network link between the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net zone and VNet2.
opzione_b: Enable the Allow gateway transit option on the peering from VNet1 to VNet2.
opzione_c: Create a second private endpoint for the storage account in VNet2.
opzione_d: Enable autoregistration on the existing virtual network link between the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net zone and VNet1.
spiegazione: Option A is correct. DNS resolution against a private DNS zone works only from virtual networks that are linked to that zone. Virtual network peering does not propagate private DNS zone resolution, so VNet2 falls through to public DNS and receives the public IP. Creating a virtual network link from the zone to VNet2 makes VNet2 a resolution virtual network and lets its VMs resolve the privatelink record. Option B is wrong because gateway transit controls whether a peered network can use the other network's VPN or ExpressRoute gateway; it has no effect on private DNS zone resolution. Option C is wrong because it is unnecessary and adds cost - the existing private endpoint is already reachable from VNet2 over the peering; only name resolution is missing. Option D is wrong because autoregistration only creates A records for virtual machines deployed in the linked virtual network. It does nothing for private endpoint records and would not affect resolution from VNet2; the zone also cannot be a registration zone for a network it is not linked to.
tags: private dns zone,virtual network link,private endpoint,peering,troubleshooting

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: A virtual network named VNet1 is already linked to a private DNS zone named corp.contoso.internal with autoregistration enabled. A colleague creates a second private DNS zone named apps.contoso.internal and attempts to create a virtual network link from that zone to VNet1 with autoregistration enabled. The operation fails. What is the cause, and what is the supported way to link VNet1 to apps.contoso.internal?
opzione_a: A virtual network can be linked to only one private DNS zone in total. VNet1 must be unlinked from corp.contoso.internal first.
opzione_b: A virtual network can be linked to only one private DNS zone with autoregistration enabled. Create the link to apps.contoso.internal without autoregistration.
opzione_c: Autoregistration requires the virtual network and the private DNS zone to be in the same resource group. Move apps.contoso.internal to the resource group of VNet1.
opzione_d: A private DNS zone can have only one registration virtual network. Create a second private DNS zone with the same name in another resource group and link VNet1 to it.
spiegazione: Option B is correct. A specific virtual network can be linked to only one private DNS zone when automatic registration is enabled - that zone becomes the registration zone for the virtual network. Linking VNet1 to apps.contoso.internal without autoregistration makes it a resolution virtual network, and a virtual network can have many resolution zones associated with it, so records in apps.contoso.internal will still resolve from VNet1. Option A is wrong because a virtual network can be linked to up to 1,000 private DNS zones; only the autoregistration link is limited to one. Option C is wrong because there is no same-resource-group requirement - a private DNS zone can be linked to virtual networks in other resource groups, subscriptions, and even other tenants, given write permissions on both objects. Option D is wrong because a private DNS zone can have multiple registration virtual networks; the restriction runs the other way. Creating duplicate zones would not lift the one-registration-zone-per-virtual-network limit.
tags: private dns zone,virtual network link,autoregistration,registration zone,resolution zone

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: Fabrikam runs a web application behind an Azure Traffic Manager profile named fabweb.trafficmanager.net that contains only external endpoints. The public DNS zone fabrikam.com is hosted in Azure DNS. Users must be able to reach the application by browsing to https://fabrikam.com, and the DNS configuration must not require manual updates if the underlying endpoints change. What should you create in the fabrikam.com zone?
opzione_a: A CNAME record set named @ that targets fabweb.trafficmanager.net
opzione_b: An A record set named @ that is qualified as an alias record set targeting the Traffic Manager profile
opzione_c: An A record set named @ that contains the IPv4 address currently returned by fabweb.trafficmanager.net
opzione_d: An NS record set named @ that contains fabweb.trafficmanager.net
spiegazione: Option B is correct. Alias record sets are supported for the A, AAAA, and CNAME record types and, unlike CNAME records, they can be created at the zone apex. An A alias record set pointing to a Traffic Manager profile lets you host a load-balanced application at the naked domain, and Azure DNS resolves the record dynamically so no manual maintenance is required. This works when the Traffic Manager profile contains only external endpoints, which is stated in the scenario. Option A is wrong because the DNS protocol prevents CNAME records at the zone apex - this is precisely the limitation that alias records exist to solve. Option C is wrong because it hard-codes an address that is not guaranteed to remain stable, producing a dangling DNS record and defeating the requirement to avoid manual updates. Option D is wrong because the apex NS record set is created and managed automatically by Azure DNS, cannot have its prepopulated name servers removed, and NS records delegate a zone rather than resolve an application name.
tags: azure dns,alias record,zone apex,traffic manager,public zone

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: Your organization plans to consolidate internal name resolution onto a single Azure Private DNS zone that is shared by workloads in several subscriptions and regions. Which statements about Azure Private DNS zones are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A single private DNS zone can be linked to virtual networks that are located in different Azure regions.
opzione_b: Virtual networks must be peered with each other before records in a shared private DNS zone can resolve across them.
opzione_c: A virtual network that belongs to a different Azure subscription can be linked to the private DNS zone.
opzione_d: You can create NS record sets in a private DNS zone to delegate a child domain to another private DNS zone.
opzione_e: When a linked virtual network is deleted, its virtual network links and autoregistered DNS records are removed automatically.
spiegazione: A, C, and E are correct. Private DNS zone data is stored as a global resource, so the same zone can be linked to virtual networks in multiple regions and remains available if one virtual network or region is affected. A virtual network in a different subscription (or even a different tenant) can be linked as long as you have write permission on both the virtual network and the private DNS zone. When you delete a linked virtual network, the virtual network links and the autoregistered DNS records associated with it are cleared automatically - no manual unlink is required. Option B is wrong because forward DNS resolution across virtual networks linked to the same private zone has no dependency on peering; you may peer networks for data-plane traffic, but resolution does not require it. Option D is wrong because you cannot create zone delegations (NS records) in a private DNS zone. If you need a child domain, you create it directly as its own private DNS zone and link it to the virtual network.
tags: private dns zone,virtual network link,cross-subscription,ns delegation,autoregistration

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: VNet1 is linked to a private DNS zone named ops.contoso.internal, and autoregistration is enabled on the link. VNet1 contains a virtual machine named VM1 that has two network interfaces, NIC1 (primary) and NIC2 (secondary), each with a private IP address. VNet1 also contains an internal load balancer named ILB1 that has a static private IP address in a subnet of VNet1. Evaluate each of the following statements. 1. An A record for VM1 that maps to the private IP address of NIC1 is created automatically in ops.contoso.internal. 2. An A record for VM1 that maps to the private IP address of NIC2 is created automatically in ops.contoso.internal. 3. If VM1 is stopped and deallocated, the autoregistered DNS record for VM1 is removed from ops.contoso.internal.
opzione_a: An A record for VM1 that maps to the private IP address of NIC1 is created automatically in ops.contoso.internal.
opzione_b: An A record for VM1 that maps to the private IP address of NIC2 is created automatically in ops.contoso.internal.
opzione_c: If VM1 is stopped and deallocated, the autoregistered DNS record for VM1 is removed from ops.contoso.internal.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes. When a virtual network link has autoregistration enabled, Azure DNS creates an address (A) record for each virtual machine deployed in that virtual network, pointing to its private IP address. Statement 2 is No. DNS records are created automatically only for the primary virtual machine NIC. If a virtual machine has more than one NIC, you must create the DNS records for the additional network interfaces manually in the private DNS zone. The same restriction is why no record is created for ILB1 - autoregistration works only for virtual machines, and records for other resources such as internal load balancers must be created manually. Statement 3 is Yes. The autoregistered records track the virtual machine life cycle: records are created when a virtual machine starts in a linked virtual network with autoregistration enabled, and when the virtual machine is stopped and deallocated or deleted, the autoregistered records are removed from the zone.
tags: private dns zone,autoregistration,a record,secondary nic,internal load balancer

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: Your company purchased the domain adatum.com from a third-party domain registrar. You create a public DNS zone named adatum.com in Azure DNS and add the required A and MX record sets. Internet clients still cannot resolve names in adatum.com. What must you do to complete the delegation of the domain to Azure DNS?
opzione_a: At the domain registrar, replace the existing name server records for adatum.com with the Azure DNS name servers assigned to the zone.
opzione_b: In the adatum.com zone in Azure DNS, modify the host property of the SOA record set to reference the registrar's name servers.
opzione_c: In the adatum.com zone in Azure DNS, remove the prepopulated Azure DNS name servers from the apex NS record set and add the registrar's name servers.
opzione_d: At the domain registrar, create a CNAME record that maps adatum.com to the first Azure DNS name server assigned to the zone.
spiegazione: Option A is correct. Azure DNS is an authoritative DNS service, not a domain registrar. Delegation is performed in the parent zone: you take the four Azure DNS name servers that were assigned to your zone and configure them as the NS records for the domain at your registrar. Until the registrar publishes those NS records, recursive resolvers never reach Azure DNS. Option B is wrong because the SOA host property is preconfigured by Azure DNS to the primary name server it provides and is the one SOA property you cannot modify; changing SOA would not affect delegation anyway. Option C is wrong because removing or modifying the prepopulated Azure DNS name servers in the apex NS record set is not allowed, and the authoritative NS records inside the child zone do not perform the delegation - the records in the parent zone do. Option D is wrong because delegation is done with NS records, not CNAME records, and a CNAME cannot exist at the zone apex in any case.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: You are designing DNS records in a public Azure DNS zone and want to use alias record sets wherever they are supported. Which targets can an alias record set in an Azure DNS zone reference? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A Standard SKU public IP address resource
opzione_b: An Azure Traffic Manager profile
opzione_c: An Azure Front Door endpoint
opzione_d: The private IP configuration of a virtual machine network interface
opzione_e: The fully qualified domain name of an on-premises web server
spiegazione: A, B, and C are correct. Azure DNS alias record sets (supported for the A, AAAA, and CNAME types) can point to a Standard SKU public IP resource, to a Traffic Manager profile, to an Azure Content Delivery Network endpoint, to an Azure Front Door endpoint, or to another DNS record set of the same type within the same zone. Coupling the record's life cycle to the Azure resource is what prevents dangling DNS records and updates the record automatically when the target IP changes or the target is deleted. Option D is wrong because alias records reference Azure resources such as public IP resources, not private IP configurations on a network interface; a public DNS zone is also the wrong place to publish private addresses. Option E is wrong because alias records must reference an Azure resource or another record set in the same zone - an arbitrary external FQDN is not a supported alias target and would be expressed as a normal (non-alias) CNAME record.
tags: azure dns,alias record,public ip,traffic manager,front door,dangling dns

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: A storage account is configured with a private endpoint for the blob subresource. Which private DNS zone name must be used so that the private endpoint DNS zone configuration is generated automatically in the Azure public cloud?
opzione_a: privatelink.blob.core.windows.net
opzione_b: privatelink.web.core.windows.net
opzione_c: privatelink.storage.azure.com
opzione_d: blob.privatelink.core.windows.net
spiegazione: Option A is correct. For a storage account private endpoint with the blob or blob_secondary subresource in the Azure public cloud, the recommended private DNS zone name is privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, with blob.core.windows.net as the public DNS zone forwarder. Private endpoint private DNS zone configurations are only generated automatically when this recommended naming scheme is used. Option B is wrong because privatelink.web.core.windows.net corresponds to the web and web_secondary subresources (static website endpoint), not blob. Option C is wrong because privatelink.storage.azure.com is not a recommended zone name for any storage subresource; Microsoft builds privatelink zones by prefixing privatelink to the existing public suffix. Option D is wrong because the privatelink label must be the leftmost label of the zone name - the correct form is privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, not blob.privatelink.core.windows.net.
tags: private dns zone,private endpoint,storage account,blob,zone naming

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: A hub-and-spoke deployment will share one Azure Private DNS zone across a large number of spoke virtual networks. Before submitting a design review, you must record the default service limits that apply. Select the appropriate value to complete each statement.
opzione_a: Maximum number of virtual network links per private DNS zone: [100 | 1000 | 25000]
opzione_b: Maximum number of virtual network links with autoregistration enabled per private DNS zone: [1 | 100 | 1000]
opzione_c: Maximum number of private DNS zones that a single virtual network can be linked to with autoregistration enabled: [1 | 100 | 1000]
spiegazione: The default Azure DNS limits for private DNS zones are: 1,000 virtual network links per private DNS zone; 100 virtual network links per private DNS zone with autoregistration enabled; and 1 private DNS zone that a given virtual network can be linked to with autoregistration enabled. The distractors are real Azure DNS limits taken from adjacent rows of the same table, which is what makes them plausible: 100 is the autoregistration link limit per zone (not the total link limit), 25,000 is the maximum number of record sets per private DNS zone, and 1,000 is both the total virtual network links per zone and the number of private DNS zones a virtual network can be linked to without autoregistration - but only one of those links may be a registration link. The one-registration-zone-per-virtual-network rule is the design constraint that most often forces a separate resolution-only zone in hub-and-spoke topologies.
tags: private dns zone,limits,virtual network link,autoregistration,hub and spoke

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure DNS
domanda: Contoso hosts the public DNS zone contoso.com in Azure DNS. An administrator attempts to create a record set with the relative name @ so that requests for contoso.com are redirected to the name webfarm.contoso.net. The operation fails. Which record type is the administrator attempting to create that the DNS standards do not permit at the zone apex?
opzione_a: CNAME
opzione_b: TXT
opzione_c: MX
opzione_d: A
spiegazione: CNAME is correct. Because the zone apex (name = @) always contains the NS and SOA record sets that are created automatically with the zone, a CNAME record set cannot coexist with them. CNAME record sets cannot coexist with any other record set of the same name, so a CNAME can never be created at the zone apex. This constraint comes from the DNS standards, not from Azure DNS. TXT is wrong because TXT record sets are fully supported at the zone apex and are routinely used there for SPF and domain-verification values. MX is wrong because MX record sets at the apex are the normal way to publish mail servers for a domain and are supported. A is wrong because an A record set at the apex is supported and is the standard way to point a naked domain at an IPv4 address; an A record set can also be qualified as an alias record set at the apex.

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: You are configuring a health probe for a public Standard Load Balancer that fronts a set of web servers in a subnet protected by a network security group. Select the correct value for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Health probe protocols supported by a Standard Load Balancer: [TCP only | TCP and HTTP | TCP, HTTP, and HTTPS]
opzione_b: Source IP address of an IPv4 health probe: [168.63.129.16 | 169.254.169.254 | The frontend IP address of the load balancer]
opzione_c: Network security group service tag that permits health probe traffic: [AzureLoadBalancer | VirtualNetwork | AzurePlatformDNS]
opzione_d: HTTP status code that marks an HTTP health probe as healthy: [200 | Any 2xx or 3xx code | 200 or 404]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - 'TCP, HTTP, and HTTPS': Standard Load Balancer supports TCP, HTTP, and HTTPS probe protocols; Basic supports only TCP and HTTP, which makes 'TCP and HTTP' the Basic-SKU distractor. 'TCP only' is incorrect for either SKU. Dropdown 2 - '168.63.129.16': All IPv4 Load Balancer health probes originate from 168.63.129.16, a Microsoft-owned virtual public IP used in all regions and national clouds. 169.254.169.254 is the Azure Instance Metadata Service endpoint, not the probe source. The frontend IP address is never the probe source. Dropdown 3 - 'AzureLoadBalancer': This service tag identifies 168.63.129.16 in network security groups and permits health probe traffic by default. VirtualNetwork covers virtual network address space and peered/on-premises ranges, not the probe source. AzurePlatformDNS is used to control Azure-provided DNS traffic. Dropdown 4 - '200': An HTTP/HTTPS probe is marked up only when the instance responds with HTTP status 200 within the timeout period; any other code (for example 403, 404, or 500) fails the probe, so the 2xx/3xx range and '200 or 404' are incorrect.

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda:
Case study: Fabrikam operates a hub-and-spoke topology in the East US region. The hub virtual network contains three third-party firewall network virtual appliances (NVAs), each with a single network interface that has one IP configuration. Spoke virtual networks force-tunnel all traffic to the hub by using user-defined routes. Fabrikam must ensure that all TCP and UDP traffic on every port is distributed across the three NVAs, that an NVA that stops responding is automatically removed from rotation, and that ingress and egress traffic for a given flow traverses the same NVA instance.

Which configuration should Fabrikam deploy in the hub virtual network?
opzione_a: An internal Standard Load Balancer with an HA ports load-balancing rule and a health probe, referenced as the next hop of the spoke user-defined routes.
opzione_b: A public Standard Load Balancer with an HA ports load-balancing rule and a health probe, referenced as the next hop of the spoke user-defined routes.
opzione_c: An internal Standard Load Balancer with individual load-balancing rules for TCP ports 80 and 443 and Floating IP enabled, referenced as the next hop of the spoke user-defined routes.
opzione_d: The NVAs placed in the backend pools of both a public Standard Load Balancer and an internal Standard Load Balancer, with the internal load balancer referenced as the next hop of the spoke user-defined routes.
spiegazione: Correct (a): This is the documented NVA high availability pattern. An HA ports rule on an internal Standard Load Balancer balances all TCP and UDP flows on all ports, per-instance health probes provide fast failover by removing an unhealthy NVA from rotation, and in exactly this hub-and-spoke force-tunnel design an HA ports rule provides flow symmetry for ingress and egress traffic. Flow symmetry is supported here because each backend instance has one NIC with one IP configuration. Wrong (b): HA ports load-balancing rules are available only for an internal Standard Load Balancer and are not supported on a public load balancer, so this configuration cannot be created. Wrong (c): Rules for TCP 80 and 443 balance only those two ports and no UDP traffic, which fails the requirement to distribute all TCP and UDP traffic on every port. Wrong (d): Flow symmetry is not supported when NVAs are placed between a public and an internal load balancer, because two independent load balancer components make uncoordinated distribution decisions. Gateway Load Balancer would be the alternative for that topology.
tags: load balancer,ha ports,nva,flow symmetry,hub and spoke,internal load balancer,case study

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: Fabrikam must load balance every TCP and UDP flow on all ports to a set of network virtual appliances by using one load-balancing rule, and must later add more load-balancing rules that target the same backend IP configurations on the same frontend IP configuration. Select the correct value for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Load balancer type required: [Public Standard | Internal Standard | Internal Basic]
opzione_b: Protocol setting in the load-balancing rule: [TCP | UDP | All]
opzione_c: Frontend and backend port values: [0 | 80 | 65535]
opzione_d: Floating IP setting required on the rules: [Disabled | Enabled | Not applicable]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - 'Internal Standard': HA ports load-balancing rules are available only for an internal Standard Load Balancer. HA ports are not supported on public load balancers or on the Basic SKU. Dropdown 2 - 'All': An HA ports rule is configured with the protocol set to All so that the load balancer balances all TCP and UDP flows. Selecting TCP or UDP alone would restrict the rule to a single protocol. Dropdown 3 - '0': HA ports rules are configured by setting the frontend and backend ports to 0, which represents all ports. Port 80 would balance a single port, and 65535 is only the highest individual port number, not a wildcard. Dropdown 4 - 'Enabled': Combining an HA ports load-balancing rule with a non-HA ports load-balancing rule that points to the same backend IP configurations is not supported on a single frontend IP configuration unless both rules have Floating IP enabled. A non-floating HA ports configuration allows no other load-balancing rule on the load balancer resource, so 'Disabled' would block the additional rules.
tags: load balancer,ha ports,floating ip,internal load balancer,load balancing rule,hotspot

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: A public Standard Load Balancer has a NIC-based backend pool that contains 60 virtual machines. The load-balancing rule has default port allocation enabled (disableOutboundSnat is set to false) and no outbound rules are configured. Select the correct value for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Default SNAT ports allocated per virtual machine with one frontend public IP address: [1024 | 512 | 256]
opzione_b: Default SNAT ports allocated per virtual machine after a second frontend public IP address is added: [512 | 1024 | 2048]
opzione_c: Default SNAT ports allocated per virtual machine after a third frontend public IP address is added: [1024 | 1536 | 2048]
opzione_d: Ephemeral ports contributed by each frontend public IP address: [64000 | 65535 | 1024]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - '512': The default SNAT port preallocation table assigns ports based on backend pool size for a single frontend IP. A pool of 60 instances falls in the 51-100 range, which receives 512 ports. 1024 applies to pools of 1-50 instances and 256 applies to pools of 101-200 instances. Dropdown 2 - '1024': Each backend receives the number of ports defined by the table per frontend IP, so a second frontend IP adds another 512 ports for a total of 1024. Dropdown 3 - '1024': Default port allocation is capped at a maximum of 1024 ports per backend instance, computed as MIN(default ports based on pool size * number of frontend IPs, 1024). Adding a third frontend IP therefore does not increase the allocation beyond 1024. Dropdown 4 - '64000': When a public IP address is added as a frontend IP to a load balancer, 64,000 ports are eligible for SNAT. Although every IP address has 65,535 ports by definition, only 64,000 are usable ephemeral SNAT ports, and 1024 is the default per-instance allocation cap rather than a per-IP total.

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda:
An internal Standard Load Balancer named ilb1 has a frontend private IP address in subnet1 of a virtual network named vnet1. The backend pool of ilb1 is NIC-based and contains virtual machines in subnet2 of vnet1. No NAT gateway is deployed, and the backend virtual machines have no instance-level public IP addresses. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true.
1. A virtual machine in the backend pool of ilb1 can successfully initiate an outbound flow to the frontend IP address of ilb1.
2. An on-premises client connected through a site-to-site VPN can reach the frontend IP address of ilb1.
3. Adding a virtual machine to the backend pool of ilb1 gives that virtual machine outbound internet connectivity.
opzione_a: A virtual machine in the backend pool of ilb1 can successfully initiate an outbound flow to the frontend IP address of ilb1.
opzione_b: An on-premises client connected through a site-to-site VPN can reach the frontend IP address of ilb1.
opzione_c: Adding a virtual machine to the backend pool of ilb1 gives that virtual machine outbound internet connectivity.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: An outbound flow from a backend virtual machine to the frontend of an internal load balancer is a documented limitation and fails. This is the classic 'VM cannot reach its own load balancer frontend' behavior. Statement 2 - Yes: An internal load balancer distributes traffic to resources inside a virtual network and is explicitly documented for private network connectivity scenarios, such as accessing a load balancer frontend from an on-premises network in a hybrid deployment. The frontend is never exposed to an internet endpoint, but it is reachable over VPN or ExpressRoute. Statement 3 - No: Outbound connectivity is not available for an internal Standard Load Balancer until it is explicitly declared through instance-level public IP addresses, a NAT gateway on the backend subnet, or by associating the backend pool members with an outbound-only public load balancer configuration. Membership in an internal load balancer backend pool provides no outbound internet access.
tags: load balancer,internal load balancer,outbound connectivity,hybrid,backend pool

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: You enable Floating IP on a load-balancing rule of a Standard Load Balancer so that multiple application instances on a backend virtual machine can reuse the same backend port. Which additional configuration must you perform inside the guest operating system of each backend virtual machine?
opzione_a: Add a secondary IP configuration to the virtual machine network interface and assign the frontend IP address of the load balancer to it.
opzione_b: Add a loopback interface and configure it with the frontend IP address of the load balancer.
opzione_c: Assign an instance-level public IP address to each virtual machine network interface.
opzione_d: Change the default gateway of the virtual machine to the frontend IP address of the load balancer.
spiegazione: Correct (b): With Floating IP enabled, Azure preserves the load balancer frontend IP address as the destination in the packet instead of rewriting it to the VM IP address. For the VM to accept that traffic, the guest OS must add a loopback interface configured with the frontend IP address, and (on Windows) the interfaces must use the weak host model; the guest firewall must also allow the frontend port. Wrong (a): The frontend IP address is not added as a secondary IP configuration on the Azure NIC; Floating IP is configured in the load-balancing rule plus the guest OS loopback, and Floating IP is not supported on secondary IP configurations for load balancing scenarios. Wrong (c): An instance-level public IP provides outbound connectivity and direct inbound addressing; it has nothing to do with accepting frontend-addressed packets. Wrong (d): Changing the default gateway is not part of the Floating IP configuration and would break the VM's normal routing through the Azure fabric.
tags: load balancer,floating ip,direct server return,loopback,port reuse

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: A network team deploys a pair of third-party network virtual appliances (NVAs) in a hub virtual network. The team must use a single load-balancing rule to distribute all TCP and UDP flows arriving on every port to the NVAs. Which configuration meets the requirement?
opzione_a: An internal Standard Load Balancer with a load-balancing rule set to protocol All and port 0
opzione_b: A public Standard Load Balancer with a load-balancing rule set to protocol All and port 0
opzione_c: An internal Standard Load Balancer with a separate load-balancing rule for each port from 1 through 65535
opzione_d: An internal Basic Load Balancer with a load-balancing rule set to protocol All and port 0
spiegazione: Correct (a): A High Availability (HA) ports rule is created by setting the frontend and backend ports to 0 and the protocol to All. HA ports load-balancing rules are available only on an internal Standard Load Balancer, and they balance all TCP and UDP flows regardless of port number. This is the documented pattern for scaling and providing high availability to NVAs. Wrong (b): HA ports are not supported on a public load balancer; the feature is documented as available only for an internal Standard Load Balancer. Wrong (c): This does not use a single rule, and creating per-port rules is exactly the operational problem HA ports were designed to eliminate. Wrong (d): Basic Load Balancer does not support HA ports at all; the SKU comparison lists HA Ports as 'Not available' for Basic.
tags: load balancer,ha ports,internal load balancer,standard sku,nva

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: Contoso publishes a Remote Desktop Gateway (RD Gateway) farm behind a public Standard Load Balancer. Users cannot establish RD Gateway sessions reliably. You must configure the load-balancing rule to use the three-tuple distribution mode that Azure recommends to resolve the known incompatibility between Azure Load Balancer and RD Gateway. Which Session persistence value should you select in the Azure portal?
opzione_a: None
opzione_b: Client IP
opzione_c: Client IP and protocol
opzione_d: Client IP and port
spiegazione: Correct (c): 'Client IP and protocol' is the three-tuple distribution mode (source IP, destination IP, and protocol type). Microsoft documents that source IP affinity with client IP and protocol solves an incompatibility between Azure Load Balancer and RD Gateway. Wrong (a): 'None' is the default hash-based mode and uses the five-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol), which provides no session persistence across new sessions because the source port changes. Wrong (b): 'Client IP' is the two-tuple mode (source IP and destination IP), not the three-tuple mode named in the requirement. Wrong (d): 'Client IP and port' is not a valid session persistence option in Azure Load Balancer; the only options are None, Client IP, and Client IP and protocol.
tags: load balancer,session persistence,distribution mode,source ip affinity,rd gateway

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: A load-balancing rule on a Standard Load Balancer references a backend pool that contains three virtual machines. A configuration error causes the health probe to fail on all three virtual machines at the same time. What happens to the TCP connections that were already established through the load balancer?
opzione_a: The established TCP flows continue, but no new flows are sent to the backend pool.
opzione_b: All established TCP flows are immediately terminated with a TCP reset.
opzione_c: The established TCP flows continue only if TCP Reset on idle is disabled on the load-balancing rule.
opzione_d: The established TCP flows are redistributed to the next healthy backend pool referenced by the load balancer.
spiegazione: Correct (a): When all instances probe down, no new flows are sent to the backend pool, but Standard Load Balancer allows established TCP flows to continue, given that the backend pool has more than one backend instance. Wrong (b): Terminating all existing TCP flows when all probes are down is Basic Load Balancer behavior, and it is the classic misconception carried over to Standard. Wrong (c): TCP Reset on idle is a separate feature that controls whether a bidirectional TCP RST is sent when the idle timeout is reached; it does not govern probe-down behavior. Wrong (d): A load-balancing rule targets a single backend pool and there is no automatic failover to another pool; when all probes are down the load balancer simply stops sending new flows.
tags: load balancer,health probe,probe down behavior,standard sku,tcp flows

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: You are documenting the differences between the Azure Load Balancer SKUs for a migration plan. Which capabilities are available with a Standard Load Balancer but NOT with a Basic Load Balancer? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: HTTPS health probes
opzione_b: Outbound rules that declaratively define SNAT
opzione_c: Zone-redundant and zonal frontend IP configurations
opzione_d: Inbound NAT rules for port forwarding to a specific virtual machine
opzione_e: TCP health probes
spiegazione: Correct (a): The SKU comparison lists health probe protocols as TCP, HTTP, and HTTPS for Standard, but only TCP and HTTP for Basic. Correct (b): Outbound rules provide declarative outbound NAT configuration and are listed as 'Not available' for Basic. Correct (c): Availability zone support (zone-redundant or zonal frontend IP configurations for inbound and outbound traffic) is a Standard-only capability; Basic is documented as not compatible with availability zones. Wrong (d): Inbound NAT rules are a core load balancer component supported by both SKUs, so this is not a difference. Wrong (e): TCP health probes are supported by both SKUs; only HTTPS probes are exclusive to Standard.
tags: load balancer,sku comparison,standard sku,basic sku,availability zones,outbound rules

sotto_argomento: Configure private endpoints for PaaS
domanda: A platform team is standardizing DNS integration for private endpoints across five services in the Azure public cloud, and must create the matching Azure private DNS zone for each one. Arrange the private DNS zone names in the order that corresponds to the following list of private-link resources and subresources: (1) Azure Cosmos DB, Sql subresource; (2) Azure Storage, file subresource; (3) Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, dfs subresource; (4) Azure Container Registry, registry subresource; (5) Azure Cache for Redis, redisCache subresource.
opzione_a: privatelink.azurecr.io
opzione_b: privatelink.file.core.windows.net
opzione_c: privatelink.redis.cache.windows.net
opzione_d: privatelink.documents.azure.com
opzione_e: privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net
spiegazione: Correct order: d, b, e, a, c. Azure Cosmos DB with the Sql subresource uses privatelink.documents.azure.com (public forwarder documents.azure.com); the other Cosmos DB APIs use different zones, such as privatelink.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and privatelink.table.cosmos.azure.com. Azure Storage with the file subresource uses privatelink.file.core.windows.net. Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 with the dfs subresource uses privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net - note that Data Lake Storage Gen2 is a storage account resource type, so its zone follows the same core.windows.net pattern but with the dfs suffix rather than blob. Azure Container Registry uses privatelink.azurecr.io. Azure Cache for Redis uses privatelink.redis.cache.windows.net, which must not be confused with privatelink.redisenterprise.cache.azure.net used by Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise or privatelink.redis.azure.net used by Azure Managed Redis. Any other ordering maps a zone to the wrong private-link resource; because private endpoint DNS zone configurations generate automatically only when the recommended naming scheme is used, a mismatched zone silently breaks name resolution to the private endpoint.
tags: private endpoint,private dns zone,cosmos db,container registry,redis,data lake storage

sotto_argomento: Configure private endpoints for PaaS
domanda: You are creating private endpoints in the Azure public cloud for a storage account (blob subresource), an Azure SQL logical server (sqlServer subresource), and a key vault (vault subresource). For each private endpoint you must create the Azure private DNS zone that uses the recommended naming scheme so that the DNS zone configuration is generated automatically. Select the correct zone name for each resource.
opzione_a: Private DNS zone for the blob private endpoint: [privatelink.blob.core.windows.net | privatelink.storage.core.windows.net | blob.privatelink.core.windows.net]
opzione_b: Private DNS zone for the Azure SQL Database private endpoint: [privatelink.database.windows.net | privatelink.sql.azuresynapse.net | privatelink.sqlserver.azure.com]
opzione_c: Private DNS zone for the key vault private endpoint: [privatelink.vault.azure.net | privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net | privatelink.keyvault.core.windows.net]
spiegazione: Correct: privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, privatelink.database.windows.net, and privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net. These are the recommended private DNS zone names for the blob, sqlServer, and vault subresources in the Azure public cloud; private endpoint private DNS zone configurations only generate automatically when the recommended naming scheme is used. Why the other choices are wrong: privatelink.storage.core.windows.net and blob.privatelink.core.windows.net invert or invent the storage zone - the pattern is always privatelink prefixed to the public forwarder (blob.core.windows.net). privatelink.sql.azuresynapse.net belongs to Azure Synapse Analytics workspaces, and privatelink.sqlserver.azure.com does not exist. privatelink.vault.azure.net is the most common Key Vault error because vault.azure.net is the FQDN users type, but vault.azure.net and vaultcore.azure.net are the public forwarders while the zone itself is privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net; privatelink.keyvault.core.windows.net does not exist. Remember also that records for multiple services must not be placed in the same DNS zone - create a separate zone per private-link service type.
tags: private endpoint,private dns zone,storage,azure sql database,key vault

sotto_argomento: Configure private endpoints for PaaS
domanda:
VNet1 is deployed in the East US region and contains a subnet named Subnet1 that is associated with a network security group named NSG1. Subnet1 was created by using an ARM template and its network policy settings have not been modified. You create a private endpoint in Subnet1 that targets the blob subresource of a general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1, which is deployed in the West Europe region. An on-premises network is connected to VNet1 by a site-to-site VPN connection. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

1. The private endpoint in Subnet1 can connect to storage1 even though storage1 is in a different region than VNet1.
2. A server in the on-premises network can reach storage1 through the private endpoint if DNS resolution returns the private endpoint IP address.
3. By default, the security rules in NSG1 are applied to traffic that is destined for the private endpoint.
opzione_a: The private endpoint in Subnet1 can connect to storage1 even though storage1 is in a different region than VNet1.
opzione_b: A server in the on-premises network can reach storage1 through the private endpoint if DNS resolution returns the private endpoint IP address.
opzione_c: By default, the security rules in NSG1 are applied to traffic that is destined for the private endpoint.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. The private endpoint must be deployed in the same region and subscription as the virtual network, but the private-link resource can be deployed in a different region than the virtual network and private endpoint. A private endpoint in East US can therefore target a storage account in West Europe. Statement 2 - Yes. Private endpoints enable connectivity from on-premises environments that use VPN or ExpressRoute. The connection works provided name resolution returns the private endpoint IP address, which is why DNS forwarding from on-premises to the Azure private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net is the standard requirement in this design. Statement 3 - No. By default, network policies are disabled for a subnet in a virtual network, so NSG rules and user-defined routes are not applied to private endpoints in that subnet. The privateEndpointNetworkPolicies property must be set to Enabled or NetworkSecurityGroupEnabled for NSG1 to filter that traffic. Note that this setting affects only private endpoints - access for other resources in Subnet1 is still controlled by the NSG security rules.

sotto_argomento: Configure private endpoints for PaaS
domanda: Subnet2 in VNet1 contains a private endpoint for a storage account and is associated with a network security group named NSG2. You add a deny rule to NSG2 that blocks outbound traffic to the private endpoint IP address on port 443, but virtual machines in VNet1 continue to reach the storage account through the private endpoint. The private endpoint connection is in an Approved state. What should you do first so that NSG2 filters the traffic?
opzione_a: Enable network policies for private endpoints on Subnet2
opzione_b: Add an application security group to the private endpoint network interface
opzione_c: Disable public network access on the storage account
opzione_d: Create a user-defined route for 0.0.0.0/0 on Subnet2 that points to a network virtual appliance
spiegazione: Correct: enable network policies for private endpoints on Subnet2. By default, network policies are disabled for a subnet, which means network security group rules and user-defined routes are not applied to private endpoints in that subnet. To have NSG rules enforced against a private endpoint you must set privateEndpointNetworkPolicies to Enabled or NetworkSecurityGroupEnabled on the subnet; the setting applies to all private endpoints in the subnet. Why the others are wrong: adding an ASG does not help, because ASG support is itself gated behind the same network policies setting. Disabling public network access hardens the storage account's public endpoint but has no effect on traffic that already flows over the private endpoint, which is what you are trying to block. A 0.0.0.0/0 user-defined route cannot override a private endpoint route: the private endpoint propagates a /32 route and, by longest prefix match, the more specific route wins - the documentation explicitly states a 0.0.0.0/0 UDR won't override private endpoint routes.

sotto_argomento: Configure private endpoints for PaaS
domanda: Your team is documenting the design constraints that apply to Azure private endpoints before a large rollout. Which statements about private endpoints are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: The private endpoint must be deployed in the same region and subscription as the virtual network that hosts it.
opzione_b: The private-link resource can be deployed in a different region than the virtual network and private endpoint.
opzione_c: Clients in an on-premises network can reach the private endpoint over a VPN or ExpressRoute connection.
opzione_d: A single private endpoint on a storage account provides access to both the blob and file subresources.
opzione_e: Private endpoints can be created on general-purpose v1 storage accounts.
spiegazione: Correct: a, b, and c. The private endpoint must be deployed in the same region and subscription as the virtual network, while the private-link resource itself can live in a different region - this is what makes cross-region private connectivity possible. Private endpoints also enable connectivity from the same virtual network, regionally peered virtual networks, globally peered virtual networks, and on-premises environments that use VPN or ExpressRoute. Why the others are wrong: a private endpoint targets one subresource (groupId). For Azure Storage you need separate private endpoints to access the file and blob subresources, because the platform validates network connections and allows only those that reach the specified private-link resource. Private endpoints can be created only on a General Purpose v2 (GPv2) storage account, so general-purpose v1 is not supported.

sotto_argomento: Configure private endpoints for PaaS
domanda: You create a private endpoint that targets the sqlServer subresource of an Azure SQL logical server. To integrate the private endpoint with Azure DNS, you must create a private DNS zone that uses the recommended name for the Azure public cloud. Which zone name should you use?
opzione_a: privatelink.database.windows.net
opzione_b: privatelink.sql.azuresynapse.net
opzione_c: privatelink.sqlserver.database.azure.com
opzione_d: privatelink.database.azure.com
spiegazione: Correct: privatelink.database.windows.net. For a Microsoft.Sql/servers private endpoint using the sqlServer subresource in the Azure public cloud, the recommended private DNS zone is privatelink.database.windows.net, and the public DNS zone forwarder is database.windows.net. Why the others are wrong: privatelink.sql.azuresynapse.net is the correct zone for Azure Synapse Analytics workspaces (Sql and SqlOnDemand subresources), not for Azure SQL Database. privatelink.sqlserver.database.azure.com and privatelink.database.azure.com are invented names - .azure.com is used by services such as Azure Cosmos DB (privatelink.documents.azure.com), but Azure SQL Database uses the database.windows.net suffix. Note also that Azure SQL Managed Instance uses a different pattern: privatelink.{dnsPrefix}.database.windows.net.
tags: private endpoint,private dns zone,azure sql database,privatelink

sotto_argomento: Configure private endpoints for PaaS
domanda: A key vault named KV1 is accessed by applications that run on virtual machines in VNet1. You create a private endpoint for KV1 that targets the vault subresource, and you plan to create an Azure private DNS zone so that the existing connection strings continue to work. Which private DNS zone name must you create?
opzione_a: privatelink.vault.azure.net
opzione_b: privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net
opzione_c: privatelink.keyvault.azure.com
opzione_d: privatelink.vaults.core.windows.net
spiegazione: Correct: privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net. In the Azure public cloud, the recommended private DNS zone for a Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults private endpoint with the vault subresource is privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net; the public DNS zone forwarders are vault.azure.net and vaultcore.azure.net. Private endpoint DNS zone configurations only generate automatically when the recommended naming scheme is used. Why the others are wrong: privatelink.vault.azure.net looks correct because vault.azure.net is the FQDN suffix users type, but it is a public forwarder, not the privatelink zone name - this is the classic Key Vault mistake. privatelink.keyvault.azure.com and privatelink.vaults.core.windows.net do not exist; the latter borrows the core.windows.net suffix used by Azure Storage.

sotto_argomento: Configure public IP addresses
domanda:
Fabrikam has a public IP address resource named pip-app1 that uses the Basic SKU with dynamic IPv4 allocation. pip-app1 is associated with the network interface of a virtual machine named vm-app1. Evaluate each of the following statements. Select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
1. If vm-app1 is stopped (deallocated) from the Azure portal and then started again, the IP address of pip-app1 can change.
2. pip-app1 can be associated with the front-end configuration of a Standard SKU public load balancer.
3. pip-app1 can be configured as zone-redundant without changing its SKU.
opzione_a: If vm-app1 is stopped (deallocated) from the Azure portal and then started again, the IP address of pip-app1 can change.
opzione_b: pip-app1 can be associated with the front-end configuration of a Standard SKU public load balancer.
opzione_c: pip-app1 can be configured as zone-redundant without changing its SKU.
spiegazione:
Statement 1 - Yes. Learn states that dynamic addresses 'can change if a resource such as a virtual machine is stopped (deallocated) and then restarted through Azure', and that 'Any associated IP address is released if the allocation method is dynamic.' The important contrast, and the reason this statement is worded carefully, is that the address remains the same if the virtual machine is merely rebooted or shut down from within the guest operating system, because the VM isn't deallocated in that case. To guarantee the address never changes, the allocation method must be static.

Statement 2 - No. Learn states that matching SKUs are required for load balancer and public IP resources: 'You can't have a mixture of basic SKU resources and standard SKU resources.' The Basic-versus-Standard table also lists Standard Load Balancer Support as 'Not supported' for the Basic SKU. A Basic public IP can only front a Basic load balancer.

Statement 3 - No. Availability zones are 'Not supported' for the Basic SKU. Learn states that 'Basic SKU Public IPs don't have any zones and are created as non-zonal', and that once created, a public IP address can't change its availability zone. Zone redundancy would require the Standard SKU, which contradicts the 'without changing its SKU' condition.
tags: public ip,basic sku,dynamic allocation,load balancer,availability zones,sku matching

sotto_argomento: Configure public IP addresses
domanda: While creating a public IP address resource in the Azure portal, an administrator selects the Standard SKU and notices that the Dynamic option for IP address assignment is unavailable. What is the reason?
opzione_a: Standard SKU public IP addresses support the static assignment method only.
opzione_b: Dynamic allocation becomes available only after the public IP address is associated with a resource.
opzione_c: Dynamic allocation requires the Global tier to be selected.
opzione_d: Dynamic allocation is unavailable because a zone-redundant public IP address was selected.
spiegazione:
Correct: Standard SKU public IP addresses support the static assignment method only. The SKU comparison table on Microsoft Learn lists the allocation method for the Standard SKU as 'Static', for both IPv4 and IPv6. Only the Basic SKU offers a choice (Basic IPv4 can be dynamic or static; Basic IPv6 is dynamic only). Learn states explicitly that dynamic IP allocation isn't supported for Standard SKU public IP addresses and there is no replacement for it besides static allocation.

Why the others are wrong:
Dynamic becomes available after association - This confuses allocation method with allocation timing. For a Basic dynamic IP, the address value is assigned when the resource is associated and started, but the choice of method is still made at creation and is never offered for Standard.
Global tier - The Tier property (Regional versus Global) controls whether the address is anycast from multiple regions for use with cross-region load balancers. It does not gate the allocation method, and Global tier addresses are still static.
Zone-redundant selection - Availability zone configuration is independent of the allocation method. A Standard public IP is static whether it is non-zonal, zonal, or zone-redundant.
tags: public ip,standard sku,static allocation,dynamic allocation,ip services

sotto_argomento: Configure public IP addresses
domanda: An administrator must upgrade an existing Basic SKU public IP address to the Standard SKU in place, so that the IP address value is preserved. Which prerequisites must be met before the upgrade can be performed? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: The public IP address must use the static assignment method.
opzione_b: The public IP address must not be associated with any resource.
opzione_c: The public IP address must have a DNS name label configured.
opzione_d: The public IP address must first be moved to a region that supports availability zones.
opzione_e: The public IP address must be assigned to a specific availability zone.
spiegazione:
Correct answers: a, b.
a - Learn's prerequisites for the upgrade require 'A static basic SKU public IP address in your subscription', and notes: 'The basic public IP you're upgrading must have static assignment. You receive a warning that the IP can't be upgraded if you try to upgrade a dynamically allocated IP address. Change the IP address assignment to static before upgrading.'
b - Learn states: 'In order to upgrade a public IP, it must not be associated with any resource.' The article also confirms 'Upgrading a public IP resource retains the IP address', which is what satisfies the requirement in the scenario.

Why the others are wrong:
c - A DNS name label is an optional property of a public IP address, not a prerequisite for changing the SKU.
d - Public IP addresses can't be moved across regions at all. Learn's move table lists 'Move across regions: No - IP addresses are tied to regional ranges and cannot be moved.' Attempting this would also lose the address, defeating the requirement.
e - Basic SKU public IPs don't support availability zones and are created as non-zonal, so a zone assignment can't be a prerequisite. Zone behavior is a consequence of the upgrade, not a precondition for it.

sotto_argomento: Configure public IP addresses
domanda: A virtual machine named vm-web1 is deployed with a Standard SKU public IP address attached to its network interface. A web server is installed and listening on TCP port 443, and the guest operating system firewall allows the traffic. No network security group is associated with the network interface or with the subnet. Connections from the internet to the public IP address time out. What is the most likely cause?
opzione_a: Standard SKU public IP addresses use a secure-by-default model and are closed to inbound traffic until a network security group explicitly allows it.
opzione_b: The public IP address must be configured as zone-redundant before it accepts inbound traffic.
opzione_c: A Standard SKU public IP address can only be associated with a load balancer front end, not with a virtual machine network interface.
opzione_d: The IP address assignment must be changed from Dynamic to Static.
spiegazione:
Correct: Secure by default. Learn states that Standard SKU public IPs use a 'Secure by default model and be closed to inbound traffic when used as a frontend. Allow traffic with network security group (NSG) is required (for example, on the NIC of a virtual machine with a Standard SKU Public IP attached).' The create-a-public-IP article repeats it: 'Communication with the resource fails until you create and associate a network security group and explicitly allow the desired traffic.' This is the single most common surprise when moving from Basic (open by default) to Standard.

Why the others are wrong:
Zone redundancy - Availability zone configuration affects resiliency to a zone failure, not the data-plane filtering of inbound traffic. A non-zonal Standard IP with a correct NSG works fine.
Standard IPs only for load balancer front ends - False. Learn lists virtual machine network interfaces first among the resources that can be associated with a public IP, and Standard is the recommended SKU for VMs.
Change Dynamic to Static - Impossible and irrelevant. Standard SKU public IP addresses are always static; dynamic allocation isn't supported for them, so this configuration can't be the cause.
tags: public ip,standard sku,secure by default,network security group,troubleshooting

sotto_argomento: Configure public IP addresses
domanda: An organization still runs several Basic SKU public IP addresses in production and asks you to explain their current support status. Which statement is correct?
opzione_a: Basic SKU public IP addresses were retired on September 30, 2025. They remain operational, but they're unsupported and aren't covered by SLA guarantees.
opzione_b: Basic SKU public IP addresses were automatically converted to the Standard SKU on the retirement date, at no cost and with no downtime.
opzione_c: Basic SKU public IP addresses stopped passing traffic on the retirement date, so every affected workload must be redeployed with a new address.
opzione_d: Basic SKU public IP addresses are still fully supported. Only Basic SKU load balancers were retired.
spiegazione:
Correct: Retired on September 30, 2025, still operational but unsupported and outside the SLA. The Learn upgrade guidance FAQ answers this directly: 'Basic public IPs will remain operational after September 30, 2025, giving users more time to transition to Standard SKU. Customers who choose to continue using Basic public IPs after retirement date accept the risks and acknowledge that the service is unsupported and not covered by SLA guarantees.'

Why the others are wrong:
Automatic conversion - Azure does not convert Basic public IPs for you. Upgrading is a customer-driven action: the address must be static and disassociated, and Microsoft publishes scripts and portal, PowerShell, and CLI procedures precisely because the work is manual.
Traffic stopped on the retirement date - Retirement means end of support, not an immediate service shutdown. The documentation states the addresses remain operational.
Still fully supported / only Basic load balancer retired - Basic SKU load balancers are also on a retirement path, but the Basic SKU public IP retirement is real and separate, and is announced at the top of every relevant public IP article.

sotto_argomento: Configure public IP addresses
domanda: Which statements about Standard SKU public IP addresses in Azure are correct? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: They always use the static assignment method.
opzione_b: They can be created as zonal or zone-redundant in regions that support availability zones.
opzione_c: They're open to inbound traffic by default, and a network security group is optional.
opzione_d: They're required in order to associate a public IP address with an Azure NAT gateway.
opzione_e: Their SKU can be downgraded to Basic at any time after creation.
spiegazione:
Correct answers: a, b, d.
a - The SKU table lists the allocation method for Standard as 'Static'. Dynamic allocation isn't supported for Standard SKU public IP addresses.
b - Learn states that Standard IPs can be non-zonal, zonal, or zone-redundant, and that zone-redundant IPs can only be created in regions where three availability zones are live.
d - The Basic-versus-Standard comparison table lists NAT Gateway Support as 'IPv4 is supported' for Standard and 'Not supported' for Basic. The at-a-glance table also confirms a NAT gateway requires a static IPv4 address.

Why the others are wrong:
c - This describes the Basic SKU, which Learn documents as 'Open by default. Network security groups are recommended but optional.' Standard is the opposite: secure by default and closed to inbound traffic until an NSG allows it.
e - There is no downgrade path. Learn states you can't change the SKU after the public IP address is created, and the only SKU change offered, the Basic-to-Standard upgrade, carries the warning 'Upgrading a basic public IP to standard SKU can't be reversed.'
tags: public ip,standard sku,basic sku,availability zones,nat gateway,sku comparison

sotto_argomento: Configure public IP addresses
domanda: Contoso must deploy an Azure NAT gateway in a region that has three live availability zones. The public IP address resource that the NAT gateway uses must continue to work if a single availability zone fails. Select the correct configuration for the public IP address resource.
opzione_a: SKU: [Basic | Standard]
opzione_b: IP address assignment: [Dynamic | Static]
opzione_c: Availability zone: [None | Zone 1 | Zone-redundant]
spiegazione:
Correct selections: Standard, Static, Zone-redundant.
SKU: Standard. The SKU comparison table lists NAT Gateway Support as 'IPv4 is supported' for Standard and 'Not supported' for Basic, so Basic can't be used here. Basic also doesn't support availability zones at all, which independently rules it out given the resiliency requirement.
IP address assignment: Static. Learn's at-a-glance table shows a NAT gateway supports Static IPv4 only ('Dynamic IPv4: No'). This is also forced by the SKU: Standard public IP addresses support the static method only, so Dynamic isn't selectable.
Availability zone: Zone-redundant. Learn defines the values: 'A zone-redundant IP is created in multiple zones for a given region and can survive any single zone failure', which is exactly the stated requirement. Zone 1 is zonal - it 'is tied to a specific availability zone, and shares fate with the health of the zone', so it fails the requirement. None (non-zonal) is 'Only valid in regions that do not support availability zones', which doesn't apply to this region.
tags: public ip,standard sku,zone-redundant,availability zones,nat gateway,static allocation

sotto_argomento: Configure service endpoints for PaaS
domanda: Litware secures a general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1 by setting Public network access to Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses, and by adding a virtual network rule for Subnet1 in VNet1. Both VNet1 and storage1 are in the East US region. An on-premises datacenter connects to Azure by using ExpressRoute with Microsoft peering. Select the appropriate options based on this configuration.
opzione_a: Source IP address that storage1 records for requests from a VM in Subnet1 after the service endpoint is enabled: [The public IPv4 address of the VM | The private IPv4 address of the VM | The public IPv4 address of the virtual network gateway]
opzione_b: Result of resolving storage1.blob.core.windows.net from the VM in Subnet1: [Resolves to a private IP address | Resolves to the public IP address of storage1 | Resolution fails]
opzione_c: Service endpoint resource that must be enabled on Subnet1 if storage1 is later moved to the West US region: [Microsoft.Storage | Microsoft.Storage.Global | Microsoft.Network]
opzione_d: Requirement to allow access to storage1 from the on-premises datacenter: [The existing virtual network rule is sufficient | An IP network rule that allows the ExpressRoute NAT IP addresses | A service endpoint enabled on the on-premises network]
risposta_corretta: The private IPv4 address of the VM,Resolves to the public IP address of storage1,Microsoft.Storage.Global,An IP network rule that allows the ExpressRoute NAT IP addresses
spiegazione: Correct answers explained. Source IP: with service endpoints, service traffic switches from using public IPv4 addresses to using virtual network private addresses as the source IP, which is why any existing storage firewall IP rules based on Azure public IPs stop working after the switch. DNS: DNS entries for Azure services remain as-is and continue to resolve to the public IP addresses assigned to the service - service endpoints change routing, not name resolution. Cross-region: Microsoft.Storage provides connectivity only to storage accounts in the same region as the virtual network, so a move to West US requires the cross-region endpoint Microsoft.Storage.Global, which provides connectivity to storage accounts in any region; only one of the two endpoint types can be associated with a subnet at a time. On-premises: endpoints can't be used for traffic from on-premises services to Azure services. By default, Azure service resources secured to virtual networks aren't reachable from on-premises networks - you must identify the NAT IP addresses used for ExpressRoute Microsoft peering and allow those public IP addresses through an IP network rule in the storage firewall. Why the other choices are wrong: the public IPv4 address of the VM is what storage1 would see without a service endpoint; the gateway public IP is unrelated to intra-VNet service traffic. A private IP resolution result would require a private endpoint, and resolution never fails because the public DNS record is unchanged. Microsoft.Network is not a service endpoint resource. The existing virtual network rule does not cover on-premises traffic, and service endpoints cannot be enabled outside an Azure virtual network.

sotto_argomento: Configure service endpoints for PaaS
domanda: VNet1 is deployed in the West Europe region and contains a subnet named Subnet1. A general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1 is deployed in the East US region. You must restrict storage1 so that it accepts traffic only from Subnet1, and you must use a virtual network rule rather than a private endpoint. Which service endpoint must you enable on Subnet1?
opzione_a: Microsoft.Storage
opzione_b: Microsoft.Storage.Global
opzione_c: Microsoft.Network
opzione_d: Microsoft.AzureActiveDirectory
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft.Storage.Global. The Azure Storage cross-region service endpoint (Microsoft.Storage.Global) provides connectivity to storage accounts in any region, which is exactly what is needed when the virtual network is in West Europe and the storage account is in East US. Why the others are wrong: Microsoft.Storage is the regional Azure Storage endpoint and provides connectivity only to storage accounts in the same region as the virtual network, so it cannot be used to reach an East US account from a West Europe VNet. Note also that only one of these two endpoint types can be associated with a subnet at a time - if one is already present you must delete it before adding the other. Microsoft.Network is not a service endpoint resource. Microsoft.AzureActiveDirectory is listed under services supporting service endpoints but is used only to support Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 virtual network integration; Microsoft Entra ID does not natively support service endpoints.

sotto_argomento: Configure service endpoints for PaaS
domanda: Subnet1 in VNet1 hosts several virtual machines that write to a storage account named storage1. You enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on Subnet1 and add a virtual network rule for Subnet1 to the storage1 firewall. From a virtual machine in Subnet1, an administrator runs nslookup against storage1.blob.core.windows.net. What will the name resolution return?
opzione_a: A private IP address from the Subnet1 address range
opzione_b: The public IP address assigned to the storage account
opzione_c: A CNAME to privatelink.blob.core.windows.net that resolves to a private IP address
opzione_d: NXDOMAIN, because public name resolution is removed when a service endpoint is enabled
spiegazione: Correct: the public IP address of the storage account. With service endpoints, DNS entries for Azure services remain as-is and continue to resolve to the public IP addresses assigned to the Azure service. A service endpoint changes routing and the source IP address of the traffic (traffic takes an optimal route over the Azure backbone and the source switches from the VM public IPv4 address to its private IPv4 address), but it never changes DNS. Why the others are wrong: resolving to a private IP address in the subnet is what a private endpoint does, not a service endpoint - a private endpoint injects a NIC with a private IP into your subnet. The privatelink CNAME chain is also created only by Private Link; no privatelink zone is involved with service endpoints. Name resolution does not fail: the public DNS record is untouched, and the storage firewall - not DNS - is what blocks unauthorized callers.

sotto_argomento: Configure user-defined network routes
domanda: Case study: Contoso Ltd. runs a hub-and-spoke topology in the East US region. Hub-VNet uses the address space 10.0.0.0/16 and contains a subnet named Subnet-NVA that hosts a third-party firewall appliance whose network interface has the private IP address 10.0.4.4 and has IP forwarding enabled. Spoke1 uses 10.1.0.0/16 and Spoke2 uses 10.2.0.0/16. Each spoke is peered with Hub-VNet only, and all peerings use the default settings and show a status of Connected. There is no peering between Spoke1 and Spoke2. A security policy states that all traffic between the spokes must be inspected by the firewall appliance in Hub-VNet. Currently, a virtual machine in Spoke1 cannot reach a virtual machine in Spoke2. You must enable spoke-to-spoke communication while complying with the security policy. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create a direct virtual network peering between Spoke1 and Spoke2.
opzione_b: In Spoke1 and Spoke2, associate a route table with the workload subnets that contains a route for the other spoke's address space with a next hop type of Virtual appliance and a next hop IP address of 10.0.4.4, and enable Allow forwarded traffic on the Hub-VNet peerings.
opzione_c: On the Hub-VNet peerings, enable Allow gateway transit, and on the Spoke1 and Spoke2 peerings, enable Use remote gateways.
opzione_d: In Hub-VNet, associate a route table with Subnet-NVA that contains a route for 0.0.0.0/0 with a next hop type of Internet.
spiegazione: Correct (b): Peering is not transitive, so Spoke1 and Spoke2 have no connectivity through Hub-VNet by default. The documented solution is service chaining: configure user-defined routes in the spokes that point to the NVA in the peered hub as the next hop IP address, and enable Allow forwarded traffic on the hub peerings so Hub-VNet accepts traffic that did not originate in the peered virtual network. Microsoft's hub-and-spoke troubleshooting guidance states exactly this: configure UDRs in spokes that have an NVA set as the next hop, and enable Allow forwarded traffic in the hub virtual network. Wrong (a): A direct peering between Spoke1 and Spoke2 would restore connectivity, but traffic would flow directly over the peering across the Microsoft backbone and completely bypass the firewall appliance, violating the requirement that all inter-spoke traffic be inspected. Wrong (c): Allow gateway transit and Use remote gateways are used to share a VPN gateway, ExpressRoute gateway, or Route Server in a peered virtual network for cross-premises connectivity. Hub-VNet contains no gateway, so Allow gateway transit cannot even be enabled, and these settings do not create spoke-to-spoke routing through an NVA. Wrong (d): Adding a 0.0.0.0/0 route with a next hop type of Internet to the NVA's own subnet does not create any path from Spoke1 to Spoke2. Microsoft also warns against applying a route table that routes traffic through a virtual appliance to the same subnet that hosts the appliance, because it can cause routing loops.

sotto_argomento: Configure user-defined network routes
domanda: To force all internet-bound traffic through a firewall appliance, you deploy a network virtual appliance named NVA1 into a dedicated subnet. NVA1 has a network interface with the private IP address 10.0.4.4. You create a route table, add a route with the address prefix 0.0.0.0/0 and a next hop type of Virtual appliance with the next hop IP address 10.0.4.4, and associate the route table with the subnet that hosts your application servers.
