The effective routes on the application servers show the route as Active, but all outbound internet traffic from the application servers is now dropped. The firewall software on NVA1 is running and configured to permit the traffic. What is the most likely cause?
opzione_a: IP forwarding is not enabled on the network interface attached to NVA1.
opzione_b: Allow forwarded traffic is not enabled on the virtual network peering.
opzione_c: Virtual network gateway route propagation is not disabled on the route table.
opzione_d: The route table is not associated with the subnet that hosts NVA1.
spiegazione: Correct (a): Any network interface attached to a virtual machine that forwards network traffic to an address other than its own must have the Azure Enable IP forwarding option enabled. This setting disables Azure's source and destination check for the interface. If custom routes direct traffic to an NVA with a Virtual appliance next hop type and IP forwarding is not enabled, packets are dropped, which precisely matches the symptom. (IP forwarding must typically also be enabled inside the appliance's operating system.) Wrong (b): Allow forwarded traffic is a peering property that lets a virtual network accept traffic that did not originate in the peered virtual network. The traffic here is internet-bound from a subnet in the same virtual network as the NVA, so no peering is involved. Wrong (c): Disabling virtual network gateway route propagation prevents BGP and gateway routes from being added to a subnet's route table. It is not required for an NVA to forward traffic, and leaving propagation enabled does not cause packets to be dropped at the NVA. Wrong (d): The route table must be associated with the subnet whose traffic you want to redirect, which has been done. In fact, Microsoft recommends deploying the NVA in a different subnet than the resources that route through it, because applying such a route table to the NVA's own subnet can cause routing loops.

sotto_argomento: Configure user-defined network routes
domanda: VNet1 uses the address space 10.0.0.0/16 and is peered with VNet2, which uses the address space 10.1.0.0/16. The peering status is Connected. A route table named RT1 is associated with Subnet1 in VNet1. RT1 contains two user-defined routes: one for the address prefix 10.1.0.0/16 with a next hop type of Virtual appliance and a next hop IP address of 10.0.100.4, and one for the address prefix 10.1.5.0/24 with a next hop type of None. Select the correct outcome for each of the following.
opzione_a: Traffic sent from Subnet1 to 10.1.5.10 is: [Sent to the virtual appliance at 10.0.100.4 | Sent directly to VNet2 over the peering | Dropped]
opzione_b: Traffic sent from Subnet1 to 10.1.20.10 is: [Sent to the virtual appliance at 10.0.100.4 | Sent directly to VNet2 over the peering | Dropped]
opzione_c: In the effective routes for a network interface in Subnet1, the state of the system route for 10.1.0.0/16 with a next hop type of Virtual network peering is: [Active | Invalid | Unknown]
risposta_corretta: Dropped,Sent to the virtual appliance at 10.0.100.4,Invalid
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - Dropped: Azure selects a route by using longest prefix match. The address 10.1.5.10 matches both 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.1.5.0/24, and /24 is the longer prefix, so the route with the None next hop type wins. Traffic routed to the None next hop type is dropped rather than routed outside the subnet. It is therefore not sent to the appliance and not sent over the peering. Dropdown 2 - Sent to the virtual appliance at 10.0.100.4: The address 10.1.20.10 is not within 10.1.5.0/24, so the longest matching prefix is 10.1.0.0/16. Two routes share that prefix: the automatically created peering system route and the UDR. When multiple routes contain the same address prefix, user-defined routes take priority over BGP routes and system routes, so traffic goes to the virtual appliance rather than directly over the peering. It is not dropped, because no matching route specifies None. Dropdown 3 - Invalid: When a UDR overrides a default or system route that has the same prefix, Azure automatically changes that system route's state from Active to Invalid in the effective routes for the subnets to which the route table is associated. Active would apply only to subnets that RT1 is not associated with, and Unknown is not a state Azure reports for effective routes.

sotto_argomento: Configure user-defined network routes
domanda: You are adding routes to a route table in an Azure virtual network. Which values can you specify as the next hop type when you create a user-defined route? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Virtual appliance
opzione_b: Virtual network peering
opzione_c: Internet
opzione_d: VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint
opzione_e: None
spiegazione: Correct (a): Virtual appliance is a valid UDR next hop type. When you use it, you also specify a next hop IP address, which can be the private IP address of a network interface attached to a VM (with IP forwarding enabled) or the private IP address of an Azure internal load balancer. Correct (c): Internet is a valid UDR next hop type. You specify it to explicitly route traffic for an address prefix to the internet, or to keep traffic destined for Azure services with public IP addresses on the Azure backbone. Correct (e): None is a valid UDR next hop type. Traffic routed to the None next hop type is dropped rather than routed outside the subnet. Wrong (b): You cannot specify Virtual network peering as the next hop type in a UDR. Azure creates routes with this next hop type automatically, and only when you configure a virtual network peering. Wrong (d): You cannot specify VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint as the next hop type in a UDR. Azure creates these routes automatically only when you enable a service endpoint on a subnet, and such routes cannot be overridden even by using a route table. Note that the other two valid UDR next hop types not listed here are Virtual network gateway and Virtual network.

sotto_argomento: Configure user-defined network routes
domanda: A subnet in an Azure virtual network has three routes that all specify the identical address prefix 172.16.0.0/16: a system route, a route learned over BGP from an on-premises network through a VPN gateway, and a user-defined route in a route table associated with the subnet. Which route does Azure use to forward traffic destined for 172.16.5.10?
opzione_a: The system route, because system routes cannot be overridden.
opzione_b: The user-defined route, because user-defined routes have the highest priority.
opzione_c: The BGP route, because dynamically learned routes are preferred over static routes.
opzione_d: Azure load balances the traffic across all three routes because the prefixes are identical.
spiegazione: Correct (b): Azure first selects routes by using the longest prefix match. When multiple routes contain the same address prefix, Azure selects the route based on this priority order: 1) user-defined route, 2) BGP route, 3) system route. Because all three routes here share the exact same 172.16.0.0/16 prefix, the user-defined route wins. Wrong (a): System routes have the lowest priority of the three and can be overridden by custom routes. Azure marks the overridden default route as Invalid in the effective routes of the subnet. (The narrow exception is that routes with a VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint next hop type cannot be overridden, which does not apply to a 172.16.0.0/16 prefix.) Wrong (c): The priority order is the opposite of what this option states. UDRs override BGP routes when the prefix is identical; BGP routes only beat system routes. Wrong (d): Azure does not perform equal-cost load balancing across routes in a route table. It deterministically selects a single route using longest prefix match and then the documented priority order.

sotto_argomento: Configure user-defined network routes
domanda:
A virtual network named VNet-Core contains three subnets named Subnet1, Subnet2, and Subnet3. You create a route table named RT-Core that contains a user-defined route with the address prefix 0.0.0.0/0 and a next hop type of Virtual appliance. You associate RT-Core with Subnet1. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
1. RT-Core can also be associated with Subnet2 and Subnet3 at the same time.
2. You can associate a second route table with Subnet1 at the same time to add more routes to that subnet.
3. Associating RT-Core with Subnet1 causes the default system routes for 10.0.0.0/8 and 192.168.0.0/16 that have a next hop type of None to be removed from Subnet1's route table.
opzione_a: RT-Core can also be associated with Subnet2 and Subnet3 at the same time.
opzione_b: You can associate a second route table with Subnet1 at the same time to add more routes to that subnet.
opzione_c: Associating RT-Core with Subnet1 causes the default system routes for 10.0.0.0/8 and 192.168.0.0/16 that have a next hop type of None to be removed from Subnet1's route table.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: In Azure you create a route table and then associate it to zero or more virtual network subnets. A single route table can be reused across multiple subnets, which is a common pattern for applying identical routing to several spoke subnets. Statement 2 - No: Each subnet can have zero or one route table associated to it. To add more routes to Subnet1, you add them to RT-Core rather than associating a second route table. By default a route table can contain up to 400 user-defined routes. Statement 3 - Yes: Microsoft's documented routing example states that Azure removed the routes for the 10.0.0.0/8, 192.168.0.0/16, and 100.64.0.0/10 address prefixes from the subnet's route table when the UDR for the 0.0.0.0/0 address prefix was added to that subnet. Once a 0.0.0.0/0 UDR sends everything to the appliance, those RFC 1918 and RFC 6598 drop routes no longer apply to the subnet.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: Case study: Contoso runs a line-of-business application in a virtual network named VNet1. A single subnet named Subnet-App hosts both the web servers and the application servers of the workload, and a network security group named nsg-app is associated with Subnet-App. The web servers must accept inbound TCP port 443 from the internet. The application servers, which are in the same subnet, must never accept inbound traffic from the internet. Contoso frequently scales the web tier in and out, so the private IP addresses of the web servers change often. The security team requires that no network security group be associated with individual network interfaces, and that the number of security rules be kept to a minimum. You need to allow inbound HTTPS to the web servers only. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create an application security group named asg-web, add the network interfaces of the web servers to it, and add a rule to nsg-app that allows TCP 443 with the source set to the Internet service tag and the destination set to asg-web
opzione_b: Associate a second network security group with the network interfaces of the application servers, and add a rule to it that denies TCP 443 from the Internet service tag
opzione_c: Add a rule to nsg-app that allows TCP 443 with the source set to the Internet service tag and the destination set to the VirtualNetwork service tag
opzione_d: Move the web servers to a dedicated subnet and create a route table that sends inbound internet traffic for the application servers to None
spiegazione: Correct: An application security group lets you group network interfaces by role and use the group as the destination of a security rule, so the policy follows the VMs as the web tier scales and IP addresses change. Only network interfaces that are members of asg-web apply the rule; the application server NICs are unaffected and remain protected by the DenyAllInBound default rule. This satisfies every requirement: no NIC-level NSG, minimal rules, and no IP maintenance. Wrong: Associating an NSG with the application server NICs violates the stated requirement that no NSG be associated with individual network interfaces, and it adds ongoing administrative overhead. Setting the destination to the VirtualNetwork service tag would allow TCP 443 from the internet to every resource in the virtual network address space, including the application servers, which breaks the security requirement. A route table controls where packets are forwarded, not whether they are permitted; user-defined routes cannot filter inbound internet traffic in place of a security rule, and moving the web servers is unnecessary work.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: A network security group named nsg-web is associated with the subnet named Subnet-Web in VNet1. nsg-web contains one custom inbound rule: priority 100, Allow, TCP, source Internet, destination the application security group asg-web, destination port 80. No other custom rules exist. VM1 and VM2 both reside in Subnet-Web, and neither of their network interfaces has a network security group associated with it. The network interface of VM1 is a member of asg-web. The network interface of VM2 is not a member of any application security group. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true. 1) Inbound HTTP traffic from the internet reaches VM1. 2) Inbound HTTP traffic from the internet reaches VM2. 3) VM1 can connect to VM2 over TCP port 80 across the virtual network.
opzione_a: Inbound HTTP traffic from the internet reaches VM1.
opzione_b: Inbound HTTP traffic from the internet reaches VM2.
opzione_c: VM1 can connect to VM2 over TCP port 80 across the virtual network.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: VM1's network interface is a member of asg-web, so the rule at priority 100 that specifies asg-web as the destination applies to it, and inbound TCP 80 from the internet is allowed. Statement 2 - No: Network interfaces that are members of an application security group apply the rules that specify that group as the source or destination; the rule does not affect other network interfaces. Because VM2's NIC is not a member of asg-web, the rule at priority 100 does not match, and the DenyAllInBound default rule at priority 65500 drops the traffic, even though nsg-web is associated with the whole subnet. Statement 3 - Yes: For this intra-virtual-network flow the rule at priority 100 does not match, because its source is the Internet service tag and its destination is asg-web. The next matching rule is the AllowVNetInBound default rule at priority 65000, which allows communication between resources in the virtual network, so VM1 can reach VM2 on TCP 80.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: You create a new network security group named nsg-app. You have not added any custom security rules to it. You review the default security rules that Azure created in the network security group. Select the correct value for each item.
opzione_a: Priority of AllowVNetInBound: [100 | 65000 | 65500]
opzione_b: Priority of AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound: [65000 | 65001 | 65500]
opzione_c: Action of DenyAllOutBound: [Allow | Deny]
opzione_d: Priority of AllowInternetOutBound: [4096 | 65001 | 65500]
spiegazione: Correct: AllowVNetInBound has priority 65000 and allows traffic from the VirtualNetwork tag to the VirtualNetwork tag. AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound has priority 65001 and allows traffic from the AzureLoadBalancer tag to 0.0.0.0/0, which is how Azure load balancer health probes reach the VM. DenyAllOutBound has priority 65500 and its action is Deny; it is the last outbound default rule and drops anything not allowed earlier. AllowInternetOutBound has priority 65001 and allows outbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet tag, which is why VMs have outbound internet access by default. Wrong: 100 is the lowest priority number available for CUSTOM rules, not a default rule. 65500 belongs to the DenyAll rules in both directions, not to the Allow defaults. 4096 is the highest priority number for a custom rule and is never used by a default rule. An Allow action for DenyAllOutBound would contradict the rule's purpose and its name.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: A virtual machine resides in a subnet that has a network security group associated with it, and the virtual machine's network interface also has a network security group associated with it. You are documenting how Azure filters traffic for this virtual machine. Select the correct value for each item.
opzione_a: For inbound traffic to the virtual machine, Azure first evaluates: [the NSG associated with the subnet | the NSG associated with the network interface | the NSG that contains the rule with the lowest priority number]
opzione_b: For outbound traffic from the virtual machine, Azure first evaluates: [the NSG associated with the subnet | the NSG associated with the network interface | both NSGs simultaneously]
opzione_c: Maximum number of network security groups that can be associated with a single subnet: [0 | 1 | 2]
opzione_d: When traffic matches a security rule, Azure: [stops processing further rules | continues evaluating all remaining rules | applies the most restrictive matching rule]
risposta_corretta: the NSG associated with the subnet,the NSG associated with the network interface,1,stops processing further rules
spiegazione: Correct: For inbound traffic Azure processes the subnet NSG first and then the NIC NSG; for outbound traffic the order is reversed, with the NIC NSG evaluated first and then the subnet NSG. Each subnet and each network interface can have zero or one NSG associated with it, so the maximum for a single subnet is 1 (the same NSG may be reused across many subnets and NICs). Once traffic matches a rule, processing stops, which means lower-priority rules with the same attributes are never processed. Wrong: Priority numbers are only compared within a single NSG; they never determine which NSG is evaluated first across the subnet/NIC boundary. The two NSGs are not evaluated simultaneously; the order is deterministic and direction-dependent. Continuing to evaluate all remaining rules, or picking the most restrictive match, describes other firewall products, not the first-match-wins model that Azure NSGs use.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: A cloud engineer is designing network segmentation for a multi-tier workload and plans to use application security groups (ASGs). Which statements about application security groups are correct? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A network interface can be a member of multiple application security groups, up to the Azure limits
opzione_b: An application security group can be specified as the source or the destination of a network security group rule
opzione_c: All network interfaces assigned to an application security group must exist in the same virtual network as the first network interface that was assigned to that group
opzione_d: An application security group can be associated directly with a subnet, replacing the need for a network security group
opzione_e: An application security group must be associated with a network security group before it can be referenced in a security rule
spiegazione: Correct: A network interface can belong to more than one application security group, up to the documented Azure limits. An ASG is a valid value for the Source and the Destination of a security rule, which lets you write rules against workload roles instead of IP addresses. All NICs assigned to an ASG must exist in the same virtual network as the first NIC assigned to it; you cannot add NICs from different virtual networks to the same ASG. Wrong: An ASG cannot be associated with a subnet. An ASG only groups network interfaces; the filtering is still performed by a network security group associated with a subnet or a NIC. There is no association between an ASG and an NSG: you simply select the existing ASG in the Source or Destination of a rule, and the rule then applies to the network interfaces that are members of that group.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: The network security group associated with a virtual machine's network interface contains an outbound rule that allows TCP port 443 to the Internet service tag. No custom inbound rules have been created in that NSG. The virtual machine initiates an HTTPS request to a public website. What must be configured so that the response traffic from the website reaches the virtual machine?
opzione_a: An inbound rule that allows TCP port 443 from the Internet service tag
opzione_b: An inbound rule that allows the ephemeral port range 1024-65535 from the Internet service tag
opzione_c: No additional rule is required, because a flow record makes the network security group stateful
opzione_d: An inbound rule that allows traffic from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag
spiegazione: Correct: A flow record is created for existing connections, and communication is allowed or denied based on the connection state of the flow record. This flow record is what makes an NSG stateful: if you allow outbound traffic on a port, you do not need a matching inbound rule for the response. An inbound rule is only needed when the communication is initiated externally. Wrong: An inbound rule allowing TCP 443 from Internet is unnecessary and would additionally expose the VM to externally initiated connections on that port. An inbound rule for the ephemeral port range is the classic stateless-firewall misconception; it is not needed and would be dangerously broad. AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound-style rules cover Azure health probe traffic, which is unrelated to the response of an outbound HTTPS session.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: Which statements accurately describe the default security rules that Azure creates in every network security group? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: AllowVNetInBound has priority 65000 and allows inbound traffic between resources that are covered by the VirtualNetwork service tag
opzione_b: Default security rules can be deleted from a network security group when they are not needed
opzione_c: AllowInternetOutBound has priority 65001 and allows outbound traffic to the Internet service tag
opzione_d: DenyAllInBound has priority 65500 and denies all inbound traffic that is not allowed by a higher-priority rule
opzione_e: Default security rules are processed before custom security rules within the same network security group
spiegazione: Correct: AllowVNetInBound (priority 65000) allows traffic from the VirtualNetwork tag to the VirtualNetwork tag on any protocol and port. AllowInternetOutBound (priority 65001) allows outbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet service tag. DenyAllInBound (priority 65500) denies traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 to 0.0.0.0/0, so anything not explicitly allowed by a lower-numbered rule is dropped. Wrong: Default rules cannot be removed; you can only override them by creating custom rules with a higher priority (a lower number). Default rules are NOT processed first: Azure deliberately assigns them the lowest priority (the highest numbers, 65000-65500) so that custom rules in the 100-4096 range are always processed before them.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: VM2 has a network interface associated with a network security group named nsg-nic, and the subnet that hosts VM2 is associated with a network security group named nsg-subnet. nsg-nic contains an outbound rule at priority 200 that denies TCP port 80 to the Internet service tag. nsg-subnet contains no custom outbound rules. VM2 attempts to open an outbound HTTP connection to a public website. Which statement describes the outcome?
opzione_a: The traffic is denied by nsg-nic, and nsg-subnet never receives the traffic to evaluate it
opzione_b: The traffic is evaluated by nsg-subnet first, and because AllowInternetOutBound permits it, the connection succeeds
opzione_c: Both nsg-nic and nsg-subnet must contain a deny rule for the outbound traffic to be blocked
opzione_d: Outbound rules in a network interface NSG are ignored; only the subnet NSG filters outbound traffic
spiegazione: Correct: For outbound traffic, Azure evaluates the NSG associated with the network interface first, and then the NSG associated with the subnet. Because nsg-nic denies TCP 80 at priority 200, the traffic is dropped there and nsg-subnet never receives it. To deny outbound traffic, either one or both NSGs need a deny rule. Wrong: Evaluating nsg-subnet first is the inbound order, not the outbound order. Requiring both NSGs to deny is the inverse of how deny works: a single deny anywhere in the path is sufficient (it is ALLOW that must exist in both NSGs). NIC-level outbound rules are absolutely enforced; they are in fact evaluated before subnet-level outbound rules.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: An application security group named AsgLogic contains network interfaces that reside in VNet1. A second application security group named AsgDb contains network interfaces that reside in VNet2. An administrator attempts to create a security rule that specifies AsgLogic as the source and AsgDb as the destination. What is the result?
opzione_a: The configuration is not supported, because the network interfaces in both the source and destination application security groups must exist in the same virtual network
opzione_b: The rule is created successfully, but it applies only to the network interfaces that are in VNet1
opzione_c: The rule is created successfully, and Azure automatically creates a virtual network peering between VNet1 and VNet2
opzione_d: The rule is created successfully, provided that AsgLogic and AsgDb reside in the same resource group
spiegazione: Correct: A documented ASG constraint states that if you specify an application security group as the source and destination in a security rule, the network interfaces in both application security groups must exist in the same virtual network. Because AsgLogic spans VNet1 and AsgDb spans VNet2, the rule cannot be assigned. Wrong: The rule does not partially apply to VNet1 only; the configuration is rejected outright. Azure never creates virtual network peering implicitly as a side effect of a security rule. Resource group membership is irrelevant to this constraint; the boundary that matters is the virtual network, not the resource group.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: A network security group named nsg-mgmt is associated with a subnet and contains the following inbound custom rules, in addition to the default rules: priority 100, Allow, TCP, source 203.0.113.10, destination Any, destination port 3389; priority 200, Deny, TCP, source Internet, destination Any, destination port 3389; priority 300, Allow, TCP, source Internet, destination Any, destination port 3389. A support technician at the public IP address 203.0.113.10 initiates an RDP connection to a VM in the subnet. Which rule determines the outcome?
opzione_a: The rule at priority 100 allows the connection
opzione_b: The rule at priority 200 denies the connection, because deny rules are always evaluated before allow rules
opzione_c: The rule at priority 300 allows the connection, because it is the last matching rule to be processed
opzione_d: The DenyAllInBound default rule at priority 65500 denies the connection
spiegazione: Correct: Rules are processed in priority order, lowest number first, and once traffic matches a rule, processing stops. The five-tuple of this flow (source 203.0.113.10, TCP, destination port 3389) matches the rule at priority 100, so the connection is allowed and no lower-priority rule is evaluated. Wrong: Azure does not give deny rules any inherent precedence; only the priority number determines order, so the rule at 200 is never reached. The rule at 300 is not evaluated either, and processing stops at the FIRST match, not the last. DenyAllInBound is only reached when no higher-priority rule matches, which is not the case here.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: In VNet1, the subnet named Subnet1 has the network security group NSG1 associated to it. VM1 resides in Subnet1, and VM1's network interface NIC1 has the network security group NSG2 associated to it. A client on the internet initiates a connection to VM1 over TCP port 443. In which order does Azure evaluate the two network security groups for this inbound flow?
opzione_a: NSG2 only, because a rule on a network interface always overrides the rules of the subnet
opzione_b: NSG1 first, then NSG2
opzione_c: NSG2 first, then NSG1
opzione_d: NSG1 and NSG2 are merged into a single rule set and evaluated together in priority order
spiegazione: Correct: For inbound traffic, Azure first processes the rules in the NSG associated with the subnet, and then processes the rules in the NSG associated with the network interface. Both NSGs must allow TCP 443 for the traffic to reach VM1; if NSG1 blocks the traffic, NSG2 never evaluates it. Wrong: A NIC-level NSG does not override a subnet-level NSG; both are enforced independently. NSG2 first, then NSG1 describes the OUTBOUND order, which is the reverse of inbound. The two NSGs are never merged into one rule set; each is evaluated separately, and priority numbers are only compared within a single NSG.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: While scripting network security group rules with Az PowerShell, an engineer must supply a Priority value for every custom security rule that is added to an NSG. Which range of values does Azure accept for the priority of a user-defined security rule?
opzione_a: 1 through 1000
opzione_b: 100 through 4096
opzione_c: 100 through 65000
opzione_d: 0 through 65500
spiegazione: Correct: A security rule priority is a number between 100 and 4096. Rules are processed in priority order, and lower numbers are processed before higher numbers because lower numbers mean higher priority. Wrong: 1 through 1000 understates the floor and the ceiling; priorities below 100 are rejected. 100 through 65000 is wrong because 65000 is reserved for the AllowVNetInBound/AllowVnetOutBound default rules; the custom range stops at 4096. 0 through 65500 is wrong for the same reason and because 0 is not a valid priority; 65500 is reserved for the DenyAllInBound/DenyAllOutBound default rules.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: A network administrator creates a new network security group (NSG) named nsg-prod in the East US region. No custom security rules have been added to it yet. Which priority is assigned to the default rule that blocks all inbound traffic that is not allowed by another rule?
spiegazione: Correct: 65500 is the priority of the DenyAllInBound default rule, which denies traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 to 0.0.0.0/0 on any protocol. Azure assigns default rules the highest priority numbers (lowest priority) so that custom rules are always processed first. Wrong: 4096 is the highest priority NUMBER you may assign to a custom rule, not a default rule. 65000 is the priority of AllowVNetInBound, which allows traffic between resources tagged VirtualNetwork. 65001 is the priority of AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound, which allows health probe traffic from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual network peering
domanda: A hub virtual network named Hub1 contains a VPN gateway with a site-to-site connection to your datacenter. You plan to peer three new spoke virtual networks with Hub1 so that virtual machines in the spokes can reach on-premises resources through the gateway in Hub1. You want to avoid deploying a gateway in each spoke. Which configuration requirements must be met? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: On each peering from Hub1 to a spoke, enable Allow gateway transit.
opzione_b: On each peering from a spoke to Hub1, enable Use remote gateways.
opzione_c: Deploy a VPN gateway in each spoke virtual network.
opzione_d: Ensure that none of the spoke virtual networks contains a virtual network gateway.
opzione_e: In each spoke, create a user-defined route for the on-premises address space with a next hop type of Virtual network peering.
spiegazione: Correct (a): Allow gateway transit (AllowGatewayTransit) is set on the peering of the virtual network that owns the gateway. It allows the peered virtual networks to receive traffic from Hub1's gateway or Route Server, and it can only be enabled because Hub1 actually contains a gateway. Correct (b): Use remote gateways (UseRemoteGateways) is set on each spoke's peering to Hub1. Microsoft notes this option can be enabled only if the peered virtual network has a gateway and that peered virtual network enables Allow gateway transit. Routes to on-premises networks then propagate to the peered spoke route tables. Correct (d): A virtual network can have only one gateway, which must be either a local gateway or a remote gateway in the peered virtual network. Microsoft states that you cannot use remote gateways if you already have a gateway configured in your virtual network, so each spoke must not contain a virtual network gateway. Wrong (c): Deploying a VPN gateway in each spoke is the exact opposite of the goal. Gateway transit exists so spokes can share the hub gateway instead of deploying gateways in every spoke, and a local gateway would block Use remote gateways. Wrong (e): Virtual network peering cannot be specified as the next hop type in a UDR. Furthermore, no UDR is needed here: routes to the gateway-connected on-premises networks propagate automatically to the peered virtual networks when gateway transit is used.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual network peering
domanda: Two business units each own an Azure subscription, and the subscriptions are associated with different Microsoft Entra tenants. VNet-Finance is in the West Europe region in the first subscription, and VNet-Sales is in the East US region in the second subscription. You must peer the two virtual networks. Which requirements apply? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: The two virtual networks must have nonoverlapping IP address spaces.
opzione_b: A peering must be configured on each of the two virtual networks.
opzione_c: The accounts used must be assigned the Network Contributor role, or a custom role with the equivalent peering actions, for each virtual network.
opzione_d: Both virtual networks must be moved into the same Azure region before the peering can be created.
opzione_e: A virtual network gateway must be deployed in each virtual network.
spiegazione: Correct (a): The virtual networks you peer must have nonoverlapping IP address spaces. This requirement applies to local and global peering alike, and Azure rejects the peering operation if the CIDR ranges intersect. Correct (b): When you peer two virtual networks created through Resource Manager, a peering must be configured for each virtual network. With only the first link, the status is Initiated; the peering isn't successfully established until the status is Connected for both peerings. Correct (c): The accounts you use to work with virtual network peering must be assigned the Network Contributor role, or a custom role assigned the necessary actions such as Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/virtualNetworkPeerings/write. For cross-tenant peering, you must also add a user from each tenant as a guest user in the opposite tenant. Wrong (d): Virtual networks can be in different regions. Peering virtual networks in different regions is supported and is referred to as Global Virtual Network Peering; the peered virtual networks can exist in any Azure public cloud region. Wrong (e): Peering does not require any virtual network gateway. Traffic between peered virtual networks is routed directly through the Microsoft backbone infrastructure, not through a gateway or over the public internet. A gateway is only relevant if you want gateway transit for cross-premises connectivity.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual network peering
domanda: Your organization is building a hub-and-spoke topology. Hub-VNet contains an Azure VPN gateway (VpnGw2 SKU) that provides site-to-site connectivity to the corporate datacenter. Spoke-VNet must use the VPN gateway in Hub-VNet to reach on-premises resources, and no gateway may be deployed in Spoke-VNet. Select the correct configuration for each of the following.
opzione_a: On the peering from Hub-VNet to Spoke-VNet, Allow gateway transit: [Enabled | Disabled | Not supported]
opzione_b: On the peering from Spoke-VNet to Hub-VNet, Use remote gateways: [Enabled | Disabled | Not supported]
opzione_c: A virtual network gateway in Spoke-VNet: [Required | Must not exist | Must use the Basic SKU]
opzione_d: Number of Spoke-VNet peerings on which Use remote gateways can be enabled: [0 | 1 | Unlimited]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - Enabled: Allow gateway transit is configured on the peering of the virtual network that contains the gateway. Enabling it on the Hub-VNet peering allows Spoke-VNet to receive traffic from Hub-VNet's gateway. Disabled would leave the spoke without transit, and the option is fully supported for both local and global peering, so Not supported is incorrect. Dropdown 2 - Enabled: Use remote gateways is configured on the spoke side and can be enabled only if the peered virtual network has a gateway and enables Allow gateway transit. Both conditions are met here. Dropdown 3 - Must not exist: A virtual network can have only one gateway, which is either a local gateway or a remote gateway in the peered virtual network. Microsoft states you can't use remote gateways if you already have a gateway configured in your virtual network. Required is wrong because it defeats the purpose of transit; Must use the Basic SKU is wrong and doubly misleading, since the transit option itself can be used with all VPN Gateway SKUs except Basic. Dropdown 4 - 1: Microsoft documents that Use remote gateways can be enabled in only one of a virtual network's peerings, which follows from a virtual network having a single gateway. 0 would mean the feature can't be used at all, and Unlimited contradicts the single-gateway constraint.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual network peering
domanda: Your company runs three virtual networks in the East US region: VNet1, VNet2, and VNet3. A peering exists between VNet1 and VNet2, and a second peering exists between VNet2 and VNet3. Both peerings show a status of Connected and use only default peering settings. Virtual machines in VNet1 cannot reach virtual machines in VNet3. You must enable direct communication between VNet1 and VNet3 with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create a virtual network peering between VNet1 and VNet3.
opzione_b: On the VNet2 peerings, enable Allow forwarded traffic in both directions.
opzione_c: On the VNet2 peerings, enable Allow gateway transit, and enable Use remote gateways on the VNet1 and VNet3 peerings.
opzione_d: Add a route table to VNet1 that contains a route for the VNet3 address space with a next hop type of Virtual network peering.
spiegazione: Correct (a): Virtual network peerings are not transitive. If VNet1 is peered with VNet2 and VNet2 is peered with VNet3, there is no connectivity between VNet1 and VNet3 through VNet2. To make VNet1 and VNet3 communicate directly, you must create an explicit peering between VNet1 and VNet3 (the only alternative is routing through an NVA in the hub, which is far more effort). Wrong (b): Allow forwarded traffic only permits a virtual network to accept traffic that did not originate in the peered virtual network; it does not create any route and does not by itself make peering transitive. Microsoft explicitly states that enabling this capability does not create any user-defined routes or network virtual appliances. Wrong (c): Allow gateway transit and Use remote gateways relate to sharing a VPN, ExpressRoute gateway, or Route Server in a peered virtual network for cross-premises connectivity. There is no gateway in this scenario, and gateway transit does not provide spoke-to-spoke transit for virtual network traffic. Wrong (d): You cannot specify Virtual network peering as the next hop type in a user-defined route. Azure creates routes with that next hop type automatically only when you configure a peering.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual network peering
domanda: A hub virtual network named Hub-VNet contains a VPN gateway that provides a site-to-site connection to your on-premises datacenter. A spoke virtual network named Spoke-VNet is peered with Hub-VNet and contains no virtual network gateway. Virtual machines in Spoke-VNet must be able to reach on-premises servers through the VPN gateway in Hub-VNet. Which peering setting must you enable on the peering from Spoke-VNet to Hub-VNet?
opzione_a: Use remote gateways
opzione_b: Allow gateway transit
opzione_c: Allow forwarded traffic
opzione_d: Allow virtual network access
spiegazione: Correct (a): Gateway transit requires two complementary settings. On the peering from the virtual network that owns the gateway (Hub-VNet), you enable Allow gateway transit (AllowGatewayTransit). On the peering from the virtual network that will consume the remote gateway (Spoke-VNet), you enable Use remote gateways (UseRemoteGateways). The question asks about the setting on the Spoke-VNet side, which is Use remote gateways. Wrong (b): Allow gateway transit is enabled on the Hub-VNet peering, not on the spoke. The portal describes it as allowing the gateway or route server in the local virtual network to forward traffic to the peered virtual network, and it can only be enabled when the local virtual network actually contains a gateway or Route Server. Wrong (c): Allow forwarded traffic permits a virtual network to receive traffic that did not originate inside the peered virtual network. It is used for service chaining through an NVA and is not the setting that lets a spoke consume a remote gateway. Wrong (d): Allow virtual network access is selected by default and simply enables communication between the peered virtual networks; it has no effect on gateway transit.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual network peering
domanda: An attempt to peer a virtual network that uses the address space 10.0.0.0/16 with a virtual network that uses the address space 10.0.4.0/24 fails. The error message states that the address space of the virtual networks overlaps. Both virtual networks are in the same subscription but in different Azure regions. Neither virtual network has subnets or resources deployed in the 10.0.4.0/24 range. Which action enables the peering to be created?
opzione_a: Modify the address space of one of the virtual networks so that the two virtual networks no longer share any CIDR range.
opzione_b: Deploy a virtual network gateway in each virtual network, and then connect them with a network-to-network connection.
opzione_c: Move both virtual networks into the same Azure region, because global peering does not support the 10.0.0.0/8 range.
opzione_d: Add a route table to each virtual network that contains a user-defined route for the overlapping range with a next hop type of None.
spiegazione: Correct (a): Virtual networks that you peer must have nonoverlapping IP address spaces. 10.0.4.0/24 is a subset of 10.0.0.0/16, so the ranges overlap and Azure rejects the peering. The documented resolution is to resize one of the virtual networks by removing or modifying the overlapping address range, which is safe here because no subnets or resources exist in that range. Wrong (b): The nonoverlapping requirement is not specific to peering transport; connecting overlapping address spaces with gateways does not resolve duplicate IP ranges and Azure would still not route correctly between identical prefixes. This also adds unnecessary cost and complexity. Wrong (c): Peering virtual networks in different regions is fully supported and is called Global Virtual Network Peering. There is no restriction against the 10.0.0.0/8 private range in global peering. The failure is caused by the overlap, not by the regions. Wrong (d): A user-defined route cannot make overlapping address spaces valid. The overlap check occurs at the control plane when the peering is created, so the peering never gets created in the first place.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual network peering
domanda:
VNet-Alpha uses the address space 10.10.0.0/16 and resides in Subscription1 in the North Europe region. VNet-Beta uses the address space 10.20.0.0/16 and resides in Subscription2 in the Central US region. Subscription1 and Subscription2 are associated with different Microsoft Entra tenants. Neither virtual network contains a virtual network gateway. You plan to connect the two virtual networks by using virtual network peering. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
1. The two virtual networks can be peered even though their subscriptions are associated with different Microsoft Entra tenants.
2. Creating a single peering link from VNet-Alpha to VNet-Beta is sufficient to establish connectivity between the two virtual networks.
3. After the peering status is Connected, virtual machines in VNet-Alpha can resolve the host names of virtual machines in VNet-Beta by using Azure-provided default name resolution.
opzione_a: The two virtual networks can be peered even though their subscriptions are associated with different Microsoft Entra tenants.
opzione_b: Creating a single peering link from VNet-Alpha to VNet-Beta is sufficient to establish connectivity between the two virtual networks.
opzione_c: After the peering status is Connected, virtual machines in VNet-Alpha can resolve the host names of virtual machines in VNet-Beta by using Azure-provided default name resolution.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: The virtual networks can be in the same or different subscriptions, and when you peer virtual networks in different subscriptions, both subscriptions can be associated with the same or different Microsoft Entra tenants. Because the regions differ, this is a Global Virtual Network Peering, which is also supported. For the cross-tenant configuration you add a user from each tenant as a guest user in the opposite tenant. Statement 2 - No: When you peer two virtual networks created through Resource Manager, a peering must be configured for each virtual network. With only the first link, the peering status is Initiated. The peering isn't successfully established until the peering status for both virtual network peerings is Connected, so a second link from VNet-Beta to VNet-Alpha is required. Statement 3 - No: You can't resolve names in peered virtual networks using default Azure name resolution. To resolve names across virtual networks, you must use Azure Private DNS or a custom DNS server. Peering provides IP connectivity, not cross-virtual-network name resolution.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual networks and subnets
domanda: A virtual network named vnet-hub has two address ranges: 10.10.0.0/16 and 172.16.0.0/16. The 172.16.0.0/16 range contains a single subnet named snet-svc, which is delegated to an Azure PaaS service and contains instances that the service injected. A network administrator must remove the 172.16.0.0/16 address range from vnet-hub, while leaving 10.10.0.0/16 in place. Arrange the four required actions in the correct order.
opzione_a: Delete the snet-svc subnet.
opzione_b: Remove the 172.16.0.0/16 address range from the vnet-hub address space.
opzione_c: Delete the resources that the delegated Azure service deployed in snet-svc.
opzione_d: Remove the subnet delegation from snet-svc.
spiegazione:
Correct order: c, d, a, b. Each step unblocks the next, and every dependency is documented on Microsoft Learn.

1. Delete the resources that the delegated service deployed in snet-svc (c). Learn states: 'If a resource for a service is already deployed in the subnet, you can't add or remove subnet delegations until you remove all the resources for the service.' Until the injected instances are gone, the delegation is frozen, so this must come first.

2. Remove the subnet delegation from snet-svc (d). The subnet delegation overview states that delegation 'Requires delegation to be removed before the subnet or virtual network can be deleted.' This step is only possible once the service's resources are removed, and it is mandatory before the subnet can be deleted.

3. Delete the snet-svc subnet (a). Learn states 'You can delete a subnet only if there are no resources in the subnet.' The subnet is now empty and undelegated, so it can be deleted.

4. Remove the 172.16.0.0/16 address range (b). Learn states: 'If a subnet exists in the address range, you can't remove the address range. To remove an address range, you must first delete any subnets (and any resources in the subnets) that exist in the address range.' With snet-svc gone, the range is empty and can finally be removed. Because vnet-hub retains 10.10.0.0/16, the virtual network still has an address space after the removal.

Reversing any pair fails: attempting b first is blocked by the existing subnet, a before d is blocked by the delegation, and d before c is blocked by the service's deployed resources.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual networks and subnets
domanda: A virtual network named vnet-core has a single address range of 10.0.0.0/16 and two subnets: snet-a (10.0.0.0/24) and snet-b (10.0.1.0/24). Both subnets contain running virtual machines. For each proposed change to the vnet-core address space, select whether the change is supported.
opzione_a: Change the address range from 10.0.0.0/16 to 10.0.0.0/23: [Supported | Not supported]
opzione_b: Change the address range from 10.0.0.0/16 to 10.0.0.0/8: [Supported | Not supported]
opzione_c: Change the address range from 10.0.0.0/16 to 10.0.0.0/25: [Supported | Not supported]
opzione_d: Remove the 10.0.0.0/16 address range from vnet-core: [Supported | Not supported]
spiegazione:
Correct selections: Supported, Supported, Not supported, Not supported. The governing rule on Microsoft Learn is: 'You can decrease the address range for a virtual network as long as it still includes the ranges of any associated subnets. Additionally, you can extend the address range, for example, changing a /16 to /8.'
10.0.0.0/16 to /23: Supported. A /23 spans 10.0.0.0 through 10.0.1.255, which still fully contains both snet-a (10.0.0.0/24) and snet-b (10.0.1.0/24). This is a decrease, but a legal one. Note that this is a change to the virtual network address space, not to a subnet range, so the running virtual machines don't block it.
10.0.0.0/16 to /8: Supported. This is an extension, which Learn calls out with this exact example. The only constraint on extending is that the new range must not overlap another range in the same virtual network, and vnet-core has no other range.
10.0.0.0/16 to /25: Not supported. A /25 spans only 10.0.0.0 through 10.0.0.127. It excludes snet-b entirely and truncates snet-a, so it no longer includes the ranges of the associated subnets.
Remove 10.0.0.0/16: Not supported. Learn states 'If a subnet exists in the address range, you can't remove the address range.' Both subnets, and the resources inside them, would have to be deleted first.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual networks and subnets
domanda: A subnet named snet-integration is delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms, and an App Service plan currently uses regional virtual network integration through that subnet. A network administrator must remove the delegation from snet-integration. What must happen first?
opzione_a: All resources of the delegated service must be removed from the subnet.
opzione_b: The network security group associated with the subnet must be dissociated.
opzione_c: The subnet must be resized to /28 or larger.
opzione_d: Private endpoint network policies must be disabled on the subnet.
spiegazione:
Correct: Remove the service's resources from the subnet first. Microsoft Learn states: 'You can modify subnet delegation to enable zero or multiple delegations. If a resource for a service is already deployed in the subnet, you can't add or remove subnet delegations until you remove all the resources for the service.' The App Service plan's integration must be removed before the delegation can be dropped.

Why the others are wrong:
Dissociate the network security group - Delegated subnets support NSG association; Learn lists network filtering with NSGs as an advantage of delegation. An NSG is not a blocker for changing a delegation.
Resize the subnet to /28 or larger - The injected service dictates the minimum number of IP addresses at deployment time, but subnet size is not a precondition for removing a delegation. This option is also self-defeating: a subnet that still contains resources can't be resized at all.
Disable private endpoint network policies - Private endpoint network policies apply to private endpoints, and Learn notes that a delegated subnet can't be used with a private endpoint in the first place. This setting is irrelevant to removing a delegation.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual networks and subnets
domanda:
A virtual network named vnet-prod contains a subnet named snet-db that is delegated to an Azure PaaS service. The service has injected instances into snet-db. Evaluate each of the following statements. Select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
1. A private endpoint can be created in snet-db while the delegation is in place.
2. The delegation on snet-db must be removed before snet-db can be deleted.
3. A network security group can be associated with snet-db while the delegation is in place.
opzione_a: A private endpoint can be created in snet-db while the delegation is in place.
opzione_b: The delegation on snet-db must be removed before snet-db can be deleted.
opzione_c: A network security group can be associated with snet-db while the delegation is in place.
spiegazione:
Statement 1 - No. Learn's list of the effects of subnet delegation states that a delegated subnet 'Can't be used with a private endpoint if the subnet is delegated. As a consequence, private endpoint network policies shouldn't be configured in these subnets.' Private endpoints require a non-delegated subnet.

Statement 2 - Yes. The same list states that delegation 'Requires delegation to be removed before the subnet or virtual network can be deleted.' In practice this makes deletion a multi-step operation: the service's injected resources must be removed first (because delegations can't be changed while the service's resources are deployed), then the delegation, then the subnet.

Statement 3 - Yes. Delegation deliberately preserves the virtual network owner's control. Learn lists 'Network filtering traffic policies with network security groups' as an advantage of delegating a subnet, and includes NSG association among the properties supported on a delegated subnet. The injected service may add its own security and route policies, but Learn notes that 'The policies or routes that these services apply are flexible and overridden by the customer.'
tags: subnet delegation,private endpoint,network security group,virtual network,subnet

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual networks and subnets
domanda: An administrator is defining the IPv4 address space of a new Azure virtual network. Which address range will Azure reject?
opzione_d: 40.65.10.0/24, a public address range that the organization owns
spiegazione:
Correct: 169.254.0.0/16. Microsoft Learn lists the address ranges that can't be added to a virtual network address space: 224.0.0.0/4 (multicast), 255.255.255.255/32 (broadcast), 127.0.0.0/8 (loopback), 169.254.0.0/16 (link-local), and 168.63.129.16/32 (internal DNS, DHCP, and Azure Load Balancer health probe). 169.254.0.0/16 is the link-local range on that list.

Why the others are wrong:
100.64.0.0/10 - This is the shared address space reserved in RFC 6598. Learn states it is treated as a private IP address space in Azure and can be deployed, which makes it a strong distractor for anyone who assumes only RFC 1918 is allowed.
172.16.0.0/12 - This is standard RFC 1918 private address space and is explicitly supported.
40.65.10.0/24 - Public address ranges are allowed. Learn states the address range you define can be public or private, and that whether it's public or private, the range is reachable only from within the virtual network, from interconnected virtual networks, and from connected on-premises networks. Microsoft recommends using private space or public space your organization owns, which is exactly this case.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual networks and subnets
domanda: A virtual network has two address ranges: 10.0.0.0/16 and 192.168.0.0/16. A single subnet named snet-legacy (192.168.0.0/24) is defined inside the second range and contains no resources. An administrator attempts to remove the 192.168.0.0/16 address range from the virtual network, and the operation fails. What should the administrator do?
opzione_a: Delete the snet-legacy subnet, and then remove the address range.
opzione_b: Decrease the 192.168.0.0/16 range to 192.168.0.0/24 first, and then remove it.
opzione_c: Remove the 10.0.0.0/16 address range first, because a virtual network can have only one address range at a time.
opzione_d: Disable service endpoints on snet-legacy, and then remove the address range.
spiegazione:
Correct: Delete the subnet first. Microsoft Learn states: 'If a subnet exists in the address range, you can't remove the address range. To remove an address range, you must first delete any subnets (and any resources in the subnets) that exist in the address range.' Because snet-legacy is empty, deleting it is straightforward and then the range can be removed.

Why the others are wrong:
Decrease the range to /24 - Resizing doesn't change anything: snet-legacy is 192.168.0.0/24, so it would still exist inside the resized range and would still block removal. Learn also notes that you can decrease an address range only as long as it still includes the ranges of any associated subnets.
Remove 10.0.0.0/16 first - This is inverted. A virtual network address space is composed of one or more non-overlapping ranges, so multiple ranges are fully supported. The presence of the other range is not the cause of the failure.
Disable service endpoints - Service endpoints are a subnet property that affects routing to Azure PaaS services. They are not a documented blocker for removing an address range; the existence of the subnet is.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual networks and subnets
domanda: You're writing your team's Azure Virtual Network design standard and must document the platform's subnet sizing rules. Select the correct value for each statement.
opzione_a: Smallest supported IPv4 subnet: [/24 | /29 | /30]
opzione_b: Usable IP addresses in an IPv4 /29 subnet: [3 | 5 | 6]
opzione_c: Supported IPv6 subnet size: [/48 | /64 | /126]
opzione_d: IP addresses that Azure reserves in every subnet: [2 | 3 | 5]
spiegazione:
Correct selections: /29, 3, /64, 5.
Smallest supported IPv4 subnet: /29. Learn states 'The smallest supported IPv4 subnet is /29, and the largest is /2 (using CIDR subnet definitions).' /24 is a common convention but far from the minimum. /30 is below the supported minimum and is rejected.
Usable addresses in a /29: 3. A /29 provides eight addresses, and Azure reserves five, leaving three. Learn says it directly: 'defining a subnet with a /29 address range gives three usable IP addresses in the subnet.' 6 is the on-premises answer (8 minus network and broadcast only) and 5 confuses the reserved count with the usable count.
Supported IPv6 subnet size: /64. Learn states 'IPv6 subnets must be exactly /64 in size' - it isn't a minimum or a maximum, it's the only allowed value. /48 and /126 are valid IPv6 prefixes elsewhere in networking but are rejected by Azure.
Reserved addresses per subnet: 5. Azure reserves the first and last address for protocol conformance plus three more for Azure service usage. 2 reflects only the network and broadcast addresses; 3 counts only the Azure-specific reservations.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual networks and subnets
domanda: A new Azure virtual network is being designed. Which address ranges can't be added to the virtual network address space? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
spiegazione:
Correct answers: a, c, e. Microsoft Learn lists exactly five ranges that can't be added to a virtual network address space: 224.0.0.0/4 (multicast), 255.255.255.255/32 (broadcast), 127.0.0.0/8 (loopback), 169.254.0.0/16 (link-local), and 168.63.129.16/32 (internal DNS, DHCP, and the Azure Load Balancer health probe).
a - 224.0.0.0/4 is the multicast range on that list. Azure virtual networks also block multicast traffic outright.
c - 168.63.129.16/32 is the Azure platform's wire-server address used for internal DNS, DHCP, and load balancer health probes, and is on the blocked list.
e - 127.0.0.0/8 is the loopback range on that list.

Why the others are wrong:
b - 10.0.0.0/8 is RFC 1918 private address space and is one of the most commonly used virtual network address spaces in Azure.
d - 100.64.0.0/10 is the shared address space reserved in RFC 6598. Learn states it is treated as a private IP address space in Azure and can be deployed, so it is allowed. This is the trap for candidates who assume only RFC 1918 ranges are permitted.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual networks and subnets
domanda: The subnet snet-web (10.30.1.0/26) hosts four virtual machines. Capacity planning shows that snet-web must be resized to 10.30.1.0/24. The 10.30.1.0/24 range is inside the virtual network address space and doesn't overlap any other subnet. What must be done before the subnet address range can be changed?
opzione_a: Move the virtual machines to another subnet, or delete them from the subnet.
opzione_b: Nothing. A subnet address range can be expanded while resources are deployed in it, as long as the new range doesn't overlap another subnet.
opzione_c: Delete the virtual network and re-create it with the larger subnet.
opzione_d: Stop (deallocate) the four virtual machines.
spiegazione:
Correct: Move or delete the resources first. Microsoft Learn is explicit about changing a subnet address range: 'If no resources are deployed within the subnet, you can change the address range. If any resources exist in the subnet, you must first either move the resources to another subnet or delete them from the subnet.'

Why the others are wrong:
Nothing is required - This is the classic misconception. Non-overlap is necessary but not sufficient; the subnet must be empty of resources regardless of the direction of the resize.
Delete and re-create the virtual network - Unnecessarily destructive and not what the documentation requires. Emptying the single subnet is enough, and deleting a virtual network has its own precondition (no resources connected to any of its subnets).
Stop (deallocate) the virtual machines - Deallocating doesn't help. The network interfaces still exist and still hold private IP configurations in snet-web, so the subnet still contains resources and the resize is still blocked.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual networks and subnets
domanda: Contoso is deploying an application tier into a new subnet named snet-app that uses the address range 10.20.4.0/27 in an Azure virtual network. How many IP addresses in snet-app are available for assignment to the network interfaces of virtual machines?
spiegazione:
Correct: 27. A /27 prefix contains 32 addresses. Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet: the first and the last address for protocol conformance (network address and broadcast address), plus three more for Azure service usage (the default gateway and two addresses that map the Azure DNS IP addresses into the virtual network space). 32 - 5 = 27 usable addresses.

Why the others are wrong:
26 - This subtracts six addresses. Azure reserves exactly five per subnet, not six.
30 - This applies the traditional on-premises convention of subtracting only the network and broadcast addresses (32 - 2). It ignores the three additional addresses that Azure reserves for platform use, and is the single most common miscalculation for this topic.
32 - This is the total size of the /27 block and ignores all reservations. No subnet in Azure makes every address available to workloads.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure virtual networks and subnets
domanda: A network engineer must create the smallest IPv4 subnet that Azure supports, to host a small management appliance in an existing virtual network. Which CIDR prefix should the engineer specify for the subnet address range?
spiegazione:
Correct: /29. Microsoft Learn states that the smallest range you can specify for a subnet is /29, which provides eight IP addresses. Because Azure reserves five addresses per subnet, a /29 subnet leaves three usable IP addresses.

Why the others are wrong:
/28 - A /28 is a perfectly valid subnet size (16 addresses, 11 usable), but it is not the smallest size Azure supports, so it does not meet the requirement.
/30 - A /30 is smaller than the documented minimum and is rejected by Azure. It is a plausible distractor because /30 is the classic point-to-point prefix in on-premises networking, where the platform does not reserve extra addresses.
/31 - A /31 is also below the supported minimum and is rejected. In traditional routing a /31 is used for point-to-point links, but Azure's five reserved addresses make anything smaller than /29 unusable.

sotto_argomento: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
domanda: Subnet-1 in VNet1 is associated with a network security group named nsg-sub. The network interface of vm-1, which resides in Subnet-1, is associated with a network security group named nsg-nic. nsg-sub contains a single custom inbound rule: priority 100, Allow, TCP, source Internet, destination Any, destination port 443. nsg-nic contains a single custom inbound rule: priority 100, Allow, TCP, source 198.51.100.5, destination Any, destination port 22. Neither network security group contains any other custom rule. Select the correct value for each item.
opzione_a: Inbound TCP 443 from a client on the internet to vm-1 is: [Allowed | Denied]
opzione_b: Inbound TCP 22 from the internet host 198.51.100.5 to vm-1 is: [Allowed | Denied]
opzione_c: Inbound TCP 443 from another virtual machine in VNet1 to vm-1 is: [Allowed | Denied]
opzione_d: To allow SSH from 198.51.100.5 to reach vm-1, you must add an allow rule to: [nsg-nic only | nsg-sub only | both nsg-sub and nsg-nic]
spiegazione: Correct: (a) Denied. nsg-sub is evaluated first and its rule at priority 100 allows TCP 443, but nsg-nic is then evaluated and contains no rule matching TCP 443 from the internet, so its DenyAllInBound default rule at 65500 drops the traffic. For inbound traffic to reach the VM, the port must be open in BOTH NSGs. (b) Denied. nsg-sub is evaluated first; no rule matches TCP 22, so DenyAllInBound in nsg-sub drops the traffic before nsg-nic is ever evaluated, even though nsg-nic would have allowed it. (c) Allowed. The custom rule in nsg-sub does not match (its source is the Internet tag, not the VirtualNetwork tag), so the AllowVNetInBound default rule at 65000 permits the flow in nsg-sub; the same default rule in nsg-nic permits it as well. (d) nsg-sub only. nsg-nic already allows TCP 22 from 198.51.100.5 at priority 100, so only the subnet NSG is missing the rule. Wrong: Adding the rule to nsg-nic only would leave the subnet NSG blocking the traffic, and adding it to both is unnecessary because nsg-nic already permits it.

sotto_argomento: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
domanda: Case study: Fabrikam hosts a reporting application on a virtual machine named vm-1 in a resource group named rg-1. vm-1 is running and resides in a subnet that is associated with a network security group named nsg-subnet. The network interface of vm-1, named nic-1, is associated with a different network security group named nsg-nic. Both network security groups have been edited by several administrators over time and now contain dozens of custom rules. Users report that they cannot reach the application on TCP port 8080. An administrator needs to review, in a single output, the aggregation of all rules from both network security groups that currently apply to nic-1, by using the Azure CLI. Which command should the administrator run?
opzione_a: az network nsg rule list --resource-group rg-1 --nsg-name nsg-subnet
opzione_b: az network nic list-effective-nsg --resource-group rg-1 --name nic-1
opzione_c: az network watcher show-next-hop --resource-group rg-1 --vm vm-1 --source-ip 10.0.0.4 --dest-ip 10.0.1.4 --nic nic-1
opzione_d: az network nsg show --resource-group rg-1 --name nsg-nic
spiegazione: Correct: az network nic list-effective-nsg returns the effective security rules for a network interface, which are the aggregation of the rules in the NSG associated with the network interface and the NSG associated with the subnet the network interface is in. This is exactly the single consolidated view the administrator needs, and it works because vm-1 is running (output is only returned when the VM is in the running state and at least one NSG is associated). Wrong: az network nsg rule list returns only the custom rules of the one NSG you name, so it shows neither the default rules nor the rules of the other NSG. az network watcher show-next-hop returns routing information (the next hop type and IP address); it does not evaluate security rules. az network nsg show returns the details of a single NSG, so it again omits the second NSG and does not produce an aggregated effective rule set.

sotto_argomento: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
domanda: VM3 resides in a subnet that is associated with a network security group named nsg-sub, and VM3's network interface is associated with a network security group named nsg-nic. nsg-nic contains an outbound custom rule: priority 150, Deny, TCP, source Any, destination Internet, destination port 443. nsg-sub contains an outbound custom rule: priority 100, Allow, TCP, source Any, destination Internet, destination port 443. VM3 attempts to establish an outbound HTTPS connection to a public endpoint. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true. 1) VM3 can currently establish the outbound HTTPS connection. 2) Changing the priority of the allow rule in nsg-sub from 100 to 50 will allow the connection. 3) Deleting the deny rule from nsg-nic will allow the connection.
opzione_a: VM3 can currently establish the outbound HTTPS connection.
opzione_b: Changing the priority of the allow rule in nsg-sub from 100 to 50 will allow the connection.
opzione_c: Deleting the deny rule from nsg-nic will allow the connection.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: For outbound traffic, Azure evaluates the NSG associated with the network interface first. nsg-nic denies TCP 443 to the Internet tag at priority 150, so the traffic is dropped and nsg-sub never receives it. Statement 2 - No: This is the classic misconception. Priority numbers are only compared between rules WITHIN the same network security group; they do not determine which NSG is evaluated first. Lowering the number to 50 in nsg-sub changes nothing, because nsg-nic is still evaluated first for outbound traffic and still denies the flow. Statement 3 - Yes: With the deny rule removed, nsg-nic no longer has a matching custom rule, so its AllowInternetOutBound default rule at priority 65001 allows the traffic. nsg-sub is then evaluated and its allow rule at priority 100 permits TCP 443 to the Internet tag, so the connection succeeds.

sotto_argomento: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
domanda: Connectivity to a virtual machine is failing intermittently, and an administrator plans to use the IP flow verify capability of Azure Network Watcher to determine whether a packet is allowed or denied. Which statements about IP flow verify are correct? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: IP flow verify evaluates the rules of all network security groups applied to the virtual machine's network interface, whether the NSG is associated with the subnet or with the network interface
opzione_b: IP flow verify returns Access allowed or Access denied together with the name of the security rule responsible for the result
opzione_c: IP flow verify can be used to test rules that apply to ICMP traffic
opzione_d: A Network Watcher instance must exist in the Azure subscription and region of the virtual machine
opzione_e: IP flow verify evaluates the effective routes of the network interface to confirm the next hop for the packet
spiegazione: Correct: IP flow verify looks at the rules of all NSGs applied to a VM's network interface, regardless of whether the NSG is associated to the subnet or the NIC, and it also considers Azure Virtual Network Manager admin rules. It returns Access denied or Access allowed plus the name of the security rule that denied or allowed the traffic and a link to the NSG (no link is provided when a default rule is responsible). A Network Watcher instance is required in the subscription and region of the VM. Wrong: IP flow verify only tests TCP and UDP rules; to test ICMP traffic rules you must use NSG diagnostics instead. IP flow verify does not evaluate routing: it tests security and admin rules only. To confirm the next hop for a packet you would use the Next hop capability of Network Watcher.
tags: ip flow verify,network watcher,nsg,troubleshooting,effective security rules

sotto_argomento: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
domanda: A support engineer must view the aggregated set of rules from both the subnet NSG and the network interface NSG that apply to the network interface of a virtual machine named vm-1, by using the Effective security rules page in the Azure portal. Which condition must be satisfied for Azure to return the effective security rules?
opzione_a: The virtual machine must be in the running state
opzione_b: The virtual machine must be stopped (deallocated) so that the platform can recalculate the rule set
opzione_c: Virtual network flow logs must be enabled on the virtual network
opzione_d: A network security group must be associated with both the subnet and the network interface
spiegazione: Correct: Azure shows effective security rules for a network interface only when an NSG is associated with the network interface or its subnet, and the VM must be in the running state. Wrong: A deallocated VM is precisely the case where no effective rules are returned; the VM must be running, not stopped. Virtual network flow logs record traffic data for analysis but are not a prerequisite for viewing effective security rules. An NSG associated with BOTH the subnet and the NIC is not required: effective rules are returned when an NSG is associated with the network interface, the subnet, or both.

sotto_argomento: Implement Azure Bastion
domanda: Fabrikam plans to deploy Azure Bastion into VNet1 so that administrators can connect to servers that run in an on-premises datacenter by specifying the private IP address of each server. The datacenter is connected to VNet1 by an ExpressRoute circuit that uses private peering. Select the appropriate options to complete the deployment requirements.
opzione_a: Minimum Bastion SKU required to connect to an on-premises server by using its private IP address: [Basic | Standard | Premium]
opzione_b: Required public IP address SKU and allocation method for the bastion host: [Basic and Dynamic | Standard and Static | Standard and Dynamic]
opzione_c: Minimum AzureBastionSubnet prefix length: [/29 | /27 | /26]
spiegazione: Correct: Standard, Standard and Static, /26. IP-based connection - targeting a machine by IP address rather than by Azure Resource Manager resource ID - requires the Standard SKU tier or higher, and the IP-based connection setting must be enabled on the Bastion Configuration page; it supports on-premises servers reached over ExpressRoute private peering or a VPN site-to-site connection. The public IP address used by a bastion host must use the Standard SKU with Static allocation. The AzureBastionSubnet must be /26 or larger for any Bastion resource deployed on or after November 2, 2021. Why the other choices are wrong: Basic does not support IP-based connection; Premium supports it but is not the minimum, since Premium only adds session recording and private-only deployment. Basic public IP SKU and any Dynamic allocation are rejected by Bastion. /29 and /27 are below the current minimum, although pre-November 2021 /27 deployments continue to work. Note also that this design must not use force tunneling or advertise a default route over the ExpressRoute circuit, because IP-based connection requires Bastion to have internet access.

sotto_argomento: Implement Azure Bastion
domanda: Security policy at your company requires a network security group on every subnet, including AzureBastionSubnet. You must add the ingress and egress rules that Azure Bastion requires so that the bastion host stays healthy and can reach the target virtual machines. Which rules are required? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Inbound TCP 443 from the GatewayManager service tag
opzione_b: Inbound TCP 3389 from the Internet service tag
opzione_c: Inbound ports 8080 and 5701 from the VirtualNetwork service tag to the VirtualNetwork service tag
opzione_d: Outbound TCP 443 to the AzureCloud service tag
opzione_e: Inbound TCP 22 from the Internet service tag
spiegazione: Correct: a, c, and d. AllowGatewayManagerInbound (TCP 443 from GatewayManager) lets the Bastion control plane communicate with the host. AllowBastionHostCommunication (ports 8080 and 5701 from VirtualNetwork to VirtualNetwork) lets the internal components of Azure Bastion communicate with each other. AllowAzureCloudOutbound (TCP 443 to AzureCloud) lets Bastion reach Azure public endpoints to store diagnostics and metering logs. If you apply an NSG to AzureBastionSubnet you must create all the required rules; omitting any of them blocks platform updates and VM connectivity.
