Why the others are wrong: inbound 3389 and inbound 22 from the Internet are not required on AzureBastionSubnet - the documentation states explicitly that ports 3389 and 22 are not required there. Users reach the bastion host over TLS on port 443 (AllowHttpsInbound), and RDP/SSH on 3389/22 appear as an outbound rule toward the VirtualNetwork tag and as an inbound rule on the target VM subnet, sourced from the AzureBastionSubnet range.

sotto_argomento: Implement Azure Bastion
domanda: You must deploy a new Azure Bastion host into an existing virtual network named VNet1 so that an administrator can open an SSH session to a Linux virtual machine by running a command from the SSH client that is installed on a local computer. VNet1 currently contains only a workload subnet. Arrange the four actions in the correct order to meet the requirement.
opzione_a: Run az network bastion ssh from the local computer to connect to the Linux virtual machine.
opzione_b: Create a subnet named AzureBastionSubnet that uses a /26 prefix in VNet1.
opzione_c: Deploy the bastion host by using the Standard SKU and select Native Client Support.
opzione_d: Create a public IP address that uses the Standard SKU and static allocation.
spiegazione: Correct order: b, d, c, a. First create the dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet with a /26 or larger prefix in the same virtual network and resource group as the bastion host; the subnet name must be exactly AzureBastionSubnet and it cannot contain other resources. Next create the public IP address, which must use the Standard SKU with Static allocation - a Basic SKU or dynamically allocated address is rejected. Then deploy the bastion host itself: native client support requires the Standard SKU, and you must select Native Client Support on the Advanced tab at deployment time (or enable it later on the Configuration page). Only after the bastion host exists and native client support is enabled can the administrator run az network bastion ssh from the local computer. The subnet and public IP are prerequisites of the deployment step, so neither can follow it, and the connection command is meaningless until the host is deployed.

sotto_argomento: Implement Azure Bastion
domanda:
Contoso deploys an Azure Bastion host named Bastion1 that uses the Basic SKU into a virtual network named VNet1. VNet1 is peered with a virtual network named VNet2 that contains several virtual machines. None of the virtual machines has a public IP address. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

1. Administrators can use Bastion1 to connect to a virtual machine in VNet2.
2. Administrators can use the az network bastion ssh command on their local computer to connect to a Linux virtual machine through Bastion1.
3. You can configure Bastion1 to use 10 instances to support additional concurrent sessions.
opzione_a: Administrators can use Bastion1 to connect to a virtual machine in VNet2.
opzione_b: Administrators can use the az network bastion ssh command on their local computer to connect to a Linux virtual machine through Bastion1.
opzione_c: You can configure Bastion1 to use 10 instances to support additional concurrent sessions.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. The Basic SKU supports virtual network peering and connecting to VMs in peered virtual networks. Deploying Bastion once and using virtual network peering to serve multiple networks is a supported design; only the Developer SKU lacks virtual network peering support. Statement 2 - No. Connecting with the native client through az network bastion ssh requires the Standard SKU or higher plus the Native Client Support setting. The Basic SKU supports only Azure portal browser-based connections. Statement 3 - No. Host scaling is available only on Standard and Premium, where you can configure 2 to 50 instances. The Basic SKU has a fixed count of two instances, giving a maximum of 40 concurrent RDP sessions and 80 concurrent SSH sessions (20 RDP and 40 SSH per instance). To scale beyond that you must upgrade the SKU - and note that upgrades are supported while downgrades are not.
tags: azure bastion,basic sku,vnet peering,host scaling,native client

sotto_argomento: Implement Azure Bastion
domanda: A bastion host currently uses the Basic SKU. You are evaluating which capabilities become available only after you upgrade the bastion host to the Standard SKU. Which capabilities require the Standard SKU or higher? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Shareable link
opzione_b: Kerberos authentication
opzione_c: Host scaling to more than two instances
opzione_d: Session recording
opzione_e: IP-based connection
spiegazione: Correct: shareable link, host scaling, and IP-based connection. All three are listed as No for Developer and Basic and Yes for Standard and Premium. Shareable link lets users connect without accessing the Azure portal. Host scaling is available only on Standard and higher and supports 2 to 50 instances, whereas Basic has a fixed count of two instances. IP-based connection lets you target a VM by IP address, including on-premises or non-Azure machines reached over ExpressRoute or VPN, and requires the Standard SKU or higher plus the IP-based connection setting enabled on the Configuration page. Why the others are wrong: Kerberos authentication is supported on every SKU tier, including Developer and Basic, so upgrading is not required for it. Session recording is not a Standard feature at all - it requires the Premium SKU, so it would not become available by upgrading to Standard.
tags: azure bastion,standard sku,host scaling,shareable link,ip-based connection

sotto_argomento: Implement Azure Bastion
domanda: An administrator wants to connect to an Azure virtual machine through Azure Bastion by running the az network bastion ssh command from the SSH client that is installed on their laptop, instead of using the Azure portal. Which is the lowest Azure Bastion SKU tier that supports this?
opzione_a: Developer
opzione_b: Basic
opzione_c: Standard
opzione_d: Premium
spiegazione: Correct: Standard. Native client support (connecting with az network bastion ssh, az network bastion rdp, or az network bastion tunnel) requires the Standard SKU or higher, and the Native Client Support setting must also be selected on the bastion host configuration. Why the others are wrong: Developer is a free shared-infrastructure SKU limited to browser-based connections to one VM at a time and does not support native client. Basic supports only Azure portal browser-based connections; native client, shareable links, IP-based connections, custom ports, and file transfer are all excluded from Basic. Premium does support native client, but the question asks for the lowest SKU that supports it, and Premium adds only session recording and private-only deployment on top of Standard.

sotto_argomento: Implement Azure Bastion
domanda: Your company plans to deploy an Azure Bastion host that uses the Standard SKU into an existing virtual network. You must create the dedicated subnet that the bastion host will use. What is the minimum subnet prefix that the AzureBastionSubnet must use?
spiegazione: Correct: /26. For any Azure Bastion resource deployed on or after November 2, 2021, the AzureBastionSubnet must be /26 or larger (/25, /24, and so on). A /26 is also the size Microsoft recommends so that host scaling has enough address space for additional scale units. Why the others are wrong: /29 and /28 are far too small and are rejected at deployment; they are the sizes associated with gateway or small workload subnets, not Bastion. /27 was the historical minimum before November 2, 2021 - existing deployments created in a /27 before that date keep working, but a new bastion host cannot be deployed into a /27, which makes /27 the classic trap answer here.

sotto_argomento: Implement Azure Bastion
domanda: A compliance team requires that every graphical RDP and SSH session made to production virtual machines through the bastion host be recorded and retained for audit. Which Azure Bastion SKU must you deploy?
opzione_a: Basic
opzione_b: Standard
opzione_c: Premium
opzione_d: Developer
spiegazione: Correct: Premium. Session recording captures the graphical RDP and SSH sessions made through the bastion host and stores the recordings in a blob container in your storage account via a SAS URL; the feature requires the Bastion Premium SKU. Why the others are wrong: Basic offers only dedicated deployment with two fixed instances and portal-based connections - no session recording. Standard adds native client, shareable links, IP-based connections, custom ports, and host scaling, but session recording is explicitly listed as No for Standard. Developer is the free shared SKU for dev/test and supports one VM connection at a time with no recording capability.

sotto_argomento: Troubleshoot load balancing
domanda: Backend virtual machines behind a public Standard Load Balancer begin failing new outbound connections to an external API during peak hours. Diagnostics indicate SNAT port exhaustion. The load balancer currently has a single frontend public IP address that is used for both inbound load-balancing rules and implicit outbound SNAT. Which actions can mitigate the SNAT port exhaustion? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Add more public IP addresses, or a public IP prefix, to the frontend of an outbound rule.
opzione_b: Set disableOutboundSnat to true on the load-balancing rule and configure an outbound rule with a higher Ports per instance value.
opzione_c: Associate a NAT gateway with the subnet that contains the backend virtual machines.
opzione_d: Change the session persistence of the load-balancing rule to Client IP.
opzione_e: Enable Floating IP on the load-balancing rule.
spiegazione: Correct (a): Each public IP address added to the frontend of an outbound rule contributes up to 64,000 extra ephemeral ports for the load balancer to use as SNAT ports, and a public IP prefix contributes 64,000 ports per address it contains. Correct (b): To tune the SNAT port allocation of an address that is also used for inbound, the automatic outbound NAT programmed by the load-balancing rule must first be disabled by setting disableOutboundSnat to true so the outbound rule can take control; you can then raise the allocation above the default. Correct (c): Azure NAT Gateway is the recommended outbound method, takes precedence over load balancer outbound connectivity, and uses dynamic port allocation that does not have the same SNAT port exhaustion concerns. Wrong (d): Session persistence (Client IP, two-tuple) only changes how inbound flows are distributed across the backend pool; it has no effect on outbound SNAT port allocation. Wrong (e): Floating IP changes inbound destination IP mapping for port reuse scenarios; it allocates no SNAT ports, and with Floating IP enabled the application must still use the primary IP configuration of the NIC for outbound.

sotto_argomento: Troubleshoot load balancing
domanda: An engineer creates a public IP address named pip1 by using the Basic SKU, then attempts to add pip1 as the frontend IP configuration of a newly created Standard Load Balancer named lb1. The operation fails. The application must remain reachable on the IP address that pip1 currently uses. What should you do?
opzione_a: Delete lb1 and recreate it by using the Basic SKU, then associate pip1 with its frontend IP configuration.
opzione_b: Associate pip1 with a NAT gateway and add the NAT gateway to the frontend IP configuration of lb1.
opzione_c: Add pip1 to a new public IP prefix and reference the public IP prefix from the frontend IP configuration of lb1.
opzione_d: Set the allocation method of pip1 to Static, upgrade pip1 to the Standard SKU, and then associate it with the frontend IP configuration of lb1.
spiegazione: Correct (d): The SKU of the public IP must match the SKU of the load balancer. When using a public Standard Load Balancer, the public IP must be Standard; Basic public IPs are not supported on a Standard Load Balancer, and Basic and Standard SKU IPs and load balancers cannot be mixed. Microsoft's upgrade guidance directs you to set the allocation method to Static (otherwise the address is lost when it is disassociated) and then upgrade the public IP to the Standard SKU, which preserves the address. Wrong (a): Basic Load Balancer was retired on September 30, 2025, is unsupported, and carries no SLA, so recreating lb1 as Basic is not an acceptable resolution. Wrong (b): A NAT gateway provides outbound-only connectivity for a subnet; it cannot be used as the frontend IP configuration of a load balancer. Wrong (c): A public IP prefix is a contiguous range of Standard SKU public IP addresses that Azure allocates; you cannot add an existing Basic public IP to a prefix, so this would not preserve the current address.
tags: load balancer,sku mismatch,public ip,standard sku,basic retirement,troubleshooting

sotto_argomento: Troubleshoot load balancing
domanda: After a security team applies a custom network security group (NSG) to the subnet that hosts the backend virtual machines of a Standard Load Balancer, the backend pool health shows every instance as unhealthy and clients receive no response. The NSG contains a custom inbound rule at priority 4000 that denies all traffic. You must restore the health probes with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create an inbound allow rule for the probe port with the source service tag Internet at a priority lower than 4000.
opzione_b: Create an outbound allow rule to destination 168.63.129.16 on the probe port at a priority lower than 4000.
opzione_c: Create a route table with a route for 168.63.129.16/32 that has a next hop type of Internet and associate it with the subnet.
opzione_d: Create an inbound allow rule for the probe port with the source service tag AzureLoadBalancer at a priority lower than 4000.
spiegazione: Correct (d): All IPv4 Load Balancer health probes originate from source IP address 168.63.129.16. The AzureLoadBalancer service tag identifies this source address in an NSG. Because NSG rules are evaluated by priority and a lower number takes precedence, an inbound allow rule for the probe port sourced from the AzureLoadBalancer tag with a priority number lower than 4000 is evaluated before the custom deny-all rule, so probes reach the VMs. Wrong (a): The Internet service tag does not represent 168.63.129.16, which is a virtual public IP of the host node rather than an internet source; the rule would not permit the probe. Wrong (b): The probe is inbound traffic to the virtual machine, so an outbound NSG rule does not unblock it. Wrong (c): 168.63.129.16 is a virtual IP of the host node and is not subject to user-defined routes, so a UDR cannot fix this; the failure is caused by NSG filtering, not routing.

sotto_argomento: Troubleshoot load balancing
domanda:
Litware runs a public Standard Load Balancer named lb1 in front of three web servers. The load-balancing rule forwards TCP port 80 on the frontend to port 80 on the backend, and it references an HTTP health probe that uses port 8080 with a request path of /health. Backend health currently shows all three instances as unhealthy, and you are reviewing the configuration. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true.
1. An HTTP health probe is marked healthy only when the backend instance responds with HTTP status 200 within the timeout period.
2. The configuration is invalid because a health probe must use the same port as the backend port of the load-balancing rule.
3. If you reconfigure the probe to use the HTTPS protocol on port 8080, the certificate chain presented by the backend must use a minimum signature hash of SHA256.
opzione_a: An HTTP health probe is marked healthy only when the backend instance responds with HTTP status 200 within the timeout period.
opzione_b: The configuration is invalid because a health probe must use the same port as the backend port of the load-balancing rule.
opzione_c: If you reconfigure the probe to use the HTTPS protocol on port 8080, the certificate chain presented by the backend must use a minimum signature hash of SHA256.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: An HTTP/HTTPS probe is marked up when the instance responds with HTTP status 200 within the timeout period. Any other response code (such as 403, 404, or 500), no response within the timeout, or a TCP reset causes the probe to fail. Statement 2 - No: The application port and the probe port are not required to be the same. Microsoft's design guidance states that in some scenarios it can be desirable for the probe port to differ from the application port, although using the same port is generally recommended. The probe port must simply be a port the VM is actually listening on, which is the more likely root cause here. Statement 3 - Yes: The HTTPS probe requires the use of certificates that have a minimum signature hash of SHA256 in the entire chain.
tags: load balancer,health probe,http probe,https probe,probe port,troubleshooting

sotto_argomento: Troubleshoot network connectivity
domanda: Case study: Litware Inc. operates two virtual networks in the same subscription. VNet-Prod uses the address space 10.10.0.0/16 and VNet-Shared uses the address space 10.20.0.0/16. The two virtual networks are peered, and both peering links show a status of Connected. To accommodate growth, a network administrator adds a second address range, 10.30.0.0/16, to VNet-Prod and deploys a new subnet and several virtual machines in that range. Virtual machines in VNet-Shared can still reach the virtual machines in the 10.10.0.0/16 range of VNet-Prod, but they cannot reach any virtual machine in the new 10.30.0.0/16 range. The effective routes on a network interface in VNet-Shared contain no route for 10.30.0.0/16. No network security groups or route tables have been changed. What should you do to restore connectivity?
opzione_a: In VNet-Shared, add a user-defined route for 10.30.0.0/16 with a next hop type of Virtual network peering.
opzione_b: Select the peering on VNet-Shared, and then select Sync.
opzione_c: Enable Allow forwarded traffic on both peering links.
opzione_d: Remove the 10.30.0.0/16 address range from VNet-Prod, and then re-add it after deleting the virtual machines.
spiegazione: Correct (b): You can resize the address space of peered virtual networks without downtime, but after the address space is resized, peers must sync with the new address space changes. Until the sync runs, the remote peer does not create system routes for the new range, which exactly matches the symptom of a missing 10.30.0.0/16 route in the effective routes. Microsoft's troubleshooting guidance lists this problem (peered virtual network doesn't reflect modified address ranges; routes for the new address space are missing) with the resolution to select the peering and select Sync, repeating for each remote peer. Microsoft also recommends running the sync after every resize operation. Wrong (a): You cannot specify Virtual network peering as the next hop type in a user-defined route. Azure creates routes with that next hop type automatically when a peering is configured and synced. Wrong (c): Allow forwarded traffic controls whether a virtual network accepts traffic that did not originate in the peered virtual network, which is relevant to NVA service chaining. It does not add missing address-space routes, and connectivity to the original 10.10.0.0/16 range already works without it. Wrong (d): Removing and re-adding the address range is destructive and unnecessary. Resizing already succeeded; only the peer sync is missing. Before removing an address range you would also have to ensure no subnets or resources are deployed in it.

sotto_argomento: Troubleshoot network connectivity
domanda: A virtual network named VNet-App uses the address space 10.0.0.0/16 and is peered with VNet-Data, which uses the address space 10.1.0.0/16. In VNet-App, a subnet named Subnet-Web has a service endpoint enabled for Azure Storage. A route table associated with Subnet-Web contains a single user-defined route: address prefix 0.0.0.0/0, next hop type Virtual appliance, next hop IP address 10.0.100.4. You run the Network Watcher Next hop tool from a virtual machine in Subnet-Web. Select the next hop type that Network Watcher returns for each destination.
opzione_a: Destination 10.1.0.4 (a virtual machine in VNet-Data): [VirtualNetworkPeering | VirtualAppliance | None]
opzione_b: Destination is a public IP address of an Azure Storage account: [VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint | VirtualAppliance | Internet]
opzione_c: Destination 203.0.113.10 (a public IP address on the internet): [Internet | VirtualAppliance | None]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - VirtualNetworkPeering: The peering causes Azure to add a system route for the peered virtual network's 10.1.0.0/16 address range. Because 10.1.0.0/16 is a longer prefix than 0.0.0.0/0, longest prefix match selects the peering route and the UDR never applies. The UDR would only win if it used the same prefix as the peering route. Dropdown 2 - VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint: When you enable a service endpoint, Azure adds routes with the address prefixes for that service to the subnet. Microsoft states that traffic to the service doesn't route to the next hop type in a route with the 0.0.0.0/0 address prefix, because the address prefixes for the service are longer than 0.0.0.0/0. Internet is wrong for the same reason, and these routes can't be overridden even with a route table. Dropdown 3 - VirtualAppliance: The internet address 203.0.113.10 doesn't fall within any other route's prefix, so the 0.0.0.0/0 route is the match. The UDR overrides the default 0.0.0.0/0 system route (whose next hop type is Internet), which Azure marks Invalid, so the traffic is sent to the appliance. None is wrong because no route directs this traffic to be dropped.

sotto_argomento: Troubleshoot network connectivity
domanda: While cleaning up resources, an administrator deleted the peering link named VNetB-to-VNetA from VNetB. On VNetA, the peering link named VNetA-to-VNetB now shows a status of Disconnected, and traffic no longer flows between the two virtual networks. You must restore connectivity between VNetA and VNetB. What should you do?
opzione_a: Delete the remaining peering link on VNetA, and then create a peering link on both VNetA and VNetB.
opzione_b: On VNetA, select the peering and then select Sync.
opzione_c: On VNetB, create a peering link to VNetA. The existing link on VNetA automatically returns to Connected.
opzione_d: On the VNetA peering, clear and then reselect Allow virtual network access, and then select Save.
spiegazione: Correct (a): A Disconnected peering status means one of the two peering links was deleted. Microsoft's guidance is explicit: you must delete the peering from both virtual networks first and then create new peering links, because you cannot re-create a peering while one side is in a Disconnected state. After both links are created, the status becomes Connected on both sides. Wrong (b): Sync is used after you resize or modify the address space of a peered virtual network so the remote peer picks up the new address ranges. It does not repair a Disconnected peering caused by a deleted link. Wrong (c): This describes the Initiated-to-Connected flow that applies when the first link is still valid. It does not work here, because the surviving link is already in the Disconnected state and a new peering cannot be created against it until the stale link is removed. Wrong (d): Allow virtual network access controls whether traffic is permitted across an established peering. Toggling it has no effect when the underlying peering link is Disconnected.

sotto_argomento: Troubleshoot network connectivity
domanda: Users report that a virtual machine named VM1 cannot reach a server with the IP address 10.5.1.4 in a peered virtual network. Before changing any configuration, you must quickly determine the next hop type, the next hop IP address, and the ID of the route table that contains the matching route for traffic from VM1 to 10.5.1.4. Which Azure Network Watcher capability should you use?
opzione_a: IP flow verify
opzione_b: Next hop
opzione_c: Effective security rules
opzione_d: Connection monitor
spiegazione: Correct (b): Next hop is the Network Watcher feature that returns the Next hop type, IP address, and Route table ID for a specific destination IP address, which is exactly what is required. If the matching route is a user-defined route, Next hop returns the route table that contains the route; otherwise it returns System Route as the route table. Wrong (a): IP flow verify detects traffic filtering issues. It checks whether a packet is allowed or denied to or from a VM and names the security rule responsible; it does not report routing or next hop information. Wrong (c): Effective security rules shows the aggregate of network security group rules applied to a network interface and its subnet. It is a filtering diagnostic, not a routing diagnostic. Wrong (d): Connection monitor provides end-to-end connection monitoring over time for Azure and hybrid endpoints. It is intended for ongoing monitoring rather than an immediate point-in-time route lookup, and it does not return a route table ID.

sotto_argomento: Troubleshoot network connectivity
domanda: You are investigating a routing problem for a virtual machine named VM1 that has a single network interface named vm1-nic. From Azure Cloud Shell, you run the following command: Get-AzEffectiveRouteTable -NetworkInterfaceName 'vm1-nic' -ResourceGroupName 'rg-prod' | Format-Table. The command completes without an error, but no routes are returned. What should you do to retrieve the effective routes?
opzione_a: Start VM1, and then run the command again.
opzione_b: Associate a route table with the subnet that contains vm1-nic, and then run the command again.
opzione_c: Register the Microsoft.Network resource provider in the subscription, and then run the command again.
opzione_d: Assign a public IP address to vm1-nic, and then run the command again.
spiegazione: Correct (a): Microsoft documents that output for effective routes is only returned if the VM is in the running state. This applies to the portal, Get-AzEffectiveRouteTable, and az network nic show-effective-route-table. A stopped (deallocated) VM returns no routes, so starting VM1 resolves the issue. Wrong (b): A route table association is not required for effective routes to be returned. Azure automatically creates default system routes for every subnet, so a running VM always shows at least the default routes even with no route table associated. Wrong (c): Microsoft.Network is registered implicitly when the virtual network and network interface are created; the resources already exist, and an unregistered provider would cause an error rather than a silent empty result. Wrong (d): Effective routes describe outbound routing from the subnet and are unrelated to whether the network interface has a public IP address assigned.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Site Recovery for Azure resources
domanda: Contoso replicates production Azure VMs from East US to West US by using Azure Site Recovery. The compliance team requires a quarterly disaster recovery drill that must not disrupt the production workload or the ongoing replication. You plan to use the Test Failover option on the replicated items. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is correct: 1) Running a test failover stops the ongoing replication of the VM until the drill is finished. 2) You should select a non-production virtual network in the target region for the test failover so that IP addresses and networking components remain available in production networks. 3) To delete the VMs created during the drill, select Cleanup test failover on the replicated item and choose Testing is complete.
opzione_a: Running a test failover stops the ongoing replication of the VM until the drill is finished.
opzione_b: You should select a non-production virtual network in the target region for the test failover so that IP addresses and networking components remain available in production networks.
opzione_c: To delete the VMs created during the drill, select Cleanup test failover on the replicated item and choose Testing is complete.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: a test failover is a disaster recovery drill that runs without impacting the production environment; the whole purpose of the drill is to validate the DR plan while replication continues, so replication is not stopped. It is a real (unplanned or planned) failover that stops replication for the VM, and Microsoft explicitly warns not to cancel a failover in progress because replication cannot be restarted. Statement 2 - Yes: the tutorial recommends choosing a non-production network for the drill, and specifically not the network that was created when you enabled replication, so that IP addresses and networking components remain available in production networks. Statement 3 - Yes: after the drill you open the Essentials page, select Cleanup test failover, optionally record notes, and select Testing is complete to delete the VMs created during the test failover. Note that a test failover is never committed - Commit applies only to a real failover.
tags: azure site recovery,test failover,dr drill,cleanup test failover,replication

sotto_argomento: Configure and interpret monitoring of virtual machines, storage accounts, and networks by using Azure Monitor Insights
domanda: Northwind is onboarding 25 Azure virtual machines to the logs-based (classic) VM insights experience so that administrators can view CPU, memory, disk, and network performance charts on the Insights page of each virtual machine. No monitoring components are currently deployed. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Agent extension to install on each virtual machine: [Azure Monitor Agent | Dependency agent | Azure Connected Machine agent]
opzione_b: Object that must be created and linked to each virtual machine before collection starts: [Diagnostic setting | Data collection rule association | Storage account SAS token]
opzione_c: Destination that the logs-based VM insights data collection rule must target: [Azure Storage account | Log Analytics workspace | Azure Monitor workspace]
opzione_d: Table that receives the VM insights performance data: [Perf | InsightsMetrics | VMConnection]
risposta_corretta: Azure Monitor Agent,Data collection rule association,Log Analytics workspace,InsightsMetrics
spiegazione: Correct: Azure Monitor Agent. Learn describes three steps to enable guest monitoring: install the Azure Monitor agent on each machine, create data collection rules, and associate the DCRs with the VMs. The Dependency agent is wrong because it only supports the VM insights Map feature (process and dependency discovery), it is not needed for performance charts, and Learn states the Dependency Agent and the Map experience are deprecated and retire on 30 June 2028. The Azure Connected Machine agent is wrong because it is only required for machines hosted outside Azure that must first be onboarded to Azure Arc; these are already Azure virtual machines. Correct: Data collection rule association. Learn states 'When you create an association between a VM and a DCR, the agent downloads that DCR and begins data collection.' A diagnostic setting is wrong because it exports platform metrics and resource logs from the Azure resource, not guest OS data from the agent. A SAS token is unrelated to agent data collection. Correct: Log Analytics workspace. Learn lists 'Log Analytics workspace if you enable logs-based metrics or collect logs', and the published logs-based VM insights DCR sends the Microsoft-InsightsMetrics stream to a logAnalytics destination. An Azure Monitor workspace is the destination for the newer OpenTelemetry metrics experience, not the logs-based classic experience, which makes it the strongest distractor. A storage account is not a valid DCR destination for this experience. Correct: InsightsMetrics. The logs-based VM insights DCR declares the stream Microsoft-InsightsMetrics with the counter specifier \VmInsights\DetailedMetrics, which lands in the InsightsMetrics table. Perf is wrong because it is populated by custom performance counter DCRs, not by the VM insights DCR. VMConnection is wrong because it is one of the Map tables written by the Dependency agent, along with VMComputer, VMProcess, and VMBoundPort.
tags: vm insights,azure monitor agent,data collection rule,insightsmetrics,log analytics workspace,dependency agent

sotto_argomento: Configure and interpret monitoring of virtual machines, storage accounts, and networks by using Azure Monitor Insights
domanda: Contoso has 40 storage accounts spread across three subscriptions. A storage administrator wants to open Azure Monitor, select Storage accounts under Insights, and immediately review availability, transaction counts, end-to-end latency, and used capacity across all of the accounts. Nothing has been configured for monitoring on any of the storage accounts. What must you do first so that the Storage insights workbooks display data?
opzione_a: Nothing. Storage insights uses the platform metrics that Azure Storage emits by default.
opzione_b: Create a diagnostic setting on each storage account that sends the Transaction metric to a Log Analytics workspace.
opzione_c: Install the Azure Monitor Agent on a virtual machine and associate it with a data collection rule that targets the storage accounts.
opzione_d: Enable Azure Storage analytics logging (classic) on each storage account.
spiegazione: Correct (a): Storage insights does not require you to enable or configure anything. The Learn documentation states explicitly that 'This feature does not require you to enable or configure anything, the storage metrics from your storage accounts are collected by default.' The workbooks read those platform metrics directly, so the Overview, Capacity, Availability, Performance, and Failures workbooks populate as soon as you open them. Wrong (b): Diagnostic settings route metrics or resource logs to a Log Analytics workspace for KQL querying, but Storage insights does not read from a workspace and works without any diagnostic setting. Wrong (c): The Azure Monitor Agent and data collection rules collect guest data from virtual machines, virtual machine scale sets, and Arc-enabled servers. Storage accounts are platform-as-a-service resources with no guest OS and cannot be targeted by a DCR association. Wrong (d): Storage analytics logging (classic) writes logs to $logs in the account itself; it is a legacy feature and is not the data source for Storage insights.
tags: storage insights,azure monitor,workbooks,platform metrics,storage account monitoring

sotto_argomento: Configure and interpret reports and alerts for backups
domanda: Fabrikam has Recovery Services vaults in several subscriptions and regions. A backup administrator must use Backup Reports to analyze job success and cloud storage consumption across the whole estate for the last 90 days, and wants to understand the configuration requirements and expected behavior before rolling it out. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: To send reporting data from each vault, configure: [A diagnostic setting on the Recovery Services vault | A metric alert rule on the Recovery Services vault | An alert processing rule on the Recovery Services vault]
opzione_b: The Log Analytics workspace that stores the reporting data can be located: [Only in the same region and subscription as the vaults | In any region and subscription, independent of the vaults | Only in the same subscription as the vaults]
opzione_c: After diagnostics are configured, the initial data push can take up to: [15 minutes | 1 hour | 24 hours]
opzione_d: To keep 90 days of history, change the Log Analytics workspace retention, which defaults to: [7 days | 30 days | 90 days]
risposta_corretta: A diagnostic setting on the Recovery Services vault,In any region and subscription, independent of the vaults,24 hours,30 days
spiegazione: Correct - diagnostic setting: Recovery Services vaults record scheduled and user-triggered operations as diagnostics data; in the Monitoring section of the vault you select Diagnostics settings and specify the Log Analytics workspace as the target. An Azure Policy definition can automate this at scale. Wrong - metric alert rule / alert processing rule: metric alert rules and alert processing rules belong to the alerting pipeline (evaluating signals and routing notifications) and do not export historical data to a workspace for reporting. Correct - any region and subscription: the documentation states that the location and subscription where the Log Analytics workspace is created is independent of the location and subscription where the vaults exist, which is what allows a single consolidated report. Wrong - the two restrictive options contradict this. Correct - 24 hours: after configuring diagnostics it might take up to 24 hours for the initial data push to complete, and Microsoft recommends viewing reports two days after configuration since the current partial day isn't shown. Wrong - 15 minutes / 1 hour: these underestimate the documented initial latency. Correct - 30 days: by default, data in a Log Analytics workspace is retained for 30 days, so you must change the retention period to see a longer time horizon such as 90 days. Wrong - 7 days / 90 days: these are not the default workspace retention.

sotto_argomento: Configure and interpret reports and alerts for backups
domanda: Recovery Services vault RSV1 protects 40 Azure VMs. You must ensure that the backup operations team receives an email message whenever a backup job for any item in RSV1 fails, by using the built-in Azure Monitor alerts that Azure Backup provides. Which three actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Create an action group that contains an email action with the operations team's addresses.
opzione_b: Create an alert processing rule (action rule) scoped to RSV1 and associate it with the action group.
opzione_c: Verify that Azure Monitor alerts for job failure scenarios are turned on for RSV1.
opzione_d: Configure a diagnostic setting on RSV1 to send the AzureBackupReport category to a Log Analytics workspace.
opzione_e: Enable Alerts (classic) in the Backup Alerts tab of RSV1 and add the operations team as recipients.
spiegazione: Correct - option A: Azure Monitor routes notifications through action groups, so an action group with an email action is required to deliver the message. Correct - option B: built-in Azure Monitor alerts for Azure Backup are fired automatically but do not send notifications on their own; you use Azure Monitor action rules (alert processing rules) together with action groups to route the alerts to a notification channel such as email. Correct - option C: backup failure alerts are Job Failure alerts (Sev 1) and, unlike security alerts, they can be turned off, so you must confirm that Azure Monitor alerts for job failure scenarios are enabled for the vault. Wrong - option D: sending AzureBackupReport diagnostics to a Log Analytics workspace powers Backup Reports and custom Log Analytics based alert rules; it is not required for the built-in Azure Monitor alerts described here. Wrong - option E: classic alerts are the older solution, they don't appear in Azure Monitor, and Microsoft is deprecating them (retirement announced for 31 March 2026) with a recommendation to migrate to Azure Monitor alerts.
tags: azure backup,azure monitor,alerts,action group,alert processing rule,notifications

sotto_argomento: Configure log settings in Azure Monitor
domanda: A security team must be able to run KQL queries against every category of resource log produced by a key vault named kv-contoso-prod, and must also be able to query the key vault's platform metrics in the same workspace. The configuration must automatically include any new log category that Microsoft adds to Key Vault in the future, and must use the fewest possible diagnostic settings. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Log category group to select: [audit | allLogs | verbose]
opzione_b: Metric category to select: [AllMetrics | ServiceApiHit | Availability]
opzione_c: Destination to select: [Azure Storage account | Log Analytics workspace | Azure Event Hubs namespace]
opzione_d: Number of diagnostic settings required: [1 | 2 | 3]
spiegazione: Correct: The allLogs category group collects all categories for the resource, and because Microsoft maintains the group definition, log collection is modified automatically when categories are added. AllMetrics is the metric category used to collect platform metrics through a diagnostic setting; metric categories other than AllMetrics aren't supported for the vast majority of Azure services. A Log Analytics workspace is the only destination that supports KQL log queries. A single diagnostic setting can define one destination of each type and can include both logs and metrics, so one setting is sufficient. Why the other options are wrong: The audit category group collects only the resource logs that record customer interactions with data or service settings, which is a subset of allLogs and would miss other categories. 'verbose' is not an Azure Monitor category group. ServiceApiHit and Availability are individual Key Vault metric names, not selectable diagnostic setting metric categories. An Azure Storage account destination supports archival only and an Azure Event Hubs namespace only streams data out of Azure; neither supports KQL. Two or three settings would be needed only if you were targeting multiple destinations of the same type.

sotto_argomento: Configure log settings in Azure Monitor
domanda: You must collect all resource log categories from a network security group named nsg-web and make them queryable with KQL. No Log Analytics workspace exists in the subscription yet. Arrange the following actions in the correct order to complete the configuration by using the Azure portal.
opzione_a: Select Save, then allow up to 90 minutes for data to begin flowing to the destination.
opzione_b: Create the Log Analytics workspace that will receive the data.
opzione_c: Select Add diagnostic setting and provide a descriptive name for the setting.
opzione_d: On the nsg-web menu, select Diagnostic settings in the Monitoring section.
opzione_e: Select the allLogs category group, select Send to Log Analytics workspace, and choose the workspace.
spiegazione: Correct order: (1) Create the Log Analytics workspace, because the destination resource must already exist before you create the diagnostic setting. (2) Open Diagnostic settings from the Monitoring section of the nsg-web resource menu, which is the documented entry point for creating a resource-scoped setting. (3) Select Add diagnostic setting and give it a descriptive name. (4) Choose the allLogs category group so that every resource log category is collected, then select Send to Log Analytics workspace and pick the workspace. (5) Save the setting; after creation, data should start flowing to the selected destination within 90 minutes, and the destination table is created automatically when the first records arrive. Common ordering errors: attempting to select the workspace before it exists causes it to be unavailable in the destination picker, and naming the setting is only possible after selecting Add diagnostic setting.
tags: azure monitor,diagnostic settings,network security group,alllogs,log analytics workspace,portal

sotto_argomento: Configure log settings in Azure Monitor
domanda: An auditor needs to determine which user created a specific virtual machine two years ago. Your organization has not changed any monitoring defaults on the subscription. Select the appropriate option to complete each statement about the Azure activity log.
opzione_a: Default retention of activity log events: [30 days | 90 days | 93 days]
opzione_b: Destination required to retain activity log events for two years: [Azure Monitor workspace | Log Analytics workspace | Azure Monitor metrics store]
opzione_c: Table that stores exported activity log data: [AzureActivity | AzureDiagnostics | AzureMetrics]
spiegazione: Correct: Azure retains activity log events for 90 days and then deletes them, at no charge regardless of volume. To keep them longer you create a diagnostic setting that exports the activity log to a Log Analytics workspace, where retention can be increased up to 12 years and there are no ingestion charges for activity logs. Exported activity log data lands in the AzureActivity table. Why the other options are wrong: 30 days is not an activity log retention value, and 93 days is the retention of platform and custom metrics, not of the activity log. An Azure Monitor workspace stores Prometheus metrics and is not an activity log destination; the Azure Monitor metrics store holds numeric time-series data, not log records. AzureDiagnostics is the table used by resource logs collected in Azure diagnostics collection mode, and AzureMetrics holds exported platform metrics; neither receives activity log entries.

sotto_argomento: Configure log settings in Azure Monitor
domanda: Fabrikam has an Azure Application Gateway named agw-prod deployed in the West US region in a subscription named Sub1. A central operations team owns a Log Analytics workspace named law-central in a different subscription named Sub2, in the East US region. You have appropriate Azure RBAC permissions on both subscriptions. You plan to create diagnostic settings for agw-prod. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true. 1. A single diagnostic setting on agw-prod can send the resource logs to two different Log Analytics workspaces. 2. law-central must be in the West US region because agw-prod is a regional resource. 3. law-central can be used as the destination even though it is in a different subscription than agw-prod.
opzione_a: A single diagnostic setting on agw-prod can send the resource logs to two different Log Analytics workspaces.
opzione_b: law-central must be in the West US region because agw-prod is a regional resource.
opzione_c: law-central can be used as the destination even though it is in a different subscription than agw-prod.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No: a single diagnostic setting can define no more than one destination of each type. To send data to two Log Analytics workspaces you must create two separate diagnostic settings, which is permitted because each resource supports up to five settings. Statement 2 is No: the same-region requirement applies only to Azure Storage account and Azure Event Hubs destinations for regional resources. A Log Analytics workspace destination is not subject to that constraint, so law-central can remain in East US. Statement 3 is Yes: the destination does not have to be in the same subscription as the resource sending the logs, provided the user configuring the setting has appropriate Azure RBAC access to both subscriptions, which is stated in the scenario. For destinations in another Microsoft Entra tenant, Azure Lighthouse would be used.

sotto_argomento: Configure log settings in Azure Monitor
domanda: Contoso runs an Azure SQL database in the West Europe region. For long-term archival you attempt to create a diagnostic setting that sends the database resource logs to an existing Standard general-purpose v2 storage account located in North Europe, but the storage account cannot be selected as a destination. You must archive the logs to Azure Storage with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create a Standard storage account in the West Europe region and select it as the destination.
opzione_b: Create a Premium block blob storage account in North Europe and select it as the destination.
opzione_c: Enable the Allow trusted Microsoft services exception on the North Europe storage account.
opzione_d: Create a second diagnostic setting on the database that targets the North Europe storage account.
spiegazione: Correct: For a regional resource, an Azure Storage account destination must be in the same region as the monitored resource. Because the SQL database is in West Europe, you must create a Standard storage account in West Europe. Why the others are wrong: A Premium block blob storage account is explicitly unsupported as a diagnostic setting destination (only Standard storage accounts are supported), and it would still be in the wrong region. The Allow trusted Microsoft services exception solves a different problem: it lets diagnostic settings reach a storage account whose firewall or virtual network rules are enabled. It does not lift the same-region requirement. Creating an additional diagnostic setting does not help, because the per-setting region requirement is identical no matter how many settings you create.

sotto_argomento: Configure log settings in Azure Monitor
domanda: An application team must correlate Azure Application Gateway resource logs with data from other Azure services by writing Kusto Query Language (KQL) queries, and must raise log alerts when specific patterns appear. You are creating a diagnostic setting for the application gateway. Which destination meets both requirements?
opzione_a: An Azure Storage account
opzione_b: A Log Analytics workspace
opzione_c: An Azure Event Hubs namespace
opzione_d: An Azure Monitor partner solution
spiegazione: Correct: A Log Analytics workspace is the only diagnostic setting destination that lets you retrieve data with KQL log queries, build workbooks, and create log alert rules on the ingested records. Why the others are wrong: An Azure Storage account is intended for archival, static analysis, and backup; logs land as PT1H.json blobs and cannot be queried with KQL or used as the source of a log alert rule. An Azure Event Hubs namespace streams the data out of Azure to external systems such as a third-party SIEM; it provides no query engine or alerting. An Azure Monitor partner solution forwards data to a non-Microsoft observability platform, so any querying and alerting happens in that partner product, not through Azure Monitor log alerts.
tags: azure monitor,diagnostic settings,log analytics workspace,kql,log alerts

sotto_argomento: Configure log settings in Azure Monitor
domanda: You are documenting the destinations that an Azure Monitor diagnostic setting can send platform logs and platform metrics to. Which three of the following are valid diagnostic setting destinations? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A Log Analytics workspace
opzione_b: An Azure Storage account
opzione_c: An Azure Service Bus queue
opzione_d: An Azure Event Hubs namespace
opzione_e: An Azure Cosmos DB container
spiegazione: Correct: A diagnostic setting can send data to a Log Analytics workspace (for KQL queries, workbooks, and log alerts), an Azure Storage account (for archive, static analysis, or backup), and an Azure Event Hubs namespace (to stream data to external systems such as a third-party SIEM). Azure Monitor partner solutions are the fourth supported destination type. Why the others are wrong: An Azure Service Bus queue is not a diagnostic setting destination; Event Hubs is the streaming destination Azure Monitor supports, and the two services are commonly confused. An Azure Cosmos DB container is not a destination either; Cosmos DB is a source that can emit resource logs through its own diagnostic setting, not a target for them.

sotto_argomento: Configure log settings in Azure Monitor
domanda: Your team wants to route the resource logs of a single Azure key vault to several independent destinations, and each team owns its own Log Analytics workspace. What is the maximum number of diagnostic settings you can create on a single Azure resource?
spiegazione: Correct: Each Azure resource can have up to five diagnostic settings. Because a single diagnostic setting can define no more than one destination of each type, you create multiple settings when you need to send data to two or more Log Analytics workspaces. Why the others are wrong: '1' reflects the outdated legacy behaviour where only a single setting existed per resource; multiple settings have been supported for years. '3' is not a documented limit and is often confused with the three classic destination types (workspace, storage, event hub). '10' exceeds the documented per-resource limit of five.

sotto_argomento: Create a Recovery Services vault
domanda: You are preparing a new Recovery Services vault named RSV-Prod that will protect Azure virtual machines and SQL Server instances running in Azure VMs. No backups have been configured yet. Select the correct answer for each statement.
opzione_a: Default storage replication type of a newly created Recovery Services vault: [Locally-redundant | Geo-redundant | Zone-redundant]
opzione_b: The storage replication type of RSV-Prod can be modified: [At any time | Only before any backup is configured in the vault | Only after the first backup completes]
opzione_c: Vault type required to protect SQL Server running in an Azure VM: [Backup vault | Recovery Services vault | Either vault type]
opzione_d: The vault must be created in: [Any region in the subscription | The same region as the datasource | The paired region of the datasource]
risposta_corretta: Geo-redundant,Only before any backup is configured in the vault,Recovery Services vault,The same region as the datasource
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - Geo-redundant: Microsoft Learn states that the storage replication type is by default set to geo-redundant storage (GRS), which is the default and recommended replication option; GRS replicates backup data to a secondary region hundreds of miles away. Locally-redundant and Zone-redundant are valid choices you can select, but neither is the default. Dropdown 2 - Only before any backup is configured in the vault: 'Be sure to change the storage replication type for a Recovery Services vault before you configure a backup in the vault. After you configure a backup, the option to modify is disabled.' 'At any time' and 'Only after the first backup completes' are wrong because configuring a backup permanently disables the control. Dropdown 3 - Recovery Services vault: SQL in Azure VM is listed as a Recovery Services vault datasource. A Backup vault supports only Azure Disks, Azure Blobs, Azure Database for PostgreSQL server, and Kubernetes services, so 'Backup vault' and 'Either vault type' are wrong. Dropdown 4 - The same region as the datasource: Learn states 'For you to create a vault to help protect any data source, the vault must be in the same region as the data source.' The Configure Backup wizard only lists VMs in the same region as the vault, so 'Any region' is wrong; the paired region is only used as a Cross Region Restore target, not as the vault location.
tags: recovery services vault,grs default,storage redundancy,sql in azure vm,vault region

sotto_argomento: Create a Recovery Services vault
domanda:
Fabrikam creates a Recovery Services vault named RSV1 in the East US region by accepting all the default settings, and immediately configures backup for 10 Azure virtual machines. The compliance team now asks whether restores can be triggered in the paired region on demand, and the finance team asks whether backup storage costs can be lowered. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
1. You can change the storage replication type of RSV1 from Geo-redundant to Locally-redundant on the vault's Backup Configuration pane.
2. Because RSV1 uses the default replication type, Cross Region Restore can be enabled on RSV1.
3. Enabling Cross Region Restore on RSV1 upgrades the vault's backup storage to read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS).
opzione_a: You can change the storage replication type of RSV1 from Geo-redundant to Locally-redundant on the vault's Backup Configuration pane.
opzione_b: Because RSV1 uses the default replication type, Cross Region Restore can be enabled on RSV1.
opzione_c: Enabling Cross Region Restore on RSV1 upgrades the vault's backup storage to read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS).
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: Backup was already configured for the 10 VMs. Microsoft Learn states 'Be sure to change the storage replication type for a Recovery Services vault before you configure a backup in the vault. After you configure a backup, the option to modify is disabled.' To actually move to LRS, Fabrikam must either stop protection and delete the data in the GRS vault and reconfigure backup in a new LRS vault, or stop protection with retained data and protect the VMs in a new LRS vault (which requires moving each VM to another resource group and paying to keep the old recovery points). Statement 2 - Yes: The default (and recommended) storage replication type for a new Recovery Services vault is Geo-redundant, and Cross Region Restore is supported only for a Recovery Services vault that uses the GRS replication type. CRR is enabled at the vault level under Properties > Backup Configuration > Cross Region Restore > Enable; after enabling it, backup items can take up to 48 hours to become available in the secondary region. Statement 3 - Yes: The Azure Backup glossary states 'For GRS vaults that have the cross-region restore feature enabled, backup storage is upgraded from GRS to RA-GRS (Read-Access Geo-Redundant Storage).' This is what allows reads from the secondary region without Azure declaring a disaster, and it incurs extra charges.
tags: recovery services vault,storage redundancy,cross region restore,ra-grs,grs to lrs

sotto_argomento: Create a Recovery Services vault
domanda: Six months ago, an administrator created a Recovery Services vault named RSV-Legacy with the default settings and configured backup for 40 Azure virtual machines. An on-premises tape system is the company's primary backup endpoint, so Azure backup storage costs must now be reduced by moving the vault's backup data to locally-redundant storage. The existing recovery points do not need to be preserved. What should you do?
opzione_a: In RSV-Legacy, open Properties > Backup Configuration > Update and set the storage replication type to Locally-redundant.
opzione_b: Run Set-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProperty and set the BackupStorageRedundancy parameter of RSV-Legacy to LocallyRedundant.
opzione_c: Disable soft delete on RSV-Legacy, stop protection and delete the backup data for the 40 VMs, create a new vault configured for Locally-redundant storage, and reconfigure backup for the VMs in the new vault.
opzione_d: Move RSV-Legacy to a new resource group, then set the storage replication type to Locally-redundant during the move operation.
spiegazione: Correct (c): Once a backup is configured in a Recovery Services vault, the storage replication type can no longer be modified, and Azure Backup cannot migrate existing recovery points between replication types or move backup data to a different vault. Microsoft Learn's documented workaround, when previous backup data does not need to be preserved, is to disable soft delete in the GRS vault, stop protection and delete the backups from the existing vault, and then configure backups for the workload in a new LRS vault. Disabling soft delete is required first, because otherwise deleted backup data is retained in a soft-deleted state. (a) is wrong: the Update control on the Backup Configuration pane is disabled after a backup has been configured, so this cannot be performed in the portal. (b) is wrong: the same service-side restriction applies to Az PowerShell, the CLI, and the REST API - the limitation is not a portal UI limitation, so the cmdlet fails for a vault with protected items. (d) is wrong: moving a vault between resource groups or subscriptions is supported, but it has no effect on the storage replication type and does not unlock the setting.
tags: recovery services vault,grs to lrs,storage redundancy,soft delete,stop protection,troubleshooting

sotto_argomento: Create a Recovery Services vault
domanda: An auditor requires that your team be able to restore Azure VM backups into the Azure paired region on demand, to run compliance drills without waiting for Microsoft to declare a disaster in the primary region. You are creating a new Recovery Services vault for this workload. Which storage replication type must you select before you configure any backups?
opzione_a: Locally-redundant
opzione_b: Zone-redundant
opzione_c: Geo-redundant
opzione_d: Geo-zone-redundant
spiegazione: Correct (c): Cross Region Restore (CRR) lets you restore data in a secondary Azure paired region at any time you choose, including for audit-compliance drills, without waiting for Azure to declare a disaster. Microsoft Learn states 'Cross Region Restore is supported only for a Recovery Services vault that uses the GRS replication type.' Because the replication type cannot be changed after backup is configured, Geo-redundant must be selected first. (a) is wrong: LRS keeps three copies within a single datacenter scale unit in the primary region - there is no secondary-region copy to restore from. (b) is wrong: ZRS replicates across availability zones within the same region, guaranteeing data residency; it enables Cross Zonal Restore, not Cross Region Restore. (d) is wrong: Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) is a real Azure Storage redundancy option, but the Recovery Services vault Backup Configuration pane offers only Geo-redundant, Locally-redundant, and Zone-redundant. Note that when CRR is enabled on a GRS vault, backup storage is upgraded to read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS).
tags: cross region restore,crr,grs,recovery services vault,storage redundancy,paired region

sotto_argomento: Create a Recovery Services vault
domanda: A colleague creates a Recovery Services vault named RSV1 by accepting all the default settings. Your company does not use Azure as its primary backup storage endpoint, so RSV1 must store its backup data in locally-redundant storage to reduce cost. When can you change the storage replication type of RSV1?
opzione_a: At any time. Azure Backup automatically migrates the existing recovery points to the new replication type.
opzione_b: Only before a backup is configured in the vault.
opzione_c: Only after the first backup job has completed successfully.
opzione_d: Only while the vault contains no backup policies.
spiegazione: Correct (b): Microsoft Learn explicitly states 'Be sure to change the storage replication type for a Recovery Services vault before you configure a backup in the vault. After you configure a backup, the option to modify is disabled.' The setting is found under Settings > Properties > Backup Configuration > Update, where you choose Geo-redundant (the default), Locally-redundant, or Zone-redundant. (a) is wrong: the option is disabled once backup is configured, and Azure Backup never migrates existing recovery points between replication types; moving from GRS to LRS requires stopping protection and deleting the data, or protecting the workload in a new LRS vault. (c) is wrong: it inverts the rule - completing a backup is exactly what locks the setting. (d) is wrong: the trigger is configuring a backup (creating a protected item), not the presence of policies. Every vault also contains default, system-managed backup policies that cannot be permanently deleted, so this condition could never be met.

sotto_argomento: Create a Recovery Services vault
domanda: Your team is standardizing on the correct Azure Backup vault type per workload. Which datasources can be protected directly in a Recovery Services vault? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: An Azure file share
opzione_b: SAP HANA running in an Azure VM
opzione_c: A container in an Azure Blob Storage account
opzione_d: An Azure Database for PostgreSQL server
opzione_e: A standalone Azure managed disk
spiegazione: Correct (a, b): Microsoft Learn lists the Recovery Services vault datasources as Azure Virtual Machine, SQL in Azure VM, Azure Files, SAP HANA in Azure VM, Azure Backup Server, Azure Backup agent (MARS), and DPM. Azure file shares (a) and SAP HANA in Azure VM (b) are both on that list. (c) is wrong: Azure Blobs are a Backup vault datasource. (d) is wrong: Azure Database for PostgreSQL server is a Backup vault datasource - it is in fact the workload Backup vaults were first introduced for. (e) is wrong: Azure Disks are a Backup vault datasource; standalone managed disks are protected through Azure Disk Backup, which uses a Backup vault and stores incremental snapshots in a snapshot resource group in your own subscription. Note the distinction from Azure VM backup, which protects the whole VM (including its disks) through a Recovery Services vault.
tags: recovery services vault,backup vault,datasources,azure files,sap hana,vault types

sotto_argomento: Create a Recovery Services vault
domanda: Your governance team asks how long backup data remains recoverable after a backup item is deleted from a Recovery Services vault when soft delete is in effect, and whether that window can be extended. What is the default soft-delete retention period, and what is the maximum value you can configure?
opzione_a: Default 14 days; can be extended up to 180 days
opzione_b: Default 7 days; can be extended up to 30 days
opzione_c: Default 30 days; can be extended up to 90 days
opzione_d: Default 14 days; the value is fixed and cannot be changed
spiegazione: Correct: Default 14 days; up to 180 days. Azure Backup soft delete retains deleted backup data in a soft-deleted state for 14 days by default, and you can configure a soft-delete retention period between 14 and 180 days. There is no retention cost for the default 14-day duration; regular backup charges apply to any retention days beyond 14. Wrong - Default 7 days, up to 30 days: these values match neither the default nor the configurable ceiling; 7 days is the minimum daily recovery point retention for MARS, not soft delete. Wrong - Default 30 days, up to 90 days: 30 days is the default data retention of a Log Analytics workspace, not the soft-delete window. Wrong - Default 14 days, fixed: the default is correct, but soft-delete retention is explicitly configurable from 14 to 180 days; what you cannot do in secure-by-default regions is disable soft delete altogether.
tags: azure backup,soft delete,recovery services vault,retention,secure by default

sotto_argomento: Create an Azure Backup vault
domanda: You must protect a standalone Azure managed disk named disk-data01 by using Azure Disk Backup. You plan to create the required vault, a backup policy, and a dedicated resource group that will hold the incremental snapshots. Select the correct answer for each statement.
opzione_a: Vault type you must create: [Recovery Services vault | Backup vault | Either vault type]
opzione_b: Recovery points created by Azure Disk Backup are stored in: [The operational (snapshot) tier only | The vault-standard tier only | Both the snapshot tier and the vault-standard tier]
opzione_c: Role to assign to the vault managed identity on disk-data01: [Disk Backup Reader | Disk Snapshot Contributor | Storage Blob Data Contributor]
opzione_d: Role to assign to the vault managed identity on the snapshot resource group: [Disk Backup Reader | Disk Snapshot Contributor | Backup Contributor]
risposta_corretta: Backup vault,The operational (snapshot) tier only,Disk Backup Reader,Disk Snapshot Contributor
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - Backup vault: Azure Disks are a Backup vault datasource; Recovery Services vaults do not support standalone managed disks, so 'Recovery Services vault' and 'Either vault type' are wrong. Dropdown 2 - The operational (snapshot) tier only: Microsoft Learn states 'Azure Disk backup supports only the operational tier backup. Copying of backups to the vault storage tier is currently not supported.' Consequently the Backup vault storage redundancy setting (LRS/GRS) does not apply to these recovery points - incremental snapshots are stored on Standard HDD storage in your snapshot resource group, and on ZRS by default in ZRS-supported regions. The other two options describe Azure VM backup behaviour, not Disk Backup. Dropdown 3 - Disk Backup Reader: Learn states 'Assign the Disk Backup Reader role to Backup Vault's managed identity on the Source disk that needs to be backed up.' Storage Blob Data Contributor is a data-plane role for blob storage and is irrelevant here. Dropdown 4 - Disk Snapshot Contributor: Learn states 'Assign the Disk Snapshot Contributor role to the Backup vault's managed identity on the Resource group where backups are created and managed by the Azure Backup service.' Disk Backup Reader belongs on the source disk, and Backup Contributor is a Recovery Services vault management role, not a snapshot-datastore role.
tags: azure disk backup,backup vault,operational tier,disk backup reader,disk snapshot contributor,managed identity

sotto_argomento: Create an Azure Backup vault
domanda: Contoso plans to use Azure Backup to protect an Azure Database for PostgreSQL server and a container in an Azure Blob Storage account. Both resources are located in the East US region. You need to identify the minimum vault configuration required to protect both datasources. What should you create?
opzione_a: One Recovery Services vault in East US
opzione_b: One Backup vault in East US
opzione_c: One Recovery Services vault and one Backup vault in East US
opzione_d: Two Recovery Services vaults in East US, one per datasource type
spiegazione: Correct (b): Azure Backup supports two vault types that target different datasources. A Backup vault (Microsoft.DataProtection/BackupVaults) is the vault used for the newer workloads, and its supported datasources include Azure Disks, Azure Blobs, Azure Database for PostgreSQL server, and Kubernetes services. Because both an Azure Database for PostgreSQL server and Azure Blobs are Backup vault datasources, a single Backup vault in the same region as the resources is sufficient. (a) is wrong: a Recovery Services vault supports Azure VMs, SQL in Azure VM, Azure Files, SAP HANA in Azure VM, MARS agent, Azure Backup Server (MABS), and DPM - it cannot protect PostgreSQL servers or Blobs. (c) is wrong: it is unnecessary, because neither datasource requires a Recovery Services vault; the requirement asks for the minimum configuration. (d) is wrong: it doubles the wrong vault type; Recovery Services vaults do not support either of these datasources, and a single vault can hold multiple datasource types anyway.
tags: azure backup,backup vault,recovery services vault,postgresql,blob backup,vault types

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a backup policy
domanda: You are authoring a grandfather-father-son (GFS) backup policy of subtype Standard for the Azure virtual machines of a regulated business unit. The policy takes one backup per day, and the retention requirements for daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly recovery points are still being negotiated with the compliance team. Select the correct answer for each statement.
opzione_a: Maximum Instant Restore snapshot retention configurable on this policy: [2 days | 5 days | 7 days | 30 days]
opzione_b: Minimum retention range supported for a daily backup point: [1 day | 7 days | 30 days]
opzione_c: Maximum retention configurable for daily recovery points: [180 days | 372 days | 9999 days]
opzione_d: The Instant Restore snapshot retention compared with the vault retention duration: [Can exceed it | Cannot exceed it | Must be identical to it]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - 5 days: For the Standard policy, the default snapshot retention is 2 days and it is configurable from a minimum of 1 day to a maximum of 5 days. 7 days is the Enhanced policy default and 30 days is the Enhanced policy maximum, so neither is available on a Standard policy. (Note: for weekly Standard policies the snapshot retention is fixed at 5 days.) Dropdown 2 - 7 days: Microsoft Learn states 'Azure Virtual Machine backup policy supports a minimum retention range from seven days up to 9999 days', and any modification to an existing VM backup policy with less than seven days requires an update to meet the seven-day minimum. 1 day is the Instant Restore snapshot minimum, not the vault retention minimum. Dropdown 3 - 9999 days: The documented maximum retentions for Azure VM backup points are 9999 days (daily), 5163 weeks (weekly), 1188 months (monthly), and 99 years (yearly). 180 days is only the default daily vault retention, and 372 days is the number of days a 12-month monthly retention actually covers (Azure Backup counts 31 days per month, so 31 x 12 = 372). Dropdown 4 - Cannot exceed it: Learn states 'Instant restore retention duration cannot exceed vault retention duration', and the retention model does not allow deleting the vault restore point (tier 2) unless the snapshot (tier 1) is deleted - Microsoft therefore recommends scheduling a vault retention period greater than the snapshot retention period.
tags: gfs,backup policy,retention,instant restore,snapshot retention,azure vm backup

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a backup policy
domanda: You are evaluating whether to adopt the Enhanced backup policy subtype for Azure virtual machine backups in a Recovery Services vault. Which three statements about the Enhanced policy are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: The backup schedule can be set to Hourly with an interval of 4, 6, 8, 12, or 24 hours.
opzione_b: Instant Restore snapshot retention can be configured up to 30 days.
opzione_c: Backup and instant restore of Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disks are supported.
opzione_d: After a VM is protected with an Enhanced policy, the policy type can be changed back to Standard.
opzione_e: The Enhanced policy writes recovery points only to the vault-standard tier and does not create local snapshots.
spiegazione: Correct (a, b, c): (a) With the Enhanced policy the backup schedule can be Hourly, Daily, or Weekly; for Hourly you can set the backup schedule to 4, 6, 8, 12, or 24 hours, giving a minimum RPO of 4 hours and a maximum of 24 hours. (b) The Enhanced policy allows Instant Restore snapshot retention from 1 to 30 days, with a default of 7 days - versus 1 to 5 days (default 2) for the Standard policy. The exact maximum depends on the hourly frequency chosen, because a higher snapshot count per day reduces the maximum allowed days, and instant restore retention cannot exceed the vault retention duration. (c) Microsoft Learn states the Enhanced policy supports backup and instant restore of Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disks, in addition to Standard HDD, Standard SSD, and Premium SSD v1 - the Standard policy does not support these newer offerings. (d) is wrong: Learn states 'Backup doesn't allow changing the policy type to Standard after you enable a VM backup with the Enhanced policy.' (e) is wrong: this describes the opposite of Instant Restore, which is enabled for everyone and cannot be disabled. The Enhanced policy uses managed disk snapshots stored alongside the disks for Instant Restore (the initial snapshot is a full copy, subsequent ones are incremental), in addition to the copy transferred to the vault-standard tier.
tags: enhanced policy,backup policy,instant restore,ultra disk,premium ssd v2,hourly backup

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a backup policy
domanda: You must protect a Trusted Launch virtual machine named VM-TL01 that runs in the West Europe region. The backup data must remain resilient to a single availability zone failure while guaranteeing data residency within West Europe, and the VM must be backed up multiple times per day. No Recovery Services vault exists yet. Drag the four actions into the correct sequence.
opzione_a: Configure backup for VM-TL01 and assign the Enhanced policy.
opzione_b: Create a Recovery Services vault in the West Europe region.
opzione_c: On the vault's Backup Configuration pane, set the storage replication type to Zone-redundant.
opzione_d: Create a backup policy of subtype Enhanced with an Hourly schedule.
spiegazione: Correct order: b, c, d, a. Step 1 (b): The vault must exist first, and it must be in the same region as the datasource - Microsoft Learn states 'For you to create a vault to help protect any data source, the vault must be in the same region as the data source', and the Configure Backup wizard only lists VMs in the same region as the vault. Step 2 (c): Zone-redundant storage replicates backup data across availability zones, guaranteeing backup data residency and resiliency within the same region, which matches the stated requirement. This must be set before any backup is configured, because 'After you configure a backup, the option to modify is disabled.' Placing this step after configuring backup would make the requirement unachievable in this vault. Step 3 (d): The policy must exist before it can be assigned. The Enhanced subtype is required here for two reasons: Trusted Launch VM backup is configured through Enhanced policies in the portal, and only the Enhanced policy supports multiple backups per day (Hourly schedules with intervals of 4, 6, 8, 12, or 24 hours). Step 4 (a): Configuring backup and assigning the policy creates the protected item and triggers the initial backup - and it is this action that locks the storage replication type, which is why it must come last.
tags: recovery services vault,zrs,zone-redundant,enhanced policy,trusted launch,backup policy,ordering

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a backup policy
domanda: A new Azure virtual machine named VM-Ledger hosts a financial application. The business requires a recovery point objective (RPO) of four hours. VM-Ledger is not yet protected by Azure Backup. You need to configure backup for VM-Ledger in an existing Recovery Services vault while meeting the RPO with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create a backup policy of subtype Standard and set the backup frequency to Hourly with an interval of every 4 hours.
opzione_b: Create a backup policy of subtype Enhanced with an Hourly schedule and a backup interval of every 4 hours, then assign it to VM-Ledger.
opzione_c: Create four Standard backup policies scheduled six hours apart and assign all of them to VM-Ledger.
opzione_d: Assign the default Standard policy to VM-Ledger and set the instant restore snapshot retention to 4 days.
spiegazione: Correct (b): Only the Enhanced backup policy subtype supports multiple backups per day for Azure VMs. With the schedule set to Hourly, you can choose an interval of 4, 6, 8, 12, or 24 hours; hourly backup has a minimum RPO of 4 hours and a maximum of 24 hours. An Enhanced hourly policy with a 4-hour interval therefore meets the 4-hour RPO. (a) is wrong: the Standard policy does not offer an Hourly schedule - it backs up an Azure VM once a day, and Microsoft Learn states the minimum RPO with the Standard policy is 1 day (24 hours). (c) is wrong: a VM can be associated with only one backup policy in one vault at a time, so you cannot stack multiple policies on the same VM; it also would not reach a 4-hour RPO.
