(d) is wrong: instant restore snapshot retention controls how many days snapshots are kept in the snapshot tier for fast restores - it has no effect on backup frequency or RPO.
tags: backup policy,enhanced policy,standard policy,rpo,hourly backup,azure vm backup

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a backup policy
domanda: Several Azure virtual machines are protected by a daily backup policy of subtype Standard. Restores are currently slow because snapshots expire too quickly, so the operations team asks you to keep instant restore snapshots for as long as the policy subtype allows. What is the maximum snapshot retention, in days, that you can configure on this policy?
spiegazione: Correct (b): For the Standard policy, Azure Backup retains Instant Restore snapshots locally for 2 days by default, and Microsoft Learn states you can configure this value from a minimum of 1 day to a maximum of 5 days. (a) is wrong: 2 days is the default value for the Standard policy, not the maximum. (c) is wrong: 7 days is the default snapshot retention for the Enhanced policy, not a value available to the Standard policy. (d) is wrong: 30 days is the maximum snapshot retention for the Enhanced policy (which supports 1 to 30 days, subject to the hourly frequency chosen); the Standard policy caps out at 5 days. Note also that Instant Restore cannot be disabled - the retention can only be reduced to a minimum of one day.
tags: instant restore,snapshot retention,standard policy,backup policy,snapshot tier

sotto_argomento: Interpret metrics in Azure Monitor
domanda: You are analyzing the Percentage CPU metric for a set of virtual machines in Azure Monitor metrics explorer. You must identify the worst CPU spike within each interval and determine which individual virtual machine is responsible. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Aggregation that shows the highest value captured in each interval: [Average | Max | Count]
opzione_b: Feature that draws a separate chart line per virtual machine: [Filtering | Splitting | Y-axis lock]
opzione_c: Smallest time granularity available on the chart: [15 seconds | 1 minute | 5 minutes]
opzione_d: How the Average aggregation is produced: [Sum divided by Count | Midpoint of Min and Max | Preaggregated and stored per interval]
spiegazione: Correct: Max returns the largest value captured over the aggregation interval, which is what surfaces a spike. Splitting controls whether the chart displays separate lines for each value of a dimension, so splitting by virtual machine (or resource ID) produces one line per machine. The current minimum time granularity in metrics explorer is 1 minute, even though the underlying system may sample faster. Average is always the Sum divided by the Count; it is never stored preaggregated and is recalculated for each time granularity from the aggregated Sum and Count so that calculation errors are avoided. Why the other options are wrong: Average would smooth away the spike, and Count only reports how many measurements were captured. Filtering chooses which dimension values are included in the chart but still aggregates them into one line unless splitting is applied; Y-axis lock only changes the visible value range. 15 seconds is the interval at which the platform samples VM CPU underneath, but it is not selectable as a chart time grain; 5 minutes is a valid grain but is not the smallest. Average is not the midpoint of Min and Max, and unlike Sum, Count, Min, and Max it is not preaggregated.

sotto_argomento: Interpret metrics in Azure Monitor
domanda: In metrics explorer you chart the Transactions metric of a storage account and apply splitting on the ResponseType dimension, which correctly shows a separate line per response type. You then create a diagnostic setting that sends AllMetrics for the same storage account to a Log Analytics workspace. In the workspace, the exported metric records show only a single total per interval, with no breakdown by ResponseType. You must make the per-dimension detail available in the workspace. What should you do?
opzione_a: Recreate the diagnostic setting and select the Transactions metric category instead of AllMetrics.
opzione_b: Extract the metric with the Azure Monitor Metrics REST API and ingest the results into the workspace by using the Logs Ingestion API.
opzione_c: Increase the retention of the workspace table so that the dimension values are preserved.
opzione_d: Install the Azure Monitor Agent on the storage account and create a data collection rule for the dimension.
spiegazione: Correct: Diagnostic settings do not currently support multidimensional metrics. Metrics with dimensions are exported as flattened, single-dimensional metrics that are aggregated across dimension values, which is exactly the behaviour observed. The documented workaround is to extract the metric manually with the Metrics REST API and import it into a Log Analytics workspace by using the Logs Ingestion API. Why the others are wrong: Metric categories other than AllMetrics aren't supported for the vast majority of Azure services; attempting to specify one returns a 'Metric category is not supported' error, and it would not restore the dimensions anyway. Retention controls how long records are kept, not whether dimension values are captured at ingestion time. The Azure Monitor Agent collects guest OS telemetry from virtual machines and cannot be installed on a platform-as-a-service storage account.
tags: azure monitor,multi-dimensional metrics,diagnostic settings,allmetrics,logs ingestion api

sotto_argomento: Interpret metrics in Azure Monitor
domanda: A development team plans to publish business telemetry to Azure Monitor as custom metrics so that the values can be charted in metrics explorer alongside platform metrics. Which three statements about Azure Monitor custom metrics are correct? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A custom metric can carry a maximum of 10 dimension keys.
opzione_b: Custom metrics are retained for the same period as platform metrics.
opzione_c: A custom metric definition must be created in Azure Monitor before the first value is emitted.
opzione_d: A subscription is limited to 50,000 active time series per region.
opzione_e: Custom metrics must be enabled through a diagnostic setting before they appear in metrics explorer.
spiegazione: Correct: Azure Monitor limits custom metrics to 10 dimension keys per metric. Custom metrics are retained for the same amount of time as platform metrics, which is 93 days. The subscription quota is 50,000 total active time series per region, where an active time series is any unique combination of metric, dimension key, and dimension value published in the past 12 hours. Why the others are wrong: You do not need to predefine a custom metric; the first time you emit a custom metric, Azure Monitor automatically creates the metric definition. Diagnostic settings route platform metrics, resource logs, and the activity log to other destinations; they play no part in ingesting custom metrics, which arrive through the Application Insights SDK, the Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule, the Telegraf agent, or the custom metrics REST API.

sotto_argomento: Interpret metrics in Azure Monitor
domanda: An engineer reports that when she sets the time picker in Azure Monitor metrics explorer to a custom 45-day range, the chart for the Percentage CPU metric of a virtual machine renders blank. The virtual machine has been running continuously for six months and the same chart displays data correctly over the last 7 days. What is the most likely cause?
opzione_a: Metrics explorer can query no more than 30 days of data on any single chart.
opzione_b: Platform metrics are retained for only 30 days, so no data exists beyond that point.
opzione_c: A diagnostic setting that sends AllMetrics to a Log Analytics workspace is required before historical metrics can be charted.
opzione_d: The time granularity is set to Automatic, which suppresses data points for ranges longer than one month.
spiegazione: Correct: Although platform metrics are stored for 93 days, metrics explorer can query a maximum of 30 days of data on any single chart. Selecting a start-to-end interval greater than 30 days produces a blank chart or a chart showing only part of the data. After selecting a 30-day interval, you can pan the chart to view the full 93-day retention window. Why the others are wrong: Platform metrics are retained for 93 days, not 30, so the data does exist. No diagnostic setting is needed to chart platform metrics in metrics explorer; platform metrics are collected automatically and a diagnostic setting is only needed to route them to other destinations. Automatic time granularity simply selects an appropriate time grain for the chosen range; it never suppresses data.

sotto_argomento: Interpret metrics in Azure Monitor
domanda: While investigating an incident in Azure Monitor metrics explorer, you need a chart that shows how many measurements a resource emitted during each aggregation interval, ignoring the numeric value of those measurements. Which aggregation type should you select?
opzione_a: Sum
opzione_b: Count
opzione_c: Average
opzione_d: Max
spiegazione: Correct: The Count aggregation returns the number of measurements captured during the aggregation interval. Count does not look at the value of each measurement, only at the number of records. Why the others are wrong: Sum adds up the values captured during the interval, so it is influenced by the magnitude of each measurement; it only equals Count in the special case where every measurement is captured with the value 1. Average is the sum of the values divided by the count, so it depends on the values. Max returns the largest single value captured during the interval, which again depends on the values rather than the number of records.

sotto_argomento: Interpret metrics in Azure Monitor
domanda: A compliance officer asks how far back you can look at CPU utilization data for a virtual machine directly in Azure Monitor Metrics, without configuring any additional collection. For how long does Azure Monitor retain platform metrics?
opzione_a: 30 days
opzione_b: 90 days
opzione_c: 93 days
opzione_d: 18 months
spiegazione: Correct: Azure Monitor stores platform and custom metrics for 93 days. This retention applies automatically with no configuration or cost for platform metrics. Why the others are wrong: '30 days' is the maximum span you can display on a single chart in metrics explorer (you can pan the chart to reach the rest of the 93-day window), not the retention period. '90 days' is the default retention of the Azure activity log, not of metrics. '18 months' is the retention for Prometheus metrics stored in an Azure Monitor workspace, which is a separate store from Azure Monitor Metrics.

sotto_argomento: Perform a failover to a secondary region
domanda: Azure Site Recovery replicated VM1 from East US to West US. Following an outage, you failed over VM1 to West US and selected Commit. The primary region is now healthy again, and you must return VM1 to East US and then restore disaster recovery protection back to West US. Select the appropriate option for each statement.
opzione_a: To begin replicating VM1 back to East US, select: [Re-Protect | Planned failover | Change recovery point | Disable replication]
opzione_b: The replication direction configured by that action is: [West US to East US | East US to West US | Bidirectional]
opzione_c: Before you can start that action, the replicated item status must be: [Failover committed | Failover in progress | Protected]
opzione_d: After you fail over to East US and commit, to protect VM1 to West US again you must: [Run Re-Protect again | Run Cleanup test failover | Take no further action]
risposta_corretta: Re-Protect,West US to East US,Failover committed,Run Re-Protect again
spiegazione: Correct - Re-Protect: after failover you reprotect the VM in the secondary region so that it replicates back to the primary region; this is the documented first step of the failback flow. Wrong - Planned failover: planned failover is a zero-data-loss option documented for Hyper-V VMs, not for Azure-to-Azure replicated items, and in any case it would not establish reverse replication. Wrong - Change recovery point: this only selects a different recovery point and is unavailable once you commit. Wrong - Disable replication: this removes protection entirely. Correct - West US to East US: in the Re-protect blade you verify the replication direction, which is secondary to primary region, and review the target settings for the primary region. Wrong - the other directions: East US to West US is the original direction, and Site Recovery replicates in one direction at a time, so bidirectional is not an option. Correct - Failover committed: the tutorial requires you to make sure the VM Status is Failover committed before you start Re-Protect. Wrong - Failover in progress / Protected: reprotect cannot start mid-failover, and Protected is the steady state before any failover. Correct - Run Re-Protect again: failing back to East US leaves replication running from East US's perspective in the reverse direction, so after the failback failover and commit you run Re-Protect once more to re-establish replication from East US to West US. Wrong - Cleanup test failover: this applies only to test failover drills. Wrong - Take no further action: protection to the secondary region is not restored automatically.

sotto_argomento: Perform a failover to a secondary region
domanda: Azure Site Recovery replicates VM1 from North Europe to West Europe. After an incident, you run a failover of VM1, validate the application on the VM created in West Europe, and then select Commit on the replicated item. What is the effect of the Commit action?
opzione_a: It deletes all recovery points available for the VM in Site Recovery, so you can no longer change the recovery point
opzione_b: It starts replicating VM1 from West Europe back to North Europe
opzione_c: It deletes the source VM and its disks in North Europe to release the primary region resources
opzione_d: It deletes the VMs that were created during the failover so that the drill resources are released
spiegazione: Correct: Commit finalizes the failover by deleting all the recovery points available for the VM in Site Recovery; after committing, the Change recovery point option is no longer available and the item's status becomes Failover committed. Wrong - starts replicating back: that is the Re-Protect action, which you run after the status is Failover committed to reverse the replication direction from the secondary to the primary region. Wrong - deletes the source VM: Commit does not delete the source VM or its disks in the primary region; that cleanup is a separate manual decision. Wrong - deletes the VMs created during the failover: that describes Cleanup test failover, which applies only to a test failover (DR drill), not to a real failover.

sotto_argomento: Perform backup and restore operations by using Azure Backup
domanda: A Recovery Services vault in East US 2 uses geo-redundant storage with Cross Region Restore enabled and protects several Azure VMs with a policy that includes instant restore snapshots. During a regional incident, an administrator opens the vault, switches the Backup Items view to the secondary region, and notices that the recovery point created two hours ago is not listed, although recovery points from previous days are available. What is the reason?
opzione_a: Snapshot-tier recovery points are not replicated to the secondary region, so only vault-tier recovery points can be restored there
opzione_b: Cross Region Restore replicates recovery points only once every 24 hours, so the newest recovery point is always excluded
opzione_c: The administrator lacks the Backup Operator role, which hides recent recovery points in the secondary region
opzione_d: Recovery points become visible in the secondary region only after Microsoft formally declares a regional outage
spiegazione: Correct: snapshots are not replicated. Azure Backup documents that during backup, snapshots aren't replicated to the secondary region - only the data stored in the vault is replicated. Therefore secondary region restores are vault-tier restores only. A recovery point taken two hours ago is likely still in the snapshot (instant restore) tier because the Transfer Data to Vault phase has not completed, so it cannot appear as a secondary region restore point. Wrong - replication once every 24 hours: Azure Backup does not document a fixed 24-hour replication interval for Cross Region Restore; the determining factor is whether the recovery point has been transferred to the vault tier. Wrong - missing Backup Operator role: the roles needed to restore in the secondary region are the same as those in the primary region, and insufficient permissions would block the restore operation rather than selectively hide the newest recovery point. Wrong - waiting for a declared outage: Cross Region Restore explicitly lets you initiate restores in the secondary region even before Azure declares an outage, and even with no outage at all for BCDR drills.
tags: azure backup,cross region restore,grs,vault tier,snapshot tier,instant restore

sotto_argomento: Perform backup and restore operations by using Azure Backup
domanda: Case study: Litware, Inc. protects its production Azure VMs with a Recovery Services vault named RSV-Prod, which is located in the East US 2 region. RSV-Prod is configured with geo-redundant storage and the Cross Region Restore feature is enabled. Litware's business continuity policy requires a quarterly recovery drill in which a backed-up VM is restored into the vault's secondary region from a vault-tier recovery point, with no outage in the primary region. During the drill, an engineer selects the backup item, switches to the secondary region view, chooses a vault-tier recovery point, and selects Create new virtual machine. The restore wizard requires a staging location. Where must the staging location storage account be created?
opzione_a: In Central US, the region that Azure treats as the paired secondary region for East US 2
opzione_b: In East US 2, the same region as RSV-Prod
opzione_c: In any region, provided the storage account is in the same subscription as RSV-Prod
opzione_d: In East US, because the staging location must be in the same geography but a different region from the source VM
spiegazione: Correct: Central US. For Cross Region Restores, the documentation states that the staging location (the storage account location) must be in the region that the Recovery Services vault treats as the secondary region, and it uses this exact example: a vault in East US 2 with geo-redundancy and Cross Region Restore enabled has Central US as its secondary region, so you must create a storage account in Central US to perform a Cross Region Restore of the VM. Wrong - East US 2: that is the vault's primary region and is where the staging account would live for an ordinary primary-region restore, not for a Cross Region Restore. Wrong - any region in the same subscription: the staging location region is constrained to the secondary region; subscription membership is not the governing rule (Cross Subscription Restore is a separate, independently controlled capability). Wrong - East US: East US is not the Azure paired region for East US 2, and no rule about 'same geography but different region' governs the staging location; the requirement is specifically the vault's paired secondary region.
tags: azure backup,cross region restore,staging location,paired region,grs,bcdr drill

sotto_argomento: Perform backup and restore operations by using Azure Backup
domanda: A failed application update has corrupted the operating system disk of VM1, a running Azure VM that uses managed disks and is not encrypted. VM1 is protected by a Recovery Services vault and has a vault-standard recovery point from yesterday. The operations team must roll VM1 back to yesterday's state while keeping the existing VM object, its network interface, and its private IP address unchanged. Which restore option should you use?
opzione_a: Replace existing
opzione_b: Create new virtual machine
opzione_c: Restore disks, then deploy the generated ARM template
opzione_d: File recovery
spiegazione: Correct: Replace existing. This option restores a disk and uses it to replace the disk on the existing VM, so the VM object, NIC, and private IP are preserved. The current VM must exist, and the option is supported for unencrypted managed VMs, which matches VM1. Azure Backup takes a snapshot of the existing VM before replacing the disk, and the original disk is retained in the resource group afterward. Wrong - Create new virtual machine: this creates a brand-new VM with a new NIC and new IP configuration, so the existing VM identity and private IP would not be preserved. Wrong - Restore disks, then deploy the generated ARM template: this also results in a new VM built from the restored disks rather than an in-place replacement, requiring manual re-creation of network settings. Wrong - File recovery: item-level recovery mounts the recovery point so you can copy individual files or folders; it cannot replace a corrupted OS disk.
tags: azure backup,vm restore,replace existing,managed disks,recovery services vault

sotto_argomento: Perform backup and restore operations by using Azure Backup
domanda: Your team plans to use the File Recovery feature of Azure VM backup to restore individual folders from recovery points of Azure VMs protected in a Recovery Services vault. Which statements about this feature are correct? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: The machine that runs the script needs outbound access on TCP port 3260 to the Recovery Services URLs, or the AzureBackup service tag allowed in the network security group.
opzione_b: The script must be run with administrator privileges and requires the password that is displayed in the Azure portal when the script is generated.
opzione_c: File recovery is supported for recovery points of VMs whose disks are encrypted with Azure Disk Encryption.
opzione_d: If the protected Linux VM uses Logical Volume Manager (LVM) or software RAID arrays, the script must be run on a machine other than the protected VM.
opzione_e: The mounted volumes remain available for 30 days unless you select Unmount Disks in the Azure portal.
spiegazione: Correct - option A: the access requirements list the Recovery Service URLs on port 3260 (outbound) for the iSCSI connection, or the AzureBackup service tag in the NSG, plus download.microsoft.com on port 443. Correct - option B: only an administrator can run the script, it must run in elevated mode, and a password shown only to the authorized user at generation time is required. Correct - option D: the documentation states that if the protected Linux VM uses LVM and/or RAID arrays, you can't run the script on the same VM and must use another machine with a compatible OS. Wrong - option C: file recovery from an encrypted VM backup isn't supported; for encrypted VMs you restore the disks and then create the VM. Wrong - option E: the script gives read-only access and is valid for only 12 hours, not 30 days; selecting Unmount Disks invalidates it immediately.

sotto_argomento: Perform backup and restore operations by using Azure Backup
domanda: A support engineer needs to recover a single configuration file from an Azure VM protected by a Recovery Services vault. From the Backup dashboard the engineer selects File Recovery, downloads the executable, and mounts the recovery point volumes on an administrative workstation. For how long does the downloaded script provide access to the recovery point before it expires automatically?
opzione_a: 1 hour
opzione_b: 12 hours
opzione_c: 24 hours
opzione_d: 14 days
spiegazione: Correct: 12 hours. The Azure Backup documentation states that the file recovery script gives read-only access to a recovery point and is valid for only 12 hours. If you want to remove access earlier, you sign in to the Azure portal, PowerShell, or CLI and select Unmount Disks for that recovery point, which invalidates the script immediately. Wrong - 1 hour: no such limit exists for the item-level recovery (ILR) script; this is closer to the lifetime of short-lived SAS or token constructs, not the ILR mount. Wrong - 24 hours: this is the documented latency for the initial diagnostics data push into a Log Analytics workspace for Backup Reports, not the ILR script validity. Wrong - 14 days: this is the default soft-delete retention period for deleted backup data in a Recovery Services vault, an unrelated setting.
tags: azure backup,file recovery,item level restore,ilr,recovery services vault,iscsi

sotto_argomento: Perform backup and restore operations by using Azure Backup
domanda: An administrator installs the Microsoft Azure Recovery Services (MARS) agent on an on-premises server that runs Windows Server 2022 and registers it with a Recovery Services vault to back up files and folders directly to Azure. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is correct: 1) You can schedule up to three daily backups per day for files and folders. 2) To conserve local disk space, you can place the cache (scratch) folder on a network share. 3) The free space in the cache folder should be at least 5 to 10 percent of the overall size of the backup data.
opzione_a: You can schedule up to three daily backups per day for files and folders.
opzione_b: To conserve local disk space, you can place the cache (scratch) folder on a network share.
opzione_c: The free space in the cache folder should be at least 5 to 10 percent of the overall size of the backup data.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: on the Specify Backup Schedule page of the Schedule Backup Wizard, the documentation states that you can schedule up to three daily backups per day; weekly schedules are also supported. Statement 2 - No: the cache folder must be locally stored on the machine that's being backed up and must be online. It cannot be on a network share, on removable media, or on an offline volume, and it must not be encrypted, on a deduplicated volume, or in a folder that is compressed, sparse, or has a reparse point. Statement 3 - Yes: the MARS support matrix specifies that free space in the cache folder should be at least 5 to 10 percent of the overall size of your backup data, because the agent snapshots the data into the local cache before sending it to Azure.
tags: azure backup,mars agent,cache folder,scratch folder,backup schedule,recovery services vault

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda:
Your subscription sends its Azure Activity log to a Log Analytics workspace. A governance review asks for the number of failed Azure Activity operations per caller over the last seven days, displayed as horizontal strips. You are completing the query:

AzureActivity
| <TimeFilter>
| <StatusFilter>
| <Aggregation>
| <Visualization>

Select the correct value for each dropdown.
opzione_a: TimeFilter: [where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where TimeGenerated < ago(7d) | where TimeGenerated == ago(7d)]
opzione_b: StatusFilter: [where ActivityStatus == "Failed" | where Level == "Failed" | where CategoryValue == "Failed"]
opzione_c: Aggregation: [summarize FailureCount = count() by Caller | summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1d) | distinct Caller]
opzione_d: Visualization: [render barchart | render timechart | render scatterchart]
risposta_corretta: where TimeGenerated > ago(7d),where ActivityStatus == "Failed",summarize FailureCount = count() by Caller,render barchart
spiegazione:
Correct selections:
TimeFilter = where TimeGenerated > ago(7d). ago() subtracts a timespan from the current UTC time, so ago(7d) is the instant seven days ago. Records generated AFTER that instant are the last seven days, matching the documented pattern 'T | where Timestamp > ago(1h)'.
StatusFilter = where ActivityStatus == "Failed". The published AzureActivity sample query 'Failed operations' is written exactly as 'AzureActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) | where ActivityStatus == "Failed"'.
Aggregation = summarize FailureCount = count() by Caller. Caller holds the identity that performed the operation, and count() with 'by Caller' yields one row per caller with the number of matching records.
Visualization = render barchart. The Azure Monitor render reference documents barchart as displaying values as horizontal strips, which is precisely what the review asked for.

Why the other choices are wrong:
'where TimeGenerated < ago(7d)' inverts the comparison and returns only records OLDER than seven days, excluding the entire period of interest. 'where TimeGenerated == ago(7d)' demands an exact match against a single instant computed at query time and would realistically return nothing.
'where Level == "Failed"' is invalid because the Level column is documented as holding one of Critical, Error, Warning, Informational, or Verbose. "Failed" is not a Level value. 'where CategoryValue == "Failed"' is also invalid because CategoryValue holds the activity log category such as Administrative, Policy, or Security.
'summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)' groups by day rather than by caller, answering a different question. 'distinct Caller' lists the unique callers but produces no count at all.
'render timechart' requires a datetime first column and plots a trend, but the result is grouped by Caller (a string), not by time. 'render scatterchart' expects a numeric first column for the x-axis and plots points rather than horizontal strips.

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda: You need to build a Log Analytics query that charts the hourly average of the "% Processor Time" performance counter for the computer named VM1 over the last seven days as a line graph over time. Following Microsoft's documented guidance, place the time filter immediately after the table name. Arrange the five query lines in the correct order from first to last.
opzione_a: | summarize avg(CounterValue) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
opzione_b: Perf
opzione_c: | render timechart
opzione_d: | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
opzione_e: | where Computer == "VM1" and CounterName == "% Processor Time"
spiegazione:
Correct order: b, d, e, a, c.

1. (b) Perf. Learn advises starting a query with a table name because it defines a clear scope and improves query performance and result relevance. Perf is the table that stores performance counter samples, exposing ObjectName, CounterName, InstanceName, CounterValue and Computer.
2. (d) | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d). The documentation states it is best to place the time filter immediately after the table name; ago(7d) subtracts seven days from the current UTC time, so this restricts the pipeline to the last week before any other work is done.
3. (e) | where Computer == "VM1" and CounterName == "% Processor Time". Filtering to a single computer and a single counter next keeps the data volume minimal. This step is essential: Learn warns that averaging across mixed performance counters produces meaningless results.
4. (a) | summarize avg(CounterValue) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h). Aggregation must follow filtering, because summarize collapses the rows the where clauses selected. bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) rounds each timestamp down to its hour so that one average is produced per hour, instead of the millisecond-granularity groups that summarizing by TimeGenerated alone would create.
5. (c) | render timechart. The render operator must be the last operator in the query, and timechart plots the datetime first column on the x-axis with the numeric aggregate as the y-axis, producing the requested line graph.

Why other orders fail: putting render anywhere but last is invalid because the reference states render must be the last operator. Putting summarize before the where clauses would aggregate every computer and every counter in the workspace, so the later filters would find no CounterName column to filter on, since summarize discards all columns that are not group keys or aggregates.

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda:
A Log Analytics workspace contains exactly the following five Perf records, all collected within the query time range:

Computer=VM1, CounterName="% Processor Time", CounterValue=20
Computer=VM1, CounterName="% Processor Time", CounterValue=40
Computer=VM1, CounterName="Available MBytes", CounterValue=1000
Computer=VM2, CounterName="% Processor Time", CounterValue=60
Computer=VM2, CounterName="% Processor Time", CounterValue=90

An analyst runs:

Perf
| where CounterName == "% Processor Time"
| summarize avg(CounterValue) by Computer

Select the correct value for each dropdown to describe the output.
opzione_a: Number of rows returned: [1 | 2 | 3]
opzione_b: Aggregated value for VM1: [20 | 30 | 60]
opzione_c: Aggregated value for VM2: [60 | 75 | 150]
opzione_d: Name of the aggregated output column: [CounterValue | avg_CounterValue | AvgCounterValue]
spiegazione:
Correct selections:
Rows = 2. The where clause removes the "Available MBytes" record, leaving four rows. The summarize reference states that the result has as many rows as there are distinct combinations of the 'by' values; the remaining rows span two distinct Computer values (VM1 and VM2), so two rows are returned.
VM1 = 30. VM1's two surviving samples are 20 and 40, and (20 + 40) / 2 = 30. The 1000 sample is excluded because its CounterName is "Available MBytes", not "% Processor Time".
VM2 = 75. VM2's samples are 60 and 90, and (60 + 90) / 2 = 75.
Column name = avg_CounterValue. The summarize syntax is '[Column=] Aggregation'; when you do not supply an explicit result column name, Learn states the name defaults to one derived from the expression. The documented outputs show exactly this convention, for example avg(x) producing avg_x and sum(y) producing sum_y, so avg(CounterValue) produces avg_CounterValue.

Why the other choices are wrong:
1 row would only occur if there were no 'by' clause at all, in which case Learn says the result has a single record. 3 rows is the trap of forgetting that the where clause already discarded the "Available MBytes" record, or of assuming the query groups by Computer and CounterName.
20 for VM1 is the minimum sample, not the mean, and 60 is the sum of the two samples misread as an average.
60 for VM2 is its minimum sample and 150 is the raw sum of 60 and 90 without dividing by the sample count.
CounterValue is the input column name; summarize does not return the raw column, it returns the aggregate. AvgCounterValue uses no underscore and is not the derived default; that name would appear only if the query were written explicitly as 'summarize AvgCounterValue = avg(CounterValue) by Computer'.

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda:
You must build a Log Analytics query that plots the hourly average of the InsightsMetrics processor utilization value for a single computer as a line graph over time. The query skeleton is:

InsightsMetrics
| where Computer == "DC00.contoso.com"
| where Namespace == "Processor" and Name == "UtilizationPercentage"
| <Operator> avg(Val) by Computer, <Grouping>
| <Visualization>

Select the correct value for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Operator: [extend | summarize | project]
opzione_b: Grouping: [bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) | ago(1h) | TimeGenerated]
opzione_c: Visualization: [render timechart | render piechart | render table]
spiegazione:
Correct selections:
Operator = summarize. summarize is the operator that arranges input rows into groups sharing the same 'by' values and computes aggregation functions such as avg() over each group. It is the only one of the three choices that accepts a 'by' clause with an aggregation.
Grouping = bin(TimeGenerated, 1h). Learn states that simply summarizing by TimeGenerated would create a group for every single millisecond because those values are unique, and that you should break the range into manageable units by using bin(). A 1h bin yields one point per hour.
Visualization = render timechart. timechart produces a line graph whose first column is the datetime x-axis and whose numeric columns become the y-axes. This exact pipeline is the published example on the render reference page.

Why the other choices are wrong:
extend adds a calculated column to every existing row and does not support a 'by' clause, so it cannot aggregate to one point per hour.
project selects or renames columns; it neither aggregates nor accepts 'by'.
ago(1h) returns a single datetime value equal to now() minus one hour. It is a filter boundary for a where clause, not a grouping expression; grouping by it would place every row into one group.
TimeGenerated used bare as the group key produces the millisecond-granularity explosion the documentation warns against.
render piechart treats the first column as a category color-axis and has no time axis, so it cannot show a trend over time.
render table is the default tabular display and produces no graph at all.

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda: A Log Analytics query that returns the 10 most recent records from a very large table takes too long to complete. You need to reduce the volume of data the query processes. Which three changes should you make? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Start the query with the table name instead of with the search operator.
opzione_b: Place '| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)' immediately after the table name.
opzione_c: Replace '| sort by TimeGenerated | take 10' with '| top 10 by TimeGenerated'.
opzione_d: Replace '| where Level == 8' with '| where Level =~ "8"'.
opzione_e: Add '| render table' as the final operator of the query.
spiegazione:
Correct answers:
a. Microsoft Learn advises starting with a table name because it defines a clear scope for the query and improves query performance and result relevance. It warns that search queries are ordinarily slower because they must process more data, and that omitting 'in (TableName)' makes the search span all tables.
b. The documentation states that it is best to place the time filter immediately after the table name. Filtering on TimeGenerated first is the single most effective way to cut the number of records the remaining pipeline must evaluate.
c. Learn explains that 'sort by' does not limit the records returned, so it sorts the entire table and the portal then truncates the display, which 'isn't optimal'. The top operator sorts on the server side and returns only the top records.

Why the others are wrong:
d. This is backwards. The string operators performance guidance says that when two operators do the same task you should use the case-sensitive one, explicitly recommending '==' rather than '=~'. Switching to =~ makes the filter slower, and it also changes a numeric comparison into a string comparison.
e. The render operator does not modify data. Learn states that it only adds a Visualization annotation to the result's extended properties instructing the user agent how to display the results, so it processes exactly the same volume of data and cannot improve query time.

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda:
A Log Analytics workspace collects Heartbeat data from Azure Monitor Agent on a fleet of virtual machines. An engineer saves the following query to detect machines that stopped reporting:

Heartbeat
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| summarize LastCall = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, _ResourceId
| where LastCall < ago(5m)

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

1. The result contains one row for each computer whose most recent heartbeat within the last 24 hours is older than five minutes.
2. The result includes the OSType column so you can tell Windows machines from Linux machines.
3. The 'where LastCall < ago(5m)' clause is evaluated before the summarize operator aggregates the records.
opzione_a: The result contains one row for each computer whose most recent heartbeat within the last 24 hours is older than five minutes.
opzione_b: The result includes the OSType column so you can tell Windows machines from Linux machines.
opzione_c: The 'where LastCall < ago(5m)' clause is evaluated before the summarize operator aggregates the records.
spiegazione:
Statement 1 = Yes. summarize returns one row per distinct combination of the 'by' expressions, here Computer and _ResourceId, and max(TimeGenerated) is that machine's newest heartbeat inside the 24-hour window. The final where keeps only rows whose newest heartbeat precedes the instant five minutes ago. Microsoft Learn publishes this exact query as the 'Not reporting VMs' sample, described as 'VMs that have not reported a heartbeat in the last 5 minutes'.

Statement 2 = No. The summarize reference states that the result contains the 'by' columns plus at least one column for each computed aggregate. Every other column of the input, including OSType, is discarded. To keep OSType you would have to add it to the 'by' clause or use an aggregate such as arg_max(TimeGenerated, *), which returns all columns of the maximizing row.

Statement 3 = No. The pipe character means the output of one command becomes the input of the next, so operators execute strictly left to right. LastCall does not even exist until summarize creates it, so a where clause referencing LastCall cannot run before summarize; placing it earlier would produce a query error. Only the first where, filtering on TimeGenerated, runs before the aggregation.

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda:
A query over a very large string column in a Log Analytics workspace is running slowly. The current filter is:

| where ResultDescription contains "Failure"

The analyst only needs records in which "Failure" appears as a complete word bounded by non-alphanumeric characters. Which replacement filter delivers that match and the best performance?
opzione_a: | where ResultDescription has "Failure"
opzione_b: | where ResultDescription =~ "Failure"
opzione_c: | where ResultDescription startswith "Failure"
opzione_d: | where ResultDescription matches regex "Failure"
spiegazione:
Correct: The KQL string operators reference explains that Kusto builds a term index of all terms of three characters or more, and that operators containing 'has' in their name use that index to match whole terms. It states directly that 'has works faster than contains, startswith, or endswith', and that a contains operator makes the query revert to scanning the column values, which is much slower than a term-index lookup. 'Failure' is a whole term, so has is both semantically correct and index-accelerated.

Why the others are wrong:
b. =~ is case-insensitive EQUALITY: it requires the entire column value to equal "Failure", so a message such as "Login Failure detected" would not match at all. The documentation also advises preferring the case-sensitive == over =~ for performance.
c. startswith only matches when the value BEGINS with the string, missing any record where the term appears later in the text, and the docs list it among the operators that has outperforms.
d. matches regex forces a regular-expression evaluation over every value. It cannot use the term index, so it is slower than has, and it matches the substring rather than enforcing a whole-term boundary.
tags: kql,has,contains,string operators,term index,query performance,azure monitor logs

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda: Your team is standardizing how KQL joins are written in Log Analytics workbooks. Which three statements about the KQL join operator are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: kind=leftanti returns all records from the left table that do not match any record in the right table.
opzione_b: kind=leftouter returns all records from the left table and only the matching records from the right table.
opzione_c: When no kind is specified, the join performs a standard inner join with no deduplication.
opzione_d: kind=leftsemi returns all columns from both the left and the right tables.
opzione_e: kind=fullouter returns all records from both tables, with unmatched cells populated with null.
spiegazione:
Correct answers:
a. The join reference documents leftanti (and its aliases anti and leftantisemi) as returning all columns from the left table and all records from the left table that don't match records from the right table. This is the standard 'find what is missing' pattern.
b. leftouter is documented as returning all columns from both tables, with all records from the left table and only matching rows from the right table.
e. fullouter is documented as returning all columns from both tables and all records from both tables, with unmatched cells populated with null.

Why the others are wrong:
c. This is the classic misconception. The reference explicitly states that the default JoinFlavor is 'innerunique', not 'inner'. innerunique performs an inner join WITH left side deduplication, so unspecified joins can silently return fewer rows than a standard inner join would.
d. leftsemi returns only the columns from the LEFT table (the rows from the left table that match records from the right). The flavor that returns all columns from both tables while keeping only matching rows is 'inner'.

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda:
A Log Analytics workspace collects agent health data from 40 servers. An operations engineer runs the following query:

Heartbeat
| summarize LastHeartbeat = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
| where LastHeartbeat < ago(5h)

What does the result set contain?
opzione_a: One row for each computer whose most recent heartbeat is older than five hours.
opzione_b: One row for each computer that sent at least one heartbeat during the last five hours.
opzione_c: Every heartbeat record generated during the last five hours, sorted by computer.
opzione_d: The total number of heartbeat records received per computer during the last five hours.
spiegazione:
Correct: 'summarize LastHeartbeat = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer' collapses the table to one row per distinct Computer, holding that computer's newest heartbeat timestamp. The subsequent 'where LastHeartbeat < ago(5h)' keeps only the rows whose newest timestamp is EARLIER than the point in time five hours ago, which is exactly the set of computers that have stopped reporting. Microsoft Learn documents this pattern under 'Unavailable computers' as 'List all known computers that didn't send a heartbeat in the last 5 hours.'

Why the others are wrong:
b. This inverts the comparison. Computers that reported within the last five hours have LastHeartbeat > ago(5h) and are filtered out by this query, not returned by it.
c. summarize is an aggregation, not a filter on raw records. It discards the individual heartbeat rows and returns only the group keys plus the aggregates, so no raw heartbeat records survive to the output.
d. Counting records would require the count() aggregation (for example, 'summarize count() by Computer'). max(TimeGenerated) returns a datetime, not a record count.

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda: An engineer writes a KQL query in Log Analytics that merges two tabular expressions with 'join (RightData) on Computer'. No kind is specified. The engineer expects a standard inner join, but observes that duplicate rows on the left side are collapsed to a single row before matching, so the result contains fewer rows than expected. Which change produces a standard inner join that returns all matching row combinations from both sides?
opzione_a: Add kind=inner to the join.
opzione_b: Add kind=innerunique to the join.
opzione_c: Add kind=leftouter to the join.
opzione_d: Add kind=leftsemi to the join.
spiegazione:
Correct: The join operator reference states that the default JoinFlavor is 'innerunique', documented as 'Inner join with left side deduplication', which is precisely the behavior the engineer observed. Explicitly specifying kind=inner selects the 'Standard inner join', which returns all columns from both tables and only the matching rows from both, without deduplicating the left side.

Why the others are wrong:
b. innerunique is already the default when no kind is given, so stating it explicitly changes nothing. The left-side deduplication the engineer is trying to eliminate would still occur.
c. leftouter returns all records from the left table plus only the matching rows from the right, padding non-matches. That returns MORE rows than an inner join and includes unmatched left rows, which is not a standard inner join.
d. leftsemi returns only the columns from the left table and only left rows that have a match. It discards the right table's columns entirely, so it cannot deliver the combined result set of an inner join.

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda: While investigating an incident in Log Analytics, you need to add one calculated column to the results of a query while retaining every column that the table already returns. Which KQL operator should you use?
opzione_a: project
opzione_b: extend
opzione_c: summarize
opzione_d: parse
spiegazione:
Correct: Microsoft Learn describes extend as the operator that keeps all original columns in the result set and defines additional ones, for example 'SecurityEvent | top 10 by TimeGenerated | extend EventCode=substring(Activity, 0, 4)'.

Why the others are wrong:
a. project also can define new columns, but it selects only the columns you name and drops everything else. It is the right tool when you want to narrow the column list, which is the opposite of the stated requirement of retaining every existing column.
c. summarize aggregates rows into groups and returns only the 'by' group keys plus the computed aggregates. All other columns are discarded, and the row count changes, so it does not add a column to the existing rows.
d. parse extracts values out of a string expression into new columns using a pattern. It is a text-extraction operator, not the general-purpose way to add a calculated column, and the question does not describe parsing a string pattern.

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda:
A Perf record was collected with TimeGenerated = 2026-03-10T14:37:22Z. An analyst runs:

Perf
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| summarize avg(CounterValue) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)

Which TimeGenerated value appears in the output row that this record contributes to?
spiegazione:
Correct: bin() rounds values DOWN to an integer multiple of the given bin size; the Learn reference states it returns 'the nearest multiple of roundTo below value' and notes that bin() and floor() are equivalent. With a 1h bin size, 14:37:22 rounds down to the start of the 14:00 hour. The documented datetime example makes this explicit: bin(datetime(1970-05-11 13:45:07), 1d) returns 1970-05-11T00:00:00Z.

Why the others are wrong:
b. 15:00:00Z would be the result of rounding UP (a ceiling). bin() never rounds up, which is the single most common misconception about this function.
c. 14:30:00Z would be the bin label if the bin size were 30m and rounding produced the nearest half-hour boundary at or below the value. The query specifies 1h, so the only valid boundaries are whole hours.
d. 14:37:00Z merely truncates the seconds, which is what bin(TimeGenerated, 1m) would produce. A 1h bin size cannot yield a label with a non-zero minute component.

sotto_argomento: Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor
domanda: In Log Analytics, you want the final operator of a KQL query to produce a line graph plotted over time. Which render visualization expects the first column of the result set to be a datetime value?
opzione_a: barchart
opzione_b: piechart
opzione_c: timechart
opzione_d: columnchart
spiegazione:
Correct: The render operator reference for Azure Monitor states that for 'timechart' the first column is the x-axis and should be datetime, while other numeric columns become the y-axes. This is why the canonical pattern is '| summarize avg(Val) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) | render timechart'.

Why the others are wrong:
a. barchart is documented as accepting a first column that can be text, datetime, OR numeric, displayed as horizontal strips. It does not require datetime, so it is not the answer to a question about a datetime requirement.
b. piechart treats the first column as the color-axis (a category) and the second column as numeric. It has no time axis at all.
d. columnchart is explicitly documented as being like barchart but with vertical strips instead of horizontal strips, so it inherits the same flexible first-column typing rather than requiring datetime.

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda:
Case study: Tailwind Traders runs its production estate in a single Azure subscription named Sub1. The platform team has grown its alerting footprint to roughly 180 metric alert rules and 40 log search alert rules, all created by different application teams. A single action group named AG-Platform contains the operations distribution list and a Logic apps action that opens a ticket. Two problems have emerged. First, application teams routinely forget to attach AG-Platform when they create new alert rules, so incidents go unticketed until someone notices. Second, Tailwind Traders also relies on built-in Azure Backup alerts for backup failures and soft-delete changes; these alerts are generated automatically and the alert rule experience does not let the team specify an action group for them, so backup incidents never reach AG-Platform at all.

The team wants a single, low-maintenance configuration that routes every fired alert in Sub1 - including alerts that no alert rule generated - to AG-Platform, without editing the 220 existing alert rules. What should the team implement?
opzione_a: Create an alert processing rule scoped to Sub1 that uses the Apply action groups action to add AG-Platform.
opzione_b: Create an Azure Policy assignment with a deployIfNotExists effect that appends AG-Platform to every Microsoft.Insights/metricAlerts and Microsoft.Insights/scheduledQueryRules resource in Sub1.
opzione_c: Enable the recommended out-of-the-box alert rules on every resource in Sub1 and attach AG-Platform to each of them.
opzione_d: Create an alert processing rule scoped to Sub1 that uses the Suppression action, and add AG-Platform to the alert processing rule.
spiegazione: Correct: This is the canonical use case for the Apply action groups action on an alert processing rule. The documentation's Management at scale section explains that instead of manually ensuring each alert rule has the right action groups as the rule count grows, "Alert processing rules allow you to specify that logic in a single rule, instead of having to set it consistently in all your alert rules." Crucially, the Add action groups to all alert types section addresses the second problem directly: "not all Azure alert sources let you specify action groups. Some examples of such alerts include Azure Backup alerts, VM Insights guest health alerts, Azure Stack Edge, and Azure Stack Hub. For those alert types, you can use alert processing rules to add action groups." A rule scoped to the whole subscription Sub1 covers all fired alerts on resources in that subscription, existing and future, without touching the 220 rules. Why the others are wrong: (b) Azure Policy can create alert rules at scale (the Azure Monitor baseline alerts pattern uses it), but the documentation warns this brings "the increased overhead of maintaining a large alert rule set", it would still require modifying the existing rules, and - decisively - it cannot help with built-in Azure Backup alerts, which are not generated by any alert rule resource for a policy to target. (c) Recommended out-of-the-box alert rules are only offered for virtual machines, AKS resources, and Log Analytics workspaces. They create additional new alert rules rather than routing existing ones, do nothing for Azure Backup alerts, and would add to the maintenance burden rather than reduce it. (d) This inverts the required action. Suppression "removes all the action groups from the affected fired alerts", so it would stop notifications entirely rather than deliver them. Suppression is used for planned maintenance windows or out-of-hours quiet periods; Apply action groups is used to add notification routing.
tags: azure monitor,alert processing rules,apply action groups,management at scale,azure backup alerts,action groups

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda:
Northwind collects Windows security events from 60 virtual machines into a Log Analytics workspace named LAW1. You must create a log search alert rule scoped to LAW1 that meets these requirements:

- The rule must count the number of matching rows returned by a KQL query against the Event table (it must not perform a calculation on a numeric column).
- Matching rows must be aggregated into 15-minute windows.
- The query must run every 5 minutes.
- A separate alert must be fired for each virtual machine that meets the condition, and each alert must target the virtual machine itself rather than LAW1.

Select the appropriate value for each setting in the alert rule wizard.
opzione_a: Measure: [Table rows | Calculation of a numeric column | Custom metric]
opzione_b: Aggregation granularity: [5 minutes | 15 minutes | 1 hour]
opzione_c: Frequency of evaluation: [1 minute | 5 minutes | 15 minutes]
opzione_d: Split by dimensions on column: [_ResourceId | TimeGenerated | Severity]
spiegazione: Correct: Measure = Table rows. The documentation states that log search alerts can measure two things: "Table rows: You can use the number of returned rows to work with events such as Windows event logs, Syslog, and application exceptions" and "Calculation of a numeric column" for numeric calculations such as CPU percentage. Counting matching Event rows is the Table rows measure. Custom metric is not a log search alert Measure option at all. Aggregation granularity = 15 minutes. Aggregation granularity is documented as the Window size: "The interval for aggregating multiple records to one numeric value." This is a distinct setting from how often the rule runs. Frequency of evaluation = 5 minutes. "Frequency of evaluation: How often the query is run. You can set it anywhere from one minute to one day (24 hours)." The requirement says every 5 minutes; note the documented note that "The frequency is not a specific time that the alert runs every day. It's how often the alert rule runs", and that granularity and frequency are configured independently. Split by dimensions on _ResourceId. The documentation explains that when the alert rule scope is a workspace, alerts fire on the workspace by default; to fire a separate alert per affected Azure resource you split by dimensions on the Azure Resource ID column - "Splitting on the Azure resource ID column makes the specified resource into the alert target." TimeGenerated is a datetime column used for time filtering, not a meaningful resource dimension, and Severity would group alerts by event severity rather than by virtual machine.
tags: azure monitor,log search alert,measure,table rows,aggregation granularity,frequency of evaluation,split by dimensions,log analytics

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: The on-call team at Woodgrove Bank reports that a single ongoing high-CPU incident on one virtual machine produced dozens of email notifications over the course of an hour, all referencing the same condition. Reviewing the metric alert rule, you find that the condition, threshold, and action group are all correct, the rule is set to Check every 1 minute with a 5-minute lookback period, and in Advanced options the Automatically resolve alerts checkbox is cleared. What is happening, and what is the appropriate remediation?
opzione_a: The rule is stateless, so it fires every time the condition is met even though it already fired. Select Automatically resolve alerts to make the rule stateful so it will not fire again until the condition resolves.
opzione_b: The evaluation frequency is too aggressive. Increase the lookback period to 24 hours so that the metric is aggregated over a longer window and the rule can only fire once per day.
opzione_c: The action group is being invoked repeatedly by Azure Monitor retries. Create an alert processing rule with a recurring suppression schedule that is active 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
opzione_d: The severity is set too high. Lower the severity from Sev0 to Sev4 so that Azure Monitor throttles notifications for the rule.
spiegazione: Correct: The Automatically resolve alerts checkbox controls whether a metric alert is stateful or stateless. The documentation says: "If you don't select this checkbox, metric alerts are stateless. Stateless alerts fire each time the condition is met, even if alert already fired." It further states that for a stateless rule with a frequency of less than 5 minutes, "While the condition continues to be met, a notification is sent sometime between one and six minutes" - which precisely matches dozens of notifications in an hour at a 1-minute frequency. Selecting the checkbox makes the alert stateful, so it fires once and does not trigger actions again until the condition resolves (for metric alerts, after the condition is not met for three consecutive checks), at which point a resolved notification is sent. Why the others are wrong: (b) The lookback period is the aggregation window, not a firing cap. Stretching it to 24 hours would badly distort the average CPU signal and delay detection, and a stateless rule would still re-fire on each evaluation. (c) The repeats are caused by stateless re-firing, not by webhook/action retries. A 24x7 suppression alert processing rule would remove all action groups from these alerts, meaning the team would receive no notification at all for genuine incidents. (d) Severity is metadata used for classification, filtering, and routing; it does not throttle notifications. Rate limiting is applied per subscription, per alert rule, and per notification target regardless of severity.
tags: azure monitor,metric alert,stateful,stateless,automatically resolve alerts,troubleshooting,notification noise

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda:
Contoso needs a metric alert rule on a production virtual machine with the following requirements:

- The rule must evaluate the average of the Percentage CPU metric over five-minute periods of data.
- The rule must perform that evaluation as often as Azure Monitor allows for metric alerts.
- Fired alerts must carry the most critical severity on the Azure Monitor 0-4 scale.
- While the high-CPU condition persists, the rule must not keep firing; it must fire once and send a resolved notification when the condition clears.

Select the appropriate value for each setting on the alert rule.
opzione_a: Lookback period (aggregation granularity): [1 minute | 5 minutes | 15 minutes]
opzione_b: Check every (evaluation frequency): [1 minute | 5 minutes | 30 minutes]
opzione_c: Severity: [Sev0 | Sev2 | Sev4]
opzione_d: Automatically resolve alerts: [Enabled | Disabled]
spiegazione: Correct: Lookback period = 5 minutes. In the When to evaluate section, "Lookback period" selects "how far back to look each time the data is checked" - this is the aggregation window over which the Average aggregation type is applied, so five-minute periods of data means a 5-minute lookback. (The Azure CLI equivalent is --window-size, described as "Time over which to aggregate metrics", default 5m.) Check every = 1 minute. "Check every" selects how often the alert rule checks whether the condition is met; 1 minute is the finest evaluation frequency for metric alerts and is the documented CLI default (--evaluation-frequency, default 1m). Note that evaluation frequency and lookback period are independent: every 1 minute, look back 5 minutes. Severity = Sev0. Severity runs "from 0 (critical) to 4 (verbose)", so the most critical level is Sev0. Sev2 is the mid-range default and Sev4 is the least critical (verbose) end. Automatically resolve alerts = Enabled. This checkbox makes the alert stateful: a stateful alert fires when the conditions are met and "will not fire again or trigger any more actions until the conditions are resolved", and a resolved notification is sent when the condition clears (for metric alerts, when the condition is not met for three consecutive checks). If the checkbox is cleared, metric alerts are stateless and fire each time the condition is met, which is exactly what the requirement forbids.
tags: azure monitor,metric alert,evaluation frequency,lookback period,aggregation granularity,severity,stateful

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: An operations engineer working in Azure public cloud creates a Service Health alert rule so that the team is notified by email and SMS about Azure outages and planned maintenance affecting the subscription. When creating the action group, which region must be selected for the action group to function correctly with Service Health alerts?
opzione_a: Global
opzione_b: The same region as the resources that Service Health reports on
opzione_c: Sweden Central, because Service Health notifications are processed only in Europe
opzione_d: Regional, so that the action group is zone-redundant within the subscription's home region
spiegazione: Correct: The action groups documentation states explicitly: "Service Health Alerts are only supported in public clouds within the global region. For Action groups to properly function in response to a Service Health Alert, the region of the action group must be set to Global." With the Global option, the action group is persisted in at least two regions for regional resiliency, and voice, SMS, and email actions performed as the result of service health alerts are resilient to Azure live-site incidents - which is exactly what you want when the alert is telling you Azure itself is having a problem. Why the others are wrong: (b) The action group region is a processing/storage region choice for the action group resource; it is not tied to the regions Service Health reports on, and any non-Global choice breaks Service Health alerts. (c) Sweden Central is one of the valid regions in the Regional processing list, but Regional processing is not supported for Service Health alerts, and there is no rule confining Service Health processing to Europe. (d) Regional processing does give a zone-redundant action group stored within a chosen geographic boundary, and it is the right choice when you must keep processing inside a specific geography - but it is explicitly not supported for Service Health alerts.
tags: azure monitor,action groups,service health,global region,regional processing,activity log alert

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: A cloud administrator is documenting how action groups behave before rolling out a standardized alerting design across the organization. Which of the following statements about Azure Monitor action groups are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: An action group can contain a maximum of 10 SMS actions.
opzione_b: An action group can contain up to 1,000 email actions.
opzione_c: The same action group can be referenced by multiple alert rules.
opzione_d: An action group can be associated with only one alert rule at a time.
opzione_e: The actions inside an action group are executed sequentially, in the order in which they are listed on the Actions tab.
spiegazione: Correct: (a) The Azure Monitor service limits table for action groups lists "10 SMS actions in an action group" (with a production rate limit of no more than one SMS message every five minutes). (b) The same table lists "1,000 email actions in an action group", along with a rate limit of no more than 100 emails every hour for each email address per region. Note that 10 is the per-action-group cap for most other action types - Azure app push, Event Hubs, ITSM, Logic app, Runbook, Secure webhook, Voice, Webhook, and Email Azure Resource Manager role - which makes Email the notable exception at 1,000. (c) The documentation states "Multiple alert rules can use the same action group" and gives the example of creating a single action group to notify User1, User2, and User3 by email and applying it to two different alert rules. Why the others are wrong: (d) This directly contradicts the documented reusability of action groups; reuse is in fact the recommended pattern, since action groups "are defined by the unique set of actions and the users to be notified." (e) The documentation states "Action groups are executed concurrently, in no specific order" - you cannot rely on the listed order to sequence actions. If you need ordered or conditional logic, use a Logic apps action to orchestrate it.

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda:
Adventure Works patches its infrastructure during a weekly maintenance window every Saturday from 00:00 to 06:00. An administrator creates an alert processing rule named APR-Maintenance in a resource group in subscription Sub1. The rule's scope is set to the entire subscription Sub1, the rule action is set to Suppression, and the Scheduling tab is configured with a Recurring weekly schedule covering Saturday 00:00 to 06:00.

Evaluate each of the following statements about APR-Maintenance and determine whether it is true (Yes) or false (No):

1. Resources hosted in a different subscription, Sub2, can be covered by APR-Maintenance if the administrator adds them to the rule's scope.
2. During the Saturday maintenance window, alerts that fire on resources in Sub1 are still visible on the Alerts page in the Azure portal, even though no action groups are invoked for them.
3. During the Saturday maintenance window, APR-Maintenance also suppresses notifications for any Azure Service Health alerts that fire in Sub1.
opzione_a: Resources hosted in a different subscription, Sub2, can be covered by APR-Maintenance if the administrator adds them to the rule's scope.
opzione_b: During the Saturday maintenance window, alerts that fire on resources in Sub1 are still visible on the Alerts page in the Azure portal, even though no action groups are invoked for them.
opzione_c: During the Saturday maintenance window, APR-Maintenance also suppresses notifications for any Azure Service Health alerts that fire in Sub1.
spiegazione:
Statement 1 = No. The documentation states that an alert processing rule applies "to alerts that fired on resources within that scope" and that the scope must be "within the same subscription as the alert processing rule": "You can't create an alert processing rule on a resource from a different subscription." Because APR-Maintenance lives in Sub1, resources in Sub2 cannot be added to its scope; a separate alert processing rule would have to be created in Sub2.

Statement 2 = Yes. The Suppression action "removes all the action groups from the affected fired alerts. So, the fired alerts won't invoke any of their action groups, not even at the end of the maintenance window. Those fired alerts will still be visible when you list your alerts in the portal, Azure Resource Graph, API, or PowerShell." Suppression stops notifications, not alert generation - which is exactly why suppression is preferred over disabling alert rules during maintenance.

Statement 3 = No. The alert processing rules documentation contains an explicit note: "Alert processing rules don't affect Azure Service Health alerts." Service Health alerts will continue to invoke their action groups during the maintenance window regardless of APR-Maintenance.
tags: azure monitor,alert processing rules,suppression,maintenance window,scheduling,service health,scope

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: Fabrikam runs 40 Azure virtual machines in a single subscription: 25 in the East US region and 15 in the West Europe region. The operations team wants to be alerted whenever the Percentage CPU platform metric on any of these VMs exceeds 85%, and wants to create as few metric alert rules as possible. What is the minimum number of metric alert rules required?
spiegazione: Correct: A single metric alert rule can monitor multiple resources of the same type only when those resources "exist in the same Azure region", and virtual machines (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines) are on the list of resource types supported for multi-resource metric alerts. Because the VMs span two regions, you need one multi-resource rule for East US and one for West Europe: two rules total. Individual notifications are still sent for each monitored resource. Why the others are wrong: (a) One rule cannot span East US and West Europe - the scope of a multi-resource metric alert rule is constrained to a single Azure region. (c) 25 would imply one rule per VM in East US only, ignoring that multi-resource rules exist and ignoring the West Europe VMs. (d) 40 (one rule per VM) works but is not the minimum, and it consumes 40 of the 5,000 metric alert rules allowed per subscription unnecessarily. Note that Percentage CPU is a platform (host) metric, so the multi-resource restriction on VM guest metrics does not apply here.

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: A metric alert fires on a virtual machine named VM1. At the moment the alert fires, VM1 is in the scope of two enabled alert processing rules: APR1 uses the Apply action groups action to add an action group named AG-OnCall, and APR2 uses the Suppression action. No schedule restricts either rule. What is the result?
opzione_a: AG-OnCall is invoked first, and suppression then stops any further notifications for the same alert.
opzione_b: AG-OnCall is invoked, because the Apply action groups action always takes precedence over Suppression.
opzione_c: No action groups are invoked for the fired alert, but the alert instance is still visible on the Alerts page in the Azure portal.
opzione_d: The alert rule is prevented from evaluating, so no alert instance is created at all.
spiegazione: Correct: The alert processing rules documentation states that "The suppression action has a higher priority over the Apply action groups action. If a single fired alert is affected by different alert processing rules of both types, the action groups of that alert will be suppressed." Suppression removes all action groups from the affected fired alert, so AG-OnCall is not called. The same documentation confirms suppressed alerts "will still be visible when you list your alerts in the portal, Azure Resource Graph, API, or PowerShell." Why the others are wrong: (a) Suppression removes the action groups entirely; AG-OnCall is never invoked, not invoked-then-stopped. (b) This inverts the documented precedence - Suppression wins over Apply action groups. (d) Alert processing rules act on alerts as they are being fired; they modify alert behavior but do not stop the alert rule from evaluating or the alert instance from being created. Disabling the alert rule itself would be needed to prevent the alert.

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: You are configuring the Scope tab of an alert processing rule and want to narrow the rule so that it affects only a specific subset of the fired alerts in its scope. Which of the following are available filters on an alert processing rule? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Severity
opzione_b: Monitor condition
opzione_c: Aggregation type
opzione_d: Resource type
opzione_e: Threshold value of the signal
spiegazione: Correct: The alert processing rules documentation lists the available filters as: Alert context (payload), Alert rule ID, Alert rule name, Description, Monitor condition, Monitor service, Resource, Resource group, Resource type, and Severity. Severity (a) filters on the selected severities. Monitor condition (b) filters on either Fired or Resolved. Resource type (d) filters on resource types such as virtual machines, and supports Contains to match a resource type and all its child resources. Why the others are wrong: (c) Aggregation type (Sum, Count, Average, Min, Max) is a property of a metric alert rule's condition, configured in the alert rule wizard - it is not an alert processing rule filter. (e) The threshold value of the signal is likewise part of the alert rule's condition definition, not an alert processing rule filter. Remember that multiple filters on one rule are combined with a logical AND, while multiple values within a single filter (up to five) are combined with a logical OR.
tags: azure monitor,alert processing rules,filters,severity,monitor condition,resource type,scope

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: Litware defines several action groups that notify different escalation tiers. While configuring the Actions tab of a single metric alert rule, an engineer tries to attach action groups for the database team, the network team, the platform team, the security team, the on-call rotation, and an ITSM bridge. What is the maximum number of action groups that can be added to a single alert rule?
opzione_d: There is no limit on action groups per alert rule.
spiegazione: Correct: The action groups documentation states under Reusability and execution: "You can add up to five action groups to a single alert rule." The engineer's six action groups exceed that limit, so the actions would need to be consolidated into fewer action groups. Why the others are wrong: (a) An alert rule can have more than one action group - and in fact action groups are optional on an alert rule entirely. (c) 10 is the documented per-action-group limit for several individual action types (for example, 10 SMS actions, 10 webhook actions, 10 Logic app actions in an action group), not the number of action groups per alert rule. (d) There is no limit on the number of action groups you can create in a subscription, but there is a hard limit of five action groups attached to one alert rule. Note also that action groups are executed concurrently, in no specific order, and one action group can be reused by many alert rules.

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: While building an action group in Azure Monitor, an engineer must distinguish between entries configured on the Notifications tab and entries configured on the Actions tab. Which of the following are action types (automated actions) rather than notification types? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Secure webhook
opzione_b: SMS
opzione_c: Automation Runbook
opzione_d: Azure app push notifications
opzione_e: Event hubs
